# Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)

# Chapter 1 — Introduction

**Document ID:** MED-CSDG-001

**Chapter:** 1

**Version:** 1.0

**Status:** Approved Baseline

---

# 1. Purpose

The **Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)** establish the mandatory engineering standards governing the design, implementation, review, testing, deployment, and maintenance of software across the **Mediverse – AI-Powered Medical Education Platform**.

This document defines the engineering rules that ensure all code produced by the Mediverse development teams is:

* Consistent
* Maintainable
* Secure
* Readable
* Testable
* Scalable
* Observable
* Performant
* Production-ready

The CSDG translates the architectural principles defined by the Software Architecture Document (SAD), Technical Design Document (TDD), API Design Specification (ADS), Database Design Document (DDD), Security Design Document (SecDD), DevOps & Infrastructure Guide (DIG), and Architecture Decision Records (ADR) into day-to-day engineering practices.   

---

# 2. Vision

The Mediverse engineering organization shall produce software that is:

```text
Correct

↓

Simple

↓

Readable

↓

Secure

↓

Reliable

↓

Scalable

↓

Maintainable

↓

Future-Proof
```

Engineering excellence is achieved through consistent application of shared standards rather than individual coding preferences.

---

# 3. Scope

This document governs every software artifact developed for Mediverse.

Including:

* Backend Services
* Frontend Applications
* Mobile Applications
* AI Services
* RAG Pipelines
* MCP Integrations
* REST APIs
* WebSocket Services
* Database Scripts
* Infrastructure as Code
* Kubernetes Manifests
* Helm Charts
* CI/CD Pipelines
* Automation Scripts
* Test Code
* Documentation
* Configuration Files

Every repository within Mediverse shall comply with this standard.

---

# 4. Objectives

The objectives of this document are to:

* Standardize software development.
* Reduce implementation inconsistencies.
* Improve maintainability.
* Increase software quality.
* Improve developer productivity.
* Reduce technical debt.
* Simplify onboarding.
* Improve security posture.
* Improve review quality.
* Enable predictable software delivery.

---

# 5. Relationship with Other Documents

The Coding Standards & Development Guidelines are part of the Mediverse engineering documentation hierarchy.

```text
Business Vision
      │
      ▼
PRD
      │
      ▼
SRS
      │
      ▼
SAD
      │
      ▼
DDD
      │
      ▼
TDD
      │
      ▼
ADS
      │
      ▼
FDS
      │
      ▼
SecDD
      │
      ▼
DIG
      │
      ▼
CSDG
      │
      ▼
Source Code
```

The CSDG defines **how engineers implement software consistently**; it does not redefine business requirements or architectural decisions. The PRD defines business intent, the SRS defines software requirements, the SAD defines architecture, the TDD defines implementation, and the DDD defines the database architecture.     

---

# 6. Intended Audience

This document is intended for:

| Role                 | Responsibility               |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Backend Developers   | Implement backend services   |
| Frontend Developers  | Implement UI applications    |
| AI Engineers         | Build AI services            |
| DevOps Engineers     | Infrastructure automation    |
| QA Engineers         | Test implementation quality  |
| Security Engineers   | Review secure implementation |
| Database Engineers   | Database implementation      |
| Architects           | Technical governance         |
| Technical Leads      | Code quality oversight       |
| Engineering Managers | Development governance       |

All engineering teams shall follow this document.

---

# 7. Engineering Philosophy

The Mediverse engineering organization follows the principle:

> **Readable code is more valuable than clever code.**

Engineers should optimize for:

* clarity
* simplicity
* maintainability
* correctness
* long-term evolution

rather than writing code that is merely concise or technically sophisticated.

---

# 8. Guiding Principles

Every software component should satisfy:

```text
Business Value

↓

Correctness

↓

Readability

↓

Maintainability

↓

Security

↓

Scalability

↓

Performance

↓

Observability
```

No single quality attribute should be optimized at the expense of critical system qualities without documented justification.

---

# 9. Engineering Values

The Mediverse engineering culture values:

* Simplicity
* Consistency
* Automation
* Reusability
* Documentation
* Collaboration
* Continuous Improvement
* Ownership
* Accountability
* Learning

These values guide engineering decisions across the platform.

---

# 10. Definition of Quality Code

Quality code exhibits the following characteristics:

* Correct
* Simple
* Predictable
* Testable
* Secure
* Modular
* Reusable
* Observable
* Documented
* Easy to modify

Quality is evaluated over the software lifecycle, not only at initial implementation.

---

# 11. Definition of Done

A feature is complete only when it satisfies all applicable engineering standards.

Minimum criteria include:

* Code implemented
* Tests passing
* Code reviewed
* Security checks completed
* Static analysis passing
* Documentation updated
* CI/CD pipeline successful
* No critical defects
* Deployment validated

---

# 12. Engineering Ownership

Every codebase shall define ownership for:

* Repository
* Modules
* APIs
* Infrastructure
* Documentation
* Production Support

Ownership ensures accountability throughout the software lifecycle.

---

# 13. Coding Standard Hierarchy

Engineering rules are applied in the following order:

```text
Architecture Decisions

↓

Enterprise Standards

↓

Language Standards

↓

Framework Standards

↓

Project Standards

↓

Team Conventions
```

Lower-level conventions shall not conflict with higher-level standards.

---

# 14. Standard Compliance

Compliance with this document is mandatory.

Exceptions require:

* documented justification
* technical lead approval
* architecture review (when applicable)
* periodic reassessment

Exceptions should remain limited and time-bound.

---

# 15. Development Lifecycle Alignment

Coding standards apply throughout:

```text
Design

↓

Implementation

↓

Review

↓

Testing

↓

Deployment

↓

Maintenance
```

Quality is enforced continuously, not only during code review.

---

# 16. Engineering Automation

The following should be automated wherever feasible:

* Formatting
* Linting
* Static Analysis
* Security Scanning
* Unit Testing
* Dependency Checks
* Build Validation
* Documentation Generation

Automation reduces manual errors and promotes consistency.

---

# 17. Continuous Improvement

Engineering standards shall evolve through:

```text
Feedback

↓

Review

↓

Refinement

↓

Approval

↓

Adoption
```

Lessons learned from production, retrospectives, and architecture reviews should inform updates.

---

# 18. Governance

The Enterprise Architecture Board and Engineering Leadership are responsible for approving and maintaining coding standards.

Engineering teams are responsible for implementing and following them.

---

# 19. Success Metrics

The effectiveness of this document should be measured using:

* Code review findings
* Static analysis issues
* Defect density
* Security vulnerabilities
* Test coverage
* Deployment success rate
* Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR)
* Technical debt trends
* Developer onboarding time

These metrics should guide future improvements.

---

# 20. Chapter Summary

This chapter establishes the foundation for engineering across the Mediverse platform.

Key principles include:

* Coding standards are mandatory across all repositories.
* Engineering practices align with the PRD, SRS, SAD, TDD, DDD, ADS, and ADRs.
* Readability, maintainability, security, and consistency are core objectives.
* Automation and governance are integral to software quality.
* Compliance with these standards is required unless formally approved exceptions exist.

---

# Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)

# Chapter 2 — Engineering Philosophy

**Document ID:** MED-CSDG-002
**Chapter:** 2
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

---

# 1. Purpose

This chapter defines the engineering philosophy that guides every technical decision within the Mediverse platform.

While coding standards define *what* developers must do, engineering philosophy defines *why* those standards exist. It establishes a shared mindset for building software that remains reliable, maintainable, and adaptable over many years.

---

# 2. Engineering Vision

The Mediverse engineering organization aims to build software that is:

```text
Simple

↓

Reliable

↓

Secure

↓

Scalable

↓

Maintainable

↓

Observable

↓

Adaptable
```

The objective is to create systems that continue to evolve successfully rather than systems that only satisfy immediate requirements.

---

# 3. Engineering Mission

Every engineering activity should contribute to one or more of the following goals:

* Deliver business value.
* Improve student learning.
* Protect user data.
* Ensure operational stability.
* Reduce technical complexity.
* Enable rapid innovation.
* Support future growth.

Technology is a means to achieve these outcomes, not an end in itself.

---

# 4. Business Before Technology

Engineering decisions shall begin with the business problem.

Decision sequence:

```text
Business Need
      │
      ▼
Functional Requirement
      │
      ▼
Architecture
      │
      ▼
Technology
      │
      ▼
Implementation
```

Technology choices should be justified by business value rather than popularity or novelty.

---

# 5. Simplicity First

The preferred solution is the simplest one that fully satisfies the requirements.

Developers should avoid:

* unnecessary abstractions
* speculative features
* excessive configuration
* premature optimization
* overly complex patterns

Simplicity improves readability, maintainability, and onboarding.

---

# 6. Readability Over Cleverness

Code is read far more often than it is written.

Therefore, prioritize:

* descriptive names
* straightforward control flow
* explicit intent
* small functions
* clear module boundaries

Avoid writing code that requires special knowledge to understand.

---

# 7. Maintainability as a Primary Goal

Software should be easy to modify without introducing regressions.

Maintainable software exhibits:

* low coupling
* high cohesion
* modular design
* clear interfaces
* comprehensive tests

Future developers should be able to extend the system with confidence.

---

# 8. Correctness Before Optimization

The order of priorities is:

```text
Correctness

↓

Reliability

↓

Maintainability

↓

Performance
```

Performance optimizations should be based on measurable evidence rather than assumptions.

---

# 9. Security by Design

Security is an architectural concern, not an afterthought.

Every component should assume:

* untrusted input
* authenticated access
* least privilege
* secure defaults
* audited actions

Security reviews should occur throughout development, not only before release.

---

# 10. Privacy by Design

Personal and educational data should receive the highest level of protection.

Engineering practices should emphasize:

* data minimization
* purpose limitation
* secure storage
* secure transmission
* controlled access

Every new feature should consider its impact on user privacy.

---

# 11. Scalability from the Beginning

Systems should be designed to grow.

Developers should consider:

* increasing users
* larger datasets
* higher traffic
* additional services
* new regions

Scalability should be incorporated into architecture rather than added after growth.

---

# 12. Reliability is Non-Negotiable

Critical educational services must remain available.

Engineering practices should include:

* graceful degradation
* retries
* timeouts
* circuit breakers
* health checks

Reliability supports user trust.

---

# 13. Observability by Default

Every service should be observable.

Required capabilities:

```text
Logs

Metrics

Tracing

Audit Records

Health Endpoints
```

Operational visibility is essential for diagnosis and improvement.

---

# 14. Automation Over Manual Work

Whenever a repetitive engineering activity exists, automation should be preferred.

Examples include:

* formatting
* linting
* testing
* deployment
* dependency updates
* documentation generation

Automation reduces human error and improves consistency.

---

# 15. Reuse Before Reinvention

Before implementing new functionality, developers should evaluate whether an existing solution can be reused.

Preferred order:

```text
Existing Platform Service

↓

Shared Library

↓

Open Standard

↓

New Implementation
```

Duplication should be avoided unless justified.

---

# 16. Ownership and Accountability

Every software component should have clear ownership.

Ownership includes responsibility for:

* implementation
* documentation
* testing
* production support
* security
* maintenance

Shared ownership without accountability should be avoided.

---

# 17. Continuous Improvement

Engineering practices should evolve based on:

* production experience
* retrospectives
* incident reviews
* architecture reviews
* developer feedback

Continuous improvement is expected from every engineering team.

---

# 18. Learning Culture

Engineers are expected to continuously develop their skills.

Areas include:

* programming languages
* frameworks
* architecture
* cloud technologies
* AI
* security
* performance engineering

Knowledge sharing should be encouraged through documentation and technical discussions.

---

# 19. Technical Excellence

Technical excellence is achieved through disciplined engineering practices rather than isolated heroic efforts.

Indicators include:

* consistent code quality
* reliable deployments
* comprehensive testing
* minimal production defects
* manageable technical debt

Excellence is the result of sustained practice.

---

# 20. Long-Term Thinking

Engineering decisions should consider the expected lifespan of the platform.

Questions to ask before implementation:

* Will this still be understandable in five years?
* Can it scale with future demand?
* Is it easy to modify?
* Does it align with architectural principles?
* Will it increase or reduce technical debt?

Long-term maintainability should outweigh short-term convenience.

---

# 21. Engineering Ethics

Developers should act with:

* integrity
* professionalism
* accountability
* transparency
* respect for user privacy
* commitment to quality

Engineering decisions can directly affect users and should reflect that responsibility.

---

# 22. Collaboration Over Individual Optimization

Successful software is built by teams.

Engineering practices should encourage:

* shared knowledge
* constructive reviews
* pair programming where appropriate
* open communication
* documentation

Knowledge silos should be actively reduced.

---

# 23. Evidence-Based Decision Making

Technical decisions should rely on measurable information such as:

* benchmarks
* production metrics
* architecture evaluations
* proof-of-concepts
* operational data

Assumptions should be validated whenever practical.

---

# 24. Innovation with Discipline

Innovation is encouraged when it:

* solves a real problem
* improves maintainability
* enhances user experience
* reduces operational complexity

Experimental technologies should undergo controlled evaluation before adoption.

---

# 25. Definition of Engineering Excellence

For Mediverse, engineering excellence means consistently delivering software that is:

* correct
* secure
* reliable
* maintainable
* observable
* scalable
* well documented
* aligned with enterprise architecture

---

# 26. Engineering Decision Framework

Every significant implementation decision should follow:

```text
Understand the Problem
        │
        ▼
Evaluate Alternatives
        │
        ▼
Choose the Simplest Viable Solution
        │
        ▼
Implement
        │
        ▼
Review
        │
        ▼
Measure
        │
        ▼
Improve
```

---

# 27. Anti-Patterns

The Mediverse engineering organization rejects:

* Clever code that sacrifices readability
* Premature optimization
* Copy-paste programming
* Hard-coded configuration
* Ignoring code reviews
* Skipping automated tests
* Uncontrolled technical debt
* Security shortcuts
* Undocumented architectural changes
* Tight coupling between modules

---

# 28. Alignment with Enterprise Architecture

This philosophy supports and operationalizes:

* Architecture Principles
* Architecture Decision Records (ADR-001 to ADR-100)
* Software Architecture Document (SAD)
* Technical Design Document (TDD)
* API Design Specification (ADS)
* Security Design Document (SecDD)
* DevOps & Infrastructure Guide (DIG)

Engineering philosophy provides the cultural foundation for implementing these architectural decisions consistently.

---

# 29. Success Indicators

The engineering philosophy is successful when teams consistently achieve:

* High code quality
* Low defect rates
* Fast onboarding
* Stable production systems
* Predictable releases
* Low technical debt
* Strong collaboration
* Continuous learning

---

# 30. Chapter Summary

This chapter establishes the engineering mindset for Mediverse.

Key principles are:

* Business value drives engineering decisions.
* Simplicity and readability take precedence over clever implementations.
* Security, privacy, reliability, and observability are built into every solution.
* Automation, reuse, and continuous improvement are expected.
* Technical excellence is achieved through disciplined, repeatable engineering practices.
* Long-term maintainability is prioritized over short-term convenience.

---

# Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)

# Chapter 3 — Development Principles

**Document ID:** MED-CSDG-003
**Chapter:** 3
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

---

# 1. Purpose

This chapter establishes the mandatory software engineering principles that govern the design and implementation of every component within the Mediverse platform.

These principles apply across:

* Backend Services
* Frontend Applications
* AI Services
* Infrastructure as Code
* DevOps Automation
* Database Development
* Integration Services
* Shared Libraries

They complement the enterprise architecture and guide engineers toward consistent, maintainable solutions.

---

# 2. Principle Hierarchy

Engineering principles should be applied in the following order:

```text
Business Value
      │
      ▼
Architecture Principles
      │
      ▼
Development Principles
      │
      ▼
Coding Standards
      │
      ▼
Framework Best Practices
      │
      ▼
Implementation Details
```

Higher-level principles always take precedence over implementation convenience.

---

# 3. Business Value First

Every implementation should solve a real business problem.

Before writing code, developers should ask:

* What user problem does this solve?
* Which business capability does it support?
* Is there a simpler solution?
* Does it align with the product roadmap?

Code without business value should not be introduced into the codebase.

---

# 4. SOLID Principles

All object-oriented code should adhere to SOLID principles:

* **Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)** – A class should have one reason to change.
* **Open/Closed Principle (OCP)** – Extend behavior without modifying existing, stable code.
* **Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)** – Derived types should be interchangeable with base types.
* **Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)** – Prefer focused interfaces over large, generalized ones.
* **Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)** – Depend on abstractions rather than concrete implementations.

SOLID improves flexibility, testability, and maintainability.

---

# 5. DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)

Knowledge should exist in one authoritative place.

Avoid duplicating:

* Business rules
* Validation logic
* Configuration
* SQL queries
* Constants
* Utility functions

Reuse through well-designed abstractions instead of copy-paste.

---

# 6. KISS (Keep It Simple)

Prefer the simplest implementation that satisfies the requirements.

Avoid:

* Unnecessary design patterns
* Over-engineering
* Deep inheritance hierarchies
* Excessive abstraction

Complexity should only be introduced when it delivers measurable value.

---

# 7. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)

Do not implement functionality based on speculative future requirements.

Implement only what is required today while designing for future extension.

---

# 8. Separation of Concerns (SoC)

Each component should focus on a single concern.

Example responsibilities:

```text
Controller
      │
      ▼
Service
      │
      ▼
Repository
      │
      ▼
Database
```

Mixing responsibilities increases coupling and reduces maintainability.

---

# 9. High Cohesion

Modules should contain closely related functionality.

Examples:

* StudentService handles student operations.
* AssessmentService handles assessment operations.
* NotificationService handles notifications.

Avoid "utility" classes that accumulate unrelated responsibilities.

---

# 10. Low Coupling

Components should interact through stable interfaces.

Avoid:

* Direct database access across modules
* Circular dependencies
* Hidden side effects
* Tight framework coupling

Low coupling enables independent evolution.

---

# 11. Composition Over Inheritance

Prefer composition to share behavior.

```text
Preferred

OrderService
      │
      ▼
Uses PaymentProcessor

Instead of

OrderService extends PaymentProcessor
```

Composition improves flexibility and reduces inheritance complexity.

---

# 12. Dependency Injection

Dependencies should be provided externally.

Benefits:

* Easier testing
* Better modularity
* Loose coupling
* Clear dependencies

Frameworks such as Spring should manage object lifecycles where appropriate.

---

# 13. Encapsulation

Internal implementation details should remain hidden.

Expose only:

* Stable interfaces
* Required behaviors
* Public contracts

Implementation changes should not affect consumers unnecessarily.

---

# 14. Immutability Where Practical

Prefer immutable objects for:

* DTOs
* Value Objects
* Configuration
* Events

Immutability reduces bugs caused by unintended state changes.

---

# 15. Fail Fast

Detect errors as early as possible.

Examples:

* Validate input at boundaries.
* Reject invalid state immediately.
* Surface configuration errors during startup.
* Avoid silently ignoring failures.

Early failure simplifies diagnosis.

---

# 16. Defensive Programming

Assume external inputs may be invalid.

Validate:

* API requests
* Configuration
* File uploads
* External integrations
* User input

Never trust data from external sources without verification.

---

# 17. Principle of Least Surprise

Code should behave as developers reasonably expect.

Examples:

* Standard HTTP method semantics
* Predictable naming
* Consistent exception handling
* Uniform response formats

Unexpected behavior increases maintenance costs.

---

# 18. Single Source of Truth (SSOT)

Critical information should have one authoritative representation.

Examples:

* Configuration
* Feature flags
* Business rules
* Enumerations
* Reference data

Multiple inconsistent sources create maintenance risks.

---

# 19. Explicit Over Implicit

Prefer explicit behavior.

Examples:

* Clear method names
* Explicit configuration
* Visible dependencies
* Well-defined contracts

Avoid hidden assumptions.

---

# 20. Idempotent Operations

Where applicable, operations should be safe to repeat without changing the final outcome.

Examples:

* Retryable API requests
* Infrastructure provisioning
* Deployment automation

Idempotency improves resilience.

---

# 21. Consistency

Maintain consistency in:

* Naming
* Project structure
* API design
* Error handling
* Logging
* Testing

Consistency reduces cognitive load.

---

# 22. Testability

Code should be designed for testing.

Characteristics include:

* Small methods
* Clear interfaces
* Dependency injection
* Minimal side effects

Testability is a design objective, not an afterthought.

---

# 23. Observability

Every component should emit useful operational signals.

Include:

* Structured logs
* Metrics
* Traces
* Health indicators

Operational visibility supports production reliability.

---

# 24. Backward Compatibility

Changes should avoid breaking existing consumers.

Strategies:

* Additive API evolution
* Deprecation periods
* Versioning
* Migration guidance

Compatibility reduces disruption.

---

# 25. Continuous Refactoring

Improve existing code as part of normal development.

Refactoring goals:

* Reduce duplication
* Improve readability
* Simplify design
* Remove obsolete code

Refactoring should preserve observable behavior.

---

# 26. Technical Debt Management

Technical debt should be:

* Identified
* Documented
* Prioritized
* Reviewed
* Reduced over time

Intentional debt should include a clear justification and remediation plan.

---

# 27. Documentation-Driven Development

Maintain documentation alongside implementation.

Update documentation whenever changes affect:

* APIs
* Architecture
* Configuration
* Deployment
* Operational procedures

Documentation should remain synchronized with the codebase.

---

# 28. Anti-Patterns

The Mediverse engineering organization rejects:

* God classes
* God methods
* Copy-paste programming
* Circular dependencies
* Deep inheritance hierarchies
* Hard-coded configuration
* Hidden side effects
* Shared mutable global state
* Feature flags without lifecycle management
* Unbounded utility classes

---

# 29. Success Indicators

Successful application of these principles results in:

* Low defect rates
* High code readability
* Predictable architecture
* Easier testing
* Faster onboarding
* Lower maintenance effort
* Reduced technical debt
* Stable production systems

---

# 30. Chapter Summary

The Mediverse development principles establish a common engineering foundation:

* Business value drives implementation.
* SOLID, DRY, KISS, and YAGNI guide design decisions.
* Separation of concerns, high cohesion, and low coupling improve maintainability.
* Composition, dependency injection, encapsulation, and immutability enhance flexibility.
* Fail-fast, defensive programming, and observability improve reliability.
* Consistency, testability, and continuous refactoring support long-term sustainability.
* Documentation and technical debt management are integral to engineering quality.

---

# Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)

# Chapter 4 — Enterprise Coding Governance

**Document ID:** MED-CSDG-004
**Chapter:** 4
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

---

# 1. Purpose

This chapter defines the governance framework that ensures all software developed for the Mediverse platform complies with enterprise engineering standards.

Coding governance establishes:

* decision authority
* accountability
* compliance processes
* review mechanisms
* exception management
* continuous improvement

Its objective is to ensure that software quality remains consistent across all teams, repositories, and releases.

---

# 2. Governance Objectives

The Enterprise Coding Governance Framework shall:

* Ensure consistent engineering practices.
* Enforce enterprise architecture decisions.
* Improve software quality.
* Reduce technical debt.
* Standardize development workflows.
* Enable secure software delivery.
* Maintain long-term maintainability.
* Support regulatory compliance.

---

# 3. Governance Principles

Coding governance follows these principles:

```text id="gov01"
Consistency

↓

Transparency

↓

Automation

↓

Accountability

↓

Continuous Improvement
```

Governance should enable engineering excellence rather than create unnecessary bureaucracy.

---

# 4. Governance Hierarchy

Engineering governance operates through multiple levels.

```text id="gov02"
Executive Leadership
        │
        ▼
Enterprise Architecture Board
        │
        ▼
Engineering Governance Board
        │
        ▼
Domain Architects
        │
        ▼
Technical Leads
        │
        ▼
Engineering Teams
```

Each level has clearly defined responsibilities.

---

# 5. Governance Scope

Coding governance applies to:

* Java services
* Spring Boot applications
* React applications
* AI services
* Infrastructure as Code
* Database scripts
* Kubernetes manifests
* Helm charts
* CI/CD pipelines
* Shared libraries
* Automation scripts
* Documentation repositories

No engineering repository is exempt.

---

# 6. Authority Levels

| Authority                     | Responsibility         |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Executive Leadership          | Engineering strategy   |
| Enterprise Architecture Board | Architecture standards |
| Engineering Governance Board  | Coding standards       |
| Domain Architects             | Domain compliance      |
| Technical Leads               | Team implementation    |
| Developers                    | Daily adherence        |

Decision-making authority should match organizational responsibility.

---

# 7. Governance Responsibilities

The governance framework is responsible for:

* maintaining standards
* approving changes
* reviewing compliance
* resolving exceptions
* auditing implementations
* improving engineering practices

Governance focuses on continuous quality improvement.

---

# 8. Engineering Policies

Mandatory engineering policies include:

```text id="gov03"
Coding Standards

Security Standards

Testing Standards

Documentation Standards

Review Standards

Release Standards
```

Policies should be version-controlled and periodically reviewed.

---

# 9. Repository Governance

Every repository shall define:

* Owner
* Maintainers
* Reviewers
* Branch protection rules
* CI/CD requirements
* Security contacts

Repository ownership ensures accountability.

---

# 10. Code Ownership

Every source file should have a responsible engineering team.

Ownership includes:

* implementation
* maintenance
* bug fixing
* documentation
* production support

Ownership should be explicit rather than assumed.

---

# 11. Branch Protection

Protected branches shall enforce:

* pull requests
* required reviews
* successful CI builds
* security checks
* signed commits (where required)

Direct commits to protected branches should be prohibited.

---

# 12. Pull Request Governance

Every pull request shall include:

* purpose
* linked work item
* testing evidence
* reviewer assignment
* documentation updates (if applicable)

Pull requests should remain focused and reviewable.

---

# 13. Code Review Policy

No production code shall be merged without review.

Minimum requirements:

* one qualified reviewer
* automated checks passing
* architecture compliance
* security considerations
* test coverage maintained

High-risk changes may require additional reviewers.

---

# 14. Architecture Compliance

Implementation shall comply with:

* Enterprise Architecture
* ADRs
* API standards
* Security standards
* Database standards
* Infrastructure standards

Architectural deviations require formal approval.

---

# 15. Static Code Analysis

Static analysis shall execute automatically.

Recommended checks include:

```text id="gov04"
Checkstyle

SpotBugs

PMD

SonarQube

ESLint

TypeScript

Dependency Analysis
```

Build pipelines should fail when critical issues are detected.

---

# 16. Security Scanning

Every build should include automated security analysis.

Examples:

* SAST
* Dependency vulnerability scanning
* Secret detection
* License compliance
* Container image scanning

Critical findings should block release until resolved or formally accepted.

---

# 17. Dependency Governance

Dependencies shall:

* be approved
* remain supported
* receive security updates
* avoid unnecessary duplication

Unmaintained libraries should be replaced or removed.

---

# 18. Open Source Governance

Open-source components should be evaluated for:

* license compatibility
* maintenance activity
* security history
* community support
* long-term viability

Approval should occur before adoption.

---

# 19. Version Governance

All software artifacts shall follow a documented versioning strategy.

Governed artifacts include:

* APIs
* Services
* Libraries
* Infrastructure modules
* Helm charts
* Documentation

Version changes should be traceable.

---

# 20. Documentation Governance

Engineering documentation shall remain synchronized with implementation.

Updates are required when changes affect:

* APIs
* architecture
* configuration
* deployment
* operational procedures

Documentation is part of the deliverable, not an optional artifact.

---

# 21. Testing Governance

No change may be released without meeting defined testing requirements.

Testing governance includes:

* unit testing
* integration testing
* contract testing
* security testing
* performance testing (where applicable)

Testing standards are defined in the TSQP.

---

# 22. CI/CD Governance

Every repository shall use approved CI/CD pipelines.

Pipeline stages include:

```text id="gov05"
Build

↓

Static Analysis

↓

Security Scan

↓

Tests

↓

Package

↓

Deploy
```

Manual bypasses should require documented approval.

---

# 23. Exception Management

Standards exceptions require:

* documented justification
* risk assessment
* approving authority
* expiration date
* review schedule

Exceptions should be temporary and periodically re-evaluated.

---

# 24. Technical Debt Governance

Technical debt shall be:

* identified
* categorized
* prioritized
* tracked
* reviewed
* resolved when appropriate

Intentional technical debt requires explicit ownership.

---

# 25. Audit and Compliance

Engineering compliance should be verified through:

* repository audits
* architecture reviews
* code reviews
* pipeline reports
* security assessments

Audit findings should generate corrective actions.

---

# 26. Metrics and Reporting

Governance metrics include:

```text id="gov06"
Review Time

Build Success Rate

Coverage

Static Analysis Issues

Security Findings

Technical Debt

Deployment Success
```

Metrics should drive improvement rather than individual performance evaluation.

---

# 27. Change Management

Changes to engineering standards follow:

```text id="gov07"
Proposal

↓

Review

↓

Approval

↓

Publication

↓

Adoption

↓

Review
```

The standards themselves are governed artifacts.

---

# 28. Governance Anti-Patterns

The Mediverse engineering organization rejects:

* Unreviewed production code
* Direct commits to protected branches
* Ignoring static analysis
* Ignoring security findings
* Unowned repositories
* Undocumented exceptions
* Manual deployments without governance
* Architecture changes without review
* Outdated documentation
* Permanent temporary workarounds

---

# 29. Success Indicators

Governance is effective when:

* Standards are consistently applied.
* Code reviews are timely and thorough.
* Build pipelines remain stable.
* Security findings decrease over time.
* Technical debt is actively managed.
* Documentation remains current.
* Architectural consistency improves.

These outcomes indicate a mature engineering organization.

---

# 30. Chapter Summary

Enterprise Coding Governance ensures that engineering standards are applied consistently across the Mediverse platform.

Key principles include:

* Clear governance hierarchy and ownership.
* Mandatory code reviews and branch protection.
* Automated quality, security, and compliance checks.
* Controlled exception and technical debt management.
* Continuous auditing, metrics, and improvement.
* Documentation and architecture compliance as part of every software change.

---

# Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)

# Chapter 5 — Software Engineering Lifecycle

**Document ID:** MED-CSDG-005
**Chapter:** 5
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

---

# 1. Purpose

This chapter defines the standard Software Engineering Lifecycle (SEL) that every Mediverse software component shall follow.

The lifecycle provides a consistent framework from idea to retirement, ensuring that every change is:

* Planned
* Designed
* Implemented
* Verified
* Deployed
* Operated
* Continuously Improved

Every repository, microservice, frontend application, AI service, infrastructure component, and automation pipeline shall follow this lifecycle.

---

# 2. Engineering Lifecycle Philosophy

Software development is a continuous engineering process rather than a sequence of isolated activities.

```text id="life01"
Idea

↓

Requirements

↓

Architecture

↓

Design

↓

Implementation

↓

Verification

↓

Deployment

↓

Operations

↓

Improvement

↓

Retirement
```

Every phase produces outputs that become inputs to the next phase.

---

# 3. Lifecycle Objectives

The lifecycle shall:

* Improve software quality.
* Reduce delivery risk.
* Standardize engineering practices.
* Ensure traceability.
* Enable continuous delivery.
* Support regulatory compliance.
* Improve maintainability.
* Reduce production failures.

---

# 4. Lifecycle Principles

Every lifecycle stage shall be:

* Repeatable
* Measurable
* Automated where possible
* Auditable
* Continuously improved

Engineering quality is built throughout the lifecycle rather than inspected at the end.

---

# 5. Lifecycle Phases

The Mediverse lifecycle consists of:

```text id="life02"
Business Planning

↓

Requirements

↓

Architecture

↓

Technical Design

↓

Development

↓

Testing

↓

Deployment

↓

Operations

↓

Maintenance

↓

Retirement
```

Each phase includes mandatory quality gates.

---

# 6. Phase 1 — Business Planning

Objectives:

* Identify business problem.
* Define expected outcomes.
* Assess feasibility.
* Identify stakeholders.
* Prioritize value.

Deliverables:

* Product Vision
* Business Case
* Initial Scope

---

# 7. Phase 2 — Requirements Engineering

Activities:

* Functional requirements
* Non-functional requirements
* Acceptance criteria
* User stories
* Business rules

Deliverables:

* PRD
* BRD
* SRS

No implementation begins before requirements reach the agreed level of completeness.

---

# 8. Phase 3 — Architecture

Objectives:

* Select architectural style.
* Define bounded contexts.
* Establish service boundaries.
* Evaluate quality attributes.
* Record significant decisions.

Deliverables:

* SAD
* ADRs
* Reference Architecture

Architecture reviews are mandatory for significant changes.

---

# 9. Phase 4 — Technical Design

Activities:

* API design
* Database design
* Component design
* Integration design
* Security design

Deliverables:

* TDD
* ADS
* DDD
* FDS
* SecDD

Design should remain consistent with the approved architecture.

---

# 10. Phase 5 — Development

Development activities include:

* Feature implementation
* Unit testing
* Code review
* Static analysis
* Documentation updates

Code should comply with the Coding Standards & Development Guidelines.

---

# 11. Phase 6 — Verification

Verification ensures the software meets requirements.

Testing includes:

* Unit Testing
* Integration Testing
* Contract Testing
* UI Testing
* Performance Testing
* Security Testing
* Accessibility Testing
* AI Evaluation (where applicable)

Verification results should be documented.

---

# 12. Phase 7 — Deployment

Deployment activities include:

```text id="life03"
Build

↓

Package

↓

Deploy

↓

Smoke Test

↓

Monitor
```

Deployments should be automated through approved CI/CD pipelines.

---

# 13. Phase 8 — Operations

Operational responsibilities include:

* Monitoring
* Logging
* Alerting
* Incident response
* Capacity management
* Backup verification

Operations begin immediately after deployment.

---

# 14. Phase 9 — Maintenance

Maintenance includes:

* Bug fixes
* Dependency updates
* Performance improvements
* Security patches
* Documentation updates
* Refactoring

Maintenance preserves software quality over time.

---

# 15. Phase 10 — Retirement

Software retirement includes:

* Consumer notification
* Data migration
* Archive documentation
* Infrastructure cleanup
* Knowledge preservation

Retirement should be planned rather than abrupt.

---

# 16. Lifecycle Roles

| Role               | Responsibilities                |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------- |
| Product Owner      | Requirements and prioritization |
| Architect          | Architecture and design         |
| Technical Lead     | Technical coordination          |
| Developers         | Implementation                  |
| QA Engineers       | Verification                    |
| DevOps Engineers   | Deployment and operations       |
| Security Engineers | Security validation             |
| SRE                | Reliability and monitoring      |

Responsibilities should be clearly assigned.

---

# 17. Lifecycle Quality Gates

Every phase concludes with a mandatory quality gate.

```text id="life04"
Requirements Approved

↓

Architecture Approved

↓

Design Approved

↓

Implementation Complete

↓

Testing Passed

↓

Deployment Approved

↓

Operational Validation
```

Progression without satisfying the quality gate requires formal approval.

---

# 18. Traceability

Every implementation should be traceable.

```text id="life05"
Business Goal

↓

Requirement

↓

Architecture

↓

Design

↓

Code

↓

Test

↓

Deployment
```

Traceability simplifies maintenance, auditing, and impact analysis.

---

# 19. Continuous Integration

Every code change should trigger:

* Compilation
* Static analysis
* Unit tests
* Security scanning
* Artifact generation

Failures should prevent progression to later stages.

---

# 20. Continuous Delivery

The delivery pipeline should support:

* Repeatable builds
* Automated deployments
* Environment consistency
* Rollback capability
* Release traceability

Continuous delivery enables frequent, low-risk releases.

---

# 21. Documentation Lifecycle

Documentation shall evolve with software.

Update documentation whenever changes affect:

* APIs
* Architecture
* Configuration
* Deployment
* User behavior

Outdated documentation is considered a defect.

---

# 22. Change Management

Every change should include:

* Business justification
* Technical design
* Testing evidence
* Risk assessment
* Rollback strategy

Significant changes require architecture review.

---

# 23. Risk Management

Lifecycle risks should be identified early.

Examples:

* Technical risk
* Security risk
* Performance risk
* Compliance risk
* Delivery risk

Mitigation plans should be documented.

---

# 24. Feedback Loops

Continuous feedback should be collected from:

* Users
* Monitoring
* Incidents
* Retrospectives
* Code reviews
* Performance metrics

Feedback drives iterative improvement.

---

# 25. Metrics

Lifecycle effectiveness should be measured through:

```text id="life06"
Lead Time

Deployment Frequency

Change Failure Rate

Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR)

Defect Density

Code Coverage
```

Metrics support continuous process improvement.

---

# 26. Continuous Improvement

The engineering lifecycle should evolve through:

```text id="life07"
Measure

↓

Analyze

↓

Improve

↓

Standardize

↓

Repeat
```

Lessons learned should update both processes and standards.

---

# 27. Lifecycle Anti-Patterns

The Mediverse engineering organization rejects:

* Coding without approved requirements
* Skipping architecture reviews
* Design after implementation
* Manual production deployments
* Untested releases
* Missing rollback plans
* Ignoring operational feedback
* Unsupported software in production
* Retiring systems without migration planning
* Stale documentation

---

# 28. Alignment with Enterprise Architecture

The lifecycle aligns with:

* Product Requirements
* Architecture Decision Records
* Software Architecture
* Technical Design
* API Design
* Security Design
* DevOps Standards
* Testing Strategy
* Operations Guides

This ensures consistency across the full software lifecycle.

---

# 29. Success Indicators

A successful lifecycle demonstrates:

* Predictable delivery
* Low production defects
* Fast recovery
* High deployment reliability
* Accurate documentation
* Strong traceability
* Continuous improvement
* Sustainable engineering practices

---

# 30. Chapter Summary

The Mediverse Software Engineering Lifecycle establishes a standardized, end-to-end process for developing and operating software.

Key principles include:

* A defined lifecycle from planning to retirement.
* Mandatory quality gates at every phase.
* Clear roles and responsibilities.
* Continuous integration and delivery.
* End-to-end traceability.
* Continuous feedback and improvement.
* Strong governance, documentation, and risk management.

---

# Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)

# Chapter 6 — Development Workflow

**Document ID:** MED-CSDG-006
**Chapter:** 6
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

---

# 1. Purpose

This chapter defines the standardized development workflow for all engineering teams working on the Mediverse platform.

The workflow ensures that every software change follows a consistent, traceable, and quality-controlled process from assignment through deployment.

It applies to:

* Backend Services
* Frontend Applications
* AI Services
* Infrastructure as Code
* DevOps Automation
* Database Changes
* Shared Libraries
* Documentation

---

# 2. Workflow Philosophy

Development is a continuous engineering workflow.

```text id="wf01"
Plan

↓

Develop

↓

Verify

↓

Review

↓

Merge

↓

Deploy

↓

Monitor

↓

Improve
```

Every stage contributes to software quality.

---

# 3. Workflow Objectives

The workflow shall:

* Standardize daily engineering activities.
* Improve collaboration.
* Reduce integration conflicts.
* Increase software quality.
* Improve traceability.
* Enable continuous delivery.
* Reduce production defects.

---

# 4. Development Lifecycle Overview

Every engineering task follows:

```text id="wf02"
Product Backlog

↓

Sprint Planning

↓

Development

↓

Testing

↓

Code Review

↓

CI/CD

↓

Deployment

↓

Monitoring

↓

Closure
```

No stage should be skipped without formal approval.

---

# 5. Work Item Creation

Every engineering activity begins with an approved work item.

Each work item shall include:

* Unique ID
* Business objective
* Description
* Acceptance criteria
* Priority
* Assignee
* Estimated effort
* Related ADRs (if applicable)

No code should be written without a tracked work item.

---

# 6. Task Analysis

Before implementation, developers should:

* Understand business requirements.
* Review architecture documents.
* Identify dependencies.
* Estimate implementation effort.
* Clarify ambiguities.

Development should begin only after requirements are sufficiently understood.

---

# 7. Branch Creation

A dedicated branch shall be created for each work item.

Recommended naming convention:

```text id="wf03"
feature/MED-123-user-registration

bugfix/MED-245-login-timeout

hotfix/MED-502-payment-error

release/v1.5.0
```

Branch names should clearly indicate purpose.

---

# 8. Local Environment Preparation

Developers should:

* Synchronize with the latest main branch.
* Install required dependencies.
* Update local databases if necessary.
* Verify environment configuration.
* Execute baseline tests.

Local environments should closely resemble shared development environments.

---

# 9. Implementation

Implementation should follow:

```text id="wf04"
Small Changes

↓

Frequent Commits

↓

Continuous Testing

↓

Continuous Refactoring
```

Large, unrelated changes should be avoided.

---

# 10. Coding Standards Compliance

During implementation, developers shall comply with:

* Coding Standards & Development Guidelines
* Architecture Decision Records
* API Design Specification
* Security standards
* Database standards
* Testing standards

Compliance should be verified continuously.

---

# 11. Local Testing

Before committing changes, developers should execute:

* Unit tests
* Static analysis
* Formatting checks
* Linting
* Security scans (where available)

Failures should be resolved before committing.

---

# 12. Commit Strategy

Commits should be:

* Small
* Focused
* Atomic
* Reversible

Each commit should represent a single logical change.

---

# 13. Commit Messages

Recommended format:

```text id="wf05"
type(scope): concise summary

Examples:

feat(student): add registration endpoint

fix(auth): resolve token expiration bug

refactor(course): simplify enrollment service

docs(api): update OpenAPI examples

test(ai): add tutor service unit tests
```

Commit messages should clearly describe intent.

---

# 14. Pull Request Creation

Every pull request shall include:

* Summary
* Related work item
* Testing performed
* Screenshots (if UI changes)
* Breaking changes
* Documentation updates

PR descriptions should enable efficient reviews.

---

# 15. Code Review

Code review should evaluate:

* Correctness
* Readability
* Maintainability
* Architecture compliance
* Security
* Performance
* Test coverage
* Documentation

Reviews should be constructive and evidence-based.

---

# 16. Addressing Review Feedback

Developers should:

* Respond to every review comment.
* Clarify decisions where needed.
* Update code promptly.
* Re-request review after changes.

Disagreements should be resolved through technical discussion.

---

# 17. Continuous Integration

Every pull request triggers:

```text id="wf06"
Build

↓

Static Analysis

↓

Security Scan

↓

Unit Tests

↓

Integration Tests

↓

Artifact Creation
```

CI failures block merging until resolved.

---

# 18. Merge Policy

A pull request may be merged only when:

* Reviews are approved.
* CI passes.
* No critical security findings exist.
* Documentation is updated.
* Acceptance criteria are satisfied.

Direct merges to protected branches are prohibited.

---

# 19. Deployment Pipeline

Approved changes proceed through:

```text id="wf07"
Development

↓

Testing

↓

Staging

↓

Production
```

Each environment should have defined validation criteria.

---

# 20. Post-Deployment Verification

After deployment, verify:

* Application startup
* Health endpoints
* Critical business workflows
* Logs
* Metrics
* Alerts

Successful deployment includes successful operational validation.

---

# 21. Rollback Readiness

Every deployment should have a documented rollback strategy.

Rollback procedures should include:

* Trigger conditions
* Recovery steps
* Validation
* Communication

Rollback capability should be tested periodically.

---

# 22. Documentation Updates

When implementation changes:

* APIs
* Configuration
* Architecture
* Deployment
* User behavior

the corresponding documentation shall be updated in the same change set.

---

# 23. Incident Handling During Development

If a critical issue is discovered:

* Pause feature work if necessary.
* Create an incident record.
* Notify stakeholders.
* Prioritize stabilization.
* Document root cause.

Engineering priorities should reflect business impact.

---

# 24. Sprint Completion

Before closing a sprint:

* Verify completed work.
* Update documentation.
* Close work items.
* Demonstrate completed features.
* Record retrospective actions.

Incomplete work should be re-planned rather than marked complete.

---

# 25. Retrospectives

Each sprint concludes with a retrospective.

Discuss:

* What worked well
* What did not
* Improvement opportunities
* Action items

Retrospectives should produce measurable improvements.

---

# 26. Continuous Improvement

The workflow should evolve based on:

```text id="wf08"
Metrics

↓

Feedback

↓

Retrospectives

↓

Incident Reviews

↓

Engineering Proposals
```

Process improvements should be documented and communicated.

---

# 27. Workflow Anti-Patterns

The Mediverse engineering organization rejects:

* Coding without a work item
* Long-lived feature branches
* Large, unrelated pull requests
* Skipping local testing
* Ignoring CI failures
* Merging without review
* Updating documentation after release instead of with the code
* Deploying without rollback plans
* Closing work items without validation
* Treating retrospectives as optional

---

# 28. Alignment with Enterprise Standards

The development workflow aligns with:

* Product Requirements
* Software Engineering Lifecycle
* Architecture Decision Records
* API Design Specification
* Security Design Document
* DevOps & Infrastructure Guide
* Testing Strategy & QA Plan

This alignment ensures that daily engineering activities consistently implement enterprise architecture and governance.

---

# 29. Success Indicators

A successful development workflow demonstrates:

* Short lead times
* High CI success rates
* Small, reviewable pull requests
* Low change failure rate
* High deployment frequency
* Accurate documentation
* Predictable releases
* Continuous process improvement

---

# 30. Chapter Summary

The Mediverse Development Workflow provides a standardized approach to software delivery.

Key principles include:

* Every change begins with an approved work item.
* Development proceeds through defined stages from implementation to deployment.
* Branches, commits, and pull requests follow consistent standards.
* Local testing, CI, and code reviews are mandatory quality gates.
* Documentation evolves with the code.
* Deployments include validation and rollback readiness.
* Continuous improvement is driven by metrics, retrospectives, and operational feedback.

---

# Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)

# Chapter 7 — Development Environment Standards

**Document ID:** MED-CSDG-007
**Chapter:** 7
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

---

# 1. Purpose

This chapter defines the mandatory standards for development environments across the Mediverse platform.

A standardized development environment ensures:

* Consistent builds
* Reproducible development
* Reduced onboarding time
* Fewer environment-specific defects
* Predictable CI/CD behavior

Every engineer should be able to clone the repository and begin development with minimal manual configuration.

---

# 2. Development Environment Philosophy

Development environments should be:

```text id="env01"
Consistent

↓

Reproducible

↓

Automated

↓

Secure

↓

Isolated

↓

Version Controlled
```

The local environment should closely resemble higher environments (integration, staging, production) while remaining practical for development.

---

# 3. Supported Operating Systems

The engineering organization officially supports:

| Platform                          | Status      |
| --------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Windows 11 (WSL2 recommended)     | ✅ Supported |
| Ubuntu LTS                        | ✅ Supported |
| macOS (latest supported versions) | ✅ Supported |

Linux-based development environments are preferred because they closely match production Kubernetes nodes.

---

# 4. Standard Development Workstation

Minimum recommended specifications:

| Resource | Recommendation                   |
| -------- | -------------------------------- |
| CPU      | 8+ logical cores                 |
| Memory   | 32 GB RAM                        |
| Storage  | 512 GB NVMe SSD (1 TB preferred) |
| Internet | Stable broadband                 |
| Monitor  | Dual-monitor recommended         |

Developers working with AI models, local Kubernetes clusters, or large datasets may require additional resources.

---

# 5. Mandatory Development Tools

Every developer workstation shall include:

```text id="env02"
Git

Java JDK

Node.js

Docker

Kubernetes CLI

Helm

Database Client

IDE

Build Tools

Package Managers
```

Versions are governed centrally to reduce compatibility issues.

---

# 6. Language Runtime Standards

Approved runtime versions should be documented in a central compatibility matrix.

Examples include:

* Java
* Node.js
* Python
* TypeScript

All projects should pin supported versions rather than relying on "latest".

---

# 7. IDE Standards

Approved IDEs include:

| Language   | Recommended IDE                 |
| ---------- | ------------------------------- |
| Java       | IntelliJ IDEA                   |
| Frontend   | Visual Studio Code              |
| Database   | DataGrip or approved SQL client |
| Kubernetes | VS Code + Kubernetes extensions |

IDE configuration should be documented and shared.

---

# 8. Required IDE Extensions

Developers should install extensions for:

* Language support
* Linting
* Formatting
* Docker
* Kubernetes
* Git
* YAML
* Markdown
* REST client support

Extensions should align with project tooling.

---

# 9. Source Control Configuration

Every workstation should configure:

* Git username
* Git email
* SSH keys (preferred)
* GPG signing (if required)
* Default branch settings

Identity should be verified before contributing.

---

# 10. Local Repository Setup

Repository initialization should follow:

```text id="env03"
Clone Repository

↓

Install Dependencies

↓

Configure Environment

↓

Run Database

↓

Start Services

↓

Execute Tests

↓

Begin Development
```

Setup should be scripted wherever possible.

---

# 11. Environment Variables

Application configuration shall use environment variables.

Examples:

* Database connection
* API endpoints
* Storage configuration
* Feature flags
* External service URLs

Sensitive values should never be committed to source control.

---

# 12. Secrets Management

Secrets include:

* API keys
* Database passwords
* Private certificates
* Access tokens
* Encryption keys

Rules:

* Never hard-code secrets.
* Never commit secrets to Git.
* Use approved secret management solutions.
* Rotate secrets according to security policy.

---

# 13. Local Database Standards

Local databases should:

* Match supported production versions where practical.
* Be initialized through migration scripts.
* Use representative sample data.
* Be resettable without manual intervention.

Schema changes should be managed through approved migration tools.

---

# 14. Local Service Dependencies

Dependent services should run using reproducible tooling such as:

* Containers
* Container Compose definitions
* Local Kubernetes clusters (when appropriate)

Developers should avoid undocumented manual setup.

---

# 15. Container Standards

Containers used for local development should:

* Be reproducible.
* Use official or approved base images.
* Match supported runtime versions.
* Avoid unnecessary privileges.

Container definitions should be version-controlled.

---

# 16. Local Kubernetes Environment

Developers working on cloud-native services should use a supported local Kubernetes solution.

The local cluster should support:

* Namespaces
* Ingress
* Persistent volumes
* Secrets
* ConfigMaps
* Helm deployments

The local environment should reflect production architecture where feasible.

---

# 17. Package Management

Package managers should:

* Lock dependency versions.
* Verify integrity.
* Avoid unnecessary transitive dependencies.
* Use approved repositories.

Dependency updates should follow the governance process.

---

# 18. Build Environment

Developers should be able to perform complete local builds including:

```text id="env04"
Compile

↓

Static Analysis

↓

Unit Tests

↓

Packaging

↓

Artifact Generation
```

Local builds should closely mirror CI builds.

---

# 19. Code Formatting

Formatting shall be automated using approved tools.

Formatting rules should be:

* Consistent
* Version-controlled
* Automatically enforceable

Manual formatting should be minimized.

---

# 20. Static Analysis

Local development should include:

* Style validation
* Static code analysis
* Security scanning (where practical)
* Dependency validation

Developers should resolve issues before creating pull requests.

---

# 21. Local Testing

Developers should execute:

* Unit tests
* Integration tests (where practical)
* API tests
* Frontend tests
* Database migration validation

Failing local tests should block commits until resolved.

---

# 22. AI Development Environment

AI engineers should additionally configure:

* Model endpoints
* Embedding services
* Vector database connections
* Prompt templates
* Evaluation datasets

AI configuration should be isolated from application configuration.

---

# 23. Development Logging

Local environments should generate:

* Structured application logs
* Build logs
* Test logs
* Container logs

Logs should be easy to inspect and rotate.

---

# 24. Debugging Standards

Debugging should support:

* Breakpoints
* Remote debugging
* Request tracing
* Database inspection
* Container inspection

Debug configurations should be shared where practical.

---

# 25. Environment Validation

Developers should execute an automated validation script that confirms:

```text id="env05"
Required Tools Installed

↓

Correct Runtime Versions

↓

Database Connectivity

↓

Container Runtime

↓

Build Success

↓

Tests Pass
```

Validation reduces onboarding issues and configuration drift.

---

# 26. Environment Documentation

Each repository should document:

* Prerequisites
* Installation steps
* Environment variables
* Required tools
* Common troubleshooting
* Known limitations

Documentation should remain synchronized with repository changes.

---

# 27. Anti-Patterns

The Mediverse engineering organization rejects:

* Manual environment configuration without documentation
* Hard-coded credentials
* Untracked dependency versions
* Inconsistent runtime versions
* "Works on my machine" assumptions
* Shared developer databases
* Production credentials in local environments
* Local-only configuration that cannot be reproduced
* Skipping local validation before committing

---

# 28. Alignment with Enterprise Standards

Development environment standards align with:

* Software Engineering Lifecycle
* Development Workflow
* Security Design Document
* DevOps & Infrastructure Guide
* Testing Strategy & QA Plan
* Enterprise Architecture
* Architecture Decision Records

This alignment ensures that local development practices support enterprise engineering goals.

---

# 29. Success Indicators

A standardized development environment is successful when:

* New developers can become productive quickly.
* Local builds consistently match CI builds.
* Environment-related defects are minimized.
* Configuration drift is controlled.
* Security policies are consistently enforced.
* Developers spend more time building features than troubleshooting environments.

---

# 30. Chapter Summary

The Mediverse Development Environment Standards establish a consistent and secure foundation for software development.

Key principles include:

* Standardized operating systems, tooling, and runtimes.
* Reproducible local environments.
* Secure handling of configuration and secrets.
* Automated formatting, analysis, and validation.
* Containerized and Kubernetes-ready development.
* Alignment between local, CI, and production environments.
* Comprehensive documentation and environment validation.
* Continuous enforcement of consistency across all engineering teams.

---

# Coding Standards & Development Guidelines (CSDG)

# Chapter 8 — IDE Configuration Standards

**Document ID:** MED-CSDG-008
**Chapter:** 8
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

---

# 1. Purpose

This chapter defines the standardized Integrated Development Environment (IDE) configuration for all Mediverse engineering teams.

The objective is to ensure every developer works within a consistent development environment, reducing configuration drift, improving code quality, and increasing engineering productivity.

The standards apply to:

* Backend Development
* Frontend Development
* AI Engineering
* DevOps Engineering
* Database Development
* Infrastructure as Code

---

# 2. Objectives

Standardized IDE configurations shall:

* Improve developer productivity
* Enforce coding standards automatically
* Reduce formatting inconsistencies
* Improve code quality
* Detect defects early
* Simplify onboarding
* Standardize debugging
* Support enterprise tooling

---

# 3. Approved IDEs

| Technology         | Approved IDE                                   |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Java / Spring Boot | IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate (Preferred) / Community |
| React / TypeScript | Visual Studio Code                             |
| Python / AI        | PyCharm Professional / VS Code                 |
| Database           | DataGrip / DBeaver                             |
| Kubernetes         | VS Code / Lens                                 |
| Infrastructure     | VS Code                                        |

Use of other IDEs requires compatibility with the project's formatting, linting, and build tooling.

---

# 4. Standard IDE Configuration

Every IDE should use:

```text id="ide01"
UTF-8 Encoding

↓

LF Line Endings

↓

4-Space Indentation

↓

Trim Trailing Spaces

↓

Insert Final Newline

↓

Automatic Formatting
```

Configuration should be version-controlled wherever possible.

---

# 5. Shared IDE Settings

Projects should include shared configuration for:

* Formatting
* Inspection profiles
* Run configurations (where appropriate)
* Code style
* EditorConfig
* Language settings

Developers should avoid personal settings that conflict with team standards.

---

# 6. IntelliJ IDEA Standards

Required configuration includes:

* Project SDK
* Maven/Gradle integration
* Annotation processing
* Automatic import optimization
* Code style profile
* Shared inspection profile
* JUnit integration
* Spring Boot support

The IDE should use the project-defined formatter rather than individual preferences.

---

# 7. Visual Studio Code Standards

Required configuration includes:

* Workspace settings
* Formatter configuration
* ESLint integration
* Prettier integration
* TypeScript support
* Docker extension
* Kubernetes extension
* Git integration

Workspace configuration should be committed when it benefits the entire team.

---

# 8. EditorConfig

Every repository shall include an `.editorconfig` file.

Minimum rules:

* UTF-8 encoding
* Consistent indentation
* Final newline
* Trim trailing whitespace
* Consistent line endings

EditorConfig provides editor-independent formatting consistency.

---

# 9. Code Formatting

Formatting should be automatic on save where supported.

Formatting must:

* Follow project rules.
* Produce deterministic output.
* Avoid manual alignment.
* Minimize formatting-only commits.

Formatting tools should not alter program behavior.

---

# 10. Import Management

Imports should be:

* Organized automatically
* Free of unused entries
* Explicit where appropriate
* Consistent across the project

Wildcard imports should be avoided unless explicitly allowed by project standards.

---

# 11. Inspection Profiles

IDE inspections should identify:

* Dead code
* Unused variables
* Nullability issues
* Duplicate code
* Deprecated APIs
* Unreachable code
* Potential resource leaks

Inspection profiles should be shared across teams.

---

# 12. Static Analysis Integration

The IDE should integrate with project tools such as:

* Checkstyle
* PMD
* SpotBugs
* SonarLint
* ESLint

Developers should resolve issues before committing code.

---

# 13. Live Templates

Common coding patterns should be available through shared templates.

Examples:

* REST controller
* Service class
* Repository
* DTO
* Test class
* Logging statements

Templates improve consistency and reduce repetitive work.

---

# 14. Code Generation

IDE code generation may be used for:

* Constructors
* Getters/Setters (where applicable)
* Equals/HashCode
* Builder patterns
* Test stubs

Generated code should be reviewed and refined rather than accepted blindly.

---

# 15. Debug Configuration

Standard debug configurations should support:

```text id="ide02"
Application

↓

Remote JVM

↓

Container

↓

Kubernetes Port Forward

↓

Test Runner
```

Debug profiles should be documented for common workflows.

---

# 16. Database Integration

Approved IDE database tools should support:

* Secure connections
* Read-only production access (where authorized)
* SQL formatting
* Query history
* Schema browsing

Production data modification should follow operational governance.

---

# 17. Git Integration

IDE Git features should support:

* Branch management
* Commit creation
* Diff viewing
* Conflict resolution
* Pull request preparation

Developers should understand Git concepts independently of IDE tooling.

---

# 18. Docker Integration

The IDE should allow developers to:

* Build images
* Run containers
* View logs
* Inspect running services
* Execute commands

Container management should complement command-line proficiency.

---

# 19. Kubernetes Integration

IDE support should include:

* Namespace selection
* Manifest editing
* Log viewing
* Resource inspection
* Port forwarding

Cluster modifications should follow environment access policies.

---

# 20. API Development Support

The IDE should facilitate:

* HTTP client requests
* OpenAPI viewing
* JSON formatting
* Request history
* Response inspection

These capabilities simplify API development and testing.

---

# 21. AI Development Support

AI engineers should configure support for:

* Python environments
* Notebook execution (where appropriate)
* Prompt template editing
* JSON schema validation
* Model endpoint testing

AI tooling should integrate with the standard development workflow.

---

# 22. Productivity Features

Developers are encouraged to use:

* Refactoring tools
* Navigation shortcuts
* Symbol search
* Code completion
* Safe rename
* Usage analysis

These features improve efficiency without altering coding standards.

---

# 23. Performance

IDE performance should be maintained through:

* Appropriate memory allocation
* Plugin management
* Cache maintenance
* Project indexing optimization

Unnecessary plugins should be removed.

---

# 24. Plugin Governance

Only approved plugins should be used.

Plugins should be evaluated for:

* Security
* Maintenance
* Compatibility
* Licensing
* Productivity impact

Unsupported or abandoned plugins should be avoided.

---

# 25. Accessibility

IDE configuration should support:

* Adjustable fonts
* High-contrast themes
* Keyboard navigation
* Screen reader compatibility (where needed)

Accessibility features should be available without affecting shared project configuration.

---

# 26. Workspace Portability

Workspace configuration should be portable across supported operating systems.

Repository-specific settings should avoid absolute file paths and user-specific values.

---

# 27. Anti-Patterns

The Mediverse engineering organization rejects:

* Personal formatting rules that conflict with project standards
* Committing IDE-specific temporary files
* Disabling mandatory inspections
* Excessive reliance on unsupported plugins
* Formatting-only commits mixed with functional changes
* Ignoring IDE warnings without justification
* Sharing user-specific workspace settings

---

# 28. Alignment with Enterprise Standards

IDE standards align with:

* Development Environment Standards
* Coding Standards
* Development Workflow
* Security Design Document
* DevOps & Infrastructure Guide
* Testing Strategy & QA Plan

This alignment ensures that developer tooling reinforces enterprise engineering practices.

---

# 29. Success Indicators

IDE standardization is successful when:

* Developers produce consistently formatted code.
* IDE setup for new team members is straightforward.
* Static analysis issues are identified early.
* Productivity improves through shared tooling.
* Environment-specific inconsistencies decrease.
* Teams spend less time resolving tooling differences.

---

# 30. Chapter Summary

The Mediverse IDE Configuration Standards establish a consistent development experience across all engineering teams.

Key principles include:

* Approved IDEs and shared configuration profiles.
* Automatic formatting and standardized code style.
* Integrated static analysis and inspections.
* Consistent debugging, Git, Docker, Kubernetes, and API tooling.
* Controlled plugin usage and workspace portability.
* Alignment between developer tooling and enterprise engineering standards.

---
