# CSDG — Chapter 13: Spring Boot Coding Standards

**Document ID:** `MED-CSDG-013`
**Chapter:** 13
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

This chapter defines the coding standards for building **Mediverse Spring Boot backend services** consistently across development, testing, CI/CD, and production.

---

## 1. Spring Boot Architecture Principle

Spring Boot code must maintain clear separation of responsibilities:

```text
HTTP
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Application / Service
 ↓
Domain Logic
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
Database
```

External systems should be accessed through clearly defined integration boundaries.

Do not allow controllers to directly contain database or business logic.

---

# 2. Standard Project Structure

A typical Mediverse service should follow a domain-oriented structure.

```text
student-service/
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/com/mediverse/student/
    │   │   ├── StudentServiceApplication.java
    │   │   │
    │   │   ├── controller/
    │   │   ├── service/
    │   │   ├── repository/
    │   │   ├── entity/
    │   │   ├── dto/
    │   │   ├── mapper/
    │   │   ├── exception/
    │   │   ├── config/
    │   │   └── security/
    │   │
    │   └── resources/
    │       ├── application.yml
    │       └── db/
    │
    └── test/
        └── java/com/mediverse/student/
```

The exact structure can be adapted when a service has substantially different domain requirements.

---

# 3. Main Application Class

The main class should remain minimal.

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class StudentServiceApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(StudentServiceApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

Do not place business logic here.

---

# 4. Component Responsibilities

| Component         | Responsibility                     |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Controller        | HTTP/API handling                  |
| Service           | Application/business orchestration |
| Repository        | Persistence                        |
| Entity            | Persistence/domain state           |
| DTO               | API contract                       |
| Mapper            | Object transformation              |
| Configuration     | Application configuration          |
| Exception Handler | Error translation                  |
| Security          | Authentication/authorization       |
| Integration       | External systems                   |

---

# 5. Controller Standards

Controllers should be thin.

Example:

```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/students")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class StudentController {

    private final StudentService studentService;

    @GetMapping("/{studentId}")
    public StudentResponse getStudent(
            @PathVariable UUID studentId) {

        return studentService.getStudent(studentId);
    }
}
```

The controller should not contain:

```text
SQL
business calculations
complex validation logic
transaction orchestration
external-system workflows
```

---

# 6. REST Mapping

Use the appropriate HTTP method.

```text
GET     → Retrieve
POST    → Create/action producing a resource
PUT     → Replace
PATCH   → Partial update
DELETE  → Delete
```

Do not use `POST` for every operation simply because it is convenient.

---

# 7. Controller Return Types

API contracts should be explicit.

Preferred:

```java
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public StudentResponse getStudent(@PathVariable UUID id) {
    return studentService.getStudent(id);
}
```

For more complex APIs, `ResponseEntity` may be used when response status or headers genuinely need to be controlled.

Do not wrap every response in `ResponseEntity` without a reason.

---

# 8. Request DTOs

Never use JPA entities as request models by default.

Preferred:

```java
public record CreateStudentRequest(
        @NotBlank String firstName,
        @NotBlank String lastName,
        @Email @NotBlank String email
) {}
```

This prevents clients from directly controlling persistence state.

---

# 9. Response DTOs

Responses should expose only the information required by the API contract.

```java
public record StudentResponse(
        UUID id,
        String firstName,
        String lastName,
        String email
) {}
```

Do not accidentally expose:

```text
passwordHash
internal audit information
security metadata
internal database fields
```

---

# 10. Service Layer

Services coordinate application behavior.

Example:

```java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class StudentService {

    private final StudentRepository studentRepository;

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public StudentResponse getStudent(UUID studentId) {

        Student student = studentRepository.findById(studentId)
                .orElseThrow(() ->
                        new StudentNotFoundException(studentId));

        return StudentMapper.toResponse(student);
    }
}
```

---

# 11. Business Logic Location

Business rules should not be scattered across:

```text
Controller
Repository
Mapper
Utility classes
```

They should live in an appropriate service/domain component.

---

# 12. Repository Standards

Spring Data repositories should focus on persistence.

Example:

```java
@Repository
public interface StudentRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Student, UUID> {

    Optional<Student> findByEmail(String email);
}
```

Avoid putting business workflows into repository interfaces.

---

# 13. Repository Query Naming

Derived queries should remain readable.

Good:

```java
findByEmail(...)
findByCourseId(...)
findByStudentIdAndStatus(...)
```

If a derived method becomes excessively long, use an explicit query or specification strategy.

Do not create unreadable method names merely to avoid writing a query.

---

# 14. JPA Entity Standards

Entities must clearly map to persistence structures.

```java
@Entity
@Table(name = "students")
@Getter
@NoArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PROTECTED)
public class Student {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private UUID id;

    private String firstName;

    private String lastName;
}
```

Entity design should protect invariants and avoid unnecessary public mutation.

---

# 15. Entity Constructors

JPA requires an accessible no-argument constructor.

Prefer restricted visibility:

```java
@NoArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PROTECTED)
```

rather than exposing an unrestricted public constructor unless required.

---

# 16. Entity Mutation

Avoid unrestricted setters.

Instead of:

```java
student.setStatus(ACTIVE);
```

prefer meaningful domain operations where appropriate:

```java
student.activate();
```

This makes domain behavior explicit.

---

# 17. JPA Fetch Strategy

Do not blindly use `EAGER`.

Prefer deliberate loading strategies.

Default to lazy loading where appropriate and explicitly fetch relationships needed by a use case.

---

# 18. JPA Cascade

Cascade operations must be intentional.

Do not automatically add:

```java
CascadeType.ALL
```

to every relationship.

Ask:

> Should the lifecycle of the child actually depend on the lifecycle of the parent?

If not, cascading may be incorrect.

---

# 19. Transactions

Transactions should normally be placed at the service/application boundary.

Example:

```java
@Transactional
public QuizResult submitQuiz(
        UUID studentId,
        UUID quizId,
        QuizSubmissionRequest request) {

    // transactional workflow
}
```

---

# 20. Read-Only Operations

Use:

```java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
```

for appropriate read-only service operations.

Example:

```java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public StudentResponse getStudent(UUID id) {
    ...
}
```

---

# 21. Transaction Boundaries

A transaction should represent a coherent business operation.

For example:

```text
Submit Quiz
    ↓
Validate Attempt
    ↓
Evaluate Answers
    ↓
Store Result
    ↓
Update Progress
```

If these operations must succeed or fail together, the transaction boundary should reflect that requirement.

---

# 22. Validation

Use Jakarta Bean Validation at API boundaries.

```java
public record CreateQuizRequest(

        @NotBlank
        String title,

        @NotNull
        UUID subjectId,

        @Min(1)
        int durationMinutes
) {}
```

---

# 23. Business Validation

Bean Validation is not a replacement for business rules.

Example:

```text
@NotBlank
    ↓
Input validation

Student must be enrolled before attempting quiz
    ↓
Business validation
```

Both may be required.

---

# 24. Exception Handling

Use centralized exception handling.

```java
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(StudentNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleStudentNotFound(
            StudentNotFoundException exception) {

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                .body(...);
    }
}
```

---

# 25. HTTP Status Codes

Use semantically correct status codes.

| Situation                       |              Status |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------: |
| Successful retrieval            |               `200` |
| Successful creation             |               `201` |
| Successful deletion             |               `204` |
| Invalid request                 |               `400` |
| Authentication required/failed  |               `401` |
| Insufficient permissions        |               `403` |
| Resource not found              |               `404` |
| Conflict                        |               `409` |
| Validation/business input issue | `422` where adopted |
| Unexpected server failure       |               `500` |

The final API contract must remain aligned with ADS.

---

# 26. Configuration

Configuration must not be hard-coded.

Bad:

```java
private static final String DATABASE_URL =
        "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mediverse";
```

Prefer external configuration:

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DATABASE_URL}
```

---

# 27. Configuration Properties

For grouped application configuration, prefer typed configuration.

Example:

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "mediverse.quiz")
public record QuizProperties(
        int maxAttempts,
        Duration submissionTimeout
) {}
```

This is preferable to scattering `@Value` fields throughout the application.

---

# 28. Profiles

Use Spring profiles deliberately.

Typical environments:

```text
dev
test
uat
staging
prod
```

Example:

```text
application.yml
application-dev.yml
application-uat.yml
application-prod.yml
```

Do not create dozens of profiles for minor configuration differences.

---

# 29. Secrets

Secrets must come from secure external mechanisms.

Never commit:

```text
JWT secrets
database passwords
API keys
cloud credentials
private keys
```

into Git.

---

# 30. Environment Variables

Environment-specific values should be externally configurable.

Example:

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DATABASE_URL}
    username: ${DATABASE_USERNAME}
    password: ${DATABASE_PASSWORD}
```

---

# 31. Configuration Precedence

Developers must understand how configuration is resolved across:

```text
application.yml
       ↓
profile configuration
       ↓
environment variables
       ↓
container/Kubernetes configuration
       ↓
runtime overrides
```

The exact deployment precedence is governed by DIG.

---

# 32. Profiles Are Not Security

Do not assume:

```text
prod profile
```

automatically makes an application secure.

Security must be explicitly configured.

---

# 33. Spring Security Integration

Security configuration must remain aligned with SecDD.

Authentication and authorization must not be bypassed for convenience.

Example conceptual flow:

```text
Request
  ↓
Security Filter Chain
  ↓
Authentication
  ↓
Authorization
  ↓
Controller
```

---

# 34. Authorization

Authentication answers:

> Who are you?

Authorization answers:

> Are you allowed to perform this operation?

Both must be handled appropriately.

For example:

```text
Student
   ↓
Can view own progress

Faculty
   ↓
Can manage assigned course content

Admin
   ↓
Can manage platform configuration
```

---

# 35. Method-Level Security

Where appropriate, authorization may be enforced at the service/method boundary.

Example:

```java
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('FACULTY')")
public void publishCourse(...) {
    ...
}
```

The exact authorization model must follow SecDD.

---

# 36. Caching

Caching should be introduced only when justified.

Potential Mediverse candidates may include:

```text
Course metadata
Subject structure
Frequently accessed learning resources
Configuration
```

Do not cache rapidly changing or security-sensitive data without a clear consistency strategy.

---

# 37. Cache Naming

Cache names should be domain-oriented.

Example:

```text
students
courses
subjects
quiz-results
```

Avoid generic names:

```text
data
cache1
temp
misc
```

---

# 38. Events

Domain/application events should have meaningful names.

Examples:

```text
StudentRegistered
CourseEnrolled
QuizSubmitted
AssessmentCompleted
LearningProgressUpdated
```

Events should communicate something that happened.

---

# 39. Event Consumers

Consumers must be designed for duplicate delivery where the messaging infrastructure provides at-least-once semantics.

Therefore, important operations should be idempotent.

Example:

```text
QuizSubmitted
    ↓
Notification Consumer
    ↓
Check duplicate/idempotency
    ↓
Send Notification
```

---

# 40. Scheduled Jobs

Scheduled jobs must define:

* Execution frequency
* Failure handling
* Concurrency behavior
* Observability
* Retry behavior

Avoid overlapping executions unless explicitly supported.

---

# 41. File Uploads

File uploads require:

* Size limits
* Content validation
* File-type validation
* Safe filenames
* Storage strategy
* Access control
* Malware/security considerations

Never trust the filename or MIME type supplied by a client.

---

# 42. External API Integration

External services must use explicit client abstractions.

Example:

```text
Quiz Service
     ↓
Content Service Client
     ↓
Content Service
```

Avoid scattering raw HTTP calls throughout business logic.

---

# 43. Timeouts

External HTTP calls must have explicit timeout behavior.

Never assume:

```text
"the other service will eventually respond."
```

An unavailable dependency should not unnecessarily consume application threads indefinitely.

---

# 44. Retry

Retries should be applied only where safe.

Do not blindly retry:

```text
POST operations
financial operations
non-idempotent mutations
```

unless idempotency has been designed.

---

# 45. Spring Actuator

Production services should expose appropriate operational endpoints through Actuator.

Useful capabilities include:

```text
health
metrics
info
```

Sensitive actuator endpoints must not be publicly exposed.

---

# 46. Health Checks

Health checks should distinguish:

```text
Liveness
```

from:

```text
Readiness
```

Conceptually:

```text
Liveness
→ Is the process alive?

Readiness
→ Can this instance receive traffic?
```

This becomes particularly important in Kubernetes.

---

# 47. Observability

Spring Boot services should support:

* Structured logging
* Metrics
* Distributed tracing where applicable
* Correlation/trace IDs
* Health checks

A service should be diagnosable without attaching a debugger to production.

---

# 48. API Documentation

REST APIs should be documented according to the ADS/OpenAPI standards.

The implementation and API documentation must not drift apart.

If an API changes:

```text
Code Change
    +
OpenAPI Change
    +
Tests
```

must be considered together.

---

# 49. Database Migration

Schema changes must be version-controlled.

Use the project's approved migration tool and maintain migrations such as:

```text
V1__create_students.sql
V2__create_courses.sql
V3__create_quizzes.sql
```

Never depend on manually modifying production schemas.

---

# 50. Startup Behavior

Application startup should be predictable.

Avoid performing expensive or fragile business operations automatically during startup unless explicitly required.

A temporary external-service outage should not unnecessarily prevent the entire service from starting if that dependency is not required for readiness.

---

# 51. Graceful Shutdown

Services should support graceful shutdown where applicable.

The application should have enough time to:

```text
Stop accepting new work
        ↓
Finish in-flight work
        ↓
Close resources
        ↓
Terminate
```

This is particularly important in Kubernetes deployments.

---

# 52. Testing Requirements

Spring Boot code should have appropriate test coverage.

Typical layers:

```text
Unit Tests
    ↓
Service tests

Integration Tests
    ↓
Database / Spring context

API Tests
    ↓
Controller / HTTP behavior

End-to-End Tests
    ↓
Complete user workflow
```

Not every class needs the same type or amount of testing.

---

# 53. Test Slices

Use focused Spring test slices where appropriate.

Examples:

```text
@WebMvcTest
@DataJpaTest
```

This can make tests faster and isolate responsibilities.

---

# 54. Testcontainers

For integration tests involving infrastructure such as PostgreSQL, Redis, or Kafka, Testcontainers should be considered where appropriate.

This reduces the gap between:

```text
Developer Test Environment
```

and:

```text
Real Infrastructure
```

---

# 55. Dependency Versions

Dependencies must be managed centrally and consistently.

Avoid introducing arbitrary versions throughout individual modules.

For multi-module systems, use a central dependency-management strategy.

---

# 56. Dependency Updates

Before upgrading a major dependency:

```text
Check compatibility
       ↓
Review breaking changes
       ↓
Run tests
       ↓
Run static/security analysis
       ↓
Validate runtime behavior
```

Never blindly upgrade Spring Boot or critical infrastructure libraries.

---

# 57. Code Quality Gates

Spring Boot services must pass the project's quality gates before release.

Typical checks:

```text
Compile
 ↓
Unit Tests
 ↓
Integration Tests
 ↓
Static Analysis
 ↓
Security Scan
 ↓
Package
```

---

# 58. Spring Boot Anti-Patterns

Avoid:

* Fat controllers
* Business logic in repositories
* Field injection
* Entity exposure through APIs
* Global mutable state
* Blind `CascadeType.ALL`
* Blind `EAGER` fetching
* Unbounded queries
* Missing transaction boundaries
* Hard-coded configuration
* Exposed secrets
* Uncontrolled retries
* Infinite external calls
* Unsecured Actuator endpoints

---

# 59. Spring Boot Review Checklist

Before merging Spring Boot changes:

```text
□ Controller is thin
□ Service owns business workflow
□ Repository owns persistence
□ DTO/entity boundary is respected
□ Validation exists
□ Exception handling is consistent
□ Transactions are intentional
□ JPA fetch behavior is understood
□ No N+1 query
□ Configuration is externalized
□ Secrets are protected
□ Security rules are enforced
□ Logs contain useful context
□ No sensitive data is logged
□ Tests pass
□ API documentation is updated
□ Database migration is included if required
□ Health/observability requirements are satisfied
```

---

# 60. Standard Mediverse Request Flow

A typical Mediverse API should follow:

```text
                    HTTP Request
                         │
                         ▼
               ┌──────────────────┐
               │ Security Filter  │
               └────────┬─────────┘
                        │
                        ▼
               ┌──────────────────┐
               │   Controller     │
               │ Validate Input   │
               └────────┬─────────┘
                        │
                        ▼
               ┌──────────────────┐
               │     Service      │
               │ Business Rules   │
               │ Transaction      │
               └──────┬─────┬─────┘
                      │     │
              ┌───────┘     └─────────┐
              ▼                       ▼
       ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────┐
       │  Repository  │       │ External API │
       └──────┬───────┘       └──────────────┘
              │
              ▼
       ┌──────────────┐
       │  PostgreSQL  │
       └──────────────┘
              │
              ▼
          DTO Mapping
              │
              ▼
         HTTP Response
```

This is the baseline pattern, not a rule that every feature must mechanically follow.

---

# 61. Chapter Summary

The Spring Boot standard establishes how Mediverse backend services should be built from API entry point through persistence and external integrations.

The central principle is:

> **Keep each layer responsible for its own job, make business behavior explicit, externalize configuration, secure the boundaries, and make the service observable and testable.**

---

# CSDG — Chapter 14: REST API Coding Standards

**Document ID:** `MED-CSDG-014`
**Chapter:** 14
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

This chapter defines how Mediverse REST APIs must be **designed, implemented, reviewed, documented, secured, versioned, and evolved**.

> **Important:** This chapter defines coding/implementation standards. The authoritative API contract remains the **API Design Specification (ADS)**. If an implementation conflicts with ADS, the conflict must be resolved rather than silently choosing one.

---

# 1. REST API Design Principles

Mediverse APIs must be:

* Resource-oriented
* Predictable
* Consistent
* Stateless
* Secure
* Versionable
* Observable
* Backward-compatible where required
* Explicit about errors

Avoid designing APIs around internal database implementation.

---

# 2. API Base Path

All public Mediverse APIs should have a consistent base path.

Recommended:

```text
/api/v1
```

Example:

```text
/api/v1/students
/api/v1/courses
/api/v1/subjects
/api/v1/quizzes
```

The exact versioning strategy remains governed by ADS.

---

# 3. Resource Naming

Use plural nouns.

Preferred:

```http
/api/v1/students
/api/v1/courses
/api/v1/subjects
/api/v1/quizzes
/api/v1/assessments
```

Avoid:

```http
/api/v1/getStudents
/api/v1/createCourse
/api/v1/deleteQuiz
```

HTTP methods already communicate the operation.

---

# 4. URI Naming Convention

Use lowercase kebab-case.

Preferred:

```http
/api/v1/student-enrollments
/api/v1/quiz-attempts
/api/v1/learning-resources
```

Avoid:

```http
/api/v1/studentEnrollments
/api/v1/StudentEnrollments
/api/v1/student_enrollments
```

---

# 5. HTTP Methods

| Method   | Purpose          |
| -------- | ---------------- |
| `GET`    | Retrieve         |
| `POST`   | Create/process   |
| `PUT`    | Full replacement |
| `PATCH`  | Partial update   |
| `DELETE` | Delete           |

Do not use `POST` for every operation simply because it is easier.

---

# 6. GET

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/students/123
```

A GET request should retrieve information and should not intentionally modify server state.

---

# 7. POST

Creating a resource:

```http
POST /api/v1/students
```

Example:

```json
{
  "firstName": "Amit",
  "lastName": "Patil",
  "email": "amit@example.com"
}
```

---

# 8. PUT

Use PUT when replacing the complete representation.

```http
PUT /api/v1/students/123
```

Do not use PUT for a small field update when PATCH better represents the operation.

---

# 9. PATCH

Use PATCH for partial modifications.

```http
PATCH /api/v1/students/123
```

Example:

```json
{
  "phoneNumber": "+91XXXXXXXXXX"
}
```

---

# 10. DELETE

Example:

```http
DELETE /api/v1/students/123
```

Typical successful response:

```http
204 No Content
```

If Mediverse implements soft deletion, the API behavior must be explicitly documented.

---

# 11. Resource Hierarchies

Use nested resources only when the relationship is meaningful.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses/{courseId}/subjects
```

But avoid excessive nesting:

```http
/api/v1/students/{studentId}/courses/{courseId}/subjects/{subjectId}/chapters/{chapterId}/topics
```

Deep nesting becomes difficult to use and maintain.

Prefer flatter resources where appropriate:

```http
/api/v1/topics/{topicId}
```

---

# 12. Path Parameters

Path parameters identify a resource.

```http
GET /api/v1/students/{studentId}
```

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/students/8f1c...
```

Use descriptive names:

```text
studentId
courseId
quizId
attemptId
```

---

# 13. Query Parameters

Query parameters should control retrieval behavior.

Examples:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?page=0&pageSize=20
```

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?status=PUBLISHED
```

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?sortBy=createdAt&sortDirection=desc
```

---

# 14. Query Parameters vs Path Parameters

Use:

```text
Path parameter → identify resource
Query parameter → filter/modify retrieval
```

Example:

```http
GET /students/123
```

means:

> Get student 123.

Whereas:

```http
GET /students?status=ACTIVE
```

means:

> Find students matching a condition.

---

# 15. Request DTOs

Every non-trivial request should have a clearly defined DTO.

Example:

```java
public record CreateCourseRequest(
        @NotBlank String title,
        @NotNull UUID subjectId,
        String description
) {}
```

Do not accept arbitrary `Map<String, Object>` payloads when a typed contract is possible.

---

# 16. Response DTOs

Responses should have explicit contracts.

```java
public record CourseResponse(
        UUID id,
        String title,
        String description,
        CourseStatus status
) {}
```

Avoid returning JPA entities directly.

---

# 17. DTO Naming

Follow:

```text
CreateStudentRequest
UpdateStudentRequest
StudentResponse

CreateCourseRequest
CourseResponse

SubmitQuizRequest
QuizResultResponse
```

Avoid:

```text
StudentDTO
CourseDTO
ResponseDTO
DataDTO
```

when a more precise name is possible.

---

# 18. HTTP Status Standards

Mediverse APIs should use status codes consistently.

| Status | Meaning                                    |
| -----: | ------------------------------------------ |
|  `200` | Successful request                         |
|  `201` | Resource created                           |
|  `202` | Accepted for asynchronous processing       |
|  `204` | Successful operation with no body          |
|  `400` | Malformed/invalid request                  |
|  `401` | Authentication required/failed             |
|  `403` | Authenticated but not authorized           |
|  `404` | Resource not found                         |
|  `409` | Conflict                                   |
|  `422` | Semantically invalid request where adopted |
|  `429` | Rate limit exceeded                        |
|  `500` | Unexpected server error                    |
|  `503` | Service temporarily unavailable            |

Do not return `200` for every situation.

---

# 19. Create Response

When a resource is successfully created:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
```

Example:

```json
{
  "id": "123",
  "title": "Human Anatomy"
}
```

Where appropriate, the response may include a `Location` header.

---

# 20. Error Response Standard

All APIs should use a consistent error model.

Recommended:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-08T12:00:00Z",
  "status": 404,
  "code": "STUDENT_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "Student was not found",
  "path": "/api/v1/students/123",
  "traceId": "abc-123"
}
```

The exact contract must remain aligned with ADS.

---

# 21. Error Codes

Error codes should be stable machine-readable identifiers.

Examples:

```text
STUDENT_NOT_FOUND
COURSE_NOT_FOUND
QUIZ_NOT_FOUND
INVALID_QUIZ_SUBMISSION
COURSE_ALREADY_ENROLLED
INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSION
```

Do not force clients to parse human-readable messages.

---

# 22. Error Messages

Messages should be:

* Clear
* Safe
* Actionable where appropriate

Avoid leaking:

```text
SQL queries
stack traces
internal class names
database details
security configuration
```

---

# 23. Validation Errors

Validation failures should identify the affected fields.

Example:

```json
{
  "status": 400,
  "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "message": "Request validation failed",
  "fieldErrors": [
    {
      "field": "email",
      "message": "must be a valid email address"
    },
    {
      "field": "firstName",
      "message": "must not be blank"
    }
  ]
}
```

---

# 24. Pagination

Collection endpoints should support pagination when datasets can grow significantly.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/students?page=0&pageSize=20
```

Recommended response:

```json
{
  "content": [],
  "page": 0,
  "pageSize": 20,
  "totalElements": 1250,
  "totalPages": 63
}
```

The exact pagination contract is defined by ADS.

---

# 25. Pagination Limits

Never allow unlimited client-controlled page sizes.

Bad:

```http
?pageSize=999999999
```

Apply a maximum:

```text
defaultPageSize = 20
maximumPageSize = 100
```

Exact values should be configuration-driven.

---

# 26. Sorting

Sorting should use explicit parameters.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?sortBy=createdAt&sortDirection=desc
```

Only approved sortable fields should be accepted.

Never blindly interpolate arbitrary client input into database queries.

---

# 27. Filtering

Filters should be predictable.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?status=PUBLISHED
```

Multiple filters:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?status=PUBLISHED&subjectId=123
```

Filtering rules should be documented in OpenAPI.

---

# 28. Search

Search APIs should distinguish search from exact filtering.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?search=anatomy
```

Avoid creating dozens of endpoint variants such as:

```text
/searchCourses
/findCourses
/searchByTitle
/findByKeyword
```

unless the use case genuinely requires different semantics.

---

# 29. Empty Collections

If a collection contains no matching resources:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?status=ARCHIVED
```

prefer:

```json
{
  "content": [],
  "page": 0,
  "pageSize": 20,
  "totalElements": 0,
  "totalPages": 0
}
```

Do not automatically return `404` for an empty collection.

---

# 30. Idempotency

Operations that may be retried must consider idempotency.

For example:

```http
POST /api/v1/payments
```

may require an idempotency key if the domain involves financial or otherwise duplicate-sensitive operations.

For Mediverse operations such as enrollment or submission, idempotency should be considered where duplicate requests could cause incorrect state.

---

# 31. Idempotency Keys

Where required:

```http
Idempotency-Key: 4f7d...
```

The server must define:

* Key format
* Retention period
* Duplicate behavior
* Response behavior

Do not add idempotency keys without defining their semantics.

---

# 32. Optimistic Concurrency

For resources that can be modified concurrently, consider:

```text
ETag
If-Match
version field
```

Example:

```http
If-Match: "v15"
```

This prevents a client from accidentally overwriting a newer update.

---

# 33. API Versioning

APIs must have an explicit versioning strategy.

A simple strategy is:

```text
/api/v1/...
/api/v2/...
```

Do not introduce `v2` merely because the implementation changed internally.

Version when the **consumer-visible contract** requires a breaking change.

---

# 34. Backward Compatibility

Avoid breaking existing clients unnecessarily.

Breaking changes include:

* Removing fields
* Renaming fields
* Changing data types
* Removing endpoints
* Changing authentication requirements
* Changing semantic meaning
* Changing required request fields

Prefer additive changes where possible.

---

# 35. Field Evolution

Safe:

```json
{
  "id": "123",
  "name": "Anatomy",
  "description": "..."
}
```

Adding:

```json
"thumbnailUrl": "..."
```

is generally less disruptive than removing or renaming existing fields.

---

# 36. API Deprecation

Deprecated APIs must have a defined lifecycle.

Example:

```text
v1
 ↓
Deprecated
 ↓
Migration period
 ↓
v2
 ↓
v1 removed
```

Consumers should receive adequate migration information.

---

# 37. Authentication

Protected APIs must enforce authentication according to SecDD.

Conceptually:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <access-token>
```

Do not implement authentication independently inside every controller.

---

# 38. Authorization

Authorization must happen according to the user's role and resource ownership.

Example:

```text
Student
 └── Access own learning progress

Faculty
 └── Manage assigned educational content

Admin
 └── Platform administration
```

Authentication alone is not sufficient.

---

# 39. Object-Level Authorization

Never assume:

```http
GET /students/{id}
```

is safe merely because the user is authenticated.

The system must determine whether the authenticated user is allowed to access that particular student resource.

---

# 40. Sensitive Data

Never expose sensitive information unnecessarily.

Especially avoid returning:

```text
password hashes
authentication secrets
internal security metadata
private tokens
unnecessary personal information
```

API DTOs should explicitly control exposed fields.

---

# 41. Rate Limiting

Rate limiting should be applied to APIs where abuse or excessive load is possible.

Potential targets:

```text
Login
Registration
Password reset
Search
File upload
Quiz submission
Public APIs
```

Excessive requests should return:

```http
429 Too Many Requests
```

---

# 42. Caching

Read-heavy resources may use HTTP caching where appropriate.

Potential headers:

```http
Cache-Control
ETag
Last-Modified
```

Do not cache private or sensitive student information publicly.

---

# 43. HTTP Headers

Important headers may include:

```text
Authorization
Content-Type
Accept
Correlation/Trace ID
ETag
Cache-Control
Location
```

Only headers relevant to the API should be introduced.

---

# 44. Content-Type

JSON APIs should use:

```http
Content-Type: application/json
```

Clients should explicitly communicate accepted representations where necessary:

```http
Accept: application/json
```

---

# 45. Correlation and Trace IDs

Requests should be traceable across distributed Mediverse services.

Example:

```http
X-Trace-Id: 7d9c...
```

The exact header name must be standardized platform-wide.

Conceptually:

```text
Frontend
   ↓
API Gateway
   ↓
Student Service
   ↓
Course Service
   ↓
Notification Service
```

The trace context should follow the request.

---

# 46. File Upload APIs

Example:

```http
POST /api/v1/learning-resources
Content-Type: multipart/form-data
```

File APIs must enforce:

* File-size limits
* Allowed formats
* Content validation
* Authorization
* Storage policy
* Safe file handling

Never trust a user-supplied filename.

---

# 47. Download APIs

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/learning-resources/{resourceId}/download
```

Authorization must be evaluated before returning protected educational resources.

Do not expose internal object-storage URLs unnecessarily.

---

# 48. Long-Running Operations

If an operation cannot complete within a normal request lifecycle, consider asynchronous processing.

Example:

```http
POST /api/v1/content-processing
```

Response:

```http
202 Accepted
```

with a job/resource identifier.

Then:

```http
GET /api/v1/content-processing/{jobId}
```

---

# 49. API Gateway

If Mediverse uses an API gateway:

```text
Client
   ↓
API Gateway
   ↓
Microservices
```

The gateway may handle:

* Routing
* Authentication integration
* Rate limiting
* TLS termination
* Observability
* Request correlation

Business logic should remain in the appropriate service.

---

# 50. OpenAPI

Every externally consumed REST API should have OpenAPI documentation.

Documentation should include:

* Endpoint
* HTTP method
* Parameters
* Request body
* Response
* Status codes
* Authentication
* Error responses
* Examples

---

# 51. OpenAPI-Code Consistency

The following must not contradict each other:

```text
ADS
 ↓
OpenAPI
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
DTO
 ↓
Tests
```

If the API contract changes, all affected artifacts must be reviewed.

---

# 52. API Contract Testing

Important APIs should have contract tests.

Tests should verify:

```text
Request
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
Response structure
 ↓
Status code
 ↓
Error behavior
```

---

# 53. API Testing Example

For:

```http
POST /api/v1/quizzes/{quizId}/submissions
```

tests should include:

```text
Valid submission
Invalid answer
Missing answer
Unauthorized user
Wrong student
Already submitted
Quiz expired
Quiz not found
```

This is much more valuable than testing only the happy path.

---

# 54. API Logging

Logs should provide enough information to diagnose API failures.

Example:

```text
traceId
endpoint
HTTP method
status
duration
user/context identifier where safe
```

Do not log:

```text
Authorization header
password
JWT
sensitive request payload
```

---

# 55. API Performance

Avoid APIs that trigger unnecessary database queries.

For example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses
```

should not execute hundreds of queries because each course loads multiple relationships individually.

Pagination and projection should be considered for large collections.

---

# 56. API Timeout

Every API should have a defined timeout strategy.

An API request should not remain open indefinitely because:

```text
Database slow
External service unavailable
Message broker unavailable
```

Timeouts should propagate appropriately.

---

# 57. API Retry

Clients and infrastructure may retry requests.

Therefore APIs must explicitly consider:

```text
Retry safety
Idempotency
Duplicate processing
Timeout behavior
```

This is particularly important for quiz submissions, enrollment, notifications, and other state-changing operations.

---

# 58. API Security Review

Before releasing an endpoint, verify:

```text
□ Authentication
□ Authorization
□ Object-level authorization
□ Input validation
□ Rate limiting where required
□ Sensitive data exposure
□ Injection risks
□ File handling
□ Error leakage
□ Audit requirements
```

---

# 59. API Review Checklist

Every significant API should pass:

```text
□ Correct resource naming
□ Correct HTTP method
□ Correct status codes
□ Request DTO defined
□ Response DTO defined
□ Validation defined
□ Error contract defined
□ Pagination considered
□ Filtering/sorting defined
□ Authorization defined
□ Idempotency considered
□ Performance considered
□ OpenAPI updated
□ Tests added
□ Logging/traceability supported
□ Backward compatibility evaluated
```

---

# 60. Mediverse API Example

A complete course API could look like:

```text
GET    /api/v1/courses
GET    /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
POST   /api/v1/courses
PUT    /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
PATCH  /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
DELETE /api/v1/courses/{courseId}

GET    /api/v1/courses/{courseId}/subjects
POST   /api/v1/courses/{courseId}/enrollments
```

Notice that the API describes **resources and relationships**, rather than implementation methods.

---

# 61. Bad vs Good API Design

### Bad

```http
POST /api/getStudent
POST /api/createCourse
POST /api/deleteQuiz
POST /api/searchStudents
```

### Better

```http
GET    /api/v1/students/{studentId}
POST   /api/v1/courses
DELETE /api/v1/quizzes/{quizId}
GET    /api/v1/students?search=Amit
```

The second design is more predictable and easier for clients to consume.

---

# 62. API Anti-Patterns

The following are prohibited unless explicitly justified:

* `POST` for every operation
* Verbs in resource URLs
* Returning `200` for errors
* Returning database entities
* Inconsistent error structures
* Unlimited pagination
* Unvalidated sort fields
* Exposing internal IDs unnecessarily
* Leaking stack traces
* Logging tokens
* Ignoring authorization
* Breaking clients without versioning
* Undocumented endpoints
* APIs without meaningful tests

---

# 63. Golden Rule

The Mediverse REST API should follow:

```text
                    API Contract
                         │
                         ▼
                    OpenAPI/ADS
                         │
                         ▼
                      DTOs
                         │
                         ▼
                    Controller
                         │
                         ▼
                     Service
                         │
                         ▼
                 Domain / Persistence
```

Every layer should reinforce the same contract rather than invent its own interpretation.

---

# 64. Chapter Summary

Chapter 14 establishes the implementation rules for Mediverse REST APIs, covering:

* Resource-oriented design
* URI conventions
* HTTP methods
* Request/response DTOs
* Status codes
* Error contracts
* Validation
* Pagination
* Filtering
* Sorting
* Search
* Idempotency
* Concurrency
* Versioning
* Backward compatibility
* Authentication
* Authorization
* Rate limiting
* Caching
* File APIs
* OpenAPI
* Contract testing
* Observability
* API security
* Performance

The core principle is:

> **An API is a long-lived contract with consumers, not merely a thin wrapper around a Java method.**

---

# CSDG — Chapter 15: JPA & Hibernate Coding Standards

**Document ID:** `MED-CSDG-015`
**Chapter:** 15
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Approved Baseline

This chapter defines how Mediverse services should implement the **persistence layer using Spring Data JPA and Hibernate with PostgreSQL**.

The goal is not merely to make entities map to tables. The persistence layer must remain **correct, performant, transactional, and resistant to common Hibernate failures**.

---

# 1. Persistence Architecture

The standard flow is:

```text
Controller
    ↓
Service
    ↓
Repository
    ↓
JPA / Hibernate
    ↓
PostgreSQL
```

The persistence layer must not become the location for application business workflows.

---

# 2. Entity Responsibility

A JPA entity represents persistent state.

Example:

```java
@Entity
@Table(name = "students")
public class Student {

    @Id
    private UUID id;

    private String firstName;
    private String lastName;
}
```

An entity should not automatically become:

* REST request
* REST response
* database query object
* UI model
* external integration contract

---

# 3. Entity Naming

Use singular Java class names:

```text
Student
Course
Subject
Chapter
Quiz
Question
QuizAttempt
LearningResource
```

Tables should normally use plural snake_case:

```text
students
courses
subjects
chapters
quizzes
quiz_attempts
learning_resources
```

---

# 4. Explicit Table Names

Prefer explicit table names.

```java
@Entity
@Table(name = "students")
public class Student {
}
```

Do not rely entirely on Hibernate naming conventions when a stable schema contract matters.

---

# 5. Primary Keys

The ID strategy must be consistent across the application.

For UUID-based identifiers:

```java
@Id
@GeneratedValue
private UUID id;
```

The exact generation strategy must align with the PostgreSQL schema and database migration strategy.

Do not mix incompatible identifier strategies arbitrarily across entities.

---

# 6. ID Exposure

Database identifiers should not automatically be treated as business identifiers.

For example:

```text
Database ID
    ≠
Student Roll Number
    ≠
University Registration Number
```

These concepts should remain distinct where the domain requires them.

---

# 7. Entity Constructors

JPA requires a no-argument constructor.

Prefer restricted visibility:

```java
@NoArgsConstructor(access = AccessLevel.PROTECTED)
```

Avoid exposing an unrestricted public constructor merely to satisfy JPA.

---

# 8. Entity Mutability

Avoid unrestricted setters.

Bad:

```java
student.setStatus(...);
student.setRole(...);
student.setEnrollmentDate(...);
student.setVerified(...);
```

when these state changes have business meaning.

Prefer:

```java
student.verify();
student.activate();
student.completeEnrollment();
```

This keeps state transitions explicit.

---

# 9. Entity Invariants

Entities should protect important invariants.

Example:

```java
public void publish() {

    if (questions.isEmpty()) {
        throw new QuizPublicationException(
                "Quiz must contain at least one question");
    }

    this.status = QuizStatus.PUBLISHED;
}
```

This is safer than allowing any caller to manipulate the status directly.

---

# 10. Enum Fields

Use enums for controlled domain states.

Example:

```java
@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
private QuizStatus status;
```

Prefer:

```text
DRAFT
PUBLISHED
ARCHIVED
```

over numeric ordinal values.

---

# 11. Never Use Enum Ordinals

Avoid:

```java
@Enumerated(EnumType.ORDINAL)
```

Why?

If:

```text
DRAFT     = 0
PUBLISHED = 1
ARCHIVED  = 2
```

and the enum order changes, existing database values can acquire different meanings.

Use:

```java
@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
```

instead.

---

# 12. Column Names

Use explicit names for important schema fields.

```java
@Column(name = "first_name", nullable = false)
private String firstName;
```

This keeps Java naming and database naming separate.

---

# 13. Nullability

Database constraints should reinforce application rules.

Example:

```java
@Column(nullable = false)
private String title;
```

Do not rely only on Java validation for critical database invariants.

The database should protect its own integrity.

---

# 14. Length Constraints

Define meaningful column sizes.

```java
@Column(
    name = "title",
    nullable = false,
    length = 200
)
private String title;
```

Do not blindly use extremely large columns for every string.

---

# 15. Validation vs Database Constraints

These solve different problems.

```text
API validation
    ↓
User-friendly input validation

Database constraint
    ↓
Data integrity
```

Both may be required.

---

# 16. Unique Constraints

If a value must be unique, enforce uniqueness at the database level.

Example:

```java
@Table(
    name = "students",
    uniqueConstraints = {
        @UniqueConstraint(
            name = "uk_student_email",
            columnNames = "email"
        )
    }
)
```

Do not rely exclusively on:

```java
if (repository.existsByEmail(email)) {
    ...
}
```

because concurrent requests can still create duplicates.

---

# 17. Indexes

Indexes should be created based on actual access patterns.

Potential Mediverse indexes:

```text
students.email
courses.status
quiz_attempts.student_id
quiz_attempts.quiz_id
learning_progress.student_id
learning_progress.course_id
```

Do not create indexes on every column.

Indexes have storage and write-performance costs.

---

# 18. Relationship Design

JPA relationships must reflect actual domain relationships.

Common relationships:

```text
Student → Enrollments
Course  → Subjects
Subject → Chapters
Chapter → Topics
Quiz    → Questions
Student → QuizAttempts
```

Relationships should be designed around ownership and lifecycle.

---

# 19. `@ManyToOne`

Example:

```java
@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(
    name = "course_id",
    nullable = false
)
private Course course;
```

Prefer lazy loading unless there is a specific reason to load the related entity immediately.

---

# 20. `@OneToMany`

Example:

```java
@OneToMany(
    mappedBy = "course",
    fetch = FetchType.LAZY
)
private List<Subject> subjects;
```

Collections should normally be lazy.

Do not make every collection eager.

---

# 21. `@OneToOne`

Use one-to-one relationships only when the domain genuinely requires a one-to-one relationship.

Do not use `@OneToOne` simply because two tables happen to be related.

---

# 22. `@ManyToMany`

Many-to-many relationships should be treated carefully.

Example:

```text
Student ↔ Course
```

Instead of immediately creating:

```java
@ManyToMany
private Set<Course> courses;
```

consider whether enrollment itself has attributes:

```text
Enrollment
 ├── student
 ├── course
 ├── enrolledAt
 ├── status
 └── completionPercentage
```

For Mediverse, an explicit association entity is often the better domain model.

---

# 23. Aggregate Boundaries

Do not create enormous entity graphs.

For example:

```text
Course
 └── Subject
      └── Chapter
           └── Topic
                └── LearningResource
                     └── ...
```

Loading an entire educational hierarchy simply because one object references another can cause severe performance problems.

---

# 24. Lazy Loading

Prefer:

```java
fetch = FetchType.LAZY
```

for relationships unless eager loading is explicitly justified.

Lazy loading allows the application to retrieve only the data required by the use case.

---

# 25. The N+1 Problem

A classic Hibernate problem:

```text
1 query → courses

then:

1 query → subjects for course 1
1 query → subjects for course 2
1 query → subjects for course 3
...
```

A request for 50 courses could therefore result in dozens of database queries.

Developers must actively watch for this.

---

# 26. Detecting N+1

Use:

* SQL logging during development
* Hibernate statistics where appropriate
* Integration tests
* Application monitoring
* Query analysis

Never assume a JPA relationship is efficient merely because the code looks clean.

---

# 27. Fetch Join

When a specific use case requires related data:

```java
@Query("""
    select c
    from Course c
    join fetch c.subjects
    where c.id = :courseId
""")
Optional<Course> findCourseWithSubjects(UUID courseId);
```

Use fetch joins deliberately.

Do not turn every repository method into a giant fetch graph.

---

# 28. Entity Graph

Entity graphs can define controlled fetching.

```java
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"subjects"})
Optional<Course> findById(UUID id);
```

This can be preferable when you want to keep the base relationship lazy but fetch it for a particular use case.

---

# 29. DTO Projection

If only a few fields are required, do not necessarily load an entire entity graph.

Example:

```java
public record CourseSummary(
    UUID id,
    String title,
    CourseStatus status
) {}
```

A projection can retrieve only the required columns.

This is particularly useful for large list APIs.

---

# 30. Repository Queries

Simple queries may use derived methods:

```java
Optional<Student> findByEmail(String email);
```

More complex queries may use:

* JPQL
* Specifications
* QueryDSL if adopted
* Native SQL when justified

Choose based on complexity and maintainability.

---

# 31. JPQL

JPQL should use entity/property names rather than database table/column names.

Example:

```java
@Query("""
    select s
    from Student s
    where s.email = :email
""")
Optional<Student> findStudentByEmail(String email);
```

---

# 32. Native SQL

Native SQL may be used when it provides clear value.

Examples:

* PostgreSQL-specific functionality
* Complex performance-critical queries
* Database features unavailable through JPQL

But native queries create stronger coupling to PostgreSQL.

Document the reason when introducing them.

---

# 33. SQL Injection

Never construct SQL by concatenating user input.

Bad:

```java
String sql =
    "SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = '" + name + "'";
```

Use parameter binding.

---

# 34. Dynamic Filtering

For complex search/filter requirements, use a controlled query mechanism.

Avoid constructing arbitrary SQL fragments from request parameters.

For example:

```text
sortBy=whatever SQL expression
```

must never be passed directly into SQL.

Maintain an allowlist of supported fields.

---

# 35. Transactions

Transactions should normally be managed at the service/application boundary.

Example:

```java
@Transactional
public QuizResult submitQuiz(...) {
    ...
}
```

The transaction should represent a coherent business operation.

---

# 36. Transaction Scope

Avoid unnecessarily large transactions.

Bad:

```text
@Transactional
entire application workflow
    ├── database
    ├── external HTTP call
    ├── file upload
    ├── email
    └── database
```

Holding a database transaction while waiting on an external service can cause connection exhaustion and lock contention.

---

# 37. External Calls Inside Transactions

Avoid this pattern unless there is a carefully designed reason:

```java
@Transactional
public void enrollStudent(...) {

    saveEnrollment();

    externalPaymentService.call();

    saveMoreData();
}
```

External calls can be slow or unavailable.

Prefer architectural patterns such as events/outbox where appropriate.

---

# 38. Read-Only Transactions

For read operations:

```java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
```

should be considered.

Example:

```java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public CourseResponse getCourse(UUID id) {
    ...
}
```

---

# 39. Persistence Context

Hibernate maintains a persistence context containing managed entities.

Conceptually:

```text
Database
   ↓
Hibernate
   ↓
Persistence Context
   ↓
Managed Entity
```

Developers must understand whether an entity is:

```text
Transient
Managed
Detached
Removed
```

before manipulating it.

---

# 40. Dirty Checking

Hibernate can detect changes to managed entities.

Example:

```java
@Transactional
public void activateStudent(UUID id) {

    Student student = repository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow();

    student.activate();
}
```

An explicit:

```java
repository.save(student);
```

may not be required for an already-managed entity because Hibernate can flush the change at transaction completion.

Do not add `save()` everywhere blindly.

---

# 41. `save()` Usage

Use repository `save()` when appropriate, particularly for newly created or detached entities according to the persistence design.

Understand what `save()` actually does rather than treating it as a mandatory operation after every mutation.

---

# 42. Flush

Avoid unnecessary explicit:

```java
repository.flush();
```

A flush forces synchronization between the persistence context and database.

Use it only when the business/transaction logic requires it.

---

# 43. Bulk Updates

Bulk JPQL/SQL operations can bypass parts of normal entity lifecycle behavior and persistence-context synchronization.

Example:

```java
@Modifying
@Query("""
    update Student s
    set s.active = false
    where s.lastLoginAt < :cutoff
""")
int deactivateInactiveStudents(...);
```

After bulk operations, understand the state of already-loaded entities.

---

# 44. Optimistic Locking

For concurrently modified entities, use optimistic locking where appropriate.

Example:

```java
@Version
private Long version;
```

Conceptually:

```text
User A reads version 5
User B reads version 5

User A updates → version 6

User B attempts update based on version 5
        ↓
Conflict detected
```

This prevents silent overwrites.

---

# 45. Pessimistic Locking

Pessimistic locking should be used only when the domain genuinely requires it.

It can introduce:

* Lock contention
* Deadlocks
* Reduced concurrency

Do not use it as the default solution for concurrent updates.

---

# 46. Auditing

Entities that require audit metadata may use:

```text
createdAt
updatedAt
createdBy
updatedBy
```

Spring Data auditing may be used where appropriate.

---

# 47. Audit vs Business History

Do not confuse:

```text
updatedAt
```

with a complete historical record.

If Mediverse needs to know:

```text
Who changed quiz content?
What was the previous value?
When was it changed?
```

a dedicated audit/history mechanism may be required.

---

# 48. Soft Delete

Soft deletion should be an explicit architectural decision.

Example:

```text
deletedAt
deletedBy
```

Do not implement soft deletion simply because physical deletion feels uncomfortable.

Soft deletion creates additional complexity:

```text
Every query
    ↓
Must correctly handle deleted records
```

---

# 49. Entity Serialization

Avoid returning entities directly from controllers.

A major risk is accidental traversal:

```text
Course
 ↓
Subjects
 ↓
Course
 ↓
Subjects
 ↓
...
```

This can produce:

* Infinite recursion
* Huge JSON payloads
* Lazy-loading surprises
* Internal field exposure

DTOs are the preferred boundary.

---

# 50. `equals()` and `hashCode()`

Entity equality must be designed carefully.

Do not blindly generate equality using every mutable field.

This is especially dangerous for entities stored in:

```java
Set<Entity>
```

The equality strategy must remain stable throughout the entity lifecycle.

---

# 51. Lombok and Entities

Be cautious with:

```java
@Data
```

on JPA entities.

`@Data` generates:

* Getters
* Setters
* `equals`
* `hashCode`
* `toString`

These generated methods can interact badly with lazy relationships and entity identity.

Prefer selective annotations.

---

# 52. `toString()` on Entities

Avoid including large relationships in `toString()`.

Bad:

```java
@Override
public String toString() {
    return "Course{" +
           "subjects=" + subjects +
           '}';
}
```

This can trigger lazy loading or enormous logs.

---

# 53. Serialization of Lazy Relationships

Do not rely on Jackson to automatically serialize Hibernate relationships.

Use explicit DTO mapping.

This avoids unexpected database queries during JSON serialization.

---

# 54. Database Migrations

Entity changes and database migrations must remain synchronized.

Example:

```text
Entity Change
      +
Migration Script
      +
Integration Test
```

Do not modify production schemas manually.

---

# 55. Schema Management

Production environments should not depend on:

```properties
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create
```

or similar destructive schema-generation behavior.

Production database schema evolution must be controlled through migration tooling.

---

# 56. `ddl-auto`

Development may use controlled settings such as:

```text
validate
```

or other environment-appropriate modes.

Production should generally validate rather than automatically mutate the schema.

The final setting is environment-specific and governed by DIG.

---

# 57. Database Migration Example

```text
db/migration/
├── V1__create_students.sql
├── V2__create_courses.sql
├── V3__create_subjects.sql
├── V4__create_quizzes.sql
└── V5__create_quiz_attempts.sql
```

Migration scripts must be immutable once applied to shared environments.

---

# 58. Pagination

Never retrieve huge tables into memory.

Bad:

```java
studentRepository.findAll()
```

when the table contains millions of records and the API only needs 20.

Prefer:

```java
Page<Student> findAll(Pageable pageable);
```

---

# 59. Cursor Pagination

For very large datasets or high-throughput APIs, cursor/keyset pagination may be more appropriate than offset pagination.

Example conceptual approach:

```text
GET /resources?limit=50&after=<cursor>
```

Use it where performance requirements justify the additional complexity.

---

# 60. Batch Operations

Large operations should avoid processing thousands of entities one at a time when a batch strategy is available.

However, batch processing must account for:

* Transaction size
* Memory usage
* Lock duration
* Failure recovery
* Database limits

---

# 61. Connection Pooling

The application must use an appropriately configured database connection pool.

Do not assume:

```text
more connections = more performance
```

An oversized pool can overwhelm PostgreSQL rather than improve throughput.

---

# 62. Query Performance

For slow queries:

```text
Application
    ↓
Identify query
    ↓
EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE
    ↓
Inspect execution plan
    ↓
Optimize query/index
    ↓
Measure again
```

Never add random indexes based purely on intuition.

---

# 63. PostgreSQL-Specific Considerations

Because Mediverse uses PostgreSQL, developers should understand:

* UUIDs
* JSON/JSONB
* Indexes
* Foreign keys
* Constraints
* Transactions
* Isolation levels
* Query planning
* Full-text search where applicable
* Connection pooling

PostgreSQL-specific features should be introduced deliberately because they increase database coupling.

---

# 64. Transaction Isolation

Use the default transaction isolation level unless the domain requires something different.

Changing isolation can have significant performance and concurrency consequences.

Do not change it as a generic "fix" for concurrency issues.

---

# 65. Deadlocks

Deadlocks can occur when concurrent transactions acquire locks in incompatible orders.

Prevent them through:

* Consistent update ordering
* Short transactions
* Appropriate indexing
* Avoiding unnecessary locks
* Proper retry strategies where safe

---

# 66. Repository Review Checklist

For every significant repository query:

```text
□ Is the query necessary?
□ Is it parameterized?
□ Could derived query work?
□ Could projection reduce data?
□ Is pagination required?
□ Could this create N+1?
□ Is an index required?
□ Is the query PostgreSQL-specific?
□ Is transaction behavior correct?
□ Has performance been measured?
```

---

# 67. Common Hibernate Anti-Patterns

Avoid:

```text
❌ EAGER everywhere
❌ CascadeType.ALL everywhere
❌ Entity returned from REST controller
❌ @Data blindly applied to entities
❌ Huge entity graphs
❌ N+1 queries
❌ LazyInitializationException ignored
❌ save() blindly everywhere
❌ Huge transactions
❌ External calls inside DB transactions
❌ Arbitrary native SQL
❌ Unbounded findAll()
❌ Missing indexes
❌ Manual production schema changes
❌ No concurrency strategy
```

---

# 68. Mediverse Persistence Example

A good quiz-submission flow:

```text
POST /api/v1/quizzes/{quizId}/submissions
                │
                ▼
          Controller
                │
                ▼
        SubmitQuizService
                │
         @Transactional
                │
        ┌───────┴────────┐
        ▼                ▼
 QuizRepository    StudentRepository
        │                │
        └───────┬────────┘
                ▼
         Evaluate Answers
                │
                ▼
          Save Attempt
                │
                ▼
        Update Progress
                │
                ▼
          Commit Tx
```

Notification should not necessarily be performed synchronously inside the database transaction.

An event/outbox architecture may be more appropriate:

```text
Transaction
    ↓
QuizAttempt + OutboxEvent
    ↓
Commit
    ↓
Event Publisher
    ↓
Notification Service
```

The exact implementation belongs to the architecture/ADR decisions.

---

# 69. Persistence Golden Rules

For Mediverse:

```text
1. Keep entities persistence-focused.
2. Never expose entities directly as API contracts.
3. Prefer LAZY relationships.
4. Detect and prevent N+1 queries.
5. Keep transactions at meaningful service boundaries.
6. Keep transactions short.
7. Never hold DB transactions across slow external calls without justification.
8. Use database constraints for data integrity.
9. Use migrations for schema changes.
10. Measure query performance instead of guessing.
11. Design concurrency explicitly.
12. Treat Hibernate behavior as something to understand, not magic.
```

---
