Investigate the entire traffic path.

---

# 40.96 Traffic Debugging

Recommended flow:

```text
Client
 ↓
DNS
 ↓
Load Balancer
 ↓
Ingress
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Endpoints
 ↓
Pod
 ↓
Application
 ↓
Database / Dependency
```

Check each boundary.

---

# 40.97 Service Endpoints

A Service with no healthy endpoints cannot route traffic.

Always inspect:

```text
Service
 ↓
EndpointSlices
 ↓
Ready Pods
```

when debugging connectivity.

---

# 40.98 Logs

Use:

```bash
kubectl logs
```

but remember logs alone are insufficient.

Combine:

```text
Logs
+
Events
+
Metrics
+
Traces
+
Pod state
```

for production troubleshooting.

---

# 40.99 Kubernetes Events

Events often reveal infrastructure problems such as:

```text
Scheduling failure
Image pull failure
Probe failure
Mount failure
Resource pressure
```

Always inspect events when a Pod does not behave as expected.

---

# 40.100 Observability

Every production workload SHOULD integrate with the Mediverse observability stack.

At minimum:

```text
Metrics
Logs
Health
```

Where appropriate:

```text
Distributed Tracing
```

---

# 40.101 Prometheus Metrics

Applications SHOULD expose useful metrics.

For Spring Boot:

```text
/actuator/prometheus
```

may be used when Micrometer/Prometheus integration is configured.

---

# 40.102 Golden Signals

Production Kubernetes services SHOULD be monitored using:

```text
Latency
Traffic
Errors
Saturation
```

These provide a practical starting point for service health.

---

# 40.103 Pod Disruption Budget

Critical production workloads SHOULD consider:

```text
PodDisruptionBudget
```

to prevent voluntary cluster operations from removing too many replicas simultaneously.

---

# 40.104 Availability Zones

Production clusters SHOULD distribute critical workloads across appropriate failure domains where the infrastructure supports it.

Three replicas on one physical failure domain are not equivalent to three replicas across independent failure domains.

---

# 40.105 Node Failure

Applications should tolerate the loss of an individual Kubernetes node where availability requirements demand it.

This requires:

```text
Multiple replicas
+
Scheduling constraints
+
Persistent storage strategy
+
External dependency resilience
```

---

# 40.106 Cluster Autoscaling

Cluster autoscaling MAY be used where workload demand is variable.

But HPA and cluster autoscaling solve different problems:

```text
HPA
→ More Pods

Cluster Autoscaler
→ More Nodes
```

Both may be required.

---

# 40.107 Pod Scheduling

Production workloads SHOULD avoid scheduling everything onto a single node.

Use appropriate:

```text
Affinity
Anti-affinity
Topology spread
Taints
Tolerations
```

only where justified.

---

# 40.108 Taints and Tolerations

Do not add tolerations simply to make scheduling succeed.

A toleration means:

> This workload is allowed to run on this specially tainted node.

It does not automatically mean:

> This workload should run there.

---

# 40.109 Node Selectors

Node selectors SHOULD be used only when workload placement genuinely requires specific node characteristics.

Avoid hard-coding infrastructure assumptions unnecessarily.

---

# 40.110 Security Updates

Kubernetes workloads MUST have a strategy for:

```text
Base image updates
Application dependency updates
Kubernetes version updates
Helm dependency updates
Security patches
```

---

# 40.111 Kubernetes Version

Production clusters SHOULD run a supported Kubernetes version.

Cluster upgrades must be planned around:

```text
API compatibility
CRDs
Ingress controller
CSI drivers
Helm
Argo CD
Application compatibility
```

---

# 40.112 Deprecated APIs

Do not introduce deprecated Kubernetes APIs.

Before upgrading a cluster, identify:

```text
Deprecated APIs
Removed APIs
CRD compatibility
Helm templates
Admission policies
```

---

# 40.113 CRDs

Custom Resource Definitions SHOULD be:

* Version-controlled
* Reviewed
* Versioned
* Tested before cluster upgrades

---

# 40.114 Operators

Operators SHOULD be introduced only when their operational value justifies the additional complexity.

Every operator introduces:

```text
Another controller
Another upgrade path
Another failure mode
Another security surface
```

---

# 40.115 Namespace Resource Quotas

Production namespaces SHOULD consider ResourceQuota to prevent one workload from consuming uncontrolled cluster resources.

---

# 40.116 LimitRange

LimitRange MAY establish default or minimum resource requirements.

This can prevent workloads from being deployed without resource configuration.

---

# 40.117 Production Access

Human access to production Kubernetes clusters MUST follow least privilege.

Avoid giving developers permanent:

```text
cluster-admin
```

access.

---

# 40.118 Break-Glass Access

Emergency elevated access SHOULD exist only through an approved break-glass process.

It should be:

```text
Audited
Time-limited
Justified
Revoked after use
```

---

# 40.119 Auditability

Production Kubernetes changes SHOULD be attributable to:

```text
Person / Automation
Time
Change
Reason
Git commit
Deployment
```

---

# 40.120 Manual Changes

If an emergency manual change is required:

```text
Manual Change
     ↓
Incident / Change Record
     ↓
Git Update
     ↓
Reconciliation
```

The manual state must not remain permanently outside Git.

---

# 40.121 Kubernetes Manifest Review

Reviewers SHOULD check:

```text
Image
Resources
SecurityContext
Probes
Service
Ingress
Secrets
ConfigMaps
RBAC
NetworkPolicy
Replicas
Affinity
Deployment strategy
```

---

# 40.122 Production Deployment Checklist

Before deployment:

* [ ] Image exists
* [ ] Image digest/tag is correct
* [ ] Image has passed security scanning
* [ ] Configuration is correct
* [ ] Secrets are available
* [ ] Database migration is reviewed
* [ ] Resource requests/limits are defined
* [ ] Probes are configured
* [ ] Security context is configured
* [ ] Network policies allow required traffic
* [ ] Service selectors are correct
* [ ] Ingress configuration is correct
* [ ] Rollback strategy is known
* [ ] Monitoring exists
* [ ] Alerts exist
* [ ] GitOps state is correct

---

# 40.123 Deployment Verification Checklist

After deployment:

* [ ] Argo CD reports Synced
* [ ] Application reports Healthy
* [ ] Pods are Running
* [ ] Pods are Ready
* [ ] No CrashLoopBackOff
* [ ] No ImagePullBackOff
* [ ] No OOMKilled
* [ ] Service has endpoints
* [ ] Ingress routes correctly
* [ ] Health endpoints respond
* [ ] Logs are healthy
* [ ] Error rate is normal
* [ ] Latency is normal
* [ ] Critical business flow works

---

# 40.124 Definition of Done

A Kubernetes deployment is complete when:

* [ ] Kubernetes manifests are version-controlled
* [ ] Namespace strategy is defined
* [ ] Resource labels are consistent
* [ ] Correct workload type is selected
* [ ] Replicas are appropriate
* [ ] Rolling strategy is defined
* [ ] Readiness probe exists
* [ ] Liveness probe exists where appropriate
* [ ] Startup probe exists where needed
* [ ] Resource requests are defined
* [ ] Resource limits are reviewed
* [ ] Security context is configured
* [ ] RBAC follows least privilege
* [ ] Secrets are securely managed
* [ ] Network policies are defined where required
* [ ] Service configuration is correct
* [ ] Ingress/TLS is configured where required
* [ ] Persistence strategy is defined
* [ ] HPA is configured where appropriate
* [ ] Observability is integrated
* [ ] GitOps configuration exists
* [ ] Rollback is tested or understood
* [ ] Production access is controlled
* [ ] Deployment is traceable to Git

---

# 40.125 Core Principles

Mediverse Kubernetes development follows:

1. **Kubernetes configuration is declarative.**
2. **Git is the desired-state source for production.**
3. **Argo CD manages production synchronization where GitOps is adopted.**
4. **Pods are disposable; persistent data belongs outside ephemeral containers.**
5. **Every production workload must have meaningful health behavior.**
6. **Resource requests and limits must be based on evidence.**
7. **Security must be enforced through least privilege.**
8. **Production workloads should not run as root.**
9. **Internal services should not be unnecessarily exposed externally.**
10. **Network communication should be explicitly controlled.**
11. **Deployment must be observable and reversible.**
12. **Application rollback and database rollback are separate problems.**
13. **Manual production changes should be exceptional and reconciled back into Git.**
14. **Scaling Pods without considering databases and downstream dependencies is not real scalability.**
15. **A Kubernetes deployment is successful only when the application is healthy, not merely when the Pods are `Running`.**

> **Kubernetes is not a magic availability layer. It can restart a broken application faster, distribute replicas, and automate scheduling—but it cannot compensate for bad application design, poor database architecture, incorrect probes, missing observability, or uncontrolled configuration.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 41: Helm Chart & Kubernetes Packaging Standards.**

# CSDG — Chapter 41

## Helm Chart & Kubernetes Packaging Standards

### 41.1 Purpose

This chapter defines standards for packaging Mediverse Kubernetes workloads using Helm.

The objective is to make Kubernetes deployments:

* Reusable
* Versioned
* Environment-aware
* Consistent
* GitOps-compatible
* Secure
* Maintainable
* Easy to validate
* Easy to promote across environments

Core principle:

> **Helm packages Kubernetes deployment configuration; it must not become a substitute for application architecture or infrastructure design.**

---

# 41.2 Scope

This chapter covers:

* Helm charts
* Chart structure
* `Chart.yaml`
* `values.yaml`
* Environment values
* Templates
* Helpers
* Deployments
* Services
* Ingress
* ConfigMaps
* Secrets
* ServiceAccounts
* RBAC
* HPA
* PDB
* NetworkPolicies
* PersistentVolumeClaims
* Jobs
* CronJobs
* Helm dependencies
* Chart versioning
* Helm linting
* Helm testing
* GitOps
* Argo CD
* Release management

---

# 41.3 Standard Mediverse Packaging Model

The preferred architecture is:

```text
Application Source
        │
        ▼
Container Image
        │
        ▼
Container Registry
        │
        ▼
Helm Chart
        │
        ├── values-dev.yaml
        ├── values-uat.yaml
        └── values-prod.yaml
        │
        ▼
GitOps Repository
        │
        ▼
Argo CD
        │
        ▼
Kubernetes
```

---

# 41.4 Helm's Responsibility

Helm SHOULD be responsible for:

```text
Kubernetes resource packaging
Environment configuration
Release versioning
Reusable templates
Deployment configuration
```

Helm SHOULD NOT be responsible for:

```text
Business logic
Database business rules
Application runtime logic
Secret generation logic
Infrastructure provisioning
Complex CI/CD orchestration
```

---

# 41.5 Recommended Repository Structure

A Mediverse service may use:

```text
helm/
└── mediverse-api/
    ├── Chart.yaml
    ├── values.yaml
    ├── values-dev.yaml
    ├── values-uat.yaml
    ├── values-prod.yaml
    ├── templates/
    │   ├── deployment.yaml
    │   ├── service.yaml
    │   ├── ingress.yaml
    │   ├── configmap.yaml
    │   ├── serviceaccount.yaml
    │   ├── hpa.yaml
    │   ├── pdb.yaml
    │   ├── networkpolicy.yaml
    │   ├── secret.yaml
    │   └── _helpers.tpl
    └── tests/
        └── test-connection.yaml
```

The exact structure may differ depending on the service.

---

# 41.6 Chart.yaml

Every Helm chart MUST contain:

```text
Chart.yaml
```

Example:

```yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: mediverse-api
description: Helm chart for Mediverse API
type: application
version: 1.0.0
appVersion: "1.0.0"
```

---

# 41.7 Chart Version

`version` represents the Helm chart version.

Example:

```yaml
version: 1.2.0
```

It should change whenever the chart itself changes in a release-significant way.

---

# 41.8 Application Version

`appVersion` identifies the application version represented by the chart.

Example:

```yaml
appVersion: "2.4.1"
```

Chart version and application version SHOULD NOT be treated as interchangeable.

Example:

```text
Chart:
1.3.0

Application:
2.4.1
```

is perfectly valid.

---

# 41.9 Semantic Versioning

Helm chart versions SHOULD follow Semantic Versioning:

```text
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
```

Example:

```text
1.4.2
```

General interpretation:

```text
MAJOR
Breaking chart behavior

MINOR
Backward-compatible functionality

PATCH
Backward-compatible fixes
```

---

# 41.10 Chart Name

Chart names SHOULD follow the Mediverse naming convention.

Example:

```text
mediverse-api
mediverse-auth
mediverse-user
mediverse-frontend
```

Avoid:

```text
chart1
testchart
new-api-chart-final
```

---

# 41.11 `values.yaml`

`values.yaml` contains the chart's default configuration.

Example:

```yaml
replicaCount: 2

image:
  repository: registry.example.com/mediverse/api
  tag: "1.0.0"

service:
  port: 8080
```

Defaults MUST be sensible and safe.

---

# 41.12 Environment Values

Environment-specific configuration MAY be separated:

```text
values-dev.yaml
values-uat.yaml
values-prod.yaml
```

Example:

```text
values-dev.yaml
    ↓
2 replicas

values-uat.yaml
    ↓
2 replicas

values-prod.yaml
    ↓
5 replicas
```

---

# 41.13 Values Precedence

When multiple values files are supplied, the more specific environment configuration should override the defaults.

Concept:

```text
values.yaml
      ↓
values-prod.yaml
      ↓
explicit deployment values
```

The deployment process MUST make the final configuration predictable.

---

# 41.14 Default Values

`values.yaml` SHOULD provide safe defaults.

Avoid dangerous defaults such as:

```yaml
privileged: true
runAsRoot: true
```

A developer should not accidentally create a privileged production workload simply because a value was omitted.

---

# 41.15 Production Values

Production values SHOULD be explicit for important properties:

```text
replicas
image
resources
probes
securityContext
ingress
autoscaling
```

Do not rely on obscure template defaults for critical production behavior.

---

# 41.16 Image Configuration

Image configuration SHOULD be centralized.

Example:

```yaml
image:
  repository: registry.example.com/mediverse/api
  tag: "1.4.2"
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
```

Do not repeat the image repository throughout multiple templates.

---

# 41.17 Image Tags

Production charts MUST NOT default to:

```yaml
tag: latest
```

Use immutable application versions or digests.

---

# 41.18 Image Digest

For high-integrity production deployments, support:

```text
repository@sha256:<digest>
```

where appropriate.

This provides stronger immutability than relying solely on tags.

---

# 41.19 Image Pull Policy

The image pull policy should reflect the tagging strategy.

For immutable versioned images:

```yaml
imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
```

may be appropriate.

For development workflows using mutable tags, different behavior may be required.

The production standard should favor immutable images.

---

# 41.20 Templates

Helm templates SHOULD remain readable.

Example:

```text
templates/
├── deployment.yaml
├── service.yaml
├── ingress.yaml
└── _helpers.tpl
```

Do not place the entire Kubernetes architecture into one enormous template.

---

# 41.21 Template Naming

Use meaningful filenames.

Good:

```text
deployment.yaml
service.yaml
ingress.yaml
hpa.yaml
```

Avoid:

```text
thing.yaml
resource1.yaml
misc.yaml
```

---

# 41.22 Helpers

Reusable naming and labels SHOULD be placed in:

```text
_helpers.tpl
```

Example conceptual helpers:

```text
mediverse-api.name
mediverse-api.fullname
mediverse-api.labels
mediverse-api.selectorLabels
mediverse-api.serviceAccountName
```

---

# 41.23 Labels Helper

Standard labels SHOULD be generated consistently.

Conceptually:

```yaml
app.kubernetes.io/name
app.kubernetes.io/instance
app.kubernetes.io/version
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by
```

This improves operational consistency.

---

# 41.24 Selector Labels

Selector labels MUST remain stable.

Do not include labels that change every deployment inside immutable selectors.

Bad:

```text
selector:
  version: "1.4.2"
```

Changing the version could break Service-to-Pod selection.

---

# 41.25 Deployment Template

A Deployment template should typically define:

```text
metadata
spec
replicas
selector
pod template
containers
image
ports
resources
probes
security context
environment
volumes
```

Only include what the workload actually requires.

---

# 41.26 Service Template

Service templates SHOULD define:

```text
service type
ports
targetPort
selector
```

Default internal services should generally use:

```yaml
type: ClusterIP
```

---

# 41.27 Ingress Template

Ingress should be conditionally enabled.

Example:

```yaml
ingress:
  enabled: true
```

Then the template can be rendered only when required.

---

# 41.28 Ingress Configuration

Ingress values may contain:

```text
hostname
TLS
paths
annotations
className
```

Avoid hard-coding environment-specific hostnames inside templates.

---

# 41.29 ConfigMap Template

Non-sensitive configuration SHOULD use ConfigMaps.

Example:

```yaml
config:
  LOG_LEVEL: INFO
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: production
```

Templates should convert these values into Kubernetes-compatible configuration.

---

# 41.30 Secret Template

Sensitive configuration MUST NOT be stored as plaintext in Helm values.

Bad:

```yaml
database:
  password: "SuperSecret123"
```

Even if the chart later converts it to a Kubernetes Secret, the secret has already been committed to Git.

---

# 41.31 External Secrets

Where supported, prefer:

```text
External Secret Manager
        ↓
External Secrets Operator
        ↓
Kubernetes Secret
        ↓
Pod
```

This avoids storing long-lived credentials in Helm values.

---

# 41.32 Secret References

Helm should ideally configure **references** to secrets rather than contain their secret values.

Example concept:

```yaml
existingSecret: mediverse-db-secret
```

---

# 41.33 ServiceAccount

Applications SHOULD use dedicated ServiceAccounts where Kubernetes API access is required.

Example:

```yaml
serviceAccount:
  create: true
  name: mediverse-api
```

---

# 41.34 Disable Unnecessary Token Mounting

If the application does not need Kubernetes API access:

```yaml
automountServiceAccountToken: false
```

should be considered.

---

# 41.35 RBAC

RBAC should be enabled only when required.

Do not automatically create:

```text
ClusterRole
ClusterRoleBinding
```

for every chart.

A normal REST API often does not need Kubernetes API permissions.

---

# 41.36 Namespace Ownership

Helm charts SHOULD NOT normally create production namespaces unless the platform architecture explicitly requires it.

Namespace lifecycle is often better managed by the platform/GitOps layer.

---

# 41.37 Resource Requests and Limits

Charts SHOULD expose resource configuration:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 512Mi
  limits:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 1Gi
```

This allows environment-specific tuning.

---

# 41.38 Probes as Values

Probe configuration SHOULD be configurable.

Example:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  enabled: true

readinessProbe:
  enabled: true

startupProbe:
  enabled: true
```

However, disabling probes in production should require deliberate justification.

---

# 41.39 Probe Paths

For Spring Boot services, probe endpoints may use:

```text
/actuator/health/liveness
/actuator/health/readiness
```

when configured according to the application's health architecture.

---

# 41.40 Probe Timing

Probe values should reflect actual application startup and recovery behavior.

Parameters include:

```text
initialDelaySeconds
periodSeconds
timeoutSeconds
failureThreshold
successThreshold
```

Do not copy arbitrary values from another application.

---

# 41.41 Security Context

Security context SHOULD be configurable but secure by default.

Example:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

---

# 41.42 Pod Security Context

Where appropriate:

```yaml
podSecurityContext:
  fsGroup: ...
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

The exact values depend on the application's filesystem and runtime requirements.

---

# 41.43 Capabilities

Where possible:

```yaml
capabilities:
  drop:
    - ALL
```

should be used.

Only required capabilities should be added back.

---

# 41.44 Read-Only Root Filesystem

Production workloads SHOULD support:

```yaml
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
```

where compatible.

If the application needs writable temporary storage, explicitly provide an appropriate volume.

---

# 41.45 Temporary Storage

For applications requiring `/tmp`, use an explicit temporary volume when necessary.

Concept:

```text
Container root filesystem
       ↓
Read-only

/tmp
       ↓
Writable ephemeral volume
```

---

# 41.46 NetworkPolicy

Charts SHOULD optionally support NetworkPolicy.

Example:

```yaml
networkPolicy:
  enabled: true
```

Production environments should define explicit allowed traffic.

---

# 41.47 Default Network Policy

A chart should not blindly create a deny-all policy without understanding required dependencies.

Before enabling it, identify:

```text
Ingress
DNS
Database
Redis
Kafka
External APIs
Monitoring
```

---

# 41.48 HPA

HPA SHOULD be optional:

```yaml
autoscaling:
  enabled: true
```

Example configuration:

```yaml
minReplicas: 2
maxReplicas: 10
targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70
```

---

# 41.49 HPA Design

Do not make HPA the default answer to performance problems.

First determine whether the bottleneck is:

```text
CPU
Memory
Database
Network
External API
Lock contention
Application code
```

Scaling the wrong component can make the system worse.

---

# 41.50 PodDisruptionBudget

PDB MAY be enabled for critical production workloads.

Example:

```yaml
pdb:
  enabled: true
  minAvailable: 2
```

A PDB should be consistent with the replica strategy.

---

# 41.51 PDB Anti-Pattern

Do not configure:

```text
replicas: 1
minAvailable: 1
```

and assume this provides meaningful high availability.

It provides no redundancy.

---

# 41.52 Persistence

Charts requiring persistent storage SHOULD expose PVC configuration.

Example:

```yaml
persistence:
  enabled: true
  size: 20Gi
  storageClass: standard
```

The default should generally be disabled for stateless applications.

---

# 41.53 StorageClass

Do not hard-code a cloud/vendor-specific StorageClass unless the deployment architecture requires it.

Environment-specific storage configuration belongs in environment values.

---

# 41.54 Jobs

Migration or initialization Jobs SHOULD be clearly separated from the main Deployment.

Avoid embedding complex migration logic inside application startup merely because Helm can execute hooks.

---

# 41.55 Helm Hooks

Helm hooks MAY be used for carefully defined lifecycle operations.

Examples:

```text
pre-install
post-install
pre-upgrade
post-upgrade
```

But hooks create lifecycle complexity.

Use them only when their behavior is well understood.

---

# 41.56 Hook Failure

A failed hook can prevent a Helm release from completing.

Therefore hook Jobs must have:

```text
Timeout
Retry strategy
Cleanup strategy
Idempotency
```

---

# 41.57 Database Migration Hooks

Do not blindly use:

```text
post-install
```

for database migrations.

During an upgrade:

```text
New application
Old database schema
```

and:

```text
Migration timing
```

must be carefully controlled.

GitOps and Kubernetes Job-based migration patterns may provide better operational clarity.

---

# 41.58 Helm Dependencies

If a chart depends on another chart, dependencies MUST be explicitly versioned.

Example:

```yaml
dependencies:
  - name: redis
    version: 20.x.x
```

Do not depend on arbitrary floating versions without governance.

---

# 41.59 Dependency Management

Helm dependencies SHOULD be reviewed like application dependencies.

Consider:

```text
Security
Compatibility
Upgrade path
Maintenance
Licensing
```

---

# 41.60 Subcharts

Do not create subcharts merely to make the directory structure look sophisticated.

Use subcharts when there is genuine reuse or independent packaging value.

---

# 41.61 Library Charts

Reusable organizational Helm logic MAY be implemented as a library chart.

Example:

```text
Mediverse Platform Library
        ↓
Common labels
Security defaults
Standard deployment
Standard service
```

This can reduce duplication across many services.

---

# 41.62 Avoid Over-Abstraction

Helm abstraction becomes harmful when developers cannot understand the rendered Kubernetes resources.

A developer should be able to trace:

```text
values.yaml
      ↓
template
      ↓
rendered Kubernetes object
```

without reverse-engineering hundreds of helper functions.

---

# 41.63 `helm lint`

Every chart MUST pass:

```bash
helm lint
```

before release.

---

# 41.64 Template Rendering

Charts SHOULD be rendered during CI:

```bash
helm template
```

and the resulting manifests SHOULD be validated.

This catches errors before they reach the cluster.

---

# 41.65 Kubernetes Schema Validation

Rendered manifests SHOULD be validated against Kubernetes schemas.

Concept:

```text
Helm Template
      ↓
Rendered YAML
      ↓
Schema Validation
      ↓
Policy Validation
      ↓
Deployment
```

---

# 41.66 Policy Validation

Production charts SHOULD be checked against security policies.

Potential checks include:

```text
No privileged containers
No root containers
Required resources
Required probes
Approved registries
No latest tags
Required labels
```

---

# 41.67 Helm Unit Testing

Complex charts SHOULD have automated tests for important rendering behavior.

Examples:

```text
Ingress enabled
Ingress disabled
HPA enabled
HPA disabled
Production security settings
Service ports
Environment configuration
```

---

# 41.68 Helm Test

Where practical, use:

```bash
helm test
```

for application-level deployment validation.

The test should validate meaningful connectivity or application behavior rather than merely confirming that a Pod exists.

---

# 41.69 Dry-Run Installation

For CI validation:

```bash
helm install --dry-run
```

or equivalent rendering/validation mechanisms MAY be used.

The exact command should match the Helm/Kubernetes version and CI architecture.

---

# 41.70 Chart Documentation

Every production chart SHOULD contain:

```text
README.md
```

Document:

```text
Purpose
Installation
Values
Dependencies
Required secrets
Configuration
Upgrade process
Rollback process
Known limitations
```

---

# 41.71 Values Documentation

Important values SHOULD be documented.

For example:

```yaml
replicaCount:
  # Number of application replicas
```

or generated documentation may be used.

---

# 41.72 Required Values

Critical values SHOULD fail clearly when missing rather than silently falling back to dangerous defaults.

Helm's:

```text
required
```

function MAY be used.

---

# 41.73 Template Fail-Fast

For critical configuration:

```text
Missing required value
       ↓
Helm rendering fails
```

This is preferable to:

```text
Missing value
       ↓
Deployment succeeds
       ↓
Application fails later
```

---

# 41.74 Environment-Specific Hostnames

Do not hard-code:

```text
api.mediverse.com
```

inside a generic template.

Use:

```yaml
ingress:
  host: ...
```

and supply the environment-specific value.

---

# 41.75 Environment-Specific Replicas

Replicas belong in values.

Example:

```text
Development → 1
UAT         → 2
Production  → 3+
```

The exact production count must come from capacity and availability requirements.

---

# 41.76 Environment-Specific Resources

Resource settings may vary by environment.

Example:

```text
Dev
  CPU: 100m
  Memory: 256Mi

Production
  CPU: 500m
  Memory: 1Gi
```

But development values must not become the production baseline accidentally.

---

# 41.77 Environment-Specific Security

Security should generally become **stricter**, not weaker, toward production.

Concept:

```text
Development
   ↓
Flexible

UAT
   ↓
Controlled

Production
   ↓
Strict
```

---

# 41.78 Environment Promotion

The same application image SHOULD be promoted:

```text
Dev
 ↓
UAT
 ↓
Production
```

The Helm configuration changes by environment, but the application artifact should remain the same unless a rebuild is explicitly required.

---

# 41.79 GitOps Repository

A possible Mediverse GitOps structure:

```text
gitops/
├── applications/
│   ├── mediverse-api/
│   ├── mediverse-auth/
│   └── mediverse-frontend/
│
├── environments/
│   ├── dev/
│   ├── uat/
│   └── prod/
│
└── charts/
    └── mediverse-api/
```

The exact repository strategy can vary.

---

# 41.80 Argo CD Integration

Argo CD SHOULD consume the Helm chart and values from Git.

Concept:

```text
Git
 │
 ├── Chart
 ├── Values
 └── Environment Configuration
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Helm Rendering
 │
 ▼
Kubernetes
```

---

# 41.81 Helm + Argo CD

When Argo CD manages Helm applications, avoid relying on developers manually executing:

```bash
helm install
```

in production.

Argo CD becomes the reconciliation mechanism.

---

# 41.82 Release Traceability

A production deployment should allow engineers to answer:

```text
Which chart?
Which chart version?
Which image?
Which image digest?
Which Git commit?
Which environment?
Which Argo CD application?
```

quickly.

---

# 41.83 Helm Release Naming

Release names SHOULD be predictable.

Example:

```text
mediverse-api
mediverse-auth
mediverse-frontend
```

Avoid random or manually invented release names.

---

# 41.84 Release Namespace

Helm releases should be explicitly associated with the intended namespace.

Do not accidentally install:

```text
Production release
        ↓
default namespace
```

---

# 41.85 Upgrade Strategy

Before upgrading a chart:

```text
Review diff
 ↓
Render manifests
 ↓
Validate
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Deploy
 ↓
Observe
```

---

# 41.86 Helm Diff

A Helm diff mechanism MAY be used to understand what will change.

The goal is to answer:

> What Kubernetes resources will actually change?

before deployment.

---

# 41.87 Destructive Changes

Changes involving:

```text
PVC
Database
Service
Ingress
RBAC
NetworkPolicy
CRD
```

require additional review.

A seemingly small Helm change can have a large operational impact.

---

# 41.88 CRD Management

CRDs require special attention during Helm upgrades.

Do not assume normal chart upgrade semantics safely handle every CRD lifecycle operation.

---

# 41.89 Deletion Safety

Templates MUST be reviewed for resources that could be accidentally deleted during chart changes.

Especially:

```text
PersistentVolumeClaims
Secrets
ConfigMaps
CRDs
```

---

# 41.90 Resource Ownership

Helm-managed resources should have consistent ownership metadata.

Do not manually modify Helm-managed resources without understanding the consequences.

---

# 41.91 Manual Kubernetes Modification

Avoid:

```bash
kubectl edit deployment ...
```

for resources managed by Helm/Argo CD.

Otherwise:

```text
Git
 ↓
Helm
 ↓
Argo CD
```

may overwrite the manual change.

---

# 41.92 Debugging Helm

When deployment fails, inspect in this order:

```text
1. Helm rendering
2. Kubernetes validation
3. Argo CD status
4. Kubernetes events
5. Pod state
6. Container logs
7. Service endpoints
8. Ingress
```

---

# 41.93 Common Helm Failure

### Missing value

```text
Helm render
   ↓
nil / missing value
```

Fix the values or template rather than manually patching the resulting Kubernetes object.

---

# 41.94 Common Helm Failure

### Wrong selector

```text
Deployment labels
       ≠
Service selector
```

Result:

```text
Service
   ↓
No endpoints
```

---

# 41.95 Common Helm Failure

### Wrong image

```text
Helm
 ↓
Invalid image tag
 ↓
ImagePullBackOff
```

Always verify:

```text
Registry
Repository
Tag
Digest
Credentials
```

---

# 41.96 Common Helm Failure

### Missing Secret

```text
Deployment
 ↓
envFrom / secretKeyRef
 ↓
Secret missing
 ↓
CreateContainerConfigError
```

---

# 41.97 Common Helm Failure

### Bad probe

```text
Application healthy
        ↓
Wrong probe path
        ↓
Kubernetes thinks unhealthy
        ↓
Traffic removed / restart
```

Probe configuration must be tested against the actual application.

---

# 41.98 Common Helm Failure

### Bad resource values

```text
Too little memory
 ↓
OOMKilled

Too little CPU
 ↓
Latency / throttling

Too much request
 ↓
Pod Pending
```

---

# 41.99 Chart Security Checklist

Every production chart SHOULD verify:

* [ ] No plaintext secrets
* [ ] No privileged containers
* [ ] Non-root execution
* [ ] Capability restrictions
* [ ] Read-only filesystem where possible
* [ ] Resource requests
* [ ] Resource limits
* [ ] Probes
* [ ] Approved image registry
* [ ] Immutable image
* [ ] Network policy
* [ ] Least-privilege RBAC
* [ ] Secure ServiceAccount
* [ ] No unnecessary host mounts

---

# 41.100 Chart Quality Checklist

Every production chart SHOULD have:

* [ ] `Chart.yaml`
* [ ] `values.yaml`
* [ ] Environment configuration
* [ ] Templates
* [ ] `_helpers.tpl`
* [ ] README
* [ ] Versioning
* [ ] Linting
* [ ] Template validation
* [ ] Security validation
* [ ] Automated tests where appropriate
* [ ] Git history
* [ ] Deployment documentation

---

# 41.101 Definition of Done

A Mediverse Helm chart is production-ready when:

* [ ] Chart follows naming conventions
* [ ] Chart version is defined
* [ ] Application version is defined
* [ ] Values are documented
* [ ] Environment configuration is separated
* [ ] Production defaults are safe
* [ ] Image is immutable
* [ ] Secrets are externalized
* [ ] Security context is configured
* [ ] Resource configuration exists
* [ ] Health probes are configured
* [ ] Service is correctly configured
* [ ] Ingress is correctly configured where needed
* [ ] HPA is configured where required
* [ ] PDB is configured where required
* [ ] NetworkPolicy is considered
* [ ] RBAC follows least privilege
* [ ] `helm lint` passes
* [ ] Rendered manifests validate
* [ ] Security policies pass
* [ ] Tests pass where applicable
* [ ] Argo CD can consume the chart
* [ ] Rollback procedure is documented
* [ ] Deployment is traceable

---

# 41.102 Core Principles

Mediverse Helm standards are based on:

1. **Charts package Kubernetes resources; they do not contain business logic.**
2. **Production charts must be deterministic and reproducible.**
3. **Environment differences belong in controlled values.**
4. **Secrets must never be committed as plaintext.**
5. **Production images must be immutable.**
6. **Helm templates must remain understandable.**
7. **Security defaults must be safe.**
8. **Every important deployment behavior must be testable.**
9. **Helm releases must be versioned and traceable.**
10. **The same application artifact should be promoted across environments.**
11. **Argo CD should reconcile production state where GitOps is adopted.**
12. **Manual modification of Helm-managed resources should be exceptional.**
13. **Rendered Kubernetes manifests—not the Helm source alone—must be validated.**
14. **Abstraction is useful only until it starts hiding operational behavior.**
15. **A Helm chart is successful when another engineer can understand, validate, deploy, troubleshoot, and roll it back without reverse-engineering it.**

> **A good Helm chart makes Kubernetes boring: predictable values, readable templates, safe defaults, deterministic output, and no surprises during deployment.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 42: GitOps & Argo CD Standards.**

# CSDG — Chapter 42

## GitOps & Argo CD Standards

### 42.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the standards for implementing **GitOps and Argo CD** for the Mediverse platform.

The objective is to establish a deployment model where:

* Git is the source of desired state.
* Kubernetes state is declarative.
* Deployments are auditable.
* Environment changes are reviewable.
* Drift is detected automatically.
* Releases are reproducible.
* Rollbacks are controlled.
* Manual production changes are minimized.

Core principle:

> **If a production Kubernetes change is not represented in Git, it is not a properly managed production change.**

---

# 42.2 GitOps Model

The standard Mediverse deployment flow is:

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Application Repository
    │
    ▼
CI Pipeline
    │
    ├── Build
    ├── Test
    ├── Scan
    └── Container Image
             │
             ▼
       Container Registry
             │
             ▼
       GitOps Repository
             │
             ▼
           Argo CD
             │
             ▼
        Kubernetes
```

---

# 42.3 GitOps Principles

Mediverse GitOps implementations SHOULD follow four fundamental principles:

### Declarative

The desired infrastructure and application state is represented declaratively.

### Versioned

Changes are stored in Git.

### Automatically Reconciled

The cluster is continuously compared against the desired state.

### Continuously Reconciled

Drift should be detected and corrected according to the environment's synchronization policy.

---

# 42.4 Source of Truth

For production Kubernetes configuration:

```text
Git
 ↓
Desired State
```

should be considered authoritative.

Kubernetes represents:

```text
Actual State
```

Argo CD compares:

```text
Desired State
        VS
Actual State
```

---

# 42.5 Desired vs Actual State

Conceptually:

```text
              ┌──────────────────┐
              │       Git        │
              │ Desired State    │
              └────────┬─────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
                 ┌───────────┐
                 │  Argo CD   │
                 └─────┬─────┘
                       │
                Reconcile
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌──────────────────┐
              │   Kubernetes     │
              │   Actual State   │
              └──────────────────┘
```

---

# 42.6 Application Repository vs GitOps Repository

Mediverse SHOULD clearly distinguish application source from deployment configuration.

Example:

```text
Application Repository
        │
        ├── Java
        ├── Spring Boot
        ├── React
        ├── Tests
        └── Dockerfile
```

while:

```text
GitOps Repository
        │
        ├── Helm
        ├── Environment values
        ├── Argo CD Applications
        └── Deployment configuration
```

---

# 42.7 Separation of Responsibilities

CI SHOULD primarily answer:

> **Can we build and verify this artifact?**

CD/GitOps SHOULD answer:

> **Should this artifact become the desired state of this environment?**

This separation prevents CI pipelines from becoming giant imperative Kubernetes scripts.

---

# 42.8 CI/CD Flow

Recommended:

```text
Code Commit
    ↓
CI
    ↓
Compile
    ↓
Unit Tests
    ↓
Static Analysis
    ↓
Security Scan
    ↓
Build Image
    ↓
Push Image
    ↓
Update GitOps Configuration
    ↓
Argo CD
    ↓
Kubernetes
```

---

# 42.9 Container Image Promotion

Prefer promoting the **same immutable artifact** through environments.

Example:

```text
mediverse-api:1.8.2
        │
        ├── DEV
        │
        ├── UAT
        │
        └── PROD
```

Do not rebuild the application separately for every environment unless there is a documented reason.

---

# 42.10 Image Immutability

Production deployments SHOULD use:

```text
Versioned tag
```

or preferably:

```text
Image digest
```

Example:

```text
registry.example.com/mediverse/api@sha256:...
```

Avoid:

```text
latest
```

for production.

---

# 42.11 GitOps Repository Structure

A possible Mediverse GitOps repository:

```text
mediverse-gitops/
│
├── applications/
│   ├── mediverse-api/
│   ├── mediverse-auth/
│   ├── mediverse-user/
│   └── mediverse-frontend/
│
├── environments/
│   ├── dev/
│   │   ├── values/
│   │   └── applications/
│   │
│   ├── uat/
│   │   ├── values/
│   │   └── applications/
│   │
│   └── prod/
│       ├── values/
│       └── applications/
│
└── charts/
    ├── mediverse-api/
    ├── mediverse-auth/
    └── mediverse-frontend/
```

The actual repository structure may differ based on the final Mediverse architecture.

---

# 42.12 Environment Isolation

Each environment SHOULD have clearly identifiable configuration.

Example:

```text
DEV
 ↓
mediverse-dev

UAT
 ↓
mediverse-uat

PROD
 ↓
mediverse-prod
```

Environment-specific configuration must not be accidentally mixed.

---

# 42.13 Argo CD

Argo CD acts as the GitOps reconciliation engine.

Conceptually:

```text
Git
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Kubernetes
```

Argo CD SHOULD continuously monitor the desired state.

---

# 42.14 Argo CD Application

An Argo CD Application typically defines:

```text
Application name
Source repository
Revision
Path
Helm configuration
Destination cluster
Destination namespace
Sync policy
```

---

# 42.15 Application Naming

Argo CD Applications SHOULD follow predictable naming.

Example:

```text
mediverse-api-dev
mediverse-api-uat
mediverse-api-prod
```

This makes operational investigation easier.

---

# 42.16 Application Ownership

Every Argo CD Application SHOULD have a clear owner.

The team responsible for the service should be identifiable through:

```text
Git repository
Documentation
Labels
Metadata
Ownership configuration
```

---

# 42.17 Repository Revision

Production Applications SHOULD reference a controlled Git revision.

Depending on the GitOps model, this may be:

```text
main
release branch
tag
specific commit
```

The chosen strategy must provide sufficient traceability.

---

# 42.18 Production Branch Strategy

Production configuration SHOULD NOT be modified casually.

A typical workflow is:

```text
Feature
   ↓
Pull Request
   ↓
Review
   ↓
Merge
   ↓
GitOps
   ↓
Argo CD
   ↓
Production
```

---

# 42.19 Pull Requests

Production deployment configuration changes SHOULD go through Pull Requests.

Reviewers should verify:

```text
Image version
Resources
Configuration
Security
Ingress
Secrets
Database changes
Scaling
Rollback
```

---

# 42.20 Commit Messages

GitOps commits SHOULD clearly describe deployment changes.

Good:

```text
deploy(api): promote 1.8.2 to production
```

Bad:

```text
update
fix
changes
final
```

---

# 42.21 Change Traceability

A production deployment should be traceable:

```text
Git commit
    ↓
PR
    ↓
Image
    ↓
Helm values
    ↓
Argo CD Application
    ↓
Kubernetes Deployment
```

An engineer should be able to trace a running Pod back to the source change.

---

# 42.22 Sync Status

Argo CD commonly reports states such as:

```text
Synced
OutOfSync
Unknown
```

Engineers MUST understand what these states mean before taking action.

---

# 42.23 Healthy vs Synced

These are different concepts.

```text
Synced
=
Cluster matches desired configuration
```

while:

```text
Healthy
=
Application/resource health is acceptable
```

A deployment can be:

```text
Synced + Unhealthy
```

or:

```text
OutOfSync + Healthy
```

depending on the situation.

---

# 42.24 OutOfSync

`OutOfSync` means the desired state and actual state differ.

Possible reasons:

```text
Git changed
Manual Kubernetes modification
Controller mutation
Defaulting
Generated fields
Incorrect configuration
```

Do not automatically click **Sync** without understanding the difference.

---

# 42.25 Drift

Example:

```text
Git:
replicas = 3

Kubernetes:
replicas = 5
```

Argo CD detects:

```text
OutOfSync
```

This is configuration drift.

---

# 42.26 Drift Prevention

The preferred approach is:

```text
Do not manually change production
        ↓
Change Git
        ↓
Review
        ↓
Argo CD reconciles
```

---

# 42.27 Manual Changes

Commands such as:

```bash
kubectl edit
kubectl scale
kubectl set image
kubectl patch
```

SHOULD NOT be used for normal production deployment changes.

They may be appropriate for emergency troubleshooting, but any lasting change must be reconciled into Git.

---

# 42.28 Emergency Change

If emergency modification is unavoidable:

```text
Emergency
   ↓
Manual Change
   ↓
Stabilize System
   ↓
Document Change
   ↓
Update Git
   ↓
Reconcile Argo CD
```

Never leave production permanently different from Git.

---

# 42.29 Auto-Sync

Auto-sync MAY be used for development environments.

Example:

```text
DEV
 ↓
Automatic reconciliation
```

This provides rapid feedback.

---

# 42.30 UAT Synchronization

UAT may use automatic synchronization or controlled synchronization depending on release governance.

The key requirement is consistency.

---

# 42.31 Production Synchronization

Production synchronization SHOULD follow the organization's release approval model.

A controlled model may be:

```text
PR Approved
    ↓
Release Approved
    ↓
Git Updated
    ↓
Argo CD Sync
    ↓
Production
```

---

# 42.32 Automated Production Deployment

Automation is not inherently unsafe.

The actual requirement is:

```text
Controlled
Auditable
Tested
Reversible
```

An automated production deployment can be safer than manual deployment if these conditions are satisfied.

---

# 42.33 Sync Windows

Where required, synchronization windows MAY be used to restrict production deployment periods.

Example:

```text
Normal business hours
      ↓
Deployment restricted

Approved release window
      ↓
Deployment allowed
```

---

# 42.34 Sync Waves

When applications/resources have dependencies, synchronization ordering MAY be used.

Example:

```text
Namespace
   ↓
Config
   ↓
Database migration
   ↓
Backend
   ↓
Frontend
```

Do not use sync ordering to hide an architecture with uncontrolled dependencies.

---

# 42.35 Application Dependencies

If Service A cannot start before Service B exists, the dependency should ideally be addressed architecturally.

Argo CD ordering should not become a replacement for resilient service design.

---

# 42.36 App-of-Apps

For larger Mediverse environments, an App-of-Apps pattern MAY be used.

Concept:

```text
                 Root Application
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ▼             ▼             ▼
      Auth App       API App      Frontend App
          │             │             │
          ▼             ▼             ▼
       Kubernetes Resources
```

---

# 42.37 App-of-Apps Governance

App-of-Apps should not become an uncontrolled recursive structure.

Keep:

```text
Ownership
Hierarchy
Environment
Dependencies
```

clear.

---

# 42.38 ApplicationSet

Where many applications follow the same deployment pattern, Argo CD ApplicationSet MAY be used.

For example:

```text
Service list
    ↓
ApplicationSet
    ↓
Generate Applications
```

This can reduce repetitive Argo CD configuration.

---

# 42.39 ApplicationSet Safety

Generated Applications should be carefully scoped.

A bad generator configuration can create or modify many applications at once.

Therefore ApplicationSet changes require careful review.

---

# 42.40 Helm Integration

Argo CD can render Helm charts.

Concept:

```text
Argo CD
   ↓
Helm Chart
   ↓
Values
   ↓
Rendered Manifests
   ↓
Kubernetes
```

Argo CD SHOULD remain the deployment controller rather than developers independently installing Helm releases in production.

---

# 42.41 Helm Values Management

Environment-specific values should remain version-controlled.

Example:

```text
values-dev.yaml
values-uat.yaml
values-prod.yaml
```

Sensitive credentials should remain outside Git or be stored using an approved encrypted-secret mechanism.

---

# 42.42 Secret Management

Preferred architecture:

```text
Secret Manager
      ↓
External Secrets
      ↓
Kubernetes Secret
      ↓
Application
```

rather than:

```text
Git
 ↓
Plaintext password
 ↓
Kubernetes
```

---

# 42.43 Argo CD and Secrets

Argo CD should not become a secret-management system.

It manages desired resources.

Secret lifecycle should be handled by the approved secret-management architecture.

---

# 42.44 RBAC

Argo CD access MUST follow least privilege.

Different users may require different capabilities:

```text
Viewer
Operator
Developer
Release Manager
Administrator
```

---

# 42.45 Production Access

Not every developer needs permission to:

```text
Delete production application
Modify sync policy
Change cluster configuration
Create cluster-admin privileges
```

Permissions should match responsibilities.

---

# 42.46 Argo CD Project

Argo CD Projects SHOULD be used to establish boundaries where appropriate.

Projects can constrain:

```text
Repositories
Clusters
Namespaces
Resource types
```

This prevents an application from deploying arbitrary resources everywhere.

---

# 42.47 Repository Restrictions

Production Argo CD Projects SHOULD allow only approved Git repositories.

Avoid:

```text
Any repository
```

for production deployments.

---

# 42.48 Destination Restrictions

Production applications SHOULD be restricted to approved clusters/namespaces.

Example conceptual policy:

```text
mediverse-prod
    ↓
production cluster only
```

---

# 42.49 Resource Restrictions

Where appropriate, restrict which Kubernetes resource types an Argo CD Application can create.

This limits accidental or malicious deployment of privileged resources.

---

# 42.50 Application Health

Argo CD health status should be treated as an operational signal, not as proof that the application works correctly.

For example:

```text
Deployment Healthy
```

does not guarantee:

```text
API business logic works
Database queries succeed
Payments work
Authentication works
```

Application-level monitoring remains required.

---

# 42.51 Deployment Verification

After synchronization:

```text
Argo CD
   ↓
Synced
   ↓
Healthy
   ↓
Kubernetes validation
   ↓
Application validation
```

---

# 42.52 Rollout Verification

Verify:

```text
Deployment
ReplicaSets
Pods
Services
EndpointSlices
Ingress
```

and application-level health.

---

# 42.53 Rollback Strategy

Rollback should preferably occur by reverting Git to a known-good state.

Example:

```text
Current
v1.8.2
   ↓
Problem detected
   ↓
Git revert
   ↓
Argo CD
   ↓
v1.8.1
```

This keeps the cluster and Git aligned.

---

# 42.54 Argo CD Rollback

Argo CD may provide rollback capabilities, but teams must ensure the rollback does not create permanent Git drift.

A temporary rollback followed by Git reconciliation is preferable to leaving production permanently divergent.

---

# 42.55 Git Revert

For GitOps-managed production, a Git revert provides:

```text
Auditable
Reviewable
Reproducible
```

rollback behavior.

---

# 42.56 Rollback Limitations

Application rollback does not guarantee database rollback.

Example:

```text
v2
 ↓
Database schema v2
 ↓
Application rollback
 ↓
v1
```

If v1 cannot operate against schema v2, the rollback fails.

Database compatibility must therefore be part of release design.

---

# 42.57 Progressive Delivery

For high-risk services, consider:

```text
Canary
Blue/Green
Traffic splitting
Automated analysis
```

Argo CD can be combined with progressive-delivery tooling where justified.

---

# 42.58 Canary Example

Conceptually:

```text
             Traffic
                │
        ┌───────┴───────┐
        ▼               ▼
       v1               v2
      95%                5%
```

Observe:

```text
Error rate
Latency
CPU
Memory
Business metrics
```

Then gradually increase v2.

---

# 42.59 Deployment Gates

Production deployments MAY require gates such as:

```text
Automated tests
Security scan
Approval
Integration tests
Smoke tests
Performance threshold
```

---

# 42.60 Quality Gates

A deployment SHOULD NOT proceed if critical quality gates fail.

Example:

```text
Build
 ↓
Tests ❌
 ↓
STOP
```

rather than:

```text
Tests ❌
 ↓
Deploy anyway
```

---

# 42.61 Security Scanning

Before an image is promoted:

```text
SAST
Dependency scan
Container scan
Secret scan
IaC scan
```

should be performed according to Mediverse security requirements.

---

# 42.62 Image Provenance

Production images SHOULD have traceable provenance.

At minimum, determine:

```text
Source commit
Build pipeline
Build timestamp
Image tag
Image digest
```

---

# 42.63 Git Commit Traceability

The deployment configuration SHOULD make it possible to determine which application version is running.

Useful metadata includes:

```text
app.kubernetes.io/version
Git SHA
Image digest
Build number
```

---

# 42.64 Deployment Metadata

Pods MAY expose useful metadata through:

```text
Labels
Annotations
Environment variables
```

Example:

```text
GIT_COMMIT
BUILD_NUMBER
APP_VERSION
```

Do not expose sensitive CI information.

---

# 42.65 Notifications

Important deployment events SHOULD be integrated with the team's notification mechanism where appropriate.

Examples:

```text
Deployment started
Deployment succeeded
Deployment failed
Sync failed
Application degraded
```

---

# 42.66 Observability

GitOps observability should cover:

```text
Argo CD
Kubernetes
Application
Infrastructure
```

For example:

```text
Argo CD
  ↓
Sync status

Kubernetes
  ↓
Pod health

Application
  ↓
HTTP errors

Infrastructure
  ↓
CPU / Memory
```

---

# 42.67 Audit Logs

Production deployment actions SHOULD be auditable.

Record:

```text
Who
What
When
Where
Why
```

---

# 42.68 Drift Monitoring

Drift should be actively monitored.

Example:

```text
Git
replicas=3

Cluster
replicas=5

        ↓

Argo CD
OutOfSync
```

This should trigger investigation.

---

# 42.69 Drift Policy

The environment must define whether drift is:

```text
Automatically corrected
or
Manually reviewed
```

For GitOps-managed production, automatic reconciliation is generally preferred unless there is a documented exception.

---

# 42.70 Ignore Differences

Argo CD allows certain differences to be ignored.

This capability MUST be used carefully.

Bad:

```text
Ignore everything that changes
```

That effectively disables drift detection.

---

# 42.71 Controller-Managed Fields

Some Kubernetes controllers legitimately mutate resources.

Examples:

```text
HPA
Service
Admission controllers
Operators
```

Specific expected differences may be ignored where justified.

---

# 42.72 Sync Failure

If synchronization fails:

```text
DO NOT
blindly retry repeatedly
```

Instead:

```text
Inspect error
 ↓
Identify resource
 ↓
Check manifest
 ↓
Check events
 ↓
Fix source
 ↓
Retry
```

---

# 42.73 Kubernetes Events

Argo CD errors should be correlated with Kubernetes events.

For example:

```text
Argo CD:
Sync failed

Kubernetes:
CreateContainerConfigError
```

The second message may contain the real root cause.

---

# 42.74 Application Degraded

When Argo CD reports degraded health:

Investigate:

```text
Pod state
Probe failures
Container logs
Resource pressure
Dependencies
Service endpoints
Ingress
```

---

# 42.75 Production Incident

During an incident:

```text
Detect
 ↓
Assess
 ↓
Stabilize
 ↓
Rollback / Mitigate
 ↓
Verify
 ↓
Document
 ↓
Fix Git
```

Do not sacrifice GitOps discipline permanently because of a temporary emergency.

---

# 42.76 Disaster Recovery

GitOps significantly improves recovery because desired configuration is version-controlled.

Recovery concept:

```text
Cluster Lost
     ↓
New Cluster
     ↓
Bootstrap Argo CD
     ↓
Connect GitOps Repository
     ↓
Reconcile
     ↓
Applications Restored
```

However, this does not automatically restore:

```text
Database data
Persistent volumes
External secrets
External infrastructure
```

These require separate recovery strategies.

---

# 42.77 Cluster Bootstrap

The Mediverse platform should document the minimum components required to bootstrap a new cluster:

```text
Ingress
Storage
Monitoring
Argo CD
Secrets
Policies
Application deployment
```

---

# 42.78 Bootstrap Ordering

A conceptual bootstrap sequence:

```text
1. Kubernetes Cluster
2. Namespace / Platform Policies
3. Storage / Networking
4. Secret Integration
5. Ingress
6. Observability
7. Argo CD
8. Applications
```

Actual ordering depends on infrastructure architecture.

---

# 42.79 Backup

Git is not a backup of runtime data.

Git stores:

```text
Configuration
```

It does not necessarily store:

```text
PostgreSQL data
Persistent files
User-uploaded medical content
Object storage
Runtime state
```

These require dedicated backup strategies.

---

# 42.80 Recovery Testing

GitOps recovery SHOULD be tested.

A recovery test should answer:

> Can Mediverse be reconstructed from the documented source repositories and infrastructure definitions?

If the answer is no, the system is not truly reproducible.

---

# 42.81 GitOps Anti-Patterns

Avoid:

### Anti-pattern 1

```text
kubectl apply
```

as the primary production deployment mechanism.

### Anti-pattern 2

Using:

```text
latest
```

in production.

### Anti-pattern 3

Plaintext production secrets in Git.

### Anti-pattern 4

Manual changes without Git reconciliation.

### Anti-pattern 5

Giving every Argo CD user administrator permissions.

### Anti-pattern 6

Using GitOps to deploy undocumented infrastructure hacks.

### Anti-pattern 7

Ignoring all Argo CD differences.

### Anti-pattern 8

Using Argo CD health as the only monitoring mechanism.

### Anti-pattern 9

Building a different application artifact for every environment without justification.

### Anti-pattern 10

Treating rollback as simply changing the application image without considering database compatibility.

---

# 42.82 GitOps Security Checklist

Before production:

* [ ] Argo CD RBAC configured
* [ ] Production projects restricted
* [ ] Approved repositories only
* [ ] Approved destination namespaces
* [ ] Secrets externalized
* [ ] Repository access secured
* [ ] Container registry secured
* [ ] Image provenance available
* [ ] No plaintext credentials
* [ ] Least privilege enforced
* [ ] Auditability enabled
* [ ] Production sync policy defined

---

# 42.83 GitOps Operational Checklist

Before production:

* [ ] Application defined in Argo CD
* [ ] Repository path verified
* [ ] Helm values verified
* [ ] Image verified
* [ ] Environment verified
* [ ] Namespace verified
* [ ] Sync policy verified
* [ ] Health checks verified
* [ ] Monitoring verified
* [ ] Rollback procedure documented
* [ ] Database migration strategy verified
* [ ] Drift policy defined

---

# 42.84 Production Release Checklist

```text
Code
 ↓
CI
 ↓
Tests
 ↓
Security
 ↓
Image
 ↓
Registry
 ↓
GitOps PR
 ↓
Review
 ↓
Merge
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Sync
 ↓
Health Check
 ↓
Smoke Test
 ↓
Monitoring
```

Every stage should have a clear success criterion.

---

# 42.85 Definition of Done

A Mediverse GitOps implementation is production-ready when:

* [ ] Git is the desired-state source
* [ ] Application and GitOps repositories are clearly separated
* [ ] Helm configuration is version-controlled
* [ ] Argo CD Applications are defined
* [ ] Environment boundaries are clear
* [ ] Production access follows least privilege
* [ ] Secrets are securely managed
* [ ] Images are immutable
* [ ] Deployment changes go through review
* [ ] Sync policy is defined
* [ ] Drift detection works
* [ ] Rollback is documented
* [ ] Application health is observable
* [ ] Deployment traceability exists
* [ ] Disaster recovery is documented
* [ ] Manual changes have an emergency/reconciliation process
* [ ] Production deployment can be reproduced

---

# 42.86 Core Principles

Mediverse GitOps follows:

1. **Git defines desired production state.**
2. **Argo CD reconciles desired state with Kubernetes.**
3. **CI builds and verifies artifacts; GitOps deploys them.**
4. **Production changes should be reviewable before they happen.**
5. **Immutable artifacts are preferred.**
6. **Secrets do not belong in plaintext Git repositories.**
7. **Drift is a condition to investigate, not something to hide.**
8. **Manual changes are emergency exceptions, not deployment strategy.**
9. **Rollback must preserve Git/Kubernetes consistency.**
10. **Application health and synchronization state are different things.**
11. **GitOps improves reproducibility but does not replace database or data backups.**
12. **The same tested artifact should move through environments whenever practical.**
13. **Production access must follow least privilege.**
14. **Automation should reduce human error, not merely automate bad processes.**
15. **A GitOps platform is successful when production can be understood, reproduced, audited, deployed, and recovered from Git with minimal manual intervention.**

> **GitOps is not "using Argo CD." The real goal is controlled desired-state management: every meaningful production change should have a clear source, review trail, reconciliation path, and rollback strategy.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 43: CI/CD Pipeline Standards.**


# CSDG — Chapter 43

## CI/CD Pipeline Standards

### 43.1 Purpose

This chapter defines standards for **Continuous Integration (CI)** and **Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD)** for Mediverse.

The objective is to create a pipeline that consistently:

* Builds source code
* Runs automated tests
* Performs code-quality checks
* Performs security scanning
* Builds immutable container images
* Publishes artifacts
* Updates GitOps configuration
* Promotes releases across environments
* Provides traceability
* Supports safe rollback

Core principle:

> **A deployment pipeline must be a quality gate, not merely an automation script.**

---

# 43.2 Standard Mediverse CI/CD Flow

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
Git Push / Pull Request
   │
   ▼
CI Pipeline
   │
   ├── Checkout
   ├── Compile
   ├── Unit Tests
   ├── Integration Tests
   ├── Static Analysis
   ├── Dependency Scan
   ├── Secret Scan
   ├── Build
   ├── Container Build
   ├── Container Scan
   └── Publish Artifact
              │
              ▼
       Container Registry
              │
              ▼
        GitOps Update
              │
              ▼
            Argo CD
              │
              ▼
         Kubernetes
```

---

# 43.3 CI vs CD

CI answers:

> **Is this code safe and valid enough to become a release artifact?**

CD answers:

> **Should this validated artifact be deployed to an environment?**

These responsibilities should remain logically separated.

---

# 43.4 Continuous Integration

Every meaningful code change SHOULD trigger CI.

Typical triggers:

```text
Pull Request
Push
Merge
Release
Manual execution
```

---

# 43.5 Pull Request Pipeline

A Pull Request pipeline SHOULD validate the change before merge.

Recommended:

```text
Checkout
 ↓
Compile
 ↓
Unit Tests
 ↓
Static Analysis
 ↓
Dependency Scan
 ↓
Secret Scan
 ↓
Build Verification
```

A PR should not require production deployment.

---

# 43.6 Main Branch Pipeline

After merge:

```text
Merge
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Security
 ↓
Package
 ↓
Container Image
 ↓
Registry
```

The resulting artifact should be uniquely identifiable.

---

# 43.7 Pipeline Stages

A standard Mediverse pipeline SHOULD follow:

```text
1. Checkout
2. Validate
3. Build
4. Unit Test
5. Integration Test
6. Static Analysis
7. Security Scan
8. Package
9. Container Build
10. Container Scan
11. Publish
12. GitOps Promotion
13. Deployment Verification
```

Not every service requires every stage, but omissions must be intentional.

---

# 43.8 Pipeline Fail-Fast

Critical quality failures SHOULD stop the pipeline.

Example:

```text
Unit Test
   ❌
   ↓
STOP
```

Do not continue to:

```text
Build Image
Push Image
Deploy
```

when a mandatory quality gate has failed.

---

# 43.9 Source Checkout

CI MUST obtain source from a controlled Git repository.

The pipeline SHOULD record:

```text
Repository
Branch
Commit SHA
Tag
Author
Build number
```

---

# 43.10 Reproducible Builds

Builds SHOULD be reproducible.

Avoid depending on:

```text
Developer workstation state
Random local files
Undocumented environment variables
Unpinned dependencies
```

---

# 43.11 Java Build

For Spring Boot services, the pipeline should consistently use the project's approved:

```text
JDK version
Maven/Gradle version
Spring Boot version
Dependency versions
```

The CI JDK MUST match the application's supported runtime.

---

# 43.12 Maven Example

A typical backend pipeline may execute:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

This should compile the application and execute the configured test lifecycle.

---

# 43.13 Gradle Example

If Gradle is used:

```bash
./gradlew clean build
```

The project should preferably use the Gradle Wrapper rather than relying on a globally installed Gradle version.

---

# 43.14 React Build

For Mediverse frontend applications, CI SHOULD execute:

```text
Install dependencies
 ↓
Lint
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Build
```

Example conceptual flow:

```text
npm ci
npm run lint
npm test
npm run build
```

Use the package manager and scripts actually defined by the project.

---

# 43.15 Dependency Installation

CI SHOULD use deterministic dependency installation.

For npm:

```bash
npm ci
```

is generally preferred over:

```bash
npm install
```

for CI builds when a lockfile is maintained.

---

# 43.16 Lockfiles

Dependency lockfiles SHOULD be committed.

Examples:

```text
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml
```

For Java, dependency versions should likewise be explicitly controlled.

---

# 43.17 Unit Tests

Unit tests SHOULD run on every CI build.

Examples:

```text
JUnit
Mockito
React Testing Library
```

depending on the component being tested.

---

# 43.18 Test Failure

If mandatory tests fail:

```text
Pipeline = FAILED
```

The artifact SHOULD NOT be promoted.

---

# 43.19 Test Coverage

Coverage should be treated as a quality signal, not the sole definition of quality.

Bad practice:

> "The project has 90% coverage, therefore the code is good."

Coverage can be high while tests remain useless.

---

# 43.20 Coverage Thresholds

Mediverse MAY define minimum coverage thresholds.

For example:

```text
Backend
→ minimum agreed line/branch coverage

Frontend
→ minimum agreed coverage
```

The exact thresholds should be defined by project maturity rather than copied blindly.

---

# 43.21 Integration Testing

Integration tests SHOULD validate important interactions:

```text
Spring Boot
   ↓
PostgreSQL

Spring Boot
   ↓
Redis

Service
   ↓
Kafka

Frontend
   ↓
Backend API
```

depending on the service's actual dependencies.

---

# 43.22 Test Containers

Where appropriate, Testcontainers MAY be used to provide realistic dependencies during CI.

Example:

```text
Test
 ↓
PostgreSQL Container
 ↓
Application
```

This is generally preferable to pretending a real database behaves exactly like an in-memory replacement.

---

# 43.23 Database Testing

Database-dependent tests should use a database environment representative enough to catch important SQL/schema issues.

Do not assume:

```text
H2
```

will behave identically to:

```text
PostgreSQL
```

---

# 43.24 Static Analysis

Static analysis SHOULD run automatically.

For the Mediverse Java backend this may include:

```text
SonarQube
Checkstyle
SpotBugs
PMD
```

depending on the project's selected tooling.

---

# 43.25 SonarQube

SonarQube SHOULD be integrated into CI where adopted.

The pipeline should evaluate:

```text
Bugs
Vulnerabilities
Code Smells
Coverage
Duplications
Quality Gate
```

---

# 43.26 Quality Gate

A failed mandatory quality gate SHOULD prevent release promotion.

Example:

```text
SonarQube
   ↓
Quality Gate ❌
   ↓
Pipeline STOP
```

---

# 43.27 Dependency Security

Dependencies SHOULD be scanned for known vulnerabilities.

Examples of areas to scan:

```text
Maven dependencies
npm dependencies
Container packages
Operating-system packages
```

---

# 43.28 Secret Scanning

CI SHOULD detect accidentally committed secrets.

Potential targets:

```text
Passwords
API keys
Tokens
Private keys
Cloud credentials
Database credentials
```

---

# 43.29 Secret Handling

Secrets MUST NOT be passed through source-controlled configuration merely to make the pipeline convenient.

Bad:

```text
DATABASE_PASSWORD=real-password
```

inside:

```text
application.yml
values-prod.yaml
Jenkinsfile
```

---

# 43.30 CI Credentials

CI credentials SHOULD be stored in the CI platform's secure credential mechanism or approved secret manager.

They should not be hard-coded in:

```text
Jenkinsfile
GitHub Actions YAML
Shell scripts
Dockerfiles
```

---

# 43.31 Credential Scope

Credentials SHOULD follow least privilege.

Example:

```text
Build Job
 ↓
Read dependency repository

Publish Job
 ↓
Push to container registry

Deployment Configuration Job
 ↓
Modify GitOps repository
```

Do not give every pipeline stage unrestricted access.

---

# 43.32 Build Artifacts

Artifacts SHOULD be uniquely identifiable.

Recommended metadata:

```text
Application
Version
Git SHA
Build number
Timestamp
```

---

# 43.33 Artifact Naming

Example:

```text
mediverse-api-1.8.2.jar
```

Container:

```text
mediverse/api:1.8.2
```

or immutable digest.

---

# 43.34 Container Build

Container images MUST be built in CI rather than manually on developer machines for production releases.

Flow:

```text
Source
 ↓
CI
 ↓
Docker Build
 ↓
Image
```

---

# 43.35 Dockerfile Standards

Dockerfiles SHOULD:

* Use approved base images
* Minimize layers where practical
* Avoid unnecessary packages
* Run as non-root
* Avoid embedding secrets
* Use multi-stage builds where beneficial
* Pin important dependencies
* Include health-related configuration only where appropriate

---

# 43.36 Multi-Stage Builds

Spring Boot:

```text
Build Image
   ↓
Compile
   ↓
Runtime Image
```

React:

```text
Node Build
   ↓
Static Files
   ↓
Minimal Web Server
```

This reduces runtime image size and attack surface.

---

# 43.37 Container Registry

Only approved registries SHOULD be used.

Example:

```text
CI
 ↓
Container Registry
 ↓
Argo CD/Kubernetes
```

The registry must support appropriate access control and retention policies.

---

# 43.38 Image Tagging

Use immutable identifiers.

Recommended:

```text
1.8.2
```

and/or:

```text
1.8.2-<git-sha>
```

Avoid:

```text
latest
```

for production.

---

# 43.39 Image Digest

Where possible, production GitOps configuration SHOULD reference immutable digests.

Example concept:

```text
mediverse/api@sha256:<digest>
```

---

# 43.40 Container Scanning

Every production image SHOULD be scanned before promotion.

Scan for:

```text
OS vulnerabilities
Library vulnerabilities
Secrets
Misconfiguration
Malware indicators
```

---

# 43.41 Vulnerability Policy

Not every vulnerability should automatically block every deployment.

Policy SHOULD distinguish:

```text
Critical
High
Medium
Low
```

and account for:

```text
Exploitability
Exposure
Runtime usage
Available fix
Business risk
```

---

# 43.42 Critical Vulnerabilities

Known critical vulnerabilities with practical exploitation risk SHOULD normally block production promotion unless formally accepted.

---

# 43.43 Base Image Management

Base images MUST be maintained.

Example:

```text
Old Java image
      ↓
Security updates
      ↓
Rebuild
      ↓
New image
```

Do not wait for application code changes before updating vulnerable runtime images.

---

# 43.44 Artifact Promotion

Recommended:

```text
Build once
   ↓
Test
   ↓
Publish
   ↓
Promote
```

rather than:

```text
Build DEV
Build UAT
Build PROD
```

with potentially different artifacts.

---

# 43.45 Development Deployment

A typical flow:

```text
Merge
 ↓
Image built
 ↓
GitOps DEV updated
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
DEV
```

---

# 43.46 UAT Promotion

Promotion should occur only after DEV validation.

```text
DEV
 ↓
Automated tests
 ↓
Smoke tests
 ↓
UAT approval
 ↓
GitOps UAT update
```

---

# 43.47 Production Promotion

Production should follow the approved release process:

```text
UAT
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
Approval
 ↓
GitOps PROD change
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Production
```

---

# 43.48 Environment Configuration

The application artifact should remain the same while configuration changes per environment.

Example:

```text
Same image
       │
       ├── DEV values
       ├── UAT values
       └── PROD values
```

---

# 43.49 GitOps Update

CI may update the GitOps repository with the new image version.

Example conceptual change:

```yaml
image:
  tag: "1.8.1"
```

to:

```yaml
image:
  tag: "1.8.2"
```

That Git change becomes the deployment request.

---

# 43.50 CI Must Not Bypass GitOps

If Argo CD manages production, CI SHOULD NOT directly execute:

```bash
kubectl apply
kubectl set image
kubectl rollout
```

as the normal production deployment mechanism.

The preferred path is:

```text
CI
 ↓
GitOps commit
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Kubernetes
```

---

# 43.51 Jenkins

If Jenkins is the selected Mediverse CI platform, pipelines SHOULD be defined as code.

Example:

```text
Jenkinsfile
```

should live with the application source where appropriate.

---

# 43.52 Jenkins Pipeline Stages

A typical backend pipeline:

```text
Checkout
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Unit Test
 ↓
SonarQube
 ↓
Dependency Scan
 ↓
Package
 ↓
Docker Build
 ↓
Image Scan
 ↓
Push Image
 ↓
GitOps Update
```

---

# 43.53 Jenkins Agents

Build workloads SHOULD run on controlled agents.

Avoid assuming:

```text
"whatever is installed on the Jenkins server"
```

is available.

---

# 43.54 Jenkins Tool Versions

The pipeline should explicitly control or declare:

```text
JDK
Maven
Node
Docker
Helm
kubectl
```

where applicable.

---

# 43.55 Jenkins Credentials

Use Jenkins Credentials rather than:

```groovy
environment {
    PASSWORD = "..."
}
```

Credentials SHOULD be injected only into stages that require them.

---

# 43.56 Jenkins Workspace

Sensitive files should not remain unnecessarily in workspaces after a build.

Use appropriate cleanup policies.

---

# 43.57 GitHub Actions

If GitHub Actions is used instead of Jenkins, the same architectural principles apply:

```text
Build
Test
Scan
Package
Publish
GitOps
```

The CI tool is an implementation detail; the quality gates are the important part.

---

# 43.58 Pipeline as Code

CI/CD configuration MUST be version-controlled.

Examples:

```text
Jenkinsfile
.github/workflows/*.yaml
.gitlab-ci.yml
```

Do not maintain critical production pipelines only through an undocumented UI.

---

# 43.59 Pipeline Reusability

Common pipeline logic SHOULD be reusable where practical.

Example:

```text
Mediverse CI Template
        │
        ├── Spring Boot Service
        ├── React Service
        └── Worker Service
```

But avoid creating abstractions so complicated that engineers cannot understand pipeline execution.

---

# 43.60 Pipeline Parameters

Parameters MAY be used for controlled operations such as:

```text
Environment
Version
Release mode
Feature flags
```

But production parameters must not allow arbitrary unsafe commands.

---

# 43.61 Manual Approval

Manual approval MAY be used before sensitive environments.

Example:

```text
UAT Passed
   ↓
Approval
   ↓
Production
```

Approval should be tied to an identifiable user and audit trail.

---

# 43.62 Approval Anti-Pattern

Do not make every deployment require meaningless approval.

If:

```text
Everything requires approval
```

then eventually:

```text
Approval becomes rubber-stamping
```

Approval gates should exist where they reduce real risk.

---

# 43.63 Release Versioning

Release versions SHOULD use semantic versioning where appropriate:

```text
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
```

Example:

```text
2.4.1
```

---

# 43.64 Git Tags

Production releases SHOULD be associated with Git tags where appropriate.

Example:

```text
v2.4.1
```

---

# 43.65 Release Notes

Production releases SHOULD have release notes containing:

```text
Features
Bug fixes
Breaking changes
Security changes
Database changes
Infrastructure changes
Known issues
Rollback information
```

---

# 43.66 Database Migration

Database migrations MUST be treated as part of the release.

Example:

```text
Application v2
      +
Database migration v2
```

must be compatible.

---

# 43.67 Backward Compatibility

Prefer expand-and-contract migrations.

Concept:

```text
Old Application
      ↓
Compatible Schema Expansion
      ↓
New Application
      ↓
Data Migration
      ↓
Old Schema Removal
```

Avoid making destructive schema changes in the same release as an application that still depends on the old schema.

---

# 43.68 Zero-Downtime Deployment

Zero downtime requires more than:

```text
replicas > 1
```

It also requires consideration of:

```text
Readiness
Graceful shutdown
Connection draining
Database compatibility
Backward-compatible APIs
Load balancing
Rolling update configuration
```

---

# 43.69 Rolling Deployment

For Kubernetes workloads, rolling updates SHOULD be configured intentionally.

Important properties include:

```text
maxUnavailable
maxSurge
```

The correct values depend on the workload.

---

# 43.70 Graceful Shutdown

Spring Boot services SHOULD support graceful shutdown where required.

Concept:

```text
SIGTERM
 ↓
Stop accepting new requests
 ↓
Complete active work
 ↓
Shutdown
```

---

# 43.71 Deployment Verification

After deployment, verify:

```text
Pods
 ↓
Readiness
 ↓
Service endpoints
 ↓
Ingress
 ↓
Application health
 ↓
Logs
 ↓
Metrics
```

---

# 43.72 Smoke Tests

A production deployment SHOULD perform basic smoke validation.

Examples:

```text
GET health endpoint
Authentication flow
Critical API
Frontend availability
Database connectivity
```

Smoke tests should validate real system behavior, not merely Pod existence.

---

# 43.73 Automated Rollback

Automatic rollback MAY be implemented for clearly measurable failure conditions.

Possible signals:

```text
Error rate
HTTP 5xx
Latency
Pod crash rate
Readiness failures
```

Automatic rollback should only be enabled when the signal is reliable.

---

# 43.74 Rollback Trigger

Example:

```text
Deployment
   ↓
5xx rate > threshold
   ↓
Rollback
```

Do not automatically rollback based on noisy or poorly understood metrics.

---

# 43.75 Pipeline Notifications

CI/CD should notify relevant teams about important events.

Example:

```text
Build Failed
Security Scan Failed
Deployment Failed
Production Deployment Succeeded
Rollback Triggered
```

---

# 43.76 Pipeline Observability

Pipeline metrics SHOULD include:

```text
Build duration
Failure rate
Deployment frequency
Lead time
Rollback frequency
Mean recovery time
```

These support DevOps performance analysis.

---

# 43.77 DORA Metrics

Mediverse MAY track:

### Deployment Frequency

How frequently changes reach production.

### Lead Time for Changes

Time from code committed to production deployment.

### Change Failure Rate

Percentage of deployments causing production problems.

### Mean Time to Restore

How quickly service is restored after failure.

These metrics should improve engineering decisions, not become vanity targets.

---

# 43.78 Pipeline Performance

Optimize pipeline execution using:

```text
Dependency caching
Docker layer caching
Parallel tests
Incremental builds
Reusable CI agents
```

Do not optimize away important quality gates simply to make the pipeline faster.

---

# 43.79 Parallelization

Independent stages MAY run in parallel.

Example:

```text
              ┌── Unit Tests ──┐
Build ────────┼── SAST ────────┼──► Package
              └── Dependency ──┘
```

Only parallelize when dependencies permit it.

---

# 43.80 Pipeline Timeout

Every potentially long-running stage SHOULD have a timeout.

Examples:

```text
Integration Tests
Docker Build
Deployment
Smoke Tests
```

A stuck pipeline should not consume resources indefinitely.

---

# 43.81 Retry Policy

Retries SHOULD be used only for genuinely transient failures.

Good candidate:

```text
Temporary network failure
```

Bad candidate:

```text
Compilation error
Test failure
Invalid configuration
```

Repeatedly retrying deterministic failures hides problems.

---

# 43.82 Artifact Retention

CI systems SHOULD define retention policies for:

```text
Build artifacts
Logs
Test reports
Container images
SBOMs
Security reports
```

Retention should satisfy operational and compliance requirements.

---

# 43.83 SBOM
