```text
Helm Values / Manifests
          ↓
       Argo CD
          ↓
     Kubernetes
          ↓
   Mediverse Runtime
```

---

## 47.3 Git as Source of Truth

For GitOps-managed resources, Git MUST represent the intended production state.

Example:

```text
Git says:
replicas = 3
image = 1.8.2

Kubernetes says:
replicas = 5
image = 1.7.9
```

Argo CD should identify the difference as **drift**.

---

## 47.4 Manual Kubernetes Changes

Manual changes to GitOps-managed resources SHOULD NOT be used as a normal deployment mechanism.

Avoid:

```bash
kubectl edit deployment
kubectl set image deployment/...
kubectl scale deployment/...
```

as permanent production changes.

The correct workflow is:

```text
Change Git
   ↓
Review
   ↓
Argo CD
   ↓
Kubernetes
```

---

## 47.5 Repository Separation

Mediverse SHOULD separate application source and deployment configuration when the project scale justifies it.

Example:

```text
mediverse-backend
mediverse-frontend
mediverse-deployment
```

The deployment repository contains:

```text
Helm
Kubernetes configuration
Environment values
Argo CD Applications
Deployment policies
```

---

# 47.6 Recommended Repository Structure

A deployment repository MAY follow:

```text
mediverse-deployment/
├── charts/
│   ├── mediverse-api/
│   ├── mediverse-frontend/
│   └── mediverse-worker/
│
├── environments/
│   ├── dev/
│   ├── uat/
│   └── prod/
│
├── argocd/
│   ├── applications/
│   └── projects/
│
└── README.md
```

---

# 47.7 Environment Separation

Mediverse environments SHOULD be explicitly separated:

```text
DEV
 ↓
UAT
 ↓
PROD
```

Each environment SHOULD have controlled:

```text
Namespace
Values
Secrets
Resource configuration
Ingress
Replica configuration
External dependencies
```

---

# 47.8 Promotion Model

A recommended promotion flow is:

```text
Development
    ↓
Automated Tests
    ↓
UAT
    ↓
Validation
    ↓
Production
```

Promotion SHOULD be represented by a Git change.

---

# 47.9 Image Promotion

The container image SHOULD be built once and promoted between environments rather than rebuilt separately for each environment.

Preferred:

```text
Build image
    ↓
Scan image
    ↓
Registry
    ↓
DEV
    ↓
UAT
    ↓
PROD
```

Avoid:

```text
Build DEV image
Build UAT image
Build PROD image
```

because the artifacts may differ.

---

# 47.10 Immutable Artifacts

The artifact deployed to production should be identifiable.

Example:

```text
mediverse-api:1.8.2
```

or preferably an immutable digest.

---

# 47.11 CI vs CD Responsibilities

CI SHOULD handle:

```text
Build
Unit tests
Integration tests
Static analysis
Security scanning
Container build
Container scanning
Image publishing
```

GitOps/CD SHOULD handle:

```text
Deployment configuration
Environment promotion
Kubernetes reconciliation
Drift detection
Deployment health
Rollback
```

---

# 47.12 CI Should Not Own Production State

CI SHOULD NOT directly become the long-term source of truth for Kubernetes state.

Avoid:

```text
Jenkins
   ↓
kubectl apply
   ↓
Production
```

as the primary GitOps model.

Prefer:

```text
Jenkins
   ↓
Update deployment repository
   ↓
Argo CD
   ↓
Production
```

---

# 47.13 Argo CD Role

Argo CD acts as the Kubernetes GitOps controller.

Conceptually:

```text
Git
 ↓
Desired State
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Compare
 ↓
Reconcile
 ↓
Kubernetes
```

---

# 47.14 Argo CD Application

Each deployable Mediverse workload SHOULD be represented by an Argo CD Application where appropriate.

Example conceptual model:

```text
Application
mediverse-api-prod
        ↓
Git repository
        ↓
Helm chart
        ↓
prod values
        ↓
mediverse-prod namespace
```

---

# 47.15 Application Naming

Argo CD Applications SHOULD use predictable names.

Example:

```text
mediverse-api-dev
mediverse-api-uat
mediverse-api-prod
```

For multiple UAT environments:

```text
mediverse-api-uat1
mediverse-api-uat2
```

---

# 47.16 Argo CD Projects

Argo CD Projects SHOULD be used to establish application boundaries.

Projects can control:

```text
Allowed repositories
Allowed destinations
Allowed resource types
Application boundaries
```

---

# 47.17 Production Project

Production applications SHOULD belong to a controlled Argo CD Project.

Example conceptual structure:

```text
mediverse-dev-project
mediverse-uat-project
mediverse-prod-project
```

---

# 47.18 Repository Access

Argo CD should have access only to repositories it actually needs.

Avoid giving Argo CD unrestricted access to unrelated repositories.

---

# 47.19 Destination Restrictions

Production Argo CD Projects SHOULD restrict allowed Kubernetes destinations.

Concept:

```text
prod project
   ↓
prod cluster
   ↓
mediverse-prod namespace
```

This reduces accidental cross-environment deployment.

---

# 47.20 Namespace Restrictions

Where possible, applications SHOULD be restricted to their intended namespaces.

For example:

```text
mediverse-api-prod
       ↓
mediverse-prod
```

rather than allowing deployment anywhere in the cluster.

---

# 47.21 Automated Sync

Automated synchronization MAY be enabled for appropriate environments.

Typical strategy:

```text
DEV
→ automatic

UAT
→ automatic or controlled

PROD
→ controlled/approved
```

The exact model should match the organization's release policy.

---

# 47.22 Production Sync

Production deployments SHOULD have appropriate safeguards.

Possible controls:

```text
Pull request approval
Git branch protection
Argo CD Project restrictions
Sync windows
Manual approval
Automated policy checks
```

Do not rely on a single control.

---

# 47.23 Sync Policy

Argo CD sync configuration should be intentional.

Example conceptual configuration:

```yaml
syncPolicy:
  automated:
    prune: true
    selfHeal: true
```

These options MUST be evaluated carefully before enabling them in production.

---

# 47.24 Self-Healing

Self-healing means Argo CD can revert unauthorized/manual changes.

Concept:

```text
Git
 ↓
Desired state
 ↓
Kubernetes manually changed
 ↓
Drift detected
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Restore desired state
```

This is a major GitOps benefit.

---

# 47.25 Pruning

Pruning removes Kubernetes resources that are no longer defined in Git.

It is powerful but potentially destructive.

Therefore:

> **Prune should be enabled only after understanding the application's resource lifecycle.**

---

# 47.26 Drift Detection

Drift SHOULD be monitored.

Example:

```text
Git:
Deployment replicas = 3

Cluster:
Deployment replicas = 4

        ↓

OUT OF SYNC
```

Drift should be investigated rather than ignored.

---

# 47.27 Drift Categories

Drift can occur because of:

```text
Manual kubectl changes
Controllers
Operators
Mutating webhooks
Cluster defaults
External automation
Incorrect Git configuration
```

Not every difference necessarily represents malicious activity.

---

# 47.28 Ignore Differences

Argo CD may be configured to ignore known legitimate differences.

However:

> **Ignore rules must be narrow and documented.**

Do not use broad ignore rules merely to make applications appear healthy.

---

# 47.29 Health Status

Argo CD health status SHOULD be monitored.

Typical states include:

```text
Healthy
Progressing
Degraded
Suspended
Missing
Unknown
```

Production workloads should not remain degraded without investigation.

---

# 47.30 Sync Status

Teams should understand the difference between:

```text
Synced
OutOfSync
```

A workload can be:

```text
Synced + Degraded
```

which means configuration matches Git but the application itself is unhealthy.

---

# 47.31 Deployment Health

GitOps success does not automatically mean application success.

Pipeline:

```text
Git commit
 ↓
Argo sync successful
 ↓
Pods deployed
 ↓
Readiness passes
 ↓
Application health
```

Every layer should be validated.

---

# 47.32 Application Health Checks

Argo CD SHOULD use appropriate health assessment for critical workloads.

For Mediverse services, health should ultimately reflect:

```text
Pod state
Readiness
Service availability
Application health
```

---

# 47.33 Sync Waves

Sync waves MAY be used when resources have dependency ordering.

Example:

```text
Wave 0
Namespaces

Wave 1
Config / Secrets

Wave 2
Database migration

Wave 3
Backend

Wave 4
Frontend / Gateway
```

Do not use sync waves to hide poor architecture.

---

# 47.34 Database Migration Ordering

Database migrations require special care.

Example:

```text
Migration
   ↓
Backend
```

may be appropriate for backward-compatible migrations.

But:

```text
Destructive DB migration
   ↓
Old application
```

can break active workloads.

Database compatibility must be considered independently from Argo CD ordering.

---

# 47.35 App-of-Apps Pattern

For larger Mediverse deployments, an App-of-Apps pattern MAY be used.

Concept:

```text
Root Application
       ↓
 ┌─────┼─────────┐
 ↓     ↓         ↓
API  Frontend  Worker
 ↓     ↓         ↓
Dev/UAT/Prod Applications
```

---

# 47.36 App-of-Apps Caution

The root Argo CD application becomes highly privileged and operationally important.

It MUST be protected carefully.

Do not treat App-of-Apps as merely a convenience folder.

---

# 47.37 ApplicationSet

For multiple environments or services, Argo CD ApplicationSet MAY reduce repetitive Application definitions.

Example:

```text
Service × Environment
```

can generate:

```text
auth-dev
auth-uat
auth-prod

user-dev
user-uat
user-prod
```

---

# 47.38 Avoid Application Duplication

If dozens of Argo CD Applications differ only by:

```text
service
environment
namespace
values
```

consider whether ApplicationSet is more maintainable.

---

# 47.39 Git Branch Strategy

GitOps deployment repositories SHOULD use a clear branch strategy.

Possible model:

```text
main
 ↓
production

develop
 ↓
development
```

Alternatively, environment promotion can be represented entirely through directories or pull requests.

The project must choose one model and document it.

---

# 47.40 Environment Branches vs Directories

Both can work:

### Branch model

```text
dev branch
uat branch
prod branch
```

### Directory model

```text
environments/
├── dev/
├── uat/
└── prod/
```

For Mediverse, a **directory-based environment structure** is generally easier to inspect and promote through pull requests.

---

# 47.41 Pull Requests

Production configuration changes SHOULD go through pull requests.

PR review should verify:

```text
Image
Replicas
Resources
Environment
Ingress
Secrets references
Security policies
Dependencies
```

---

# 47.42 CODEOWNERS

Deployment repositories SHOULD use CODEOWNERS where supported.

Example concept:

```text
prod/
 ↓
Platform team approval

security/
 ↓
Security approval
```

---

# 47.43 Branch Protection

Protected branches SHOULD enforce:

```text
Pull request
Required review
Status checks
No force push
No direct production changes
```

---

# 47.44 Commit Messages

Deployment commits SHOULD be descriptive.

Good:

```text
Deploy mediverse-api 1.8.2 to UAT
```

Bad:

```text
update
fix
test
changes
```

---

# 47.45 Commit Traceability

A production deployment should be traceable:

```text
Git commit
 ↓
Helm values
 ↓
Image version
 ↓
Argo CD sync
 ↓
Kubernetes resources
```

An engineer should be able to answer:

> **Which source code version is running in production?**

---

# 47.46 Image-to-Commit Mapping

The CI pipeline SHOULD attach source version metadata to the image.

Example:

```text
Image:
mediverse-api:1.8.2

Git:
commit abc1234
```

This dramatically improves incident investigation.

---

# 47.47 Deployment Metadata

Kubernetes workloads SHOULD expose useful metadata such as:

```text
Application
Version
Environment
Git commit
Build number
```

through labels or annotations where appropriate.

---

# 47.48 Secret Management

GitOps repositories MUST NOT become secret dumps.

Preferred architecture:

```text
Git
 ↓
Secret reference
 ↓
External Secret Manager
 ↓
Kubernetes Secret
 ↓
Application
```

---

# 47.49 Sealed Secrets / External Secrets

If a Git-managed secret mechanism is used, the selected solution must be formally standardized.

Possible technologies include:

```text
Sealed Secrets
External Secrets Operator
Vault integrations
Cloud secret managers
```

Do not mix multiple approaches without architectural justification.

---

# 47.50 Argo CD RBAC

Argo CD users SHOULD receive least-privilege permissions.

Possible roles:

```text
Viewer
Developer
Release Operator
Platform Administrator
```

---

# 47.51 Production Argo CD Access

Production Argo CD access SHOULD be more restrictive than development access.

Example:

```text
Developer
 ↓
View DEV
Sync DEV

Release Operator
 ↓
View UAT
Sync UAT

Production Operator
 ↓
Controlled PROD sync
```

---

# 47.52 SSO

Argo CD SHOULD integrate with an organizational identity provider where available.

This provides:

```text
Central identity
Access control
User lifecycle
Auditability
```

---

# 47.53 Shared Argo CD Accounts

Shared administrative accounts SHOULD NOT be used as the normal operating model.

Individual identities provide better accountability.

---

# 47.54 Argo CD Secrets

Argo CD credentials and repository credentials MUST be protected.

Never commit:

```text
Repository passwords
SSH private keys
API tokens
Cloud credentials
```

into Git repositories.

---

# 47.55 Argo CD Repository Authentication

Repository access SHOULD use appropriate credentials such as:

```text
Deploy keys
Access tokens
SSH credentials
```

with minimum required permissions.

---

# 47.56 Argo CD Monitoring

Monitor:

```text
Application sync status
Application health
Sync failures
Repository errors
Controller errors
API errors
Resource failures
```

---

# 47.57 Notifications

Argo CD SHOULD integrate with the Mediverse notification system where appropriate.

Important events:

```text
Production deployment
Deployment failure
Application degraded
Sync failure
Repeated reconciliation failure
```

---

# 47.58 Deployment Failure Handling

When Argo CD reports failure:

```text
STOP
 ↓
Inspect sync operation
 ↓
Inspect Kubernetes events
 ↓
Inspect application logs
 ↓
Inspect rendered configuration
 ↓
Identify root cause
 ↓
Fix Git
 ↓
Reconcile
```

Do not repeatedly press **Sync** without understanding the failure.

---

# 47.59 Rollback Strategy

GitOps rollback SHOULD preferably be Git-based.

Example:

```text
Current:
1.8.2

Problem detected

Git:
revert to 1.8.1

      ↓

Argo CD
      ↓
1.8.1
```

This preserves the audit trail.

---

# 47.60 Emergency Rollback

An emergency operational rollback MAY use Argo CD/Helm capabilities directly when necessary.

However, the Git repository must subsequently be reconciled so that the emergency state does not become undocumented drift.

---

# 47.61 Roll Forward vs Rollback

Rollback is not always the correct solution.

If the problem is:

```text
Application bug
```

rollback may be appropriate.

If the problem is:

```text
Database migration
```

rollback may be dangerous.

If the problem is:

```text
Infrastructure capacity
```

scaling/resource correction may be better.

Always determine the failure class first.

---

# 47.62 Sync Windows

Production deployment windows MAY be defined to prevent deployments during sensitive periods.

Example:

```text
Business-critical hours
 ↓
No automatic production sync
```

Emergency deployment procedures should remain available.

---

# 47.63 Progressive Delivery

For critical Mediverse services, GitOps MAY integrate with progressive delivery mechanisms:

```text
Canary
Blue-Green
Rolling
A/B
```

Example:

```text
v1
 ↓
5% v2
 ↓
Metrics
 ↓
25%
 ↓
50%
 ↓
100%
```

---

# 47.64 Deployment Verification

Progressive delivery should use measurable signals:

```text
Error rate
Latency
HTTP 5xx
CPU
Memory
Application health
Business metrics
```

---

# 47.65 GitOps Security Checklist

### Git

* [ ] Branch protection
* [ ] PR review
* [ ] CODEOWNERS
* [ ] No secrets
* [ ] Immutable image references
* [ ] Traceable commits

### Argo CD

* [ ] RBAC
* [ ] SSO where possible
* [ ] Project restrictions
* [ ] Repository restrictions
* [ ] Destination restrictions
* [ ] Auditability
* [ ] Notifications
* [ ] Monitoring

### Kubernetes

* [ ] Namespace restrictions
* [ ] NetworkPolicies
* [ ] ServiceAccount restrictions
* [ ] Pod security
* [ ] Resource controls

---

# 47.66 Operational Checklist

Before production sync:

```text
[ ] Correct repository
[ ] Correct branch/revision
[ ] Correct environment
[ ] Correct namespace
[ ] Correct image
[ ] Correct image digest/tag
[ ] Correct values
[ ] No secret leakage
[ ] Security validation passed
[ ] Health checks configured
[ ] Migration compatibility verified
[ ] Rollback strategy understood
```

---

# 47.67 Definition of Done

Mediverse GitOps implementation is production-ready when:

* [ ] Git is the source of truth
* [ ] Application and deployment repositories are appropriately structured
* [ ] Helm charts are standardized
* [ ] Environment configuration is controlled
* [ ] Argo CD Applications are defined
* [ ] Argo CD Projects restrict access
* [ ] Repository access is secured
* [ ] Kubernetes destinations are restricted
* [ ] RBAC is implemented
* [ ] Production sync is controlled
* [ ] Drift detection is active
* [ ] Health status is monitored
* [ ] Secrets are externally managed
* [ ] Image versions are immutable
* [ ] Deployment traceability exists
* [ ] Rollback has been tested
* [ ] Notifications are configured
* [ ] Production deployment procedure is documented

---

# 47.68 Core Principles

Mediverse GitOps follows these rules:

1. **Git is the source of truth.**
2. **Kubernetes should be reconciled, not manually maintained.**
3. **CI builds artifacts; GitOps deploys them.**
4. **Build once and promote the same artifact.**
5. **Production configuration requires controlled review.**
6. **Argo CD permissions must follow least privilege.**
7. **Environment boundaries must be explicit.**
8. **Drift must be visible and investigated.**
9. **Rollback should preserve auditability.**
10. **Secrets must never become part of the Git history.**
11. **Deployment success and application health are different things.**
12. **Automated synchronization must not bypass production safety controls.**
13. **Every production workload must be traceable from source commit → image → Helm → Argo CD → Kubernetes.**
14. **GitOps automation should reduce human error, not automate bad configuration faster.**
15. **If engineers routinely need `kubectl` to keep production working, the GitOps implementation is incomplete.**

> **The goal of Mediverse GitOps is not simply automated deployment. It is a reproducible, auditable, self-correcting path from approved source code to a known production state.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 48: CI/CD Pipeline Standards.**

# CSDG — Chapter 48

## CI/CD Pipeline Standards

### 48.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the standards for building, testing, scanning, packaging, publishing, and promoting Mediverse applications through CI/CD.

Core principle:

> **CI proves that an artifact is buildable, testable, secure, and deployable. CD promotes that verified artifact through controlled environments.**

---

## 48.2 Mediverse CI/CD Flow

The standard pipeline SHOULD follow:

```text
Developer
   ↓
Git Push / Pull Request
   ↓
Source Validation
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Unit Tests
   ↓
Integration Tests
   ↓
Static Analysis
   ↓
Security Scan
   ↓
Package
   ↓
Container Build
   ↓
Container Scan
   ↓
Push Image
   ↓
Update Deployment Configuration
   ↓
Argo CD
   ↓
DEV
   ↓
UAT
   ↓
PROD
```

---

# 48.3 CI/CD Responsibilities

### CI

CI SHOULD perform:

* Compilation
* Unit testing
* Integration testing
* Static code analysis
* Dependency analysis
* Security scanning
* Packaging
* Container image creation
* Container image scanning
* Artifact publishing

### CD / GitOps

CD SHOULD handle:

* Environment promotion
* Deployment configuration
* Kubernetes reconciliation
* Deployment health
* Drift detection
* Rollout verification
* Rollback

---

# 48.4 Pipeline as Code

CI/CD pipelines MUST be defined as code.

Examples:

```text
Jenkinsfile
.github/workflows/*.yml
.gitlab-ci.yml
```

Pipeline configuration should NOT depend on undocumented manual configuration inside the CI server.

---

# 48.5 Jenkins Standard

If Jenkins is used for Mediverse, pipelines SHOULD be implemented using:

```text
Jenkinsfile
```

stored with the application source.

Recommended model:

```text
Repository
├── src/
├── Dockerfile
├── Jenkinsfile
└── ...
```

---

# 48.6 Pipeline Stages

A standard Mediverse backend pipeline SHOULD contain stages similar to:

```text
Checkout
   ↓
Validate
   ↓
Compile
   ↓
Unit Test
   ↓
Integration Test
   ↓
Code Quality
   ↓
Security Scan
   ↓
Package
   ↓
Docker Build
   ↓
Image Scan
   ↓
Push Image
   ↓
Update Deployment
```

Not every service requires every stage, but skipped stages must have a documented reason.

---

# 48.7 Pull Request Pipeline

Pull requests SHOULD execute a validation pipeline.

Typical flow:

```text
PR
 ↓
Compile
 ↓
Unit Tests
 ↓
Static Analysis
 ↓
Dependency Scan
 ↓
Build Verification
```

A PR SHOULD NOT merge if mandatory quality gates fail.

---

# 48.8 Main Branch Pipeline

After merge:

```text
main
 ↓
Full CI
 ↓
Build Artifact
 ↓
Security Scan
 ↓
Container Build
 ↓
Registry
```

Production deployment should occur through the approved GitOps promotion process.

---

# 48.9 Branch Protection

Protected branches SHOULD require:

* Pull request
* Required reviews
* Successful CI
* Security checks
* No direct force-push
* No direct unauthorized production changes

---

# 48.10 Build Once

A major Mediverse CI/CD principle:

> **Build once; promote the same artifact.**

Bad:

```text
DEV
 ↓
build image A

UAT
 ↓
build image B

PROD
 ↓
build image C
```

Preferred:

```text
Source
 ↓
Build image A
 ↓
DEV
 ↓
UAT
 ↓
PROD
```

---

# 48.11 Artifact Identity

Every build artifact MUST be uniquely identifiable.

Example:

```text
mediverse-api:1.8.2
```

Better:

```text
mediverse-api:1.8.2-abc1234
```

or use a digest.

---

# 48.12 `latest` Tag

Production pipelines MUST NOT use:

```text
latest
```

as the deployment identifier.

Why?

Because:

```text
latest
```

does not guarantee which artifact is actually running.

---

# 48.13 Versioning

Artifact versions SHOULD be generated consistently.

Possible sources:

```text
Git tag
Semantic version
Build number
Commit SHA
Release version
```

The project MUST choose a consistent strategy.

---

# 48.14 Git Commit Traceability

Each production artifact SHOULD be traceable to:

```text
Git repository
Commit SHA
Branch/tag
Build number
Pipeline execution
Container image
Deployment
```

---

# 48.15 Build Reproducibility

Builds SHOULD be reproducible.

Avoid depending on:

```text
Developer machine state
Unpinned dependencies
Mutable external binaries
Undocumented environment variables
```

---

# 48.16 Java Build Standard

For Spring Boot services, the pipeline SHOULD explicitly define:

```text
Java version
Maven/Gradle version
Build command
Test command
Packaging command
```

Example:

```bash
./mvnw clean verify
```

Using the Maven Wrapper is preferred when available.

---

# 48.17 Maven Wrapper

For Maven applications, prefer:

```text
mvnw
mvnw.cmd
```

over assuming that the Jenkins agent has the correct Maven version installed.

This reduces environment inconsistency.

---

# 48.18 Node / React Build

For React applications, CI SHOULD explicitly control:

```text
Node.js version
Package manager
Dependency installation
Build command
Test command
```

Example:

```bash
npm ci
npm run build
```

---

# 48.19 Lock Files

Dependency lock files MUST be committed where supported.

Examples:

```text
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml
```

Do not casually regenerate lock files during CI.

---

# 48.20 Dependency Installation

CI SHOULD prefer deterministic installation.

For npm:

```bash
npm ci
```

is generally preferred over:

```bash
npm install
```

for CI environments.

---

# 48.21 Unit Tests

Unit tests SHOULD execute before expensive downstream stages.

Example:

```text
Compile
 ↓
Unit Tests
 ↓
Fail fast
```

There is no reason to build and publish a Docker image if the unit test suite already failed.

---

# 48.22 Test Failure

A mandatory test failure MUST fail the pipeline.

Bad:

```text
Tests failed
 ↓
Pipeline continues
 ↓
Image published
```

Good:

```text
Tests failed
 ↓
Pipeline STOP
```

---

# 48.23 Integration Tests

Integration tests SHOULD validate interactions between components such as:

```text
Spring Boot
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka
External services
```

where required.

---

# 48.24 Test Isolation

Tests SHOULD avoid depending on shared mutable environments whenever possible.

Prefer isolated resources such as:

```text
Testcontainers
Ephemeral databases
Mock services
Dedicated test namespaces
```

depending on the test type.

---

# 48.25 Testcontainers

For Spring Boot integration testing, Testcontainers MAY be used to provide realistic infrastructure dependencies.

Example:

```text
JUnit
 ↓
Testcontainers
 ↓
PostgreSQL
 ↓
Application
```

This is often more reliable than assuming a developer-installed PostgreSQL instance.

---

# 48.26 Code Coverage

Code coverage SHOULD be measured for meaningful test suites.

Coverage should not become a vanity metric.

Example:

```text
80% coverage
```

does not automatically mean:

```text
80% quality
```

Critical business and security paths require appropriate tests regardless of the raw percentage.

---

# 48.27 Quality Gates

Quality gates SHOULD evaluate:

```text
Test success
Coverage
Bugs
Vulnerabilities
Code smells
Duplications
Security issues
```

---

# 48.28 SonarQube

If SonarQube is part of Mediverse CI, the pipeline SHOULD integrate it before artifact publication.

Concept:

```text
Build
 ↓
Tests
 ↓
SonarQube
 ↓
Quality Gate
 ↓
Continue
```

---

# 48.29 Quality Gate Failure

If the project defines SonarQube as a mandatory gate:

```text
Quality Gate failed
       ↓
Pipeline failed
       ↓
No production artifact
```

Do not ignore quality-gate failures simply to get a green deployment.

---

# 48.30 Security Scanning

CI SHOULD include multiple security layers.

Recommended:

```text
Source Code
   ↓
SAST

Dependencies
   ↓
SCA

Container
   ↓
Image Scan

Deployment
   ↓
IaC / Kubernetes Scan
```

---

# 48.31 SAST

Static Application Security Testing SHOULD identify issues such as:

```text
Injection risks
Unsafe APIs
Hard-coded secrets
Authentication weaknesses
Authorization problems
Dangerous coding patterns
```

---

# 48.32 Dependency Scanning

Third-party dependencies MUST be scanned for known vulnerabilities.

For Java:

```text
Maven dependencies
```

For React:

```text
npm dependencies
```

---

# 48.33 Dependency Pinning

Avoid uncontrolled dependency upgrades inside CI.

A pipeline should not unexpectedly deploy:

```text
Dependency version changed overnight
```

without a source-control change.

---

# 48.34 Secret Scanning

Repositories SHOULD be scanned for accidental secrets.

Detect:

```text
API keys
Passwords
Tokens
Private keys
Cloud credentials
Database credentials
```

---

# 48.35 Secret Leak Response

If a secret is committed:

> **Deleting the file is not enough.**

The secret SHOULD be:

```text
Revoked
Rotated
Removed from repository history where required
Audited
```

---

# 48.36 Container Build

Container images SHOULD be built only after application validation.

Preferred:

```text
Tests
 ↓
Quality
 ↓
Security
 ↓
Docker Build
```

---

# 48.37 Multi-Stage Docker Builds

Production images SHOULD use multi-stage builds where appropriate.

Example concept:

```text
Build Stage
   ↓
Compile
   ↓
Runtime Stage
   ↓
Minimal Image
```

This reduces unnecessary packages and attack surface.

---

# 48.38 Container Image Size

Images SHOULD contain only what the application needs.

Avoid shipping:

```text
Build tools
Compilers
Source code
Debug utilities
Unused packages
```

in the final runtime image unless required.

---

# 48.39 Base Images

Base images SHOULD be:

* Official
* Trusted
* Maintained
* Minimal
* Version controlled
* Security scanned

Avoid arbitrary images from unknown registries.

---

# 48.40 Container Scanning

Every production-bound image SHOULD be scanned.

Example findings:

```text
Critical
High
Medium
Low
```

The project must define which severities block deployment.

---

# 48.41 Critical Vulnerabilities

Critical vulnerabilities SHOULD block production publication unless an approved exception exists.

Exceptions MUST be documented.

---

# 48.42 Vulnerability Exceptions

Security exceptions SHOULD include:

```text
Vulnerability
Reason
Affected component
Risk assessment
Mitigation
Owner
Expiration date
```

Do not create permanent "false positive" exceptions without review.

---

# 48.43 Artifact Registry

Container images SHOULD be pushed to a controlled registry.

Example:

```text
Nexus
AWS ECR
Azure Container Registry
Google Artifact Registry
Harbor
```

The selected registry must be standardized for the environment.

---

# 48.44 Registry Naming

Use predictable image names.

Example:

```text
registry.example.com/mediverse/api
registry.example.com/mediverse/frontend
registry.example.com/mediverse/notification
```

---

# 48.45 Registry Access

CI credentials for registries MUST follow least privilege.

The pipeline should have permission to:

```text
Push
Pull
```

only where necessary.

---

# 48.46 Credentials

CI credentials MUST NOT be embedded in:

```text
Jenkinsfile
Shell scripts
Dockerfile
Git repository
Application configuration
```

Use the CI platform's credential management.

---

# 48.47 Pipeline Secrets

Credentials SHOULD be injected only for the stage that needs them.

Avoid making all credentials globally available to the entire pipeline.

---

# 48.48 Environment Variables

Pipeline configuration MAY use environment variables for non-sensitive configuration.

Sensitive values should use secure credential mechanisms.

---

# 48.49 Deployment Repository Update

After a successful image build:

```text
CI
 ↓
Image published
 ↓
Update image version in deployment repository
 ↓
Git commit / PR
 ↓
Argo CD
```

This creates an auditable promotion event.

---

# 48.50 Automated Image Update

An automation tool MAY update:

```yaml
image:
  tag: "1.8.2"
```

in the deployment repository.

However, automated updates MUST still follow repository protection rules.

---

# 48.51 GitOps Boundary

The CI pipeline SHOULD NOT bypass GitOps by directly changing production Kubernetes resources when GitOps is the designated deployment mechanism.

Preferred:

```text
CI
 ↓
Git
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Kubernetes
```

---

# 48.52 Environment Promotion

Promotion SHOULD be explicit.

Example:

```text
Image 1.8.2
     ↓
DEV
     ↓
UAT
     ↓
Approval
     ↓
PROD
```

---

# 48.53 Promotion Evidence

Before production promotion, retain evidence such as:

```text
Test results
Security scan
Quality gate
Image digest
UAT verification
Approval
Deployment commit
```

---

# 48.54 Production Approval

Production promotion SHOULD require appropriate authorization.

Possible controls:

```text
PR approval
Manual approval gate
Release manager approval
Change-management process
Automated policy
```

---

# 48.55 Pipeline Failure Strategy

A failed pipeline should provide enough information to determine:

```text
What failed?
Where did it fail?
Why did it fail?
What artifact was produced?
Was anything published?
Was anything deployed?
```

---

# 48.56 Fail Fast

Cheap validation should happen before expensive operations.

Preferred:

```text
Syntax
 ↓
Compile
 ↓
Unit Tests
 ↓
Static Analysis
 ↓
Integration Tests
 ↓
Container Build
 ↓
Image Scan
```

Do not spend several minutes building an image if compilation already fails.

---

# 48.57 Parallelization

Independent pipeline stages MAY execute in parallel.

Example:

```text
             ┌── Unit Tests ──┐
Build ───────┼── SAST ────────┼──→ Continue
             └── Dependency ──┘
```

Parallelization should improve speed without making the pipeline difficult to understand.

---

# 48.58 Pipeline Timeout

Long-running stages SHOULD have explicit timeouts.

This prevents:

```text
Hung build
 ↓
Agent occupied indefinitely
```

---

# 48.59 Retry Strategy

Retries SHOULD be used only for transient failures.

Good candidates:

```text
Temporary network failure
Registry timeout
Transient infrastructure issue
```

Do not automatically retry deterministic failures such as:

```text
Compilation failure
Test failure
Security failure
Invalid configuration
```

---

# 48.60 Workspace Cleanup

CI agents SHOULD clean workspaces appropriately.

Avoid stale files causing:

```text
False build success
Unexpected dependency behavior
Incorrect artifacts
```

---

# 48.61 Build Agents

Build agents SHOULD be:

```text
Version controlled
Reproducible
Secure
Minimal
Consistently configured
```

Containerized build agents are often useful for this purpose.

---

# 48.62 Jenkins Agent Security

Jenkins agents MUST NOT have unnecessary privileges.

Avoid giving a generic build agent unrestricted:

```text
Cluster admin
Cloud admin
Database admin
```

permissions.

---

# 48.63 Docker-in-Docker

Docker build strategies such as:

```text
Docker-in-Docker
Docker socket mounting
Kaniko
BuildKit
```

must be selected deliberately based on security and operational requirements.

Do not expose the host Docker socket to builds without understanding the security implications.

---

# 48.64 Pipeline Isolation

Untrusted pull-request builds SHOULD be isolated from highly privileged credentials.

A malicious PR should not be able to access:

```text
Production credentials
Cloud admin credentials
Production registry credentials
```

---

# 48.65 Artifact Retention

CI artifacts SHOULD have defined retention policies.

Examples:

```text
Test reports
Coverage reports
Build logs
SBOM
Scan results
Packages
```

Retention should balance auditability and storage cost.

---

# 48.66 SBOM

Production artifacts SHOULD have a Software Bill of Materials where practical.

The SBOM should help answer:

```text
What dependencies exist inside this artifact?
```

---

# 48.67 SBOM Traceability

An SBOM SHOULD be associated with:

```text
Application
Version
Image
Digest
Build
```

---

# 48.68 Build Metadata

The generated application/container SHOULD expose build information where appropriate:

```text
Version
Git commit
Build timestamp
Build number
```

Do not expose sensitive CI information.

---

# 48.69 Release Pipeline

A production release pipeline SHOULD look like:

```text
PR
 ↓
CI Validation
 ↓
Merge
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Scan
 ↓
Publish Artifact
 ↓
DEV
 ↓
UAT
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
Production Approval
 ↓
GitOps Promotion
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Production
```

---

# 48.70 Rollback

Rollback MUST be possible.

Preferred:

```text
Git revert
 ↓
Deployment repository
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Previous known-good image
```

Emergency rollback MAY use operational tooling, but Git must subsequently be reconciled.

---

# 48.71 Database Changes

Database migrations MUST be treated separately from application deployment.

A pipeline must consider:

```text
Backward compatibility
Migration ordering
Rollback feasibility
Data loss
Long-running migrations
Locking
Downtime
```

---

# 48.72 Backward-Compatible Migration

A safer deployment pattern is:

```text
Deploy compatible schema
       ↓
Deploy application
       ↓
Migrate traffic
       ↓
Remove obsolete schema later
```

Avoid combining destructive database changes with the first application release that requires them.

---

# 48.73 Zero-Downtime Deployment

Where required, the pipeline and Kubernetes strategy SHOULD support:

```text
Rolling deployment
Readiness probes
Graceful shutdown
Connection draining
Backward-compatible APIs
```

---

# 48.74 Deployment Verification

After deployment:

```text
Argo CD Healthy
       ↓
Pods Ready
       ↓
Service Available
       ↓
Smoke Test
       ↓
Metrics Healthy
```

---

# 48.75 Smoke Tests

Production deployment SHOULD have lightweight smoke tests.

Examples:

```text
GET /actuator/health
GET /api/health
Authentication endpoint
Critical read operation
```

Smoke tests should not mutate critical production data.

---

# 48.76 Automated Rollback

Automated rollback MAY be used when clear health criteria exist.

Example:

```text
5xx > threshold
       ↓
Rollback
```

But automated rollback should not be introduced without reliable observability.

Otherwise the system can repeatedly deploy and rollback without solving the root problem.

---

# 48.77 Pipeline Observability

CI/CD itself SHOULD be observable.

Track:

```text
Pipeline duration
Failure rate
Deployment frequency
Lead time
Rollback frequency
Mean time to recovery
```

These support engineering-performance analysis.

---

# 48.78 DORA Metrics

Mediverse SHOULD consider tracking:

```text
Deployment Frequency
Lead Time for Changes
Change Failure Rate
Mean Time to Recovery
```

These metrics should improve engineering decisions, not become targets that encourage reckless releases.

---

# 48.79 Pipeline Notifications

Important events SHOULD be communicated through the team's approved notification channels.

Examples:

```text
Build failed
Security gate failed
UAT deployment completed
Production deployment completed
Production deployment failed
Rollback executed
```

---

# 48.80 CI/CD Audit Trail

The system SHOULD preserve:

```text
Who triggered the pipeline
What commit was built
What artifact was produced
What scans ran
What approval occurred
What was deployed
Where it was deployed
When it happened
```

---

# 48.81 Pipeline Security Checklist

* [ ] Pipeline as code
* [ ] Protected branches
* [ ] Least-privilege CI credentials
* [ ] No hard-coded secrets
* [ ] Secret scanning
* [ ] Dependency scanning
* [ ] SAST
* [ ] Container scanning
* [ ] Controlled registry
* [ ] Immutable artifacts
* [ ] PR isolation
* [ ] Secure build agents
* [ ] Artifact traceability

---

# 48.82 CI/CD Quality Checklist

* [ ] Compilation
* [ ] Unit tests
* [ ] Integration tests
* [ ] Code coverage
* [ ] SonarQube quality gate
* [ ] Dependency scan
* [ ] Container scan
* [ ] SBOM
* [ ] Artifact publication
* [ ] Deployment verification
* [ ] Smoke tests
* [ ] Rollback capability

---

# 48.83 Definition of Done

The Mediverse CI/CD implementation is production-ready when:

* [ ] Pipeline is defined as code
* [ ] PR validation is automated
* [ ] Main branch validation is automated
* [ ] Tests execute automatically
* [ ] Quality gates are enforced
* [ ] Security scanning is integrated
* [ ] Container images are scanned
* [ ] Artifacts are immutable
* [ ] Registry access is secured
* [ ] Deployment repository is integrated
* [ ] Argo CD performs deployment
* [ ] Environment promotion is controlled
* [ ] Production approval is enforced
* [ ] Deployment verification exists
* [ ] Rollback has been tested
* [ ] Auditability exists
* [ ] Pipeline metrics are available

---

# 48.84 Core Principles

Mediverse CI/CD follows:

1. **Fail fast.**
2. **Build once.**
3. **Test before publishing.**
4. **Scan before deployment.**
5. **Never deploy mutable artifacts to production.**
6. **CI creates verified artifacts; GitOps deploys them.**
7. **Production deployments must be traceable.**
8. **Secrets belong in secure credential systems, not pipeline code.**
9. **Security gates are engineering controls, not optional decorations.**
10. **Retries are for transient failures, not broken code.**
11. **Rollback must be tested.**
12. **Database changes require independent compatibility analysis.**
13. **Production promotion must have appropriate authorization.**
14. **The pipeline should make the safe path the easiest path.**
15. **A green pipeline is not proof that the application is healthy; post-deployment verification is mandatory.**

> **The objective of Mediverse CI/CD is not simply to automate Jenkins jobs. It is to create a reliable chain of evidence from source code → tested artifact → secured image → approved environment → healthy production workload.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 49: Observability, Logging & Monitoring Standards.**

# CSDG — Chapter 49

## Observability, Logging & Monitoring Standards

### 49.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the standards for **logging, metrics, monitoring, tracing, alerting, and operational visibility** across the Mediverse platform.

Core principle:

> **If a production system cannot tell us what happened, where it happened, and why it happened, it is not operationally complete.**

---

## 49.2 Observability Model

Mediverse observability SHOULD be based on three primary signals:

```text
                OBSERVABILITY
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       ↓             ↓             ↓
     Logs         Metrics        Traces
       │             │             │
   What happened?  How much?    Where/Why?
```

These signals SHOULD work together rather than being treated as independent systems.

---

## 49.3 Observability Architecture

Recommended conceptual architecture:

```text
Mediverse Applications
        │
        ├── Logs ───────→ Log Platform
        │
        ├── Metrics ────→ Prometheus
        │                       ↓
        │                    Grafana
        │
        └── Traces ─────→ OpenTelemetry
                                ↓
                         Trace Backend
```

---

# 49.4 Observability Responsibilities

### Application

Applications SHOULD produce:

```text
Structured logs
Business metrics
Application metrics
Trace context
Health information
```

### Platform

The platform SHOULD provide:

```text
Collection
Storage
Visualization
Alerting
Retention
Access control
```

---

# 49.5 Logging Standard

All Mediverse backend services SHOULD use structured logging.

Preferred:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-09T10:15:22Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "mediverse-api",
  "traceId": "abc123",
  "message": "Unable to retrieve patient record"
}
```

Avoid relying exclusively on unstructured messages such as:

```text
Something went wrong!!!
```

---

# 49.6 Log Levels

Standard log levels:

```text
TRACE
DEBUG
INFO
WARN
ERROR
```

Use them intentionally.

### TRACE

Extremely detailed diagnostic information.

Normally disabled in production.

### DEBUG

Developer-level troubleshooting information.

Should normally be disabled or restricted in production.

### INFO

Normal application lifecycle and important business events.

### WARN

Unexpected situation that does not necessarily mean failure.

### ERROR

An operation failed or an important system problem occurred.

---

# 49.7 Production Log Level

Production SHOULD generally use:

```text
INFO
WARN
ERROR
```

with DEBUG temporarily enabled only when justified.

Do not run every production service permanently at DEBUG.

---

# 49.8 Logging Sensitive Data

The following MUST NOT be logged:

```text
Passwords
JWT tokens
Refresh tokens
API secrets
Private keys
Database passwords
Patient-sensitive information
Unnecessary personal information
```

This is especially important for a medical platform.

---

# 49.9 Medical Data Logging

Mediverse MUST follow the principle:

> **Log the event, not the sensitive payload.**

Bad:

```text
Patient:
Name = ...
Diagnosis = ...
Prescription = ...
```

Better:

```text
Patient record access completed
patientIdHash=...
userId=...
action=READ
```

Even identifiers should be minimized according to the platform's privacy requirements.

---

# 49.10 Exception Logging

Exceptions SHOULD contain enough context to troubleshoot the problem.

Bad:

```text
ERROR: failed
```

Better:

```text
ERROR
service=mediverse-api
operation=fetchPatientRecord
patientRecordId=<safe-reference>
errorType=RecordNotFoundException
```

Do not log sensitive exception payloads.

---

# 49.11 Stack Traces

Stack traces SHOULD be captured for unexpected server-side failures.

However, they MUST NOT expose:

```text
Secrets
Credentials
Sensitive request data
Authorization headers
Patient information
```

---

# 49.12 Correlation ID

Requests SHOULD have a correlation identifier.

Example:

```text
X-Correlation-ID
```

Concept:

```text
Client
  ↓
API Gateway
  ↓
Auth Service
  ↓
Patient Service
  ↓
Database
```

All relevant services should be able to associate logs with the same request.

---

# 49.13 Trace ID

Where distributed tracing is implemented, a trace ID SHOULD identify the complete distributed request.

Example:

```text
Trace
abc123
 │
 ├── API Gateway
 ├── Auth Service
 ├── Patient Service
 └── Notification Service
```

---

# 49.14 Correlation vs Trace ID

These should not be confused.

```text
Correlation ID
→ Application-level request association

Trace ID
→ Distributed tracing context
```

Where OpenTelemetry is used, trace context should be propagated consistently.

---

# 49.15 Structured Log Fields

Common fields SHOULD include:

```text
timestamp
level
service
environment
host/pod
logger
message
traceId
spanId
correlationId
```

Additional fields should be added only when useful.

---

# 49.16 Environment

Logs SHOULD identify the environment.

Example:

```text
environment=dev
environment=uat
environment=prod
```

This prevents confusion during incident analysis.

---

# 49.17 Service Identification

Every log should make it possible to identify the originating service.

Example:

```text
service=mediverse-auth
service=mediverse-user
service=mediverse-api
service=mediverse-notification
```

---

# 49.18 Kubernetes Context

Where useful, logs SHOULD include:

```text
namespace
pod
container
node
```

This helps identify infrastructure-specific failures.

---

# 49.19 Log Aggregation

Application logs SHOULD be centrally collected.

Concept:

```text
Pods
 ↓
Log Collector
 ↓
Central Log Platform
 ↓
Search / Dashboard / Alert
```

Possible technologies include:

```text
ELK
OpenSearch
Loki
Fluent Bit
Fluentd
```

The project should standardize one primary approach rather than creating an unnecessary mixture.

---

# 49.20 Logging Format

JSON logging is RECOMMENDED for backend services because it makes logs easier to:

```text
Search
Filter
Aggregate
Parse
Correlate
Analyze
```

---

# 49.21 Log Retention

Retention MUST be defined by environment and operational requirements.

Example conceptual policy:

```text
DEV
→ short retention

UAT
→ moderate retention

PROD
→ longer retention
```

Actual retention should be determined by compliance, operational, and storage requirements.

---

# 49.22 Log Rotation

Local application/container logging MUST NOT allow unlimited disk growth.

Log rotation or centralized collection MUST prevent:

```text
Disk exhaustion
Node instability
Pod failures
```

---

# 49.23 Metrics

Metrics SHOULD provide quantitative information about system behavior.

Examples:

```text
Request count
Request latency
Error rate
CPU
Memory
Database connections
Queue depth
Cache hit rate
```

---

# 49.24 RED Metrics

For HTTP services, the RED method is recommended:

```text
Rate
Errors
Duration
```

Example:

```text
Requests/sec
5xx/sec
P95 latency
```

---

# 49.25 USE Metrics

For infrastructure resources, the USE method is useful:

```text
Utilization
Saturation
Errors
```

Examples:

```text
CPU utilization
Disk saturation
Network errors
```

---

# 49.26 Golden Signals

Critical services SHOULD monitor:

```text
Latency
Traffic
Errors
Saturation
```

---

# 49.27 Application Metrics

Mediverse services SHOULD expose application-level metrics.

Examples:

```text
HTTP requests
Authentication attempts
Failed logins
Database query latency
File uploads
Notification delivery
Background jobs
```

Metrics should be selected based on operational usefulness.

---

# 49.28 Business Metrics

Important business operations MAY have metrics.

Examples:

```text
Courses viewed
Learning sessions started
Quiz attempts
Quiz completion rate
Content access failures
```

Business metrics MUST avoid exposing sensitive individual information.

---

# 49.29 Prometheus

If Prometheus is used, applications SHOULD expose metrics through a standardized endpoint where appropriate.

For Spring Boot:

```text
/actuator/prometheus
```

Access to metrics endpoints MUST be controlled appropriately.

---

# 49.30 Metric Naming

Metrics SHOULD use consistent naming.

Example:

```text
http_server_requests_total
```

Avoid arbitrary names such as:

```text
my_random_counter
```

---

# 49.31 Metric Labels

Labels SHOULD be carefully controlled.

Good:

```text
method
status
service
endpoint
```

Potentially dangerous:

```text
patientId
userId
requestId
```

High-cardinality identifiers can severely damage metric-system performance.

---

# 49.32 High Cardinality

Do NOT put arbitrary IDs into metric labels.

Bad:

```text
http_requests{userId="123456"}
```

This can create millions of unique time series.

Better:

```text
http_requests{endpoint="/api/patients",status="200"}
```

---

# 49.33 Metrics Cardinality

Every new label should be evaluated for:

```text
Number of possible values
Number of resulting time series
Memory consumption
Query cost
```

---

# 49.34 Kubernetes Metrics

Monitor:

```text
Pod CPU
Pod memory
Container restarts
Pod readiness
Deployment availability
Node CPU
Node memory
Node disk
```

---

# 49.35 Resource Saturation

Critical services SHOULD have visibility into:

```text
CPU saturation
Memory pressure
Disk pressure
Connection pool saturation
Thread pool saturation
Queue saturation
```

---

# 49.36 JVM Metrics

Spring Boot services SHOULD expose relevant JVM metrics.

Examples:

```text
Heap usage
Non-heap usage
GC activity
Thread count
Class loading
CPU
```

---

# 49.37 Garbage Collection

Unexpected GC behavior SHOULD be observable.

Watch for:

```text
Long GC pauses
High allocation rate
Frequent full GC
Heap exhaustion
```

---

# 49.38 Database Metrics

PostgreSQL monitoring SHOULD include:

```text
Connections
Connection saturation
Query latency
Transactions
Locks
Deadlocks
Cache behavior
Disk usage
Replication status where applicable
```

---

# 49.39 Connection Pool Metrics

For Spring Boot services using a connection pool, monitor:

```text
Active connections
Idle connections
Pending requests
Maximum pool size
Connection acquisition time
```

A database can be healthy while the application is failing because its connection pool is exhausted.

---

# 49.40 Redis Metrics

Where Redis is used, monitor:

```text
Memory usage
Evictions
Hit/miss ratio
Connected clients
Commands/sec
Latency
Persistence health
```

---

# 49.41 Kafka / Messaging Metrics

Where messaging infrastructure is used, monitor:

```text
Consumer lag
Messages/sec
Producer errors
Consumer errors
Partition health
Broker health
Retry volume
Dead-letter volume
```

---

# 49.42 Dead-Letter Queues

DLQ growth SHOULD trigger monitoring and potentially alerting.

Example:

```text
Messages
 ↓
Processing failure
 ↓
Retry
 ↓
Retry exhausted
 ↓
DLQ
```

A growing DLQ is an operational signal, not merely a storage location.

---

# 49.43 Health Endpoints

Applications SHOULD expose health information.

Spring Boot may provide:

```text
/actuator/health
```

Health endpoints should distinguish appropriate states such as:

```text
UP
DOWN
OUT_OF_SERVICE
UNKNOWN
```

---

# 49.44 Liveness vs Readiness

These are different concepts.

### Liveness

Answers:

> Is the process alive?

### Readiness

Answers:

> Can this instance safely receive traffic?

Do not make liveness dependent on every external dependency.

---

# 49.45 Liveness Probe

A liveness failure should normally indicate that restarting the container is likely to help.

Do not configure liveness to fail merely because:

```text
Database temporarily unavailable
External API unavailable
Kafka temporarily unavailable
```

unless restart is actually the correct recovery mechanism.

---

# 49.46 Readiness Probe

Readiness SHOULD prevent traffic from reaching an instance that cannot serve requests correctly.

Example:

```text
Pod running
but
database connection unavailable

        ↓

Pod may remain alive
Pod becomes NotReady
```

---

# 49.47 Startup Probe

Applications with slow startup MAY use a startup probe to prevent premature liveness failures.

---

# 49.48 Alerting

Alerts SHOULD indicate actionable problems.

Bad alert:

```text
CPU = 70%
```

if no action is required.

Better:

```text
CPU > 90%
for 15 minutes
AND
request latency increasing
```

---

# 49.49 Alert Design

Every alert SHOULD answer:

```text
What happened?
Why does it matter?
Who should respond?
What should they investigate?
```

---

# 49.50 Alert Severity

A standardized severity model SHOULD be used.

Example:

```text
SEV1
Critical production outage

SEV2
Major degradation

SEV3
Important but non-critical issue

SEV4
Informational
```

The exact terminology can vary, but it must be consistent.

---

# 49.51 Alert Fatigue

The platform MUST avoid excessive alerting.

If engineers routinely ignore alerts because there are too many:

> **The alerting system is broken.**

---

# 49.52 Symptoms vs Causes

Alerts should preferably detect user-impacting symptoms.

Example:

Weak:

```text
CPU high
```

Stronger:

```text
API error rate > 5%
```

Infrastructure alerts remain useful, but user-facing symptoms should receive priority.

---

# 49.53 Alert Thresholds

Thresholds SHOULD be based on:

```text
Historical behavior
Capacity
SLOs
Business impact
Failure characteristics
```

Do not select arbitrary numbers without understanding the workload.

---

# 49.54 Alert Duration

Transient spikes SHOULD not always trigger incidents.

Example:

```text
CPU > 90%
for 1 minute
```

may be noise.

Instead:

```text
CPU > 90%
for 10 minutes
```

may be more actionable depending on the service.

---

# 49.55 Alert Routing

Alerts SHOULD be routed according to ownership.

Example:

```text
Application error
      ↓
Application team

Kubernetes failure
      ↓
Platform team

Security issue
      ↓
Security team

Database failure
      ↓
Database/platform owner
```

---

# 49.56 On-Call Information

Critical alerts SHOULD contain:

```text
Service
Environment
Severity
Current condition
Dashboard
Logs
Trace information
Runbook
```

---

# 49.57 Runbooks

Important alerts SHOULD have associated runbooks.

Example:

```text
Alert:
High API Error Rate

Runbook:
1. Check Grafana
2. Check application logs
3. Check recent deployment
4. Check dependency health
5. Check database
6. Roll back if required
```

---

# 49.58 Dashboards

Each critical Mediverse service SHOULD have a dashboard.

Minimum dashboard sections:

```text
Availability
Traffic
Latency
Errors
Resources
Dependencies
Deployments
```

---

# 49.59 Service Dashboard

Example:

```text
MEDIVERSE API
────────────────────────
Requests/sec
Error Rate
P50
P95
P99

CPU
Memory
Pods

Database
Redis
Kafka

Recent Deployments
```

---

# 49.60 Kubernetes Dashboard

Platform dashboards SHOULD include:

```text
Cluster health
Nodes
Namespaces
Pods
Deployments
CPU
Memory
Restarts
Pending pods
Failed pods
```

---

# 49.61 Deployment Dashboard

Deployment visibility SHOULD include:

```text
Version
Commit
Deployment time
Replica status
Rollout status
Error rate before/after deployment
```

---

# 49.62 Before/After Deployment Analysis

A deployment should be evaluated against the previous state.

Example:

```text
Before deployment:
5xx = 0.3%

After deployment:
5xx = 8.4%
```

This is a strong deployment health signal.

---

# 49.63 Distributed Tracing

Mediverse SHOULD use distributed tracing for sufficiently complex service interactions.

Example:

```text
Frontend
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Auth
 ↓
Learning Service
 ↓
PostgreSQL
```

Tracing should make latency propagation visible.

---

# 49.64 OpenTelemetry

OpenTelemetry MAY be used as the standard instrumentation layer.

It can provide:

```text
Traces
Metrics
Logs
```

The implementation should avoid unnecessary duplication with existing instrumentation.

---

# 49.65 Trace Sampling

Tracing every request may be expensive at scale.

Sampling strategies MAY be used:

```text
Head sampling
Tail sampling
Error-based sampling
Priority sampling
```

Critical/error traces should receive appropriate visibility.

---

# 49.66 Trace Context Propagation

Trace context SHOULD propagate across:

```text
HTTP
Messaging
Async processing
Service boundaries
```

Otherwise distributed traces become fragmented.

---

# 49.67 Database Tracing

Database operations MAY be traced for troubleshooting.

However, SQL parameters MUST be carefully controlled so sensitive information is not exposed.

---

# 49.68 External Dependency Monitoring

Critical external dependencies SHOULD be monitored.

Examples:

```text
Email provider
Object storage
Authentication provider
Payment provider
Third-party APIs
```

---

# 49.69 Dependency Failure

Application observability should make it possible to distinguish:

```text
Application failure
vs
Database failure
vs
External service failure
vs
Network failure
```

---

# 49.70 SLOs

Critical services SHOULD define Service Level Objectives.

Examples:

```text
Availability ≥ 99.9%

P95 API latency < 500 ms

Error rate < 1%
```

Actual values must be derived from business requirements and workload characteristics.

---

# 49.71 SLIs

SLIs measure actual service behavior.

Examples:

```text
Successful requests / total requests
P95 latency
Availability
Queue processing latency
```

---

# 49.72 SLO vs Alert

Not every SLO violation should produce an immediate alert.

Alerting should consider:

```text
Severity
Duration
Error budget
User impact
```

---

# 49.73 Error Budgets

Where SRE practices are adopted, error budgets MAY be used to balance:

```text
Reliability
vs
Release velocity
```

Example:

```text
SLO = 99.9%

Allowed unreliability:
0.1%
```

---

# 49.74 Incident Correlation

During incidents, engineers SHOULD correlate:

```text
Logs
+
Metrics
+
Traces
+
Deployments
+
Infrastructure events
```

Example:

```text
Deployment 14:30
      ↓
Latency increases 14:32
      ↓
5xx increases 14:33
      ↓
Trace shows DB timeout
      ↓
Root cause investigation
```

---

# 49.75 Deployment Markers

Dashboards SHOULD show deployment events where possible.

This makes changes easier to correlate with incidents.

---

# 49.76 Monitoring the Monitoring System

Observability infrastructure itself MUST be monitored.

Monitor:

```text
Prometheus health
Grafana availability
Log collector health
Log ingestion failures
Trace collector health
Storage capacity
Alert manager health
```

---

# 49.77 Monitoring Gaps

A missing metric should not silently become a false "healthy" state.

Example:

```text
No metrics received
```

must be distinguishable from:

```text
Metric = 0
```

---

# 49.78 Missing Telemetry

Telemetry collection failures SHOULD produce appropriate alerts.

Otherwise:

```text
Application broken
 ↓
Telemetry broken
 ↓
Dashboard looks normal
```

This is dangerous.

---

# 49.79 Logging During Incidents

During incidents:

```text
Increase diagnostic visibility
```

may be appropriate.

But temporary DEBUG logging MUST have:

```text
Reason
Owner
Start time
End time
```

and should be reverted afterward.

---

# 49.80 Observability Security

Observability systems contain potentially sensitive information and MUST be secured.

Controls SHOULD include:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Encryption
Retention
Audit logs
Environment separation
```

---

# 49.81 Access Control

Not every engineer needs access to every production log.

Use least privilege.

Example:

```text
Developer
→ DEV logs

Application engineer
→ Application logs

Platform engineer
→ Platform logs

Security team
→ Security logs
```

---

# 49.82 Data Masking

Sensitive values SHOULD be masked before logs reach centralized storage.

Examples:

```text
Authorization: Bearer ********
password: ********
secret: ********
```

---

# 49.83 Observability Checklist

### Logs

* [ ] Structured logging
* [ ] Consistent levels
* [ ] Correlation ID
* [ ] Trace ID
* [ ] No secrets
* [ ] No unnecessary medical data
* [ ] Centralized collection
* [ ] Retention policy

### Metrics

* [ ] RED metrics
* [ ] Infrastructure metrics
* [ ] JVM metrics
* [ ] Database metrics
* [ ] Dependency metrics
* [ ] Cardinality controlled

### Tracing

* [ ] Distributed tracing
* [ ] Context propagation
* [ ] Error visibility
* [ ] Sampling strategy

### Alerting

* [ ] Actionable alerts
* [ ] Severity
* [ ] Routing
* [ ] Runbooks
* [ ] Noise reduction

---

# 49.84 Definition of Done

Mediverse observability is production-ready when:

* [ ] Centralized logging exists
* [ ] Structured logs are standardized
* [ ] Sensitive data is protected
* [ ] Correlation IDs are available
* [ ] Distributed tracing is implemented where needed
* [ ] Application metrics exist
* [ ] Infrastructure metrics exist
* [ ] Database metrics exist
* [ ] Dashboards exist
* [ ] Critical alerts exist
* [ ] Alert ownership exists
* [ ] Runbooks exist
* [ ] Health probes are correctly configured
* [ ] SLOs/SLIs are defined for critical services
* [ ] Deployment events can be correlated with telemetry
* [ ] Observability infrastructure itself is monitored

---

# 49.85 Core Principles

Mediverse observability follows:

1. **Logs explain events.**
2. **Metrics quantify behavior.**
3. **Traces explain distributed execution.**
4. **Every critical request should be traceable.**
5. **Never log sensitive medical or authentication data unnecessarily.**
6. **Avoid high-cardinality metrics.**
7. **Alerts must be actionable.**
8. **A missing metric is not the same as a zero metric.**
9. **Health checks must reflect actual operational semantics.**
10. **Deployment events must be correlated with system behavior.**
11. **Observability infrastructure must itself be observable.**
12. **Temporary diagnostic changes must be reverted.**
13. **Dashboards should help answer questions, not merely display graphs.**
14. **The goal is faster diagnosis, not maximum telemetry volume.**
15. **If an incident requires guessing, the observability design has a gap.**

> **Mediverse observability must allow an engineer to move from symptom → service → request → trace → log → dependency → root cause without guessing.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 50: Incident Management, Error Handling & Production Troubleshooting Standards.**

# CSDG — Chapter 50

## Incident Management, Error Handling & Production Troubleshooting Standards

### 50.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the standards for handling:

* Production incidents
* Application failures
* Infrastructure failures
* API errors
* Database failures
* Kubernetes failures
* Deployment failures
* Security incidents
* Service degradation
* Recovery and post-incident analysis

Core principle:

> **The objective during an incident is to restore a safe, stable service first, then determine and permanently eliminate the root cause.**

---

## 50.2 Incident Lifecycle

Every significant incident SHOULD follow:

```text
Detection
   ↓
Triage
   ↓
Classification
   ↓
Containment
   ↓
Diagnosis
   ↓
Recovery
   ↓
Verification
   ↓
Root Cause Analysis
   ↓
Corrective Actions
   ↓
Post-Incident Review
```

---

# 50.3 Incident Detection

Incidents MAY be detected through:

```text
Monitoring alerts
Logs
Metrics
Traces
User reports
Synthetic monitoring
Health checks
Deployment failures
Security alerts
Infrastructure alerts
```

---

# 50.4 Incident Classification

Every incident SHOULD be classified.

### Application

```text
API failure
Authentication failure
Business logic failure
Memory leak
Thread exhaustion
```

### Database

```text
Connection exhaustion
Slow queries
Deadlocks
Storage exhaustion
Migration failure
```

### Infrastructure

```text
Node failure
Pod failure
Network failure
Storage failure
Kubernetes failure
```

### Deployment

```text
Bad release
Configuration error
Image failure
Failed rollout
GitOps failure
```

### Security

```text
Credential exposure
Unauthorized access
Suspicious activity
Vulnerability exploitation
```

---

# 50.5 Severity

A consistent severity model SHOULD be used.

```text
SEV1
Critical outage / severe security incident

SEV2
Major service degradation

SEV3
Limited functionality impact

SEV4
Minor or informational issue
```

Severity should reflect **user/business impact**, not merely technical complexity.

---

# 50.6 SEV1 Example

Examples:

```text
Entire Mediverse platform unavailable
Critical authentication failure
Major data integrity incident
Widespread production API failure
Critical security compromise
```

---

# 50.7 SEV2 Example

Examples:

```text
Major service degraded
Large percentage of API requests failing
Important learning functionality unavailable
Database performance severely degraded
```

---

# 50.8 SEV3 Example

Examples:

```text
Single non-critical feature unavailable
Limited API degradation
Intermittent failure affecting small user population
```

---

# 50.9 Incident Commander

For significant incidents, an Incident Commander SHOULD be assigned.

Responsibilities:

```text
Coordinate response
Control communication
Assign investigation tasks
Prevent duplicated effort
Drive recovery
Ensure documentation
```

The Incident Commander does not necessarily need to be the person who understands the technical root cause.

---

# 50.10 Incident Roles

For major incidents, useful roles include:

```text
Incident Commander
Technical Lead
Application Owner
Platform Engineer
Database Owner
Security Lead
Communications Lead
Scribe
```

One person MAY temporarily perform multiple roles in a small team.

---

# 50.11 First Rule: Stabilize

During an incident:

> **Restore service before optimizing the architecture.**

Example:

```text
Production API failing
       ↓
Restore availability
       ↓
Investigate root cause
```

Do not spend 45 minutes redesigning a component while users remain unable to use the platform.

---

# 50.12 Incident Triage

Initial triage SHOULD answer:

```text
What is broken?
Who is affected?
When did it start?
Is it getting worse?
What changed recently?
Is the issue isolated or widespread?
```

---

# 50.13 Recent Changes

Always investigate recent changes early.

Check:

```text
Deployment
Configuration
Database migration
Infrastructure change
Dependency upgrade
Secret rotation
Certificate change
Network change
Kubernetes change
```

A strong correlation does not automatically prove causation, but recent changes are high-value investigation points.

---

# 50.14 First Five Minutes

A practical initial sequence:

```text
1. Confirm the incident.
2. Determine user impact.
3. Check monitoring.
4. Check recent deployments.
5. Check application health.
6. Check infrastructure health.
7. Decide whether rollback/containment is required.
```

---

# 50.15 Incident Communication

During significant incidents, communication SHOULD be:

```text
Short
Factual
Frequent enough
Non-speculative
Action-oriented
```

Avoid:

```text
"We think maybe something could possibly..."
```

Prefer:

```text
"API error rate increased from 0.4% to 18% after deployment 1.8.2. Rollback is in progress."
```

---

# 50.16 Do Not Speculate

During incidents, separate:

```text
Known
Suspected
Unknown
```

Example:

```text
KNOWN:
5xx increased after deployment.

SUSPECTED:
Database connection exhaustion.

UNKNOWN:
Whether the deployment caused the connection leak.
```

This prevents false certainty.

---

# 50.17 Error Handling Philosophy

Application errors SHOULD be:

```text
Predictable
Consistent
Traceable
Safe
Actionable
```

---

# 50.18 API Error Contract

Mediverse APIs SHOULD return a consistent error structure.

Example:

```json id="jm8fba"
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-09T10:20:00Z",
  "status": 404,
  "code": "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "Requested resource was not found",
  "path": "/api/resource/123",
  "traceId": "abc123"
}
```

The exact schema should be standardized across services.

---

# 50.19 Do Not Expose Internal Errors

Never return:

```text id="rvxtq5"
Stack trace
SQL query
Database hostname
Internal filesystem path
Secret
Internal infrastructure details
```

to API consumers.

---

# 50.20 HTTP Status Codes

Use HTTP status codes semantically.

Examples:

```text
400
Bad Request

401
Unauthenticated

403
Forbidden

404
Not Found

409
Conflict

422
Validation / semantic failure where appropriate

429
Too Many Requests

500
Internal Server Error

502
Bad Gateway

503
Service Unavailable

504
Gateway Timeout
```

Do not return `500` for every possible application error.

---

# 50.21 Error Codes

Human-readable messages can change.

Machine-readable error codes SHOULD remain stable.

Example:

```text
USER_NOT_FOUND
INVALID_CREDENTIALS
RESOURCE_CONFLICT
VALIDATION_FAILED
RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE
```

---

# 50.22 Validation Errors

Validation failures SHOULD identify the affected fields without exposing sensitive information.

Example:

```json id="lq0u8m"
{
  "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "fields": {
    "email": "Invalid email format",
    "password": "Password does not meet requirements"
  }
}
```

---

# 50.23 Exception Handling

Spring Boot services SHOULD use centralized exception handling.

Typical approach:

```text id="c3aw3m"
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Exception
   ↓
Global Exception Handler
   ↓
Standard API Error
```

Avoid duplicating error-response construction across every controller.

---

# 50.24 Exception Hierarchy

Applications SHOULD distinguish between:

```text id="y6z9ul"
Business exceptions
Validation exceptions
Authentication exceptions
Authorization exceptions
Infrastructure exceptions
Unexpected exceptions
```

---

# 50.25 Business Exceptions

Business exceptions represent expected domain conditions.

Example:

```text id="x8p5n4"
CourseAlreadyCompletedException
ResourceNotAvailableException
DuplicateEnrollmentException
```

These should not be treated as unexpected system crashes.

---

# 50.26 Unexpected Exceptions

Unexpected exceptions SHOULD:

```text id="x5e4pm"
Be logged
Include trace context
Return safe error response
Generate appropriate telemetry
Potentially trigger alerting
```

---

# 50.27 Retry Strategy

Retries SHOULD be used only when an operation is likely to succeed if attempted again.

Good candidates:

```text id="m5ut4a"
Transient network error
Temporary service unavailable
Temporary database connectivity issue
```

Poor candidates:

```text id="w6xq9m"
Validation failure
Authentication failure
Authorization failure
Invalid request
Business rule violation
```

---

# 50.28 Retry Storms

Uncontrolled retries can turn a small outage into a major outage.

Example:

```text id="r5t1a4"
Service B fails
 ↓
Service A retries 10 times
 ↓
1000 requests × 10 retries
 ↓
Service B overloaded further
```

Retries MUST have limits.

---

# 50.29 Exponential Backoff

Transient retries SHOULD generally use exponential backoff.

Concept:

```text id="e4os2x"
Attempt 1 → immediate
Attempt 2 → short delay
Attempt 3 → longer delay
Attempt 4 → longer delay
```

Jitter SHOULD be considered to prevent synchronized retry storms.

---

# 50.30 Circuit Breaker

For unstable dependencies, a circuit breaker MAY be used.

Concept:

```text id="u2f7lq"
Healthy
  ↓
Failures
  ↓
OPEN
  ↓
Stop sending requests
  ↓
Recovery check
  ↓
HALF-OPEN
  ↓
Healthy
  ↓
CLOSED
```

---

# 50.31 Timeouts

Every network dependency SHOULD have an appropriate timeout.

Never rely indefinitely on:

```text id="b9a5h7"
HTTP request
Database connection
Redis operation
Kafka operation
External API
```

An absent timeout can convert one failure into thread/resource exhaustion.

---

# 50.32 Timeout Hierarchy

Timeouts should be consistent across layers.

Concept:

```text id="8u8c7g"
Client timeout
   >
Gateway timeout
   >
Service timeout
   >
Dependency timeout
```

The exact values depend on workload and architecture.

---

# 50.33 Graceful Degradation

Where appropriate, services SHOULD degrade gracefully.

Example:

```text id="xwzq2c"
Recommendation service unavailable
        ↓
Core learning functionality remains available
```

Do not allow a non-critical dependency to take down the entire platform.

---

# 50.34 Bulkhead Isolation

Critical services MAY use bulkhead patterns to isolate resources.

Example:

```text id="7q49sj"
Critical API thread pool
        ≠
Background processing thread pool
```

This prevents one workload from consuming all available resources.

---

# 50.35 502 Bad Gateway

A `502` usually indicates that a gateway/proxy received an invalid response or encountered an upstream failure.

Troubleshooting should examine:

```text id="a7c0f7"
Ingress
Load balancer
Gateway
Service
Pod
Application
Upstream dependency
```

Do not automatically assume the frontend is responsible.

---

# 50.36 503 Service Unavailable

Investigate:

```text id="j1f8eo"
Service endpoints
Pod readiness
Deployment replicas
Ingress routing
Resource exhaustion
Application health
```

---

# 50.37 504 Gateway Timeout

Investigate:

```text id="4kwmcs"
Request duration
Application thread pool
Database latency
External dependencies
Gateway timeout
Service timeout
Network latency
```

A `504` is often a symptom rather than the root cause.

---

# 50.38 Kubernetes Troubleshooting Order

For an application failure, use:

```text id="q7f7pr"
Ingress
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Endpoints
  ↓
Deployment
  ↓
Pods
  ↓
Containers
  ↓
Application logs
  ↓
Dependencies
```

This prevents random troubleshooting.

---

# 50.39 Kubernetes Pod Investigation

First inspect:

```bash id="h7qk2s"
kubectl get pods -n <namespace>
```

Then:

```bash id="r8t8qu"
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <namespace>
```

Then:

```bash id="e3b5yd"
kubectl logs <pod> -n <namespace>
```

If necessary:

```bash id="k6qz0w"
kubectl logs <pod> -n <namespace> --previous
```

---

# 50.40 Restart Investigation

Do not blindly restart pods.

A restart can:

```text id="7y9xgf"
Hide symptoms
Destroy useful evidence
Temporarily restore service
```

Always capture enough diagnostic information first when the incident allows it.

---

# 50.41 CrashLoopBackOff

Investigate:

```text id="o1mxo4"
Application startup
Environment variables
Secrets
ConfigMaps
Dependencies
Memory limits
Liveness probes
Image
Recent deployment
```

---

# 50.42 OOMKilled

If a pod is `OOMKilled`, inspect:

```text id="w4zj62"
Memory usage
Container limit
JVM heap
GC
Memory leak
Traffic increase
Recent code changes
```

Do not simply increase memory indefinitely.

---

# 50.43 Pending Pods

Investigate:

```text id="c3f7mz"
Node capacity
CPU requests
Memory requests
Taints
Tolerations
Affinity
Volume availability
Scheduling constraints
```

---

# 50.44 ImagePullBackOff

Investigate:

```text id="b8nqj4"
Image name
Image tag
Registry availability
Registry credentials
Image existence
Network connectivity
ImagePullSecrets
```

---

# 50.45 CreateContainerConfigError

Investigate:

```text id="2o5yqu"
Missing ConfigMap
Missing Secret
Incorrect environment variable
Invalid volume reference
Incorrect configuration
```

This should be resolved at configuration/deployment level rather than by repeatedly restarting the pod.

---

# 50.46 Service Troubleshooting

Check:

```bash id="h0f3nr"
kubectl get svc -n <namespace>
```

Then:

```bash id="h0t0jv"
kubectl get endpoints -n <namespace>
```

Then inspect:

```text id="9i1hdf"
Selector
Target ports
Pod labels
Readiness
```

A Service without healthy endpoints cannot route traffic successfully.

---

# 50.47 Ingress Troubleshooting

For ingress failures inspect:

```text id="y3l1ce"
Ingress rules
Host
Path
TLS
Backend service
Service port
Ingress controller
Controller logs
```

---

# 50.48 DNS Troubleshooting

If service discovery fails, inspect:

```text id="j6n4xp"
Service name
Namespace
CoreDNS
NetworkPolicy
Cluster DNS configuration
```

---

# 50.49 Database Incident

Database incidents SHOULD be investigated through:

```text id="bqv1lc"
Application logs
 ↓
Connection pool
 ↓
Database connections
 ↓
Slow queries
 ↓
Locks
 ↓
Deadlocks
 ↓
Storage
 ↓
Database health
```

---

# 50.50 Connection Pool Exhaustion

Symptoms may include:

```text id="u2b9f7"
Request timeouts
Unable to acquire connection
High latency
Thread waiting
502/504
```

Do not immediately increase the pool size.

First determine:

```text id="r3jqhy"
Why connections are not being released
Whether queries are too slow
Whether traffic increased
Whether the database can handle additional connections
```

---

# 50.51 Slow Queries

Investigate:

```text id="d0e4h4"
Query execution plan
Indexes
Locks
Data volume
Connection count
Recent schema changes
```

---

# 50.52 Deadlocks

When deadlocks occur:

```text id="0w5x7f"
Identify transactions
Identify locked resources
Identify ordering
Review transaction boundaries
```

Do not solve recurring deadlocks simply by increasing retry counts.

---

# 50.53 Redis Incident

Investigate:

```text id="5u0z7w"
Memory
Evictions
Connection count
Latency
Network
Persistence
Key distribution
```

---

# 50.54 Kafka Incident

Investigate:

```text id="y6h9xa"
Broker health
Consumer lag
Partition assignment
Producer errors
Consumer errors
Dead-letter queue
Network
Disk
```

---

# 50.55 External Dependency Incident

When an external service fails:

```text id="k1v3g8"
Confirm dependency status
 ↓
Measure timeout/error rate
 ↓
Enable fallback if available
 ↓
Reduce retries
 ↓
Protect resources
 ↓
Monitor recovery
```

---

# 50.56 Security Incident

Security incidents MUST follow the organization's security incident process.

Initial priorities:

```text id="4x0q8n"
Contain
Preserve evidence
Protect credentials
Assess scope
Notify responsible teams
Recover
Rotate compromised secrets
```

Do not casually delete logs or restart infrastructure if doing so could destroy evidence.

---

# 50.57 Credential Compromise

If a credential is suspected to be compromised:

```text id="m4l4v9"
1. Revoke
2. Rotate
3. Identify usage
4. Investigate scope
5. Update dependent systems
6. Verify old credential no longer works
```

---

# 50.58 Data Integrity Incident

If incorrect data may have been written:

> **Stop destructive actions until the data situation is understood.**

Investigate:

```text id="z7ukmg"
Affected records
Time window
Transactions
Backups
Audit logs
Application version
Database changes
```

---

# 50.59 Backup Verification

A backup that has never been restored is only an assumption.

Backup recovery SHOULD be tested periodically.

Verify:

```text id="1kr4g5"
Backup exists
Backup is readable
Restore works
Recovery time is acceptable
Data integrity is maintained
```

---

# 50.60 Disaster Recovery

Critical Mediverse services SHOULD have documented:

```text id="7q1yzw"
RPO
RTO
Backup strategy
Recovery procedure
Dependencies
Ownership
```

### RPO

Maximum acceptable data loss.

### RTO

Maximum acceptable recovery time.

---

# 50.61 Rollback Decision

Before rollback ask:

```text id="6drb7j"
Is the release clearly responsible?
Is rollback technically safe?
Are database changes backward compatible?
Will rollback restore functionality?
Will rollback cause additional damage?
```

---

# 50.62 Roll Forward Decision

Roll forward may be better when:

```text id="f0w7z7"
Database migration cannot safely reverse
Schema is incompatible
Fix is small and well understood
Rollback would increase risk
```

---

# 50.63 Incident Timeline

Every significant incident SHOULD maintain a timeline.

Example:

```text id="5krf4f"
14:20 Deployment started
14:23 Pods became Ready
14:26 Error rate increased
14:28 Incident declared
14:31 Rollback started
14:34 Error rate normalized
14:40 Incident resolved
```

---

# 50.64 Root Cause Analysis

After recovery, determine:

```text id="brg4i8"
What failed?
Why did it fail?
Why wasn't it detected earlier?
Why did existing controls not prevent it?
Why did recovery take this long?
```

---

# 50.65 Five Whys

The Five Whys technique MAY be used.

Example:

```text id="0fj5py"
Why did API fail?
→ Database connections exhausted.

Why?
```
