## Frontend Coding, React Architecture & UI Development Standards

### 54.1 Purpose

This chapter defines coding and architectural standards for the Mediverse frontend.

It covers:

* React architecture
* Component design
* Folder structure
* Pages
* Reusable components
* Hooks
* State management
* API integration
* Forms
* Validation
* Routing
* Authentication
* Authorization
* Error handling
* Loading states
* Accessibility
* Responsive UI
* Performance
* Testing
* Frontend security

Core principle:

> **The frontend is a presentation and interaction layer—not the source of truth for business rules, security, or authorization.**

---

# 54.2 Frontend Technology Standards

The Mediverse frontend SHOULD follow the established project stack:

```text
React
Vite
TypeScript / JavaScript according to project decision
React Router
Axios / approved HTTP client
Redux Toolkit where global state is required
Material UI / approved UI system
Tailwind CSS where adopted
```

Do not introduce additional libraries merely because they are popular.

Every new dependency should have a reason.

---

# 54.3 Frontend Architecture

Recommended high-level structure:

```text
src/
├── app/
├── assets/
├── components/
├── features/
├── hooks/
├── layouts/
├── pages/
├── routes/
├── services/
├── store/
├── utils/
├── validations/
├── constants/
├── types/
└── main.jsx
```

The exact structure can evolve, but responsibilities must remain clear.

---

# 54.4 Feature-Based Organization

Mediverse SHOULD prefer feature-oriented organization as the application grows.

Example:

```text
features/
├── auth/
├── courses/
├── lessons/
├── quizzes/
├── progress/
├── users/
├── notifications/
└── dashboard/
```

Each feature may contain:

```text
components/
hooks/
services/
pages/
schemas/
types/
```

where useful.

---

# 54.5 Avoid Giant Components

Do not create components such as:

```text
CoursePage.jsx
```

containing:

```text
1000+ lines
API calls
Business logic
Form validation
UI rendering
State management
Navigation
Modal logic
```

Break responsibilities into smaller components.

---

# 54.6 Component Responsibility

A component should have a clear responsibility.

Example:

```text
CoursePage
 ├── CourseHeader
 ├── CourseOverview
 ├── LessonList
 ├── ProgressCard
 └── EnrollmentButton
```

This improves:

```text
Maintainability
Testing
Reuse
Readability
```

---

# 54.7 Presentational Components

Presentational components SHOULD primarily focus on rendering.

Example:

```jsx
<CourseCard
  title={course.title}
  instructor={course.instructor}
  progress={course.progress}
/>
```

They should not contain unrelated application-level behavior.

---

# 54.8 Container / Feature Logic

Application logic can be placed in:

```text
hooks
feature services
state management
feature-level components
```

depending on complexity.

Do not blindly force every component into a container/presentational pattern.

---

# 54.9 Props

Props should be explicit and meaningful.

Good:

```jsx
<CourseCard
  title={course.title}
  progress={course.progress}
  onOpen={handleOpen}
/>
```

Avoid passing massive objects when only a few fields are needed.

---

# 54.10 Prop Drilling

Avoid excessive prop drilling.

Bad:

```text
App
 ↓
Dashboard
 ↓
CoursePage
 ↓
CourseSection
 ↓
LessonList
 ↓
LessonCard
```

passing the same unrelated values through every level.

Use:

```text
Context
Redux
Feature hooks
Composition
```

when genuinely appropriate.

Do not introduce global state merely to eliminate two levels of props.

---

# 54.11 React State

State should exist at the narrowest reasonable scope.

Use local state for:

```text
Modal open/close
Input state
Tabs
Temporary UI state
```

Use global state for things such as:

```text
Authenticated user
Global application configuration
Cross-feature state
```

only when genuinely shared.

---

# 54.12 Server State vs Client State

Do not treat server data as ordinary UI state without considering its lifecycle.

Server state includes:

```text
Courses
Lessons
Quiz results
User profile
Notifications
Progress
```

It has concerns such as:

```text
Caching
Refetching
Staleness
Synchronization
Loading
Errors
```

The chosen data-fetching strategy should account for these.

---

# 54.13 Redux Usage

Redux SHOULD be used when application-wide client state genuinely benefits from centralized management.

Do not create Redux state for every input field.

Bad:

```text
Redux:
firstName
lastName
email
searchText
modalOpen
```

when those values are local to one page.

---

# 54.14 Redux Toolkit

If Redux is used, prefer Redux Toolkit patterns.

Avoid legacy Redux boilerplate unless there is a specific compatibility reason.

---

# 54.15 API Service Layer

API calls SHOULD be separated from UI components.

Avoid:

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  axios.get("/api/v1/courses");
}, []);
```

repeated throughout many components.

Prefer a service abstraction:

```text
services/
└── courseService.js
```

Example:

```js
courseService.getCourses()
```

---

# 54.16 API Client

Use a centralized HTTP client configuration where appropriate.

Example responsibilities:

```text
Base URL
Headers
Authentication
Timeout
Interceptors
Error normalization
Correlation ID
```

---

# 54.17 API URLs

Do not scatter hardcoded URLs throughout components.

Avoid:

```js
axios.get("http://localhost:8080/api/v1/courses");
```

Use configuration/environment-based values.

---

# 54.18 Environment Configuration

Frontend environment configuration SHOULD distinguish environments.

Example:

```text
.env.development
.env.test
.env.production
```

Never place secrets into frontend environment variables expecting them to remain secret.

Anything bundled into browser JavaScript can potentially be inspected by the user.

---

# 54.19 Frontend Secrets

Never store:

```text
Database passwords
Private API keys
JWT signing keys
Cloud credentials
Service account secrets
```

in frontend code.

---

# 54.20 Authentication State

Authentication state should be represented centrally enough that all relevant application areas can determine:

```text
Is authenticated?
Who is the user?
What roles/permissions exist?
Is authentication loading?
```

---

# 54.21 Protected Routes

Protected routes SHOULD prevent unauthorized navigation.

Concept:

```text
User
 ↓
Route Guard
 ↓
Authenticated?
 ├── No → Login
 └── Yes → Page
```

But route guards are a UX mechanism, **not the actual security boundary**.

The backend must still authorize requests.

---

# 54.22 Role-Based UI

The frontend MAY hide controls that the user cannot use.

Example:

```text
Student:
[View Course]

Faculty:
[View] [Edit]

Admin:
[View] [Edit] [Delete]
```

However:

> Hiding a button does not provide security.

---

# 54.23 Permission-Based UI

Where permissions are used, centralize UI permission checks.

Concept:

```js
can("COURSE_PUBLISH")
```

rather than scattering role comparisons everywhere:

```js
user.role === "ADMIN"
```

---

# 54.24 Routing

Routes SHOULD have a clear structure.

Example:

```text
/
 /login
 /dashboard
 /courses
 /courses/:courseId
 /courses/:courseId/lessons/:lessonId
 /quizzes
 /profile
 /admin
```

Avoid unnecessarily complicated route structures.

---

# 54.25 Route Naming

Routes should be:

```text
Predictable
Consistent
Resource-oriented
Readable
```

Avoid:

```text
/getCoursePage
/openCourseDetails
```

Prefer:

```text
/courses/:courseId
```

---

# 54.26 Lazy Loading

Large application sections SHOULD be lazy-loaded where appropriate.

Example:

```text
Admin module
 ↓
Loaded only when required
```

This reduces initial bundle size.

---

# 54.27 Code Splitting

Code splitting should focus on meaningful boundaries:

```text
Dashboard
Courses
3D learning module
Admin
Analytics
```

Do not create hundreds of tiny chunks without measuring the result.

---

# 54.28 Loading States

Every asynchronous operation should have a defined loading state.

Examples:

```text
Course loading
Lesson loading
Quiz submission
Profile update
File upload
3D asset loading
```

Never leave the user staring at an unresponsive interface.

---

# 54.29 Loading UI

Use appropriate indicators:

```text
Skeleton
Spinner
Progress indicator
Placeholder
```

For page-level loading, skeletons are often preferable to a generic spinner.

---

# 54.30 Error States

Every important asynchronous operation should define:

```text
Loading
Success
Empty
Error
```

state.

Concept:

```text
Loading
   ↓
 ┌───────┬────────┐
Success Empty    Error
```

---

# 54.31 Empty States

An empty result is not necessarily an error.

Example:

```text
No enrolled courses yet.
Explore available courses.
```

Do not display:

```text
ERROR 500
```

when the API successfully returned zero courses.

---

# 54.32 Error Boundaries

React Error Boundaries SHOULD be used to prevent a rendering failure in one part of the UI from crashing the entire application.

Example:

```text
Application
 ├── Header
 ├── Dashboard
 ├── Course Module ← error
 └── Footer
```

The application should provide an appropriate fallback.

---

# 54.33 Error Messages

User-facing messages should be understandable.

Avoid exposing:

```text
NullPointerException
AxiosError
SQL exception
Stack trace
```

Instead:

```text
Unable to load the course.
Please try again.
```

Detailed technical information belongs in logs/monitoring.

---

# 54.34 Form Architecture

Forms SHOULD have:

```text
Clear labels
Validation
Error messages
Loading state
Success state
Accessible controls
```

---

# 54.35 Client-Side Validation

Client-side validation improves UX.

Examples:

```text
Required fields
Email format
Password confirmation
Maximum length
File size
```

But:

> Client-side validation is not a security boundary.

Backend validation remains mandatory.

---

# 54.36 Form Submission

Prevent duplicate submissions.

Concept:

```text
Submit
 ↓
Disable / protect action
 ↓
Request
 ↓
Success/Error
 ↓
Re-enable
```

This is particularly important for:

```text
Enrollment
Quiz submission
Payment
Content publishing
```

---

# 54.37 Unsaved Changes

Forms with significant user input SHOULD warn users before losing unsaved work where appropriate.

Examples:

```text
Course editor
Medical learning notes
Long quiz
Content authoring
```

---

# 54.38 Accessibility

Mediverse SHOULD target WCAG-aligned accessibility practices.

Accessibility is not an optional visual enhancement.

---

# 54.39 Semantic HTML

Prefer:

```html
<button>
<nav>
<main>
<header>
<section>
<article>
<form>
<label>
```

over using `<div>` for everything.

---

# 54.40 Buttons vs Links

Use:

```text
<button>
```

for actions.

Use:

```text
<a>
```

or router links for navigation.

Do not use:

```html
<div onClick={...}>
```

as a replacement for a button.

---

# 54.41 Keyboard Navigation

All important interactions SHOULD be accessible using a keyboard.

Test:

```text
Tab
Shift + Tab
Enter
Space
Escape
Arrow keys
```

where appropriate.

---

# 54.42 Focus Management

When opening:

```text
Modal
Dialog
Drawer
```

focus should be managed appropriately.

After closing, focus should return to a sensible element.

---

# 54.43 Form Labels

Every form control SHOULD have an accessible label.

Bad:

```text
<input placeholder="Email">
```

Preferred:

```text
<label>Email</label>
<input ... />
```

---

# 54.44 Images

Images SHOULD have meaningful alternative text where appropriate.

Example:

```html
<img
  src="heart.png"
  alt="Human heart anatomy"
/>
```

Decorative images should not create unnecessary screen-reader noise.

---

# 54.45 3D Learning Module Accessibility

Mediverse's 3D educational content requires special consideration.

Do not make critical educational information available **only** through 3D interaction.

Provide alternative representations such as:

```text
Text
2D diagrams
Labels
Descriptions
Audio
Accessible explanations
```

---

# 54.46 Responsive Design

Mediverse MUST work across:

```text
Mobile
Tablet
Laptop
Desktop
Large screens
```

---

# 54.47 Mobile-First

For major learning workflows, design from the smallest practical viewport upward.

Validate:

```text
Navigation
Cards
Tables
Forms
Videos
3D modules
Quizzes
```

on mobile.

---

# 54.48 Responsive Breakpoints

Use the project's design-system breakpoints consistently.

Do not create arbitrary breakpoints inside individual components without reason.

---

# 54.49 Design System

Mediverse SHOULD maintain centralized design tokens for:

```text
Colors
Typography
Spacing
Borders
Radius
Elevation
Breakpoints
Transitions
```

This prevents every component from inventing its own visual language.

---

# 54.50 Theme Management

If Mediverse supports light/dark themes:

```text
Theme
 ↓
Design tokens
 ↓
Components
```

Components should not independently hardcode theme-specific colors everywhere.

---

# 54.51 Color Usage

Color should not be the only indicator of meaning.

Bad:

```text
Green = correct
Red = incorrect
```

without any additional semantic indicator.

Use:

```text
Icon
Text
Pattern
ARIA information where appropriate
```

as well.

---

# 54.52 Medical Learning UI

Because Mediverse is an educational medical platform, UI terminology should be:

```text
Clear
Consistent
Educational
Professional
```

Do not unnecessarily use complex technical terminology in student-facing interfaces.

---

# 54.53 Content Separation

Educational content SHOULD remain separate from presentation logic.

Avoid:

```jsx
<div>
  The heart pumps blood through...
</div>
```

repeated across application code.

Prefer structured content from an appropriate content/data layer.

---

# 54.54 Content Components

Create reusable components for:

```text
Learning objectives
Key concepts
Clinical correlation
Important notes
Definitions
Flowcharts
Tables
Quiz questions
References
```

---

# 54.55 Medical Content Disclaimer

Where Mediverse presents educational medical content, the UI SHOULD clearly distinguish:

```text
Educational content
```

from:

```text
Personalized medical advice
```

The frontend must not imply that educational material constitutes diagnosis or treatment guidance for an individual.

---

# 54.56 State Naming

Use descriptive state names.

Good:

```js
const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);
const [isDialogOpen, setIsDialogOpen] = useState(false);
```

Avoid:

```js
const [x, setX] = useState(false);
const [flag, setFlag] = useState(false);
```

---

# 54.57 Boolean Naming

Boolean variables SHOULD use clear prefixes:

```text
is
has
can
should
```

Examples:

```js
isLoading
isAuthenticated
hasPermission
canEdit
```

---

# 54.58 Event Handler Naming

Use:

```text
handleSubmit
handleChange
handleDelete
handleOpen
```

for internal handlers.

Props can use:

```text
onSubmit
onDelete
onOpen
```

---

# 54.59 Hooks

Custom hooks SHOULD represent reusable behavior.

Good:

```text
useAuth()
useCourses()
usePermissions()
useDebounce()
useQuiz()
```

Avoid hooks that merely rename one line of code unless there is meaningful reuse.

---

# 54.60 Hook Rules

React Hooks MUST follow React's Rules of Hooks.

Do not call hooks:

```text
Inside conditions
Inside loops
Inside nested functions
```

---

# 54.61 useEffect

Do not use `useEffect` as a general-purpose substitute for application logic.

Bad patterns include chains such as:

```text
useEffect
 ↓
setState
 ↓
another useEffect
 ↓
setState
 ↓
another effect
```

This creates difficult-to-reason state flows.

---

# 54.62 Derived State

Do not store values that can be calculated from existing state.

Avoid:

```js
const [firstName, setFirstName] = ...
const [lastName, setLastName] = ...
const [fullName, setFullName] = ...
```

when:

```js
const fullName = `${firstName} ${lastName}`;
```

is sufficient.

---

# 54.63 Memoization

Do not blindly use:

```text
useMemo
useCallback
memo
```

everywhere.

Use them when:

```text
Expensive computation exists
Referential equality matters
Measured rendering problem exists
```

Premature memoization adds complexity.

---

# 54.64 Lists and Keys

React lists MUST use stable keys.

Preferred:

```jsx
{courses.map(course => (
  <CourseCard key={course.id} />
))}
```

Avoid array indexes as keys when list order can change.

---

# 54.65 Rendering Large Lists

For large datasets, consider:

```text
Pagination
Virtualization
Incremental loading
Server-side filtering
```

Do not render thousands of DOM nodes unnecessarily.

---

# 54.66 Debouncing

Search fields that trigger API calls SHOULD use debouncing.

Concept:

```text
User types:
car
card
cardi
cardio
```

Do not send an API request for every keystroke unless there is a deliberate reason.

---

# 54.67 Caching

Frequently accessed relatively stable data MAY be cached.

Examples:

```text
Course categories
Reference data
Static educational metadata
```

Caching strategy must account for invalidation.

---

# 54.68 Optimistic UI

Optimistic updates MAY be used when:

```text
Operation is likely to succeed
Rollback is manageable
UX benefits significantly
```

Do not use optimistic UI for operations where incorrect temporary state could cause serious confusion.

---

# 54.69 API Retry

Frontend retries SHOULD be limited.

Do not automatically retry every request indefinitely.

Be particularly careful with non-idempotent operations.

---

# 54.70 Network Failure

The UI should distinguish:

```text
No network
Server error
Authentication expired
Authorization denied
Validation failure
Resource not found
```

These should not all become:

```text
Something went wrong.
```

---

# 54.71 Authentication Expiration

When authentication expires:

```text
API
 ↓
401
 ↓
Refresh / re-authenticate if supported
 ↓
Retry safely
```

Do not create infinite retry loops.

---

# 54.72 Axios Interceptors

If Axios interceptors are used for token refresh, they MUST prevent concurrent refresh storms.

Example failure:

```text
10 requests
 ↓
10 x 401
 ↓
10 refresh calls
```

Use a controlled refresh mechanism.

---

# 54.73 File Upload UX

Uploads SHOULD provide:

```text
Selected file
Size
Type
Progress
Success
Failure
Retry
```

For large uploads, consider resumability where justified.

---

# 54.74 Media Handling

For educational media:

```text
Images
Videos
Audio
3D models
```

the frontend should handle:

```text
Loading
Fallback
Unsupported format
Network failure
Accessibility
Performance
```

---

# 54.75 3D Performance

Mediverse 3D modules can be expensive.

Use:

```text
Lazy loading
Asset compression
LOD where appropriate
Texture optimization
Model optimization
Progressive loading
```

Do not load every 3D model on initial page load.

---

# 54.76 WebGL Failure

If WebGL or the required rendering capability is unavailable:

```text
3D
 ↓
Unsupported
 ↓
Fallback content
```

The student should still receive useful educational content.

---

# 54.77 Audio and Video

Educational media should provide:

```text
Play/pause
Volume
Progress
Captions where applicable
Transcript where useful
Fallback
```

Autoplay should be used cautiously.

---

# 54.78 Frontend Security

Never trust:

```text
URL parameters
Query parameters
Local storage
Cookies
Form fields
API responses
```

as inherently safe.

Validate and safely render data.

---

# 54.79 XSS Prevention

Avoid unsafe HTML rendering.

Do not use:

```jsx
dangerouslySetInnerHTML
```

unless absolutely necessary and the content has been appropriately sanitized.

---

# 54.80 URL Safety

Do not blindly construct navigation URLs from untrusted input.

Be careful with:

```text
redirect
returnUrl
next
callback
```

to avoid open redirects.

---

# 54.81 Sensitive Data in Browser

Do not unnecessarily retain sensitive information in:

```text
localStorage
sessionStorage
URL
query parameters
browser logs
```

---

# 54.82 Browser Storage

Anything stored in browser storage may be accessible to JavaScript executing in the origin.

Therefore:

> **Browser storage is not a secure vault.**

---

# 54.83 Dependency Management

Frontend dependencies SHOULD be:

```text
Minimal
Maintained
Version-controlled
Security-scanned
Justified
```

Avoid installing packages for trivial functionality.

---

# 54.84 Dependency Updates

Before upgrading major frontend dependencies:

```text
Review changelog
Check breaking changes
Run tests
Run build
Test critical workflows
```

---

# 54.85 Linting

The frontend SHOULD use automated linting.

Typical tooling:

```text
ESLint
Prettier
```

or the project's approved alternatives.

---

# 54.86 Formatting

Formatting should be automated.

Developers should not waste review time arguing about:

```text
Spaces
Quotes
Indentation
Semicolons
```

when tooling can enforce them.

---

# 54.87 Type Safety

If TypeScript is adopted, new frontend code SHOULD use strong typing.

Avoid excessive:

```ts
any
```

because it defeats much of TypeScript's value.

---

# 54.88 API Types

Frontend API models SHOULD correspond to documented backend contracts.

Example:

```ts
interface Course {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  description: string;
}
```

---

# 54.89 API Contract Drift

If backend changes:

```text
CourseResponse
```

the frontend contract should be updated deliberately.

Do not silently patch production UI based on assumptions.

---

# 54.90 Testing Pyramid

Frontend testing SHOULD cover multiple levels:

```text
Unit
 ↓
Component
 ↓
Integration
 ↓
End-to-End
```

---

# 54.91 Component Tests

Important components SHOULD test:

```text
Rendering
User interaction
Validation
Loading
Error
Accessibility behavior
```

---

# 54.92 End-to-End Tests

Critical Mediverse workflows SHOULD have E2E coverage.

Examples:

```text
Login
Course discovery
Enrollment
Lesson completion
Quiz submission
Progress tracking
Faculty content creation
Admin workflows
```

---

# 54.93 Test Selectors

Prefer stable selectors.

Avoid depending heavily on:

```text
CSS class names
Generated DOM structure
Implementation details
```

Prefer semantic selectors or deliberate test IDs where necessary.

---

# 54.94 Visual Regression

Important UI areas MAY use visual regression testing.

Especially useful for:

```text
Design system
Learning pages
Responsive layouts
Complex dashboards
3D module shell
```

---

# 54.95 Performance Testing

Measure:

```text
Initial load
Largest content
Interaction latency
Bundle size
API latency
3D asset loading
```

Do not optimize based solely on intuition.

---

# 54.96 Frontend Observability

Production frontend SHOULD provide appropriate monitoring for:

```text
JavaScript errors
Failed API requests
Performance
Route failures
Critical user workflows
```

Avoid collecting unnecessary personal information.

---

# 54.97 Logging

Frontend logs MUST NOT contain:

```text
Passwords
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
Secrets
Sensitive personal information
```

---

# 54.98 Production Debugging

Do not leave verbose debugging enabled in production.

Remove or control:

```js
console.log(...)
```

especially when it exposes sensitive or noisy data.

---

# 54.99 Definition of Done

A Mediverse frontend feature is production-ready when:

* [ ] Component responsibilities are clear
* [ ] Feature structure is appropriate
* [ ] API calls are separated from UI where appropriate
* [ ] Loading state exists
* [ ] Error state exists
* [ ] Empty state exists
* [ ] Validation exists
* [ ] Authentication state is handled
* [ ] Authorization-aware UI exists where appropriate
* [ ] Backend authorization remains authoritative
* [ ] Responsive design is implemented
* [ ] Accessibility has been considered
* [ ] Sensitive data is not exposed
* [ ] No secrets exist in frontend code
* [ ] Error boundaries exist where appropriate
* [ ] Tests exist
* [ ] Linting passes
* [ ] Formatting passes
* [ ] Production build succeeds
* [ ] Performance is acceptable
* [ ] 3D/media fallbacks exist where required
* [ ] Observability is available for critical workflows

---

# 54.100 Core Principles

1. **Keep components focused.**
2. **Separate UI from API integration.**
3. **Keep state as local as possible.**
4. **Do not put everything into Redux.**
5. **Treat server state differently from UI state.**
6. **Never treat frontend authorization as security.**
7. **Never expose secrets in browser code.**
8. **Validate user input on both frontend and backend.**
9. **Every asynchronous workflow needs loading, success, empty, and error handling.**
10. **Accessibility is part of implementation, not a final polish step.**
11. **Design mobile and desktop experiences deliberately.**
12. **Do not blindly optimize or memoize without a reason.**
13. **Large media and 3D assets must be loaded progressively.**
14. **Educational information must not depend exclusively on 3D/WebGL.**
15. **Do not expose sensitive information through browser storage or logs.**
16. **Automate linting and formatting.**
17. **Test critical user journeys end-to-end.**
18. **Measure frontend performance instead of guessing.**
19. **Do not allow API contract drift.**
20. **The frontend can improve UX, but the backend remains the authority for security and business rules.**

> **For Mediverse, the frontend must make complex medical learning feel simple without making the underlying architecture fragile. Components should remain modular, the UI should remain accessible, API interactions should remain predictable, and educational content should remain usable even when advanced features such as WebGL, media, or network services fail.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 55: Database Coding, JPA/Hibernate & Data Access Standards.**

# CSDG — Chapter 55

## Database Coding, JPA/Hibernate & Data Access Standards

### 55.1 Purpose

This chapter defines standards for database design, PostgreSQL usage, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, transactions, repositories, queries, migrations, performance, and data-access security for Mediverse.

Core principle:

> **The database is the authoritative persistence layer. Application code must respect data integrity, transaction boundaries, and explicit access patterns rather than relying on ORM magic.**

---

## 55.2 Database Technology

The Mediverse backend SHOULD use:

```text
PostgreSQL
Spring Data JPA
Hibernate
Flyway / approved migration framework
```

The exact versions must follow the project's dependency-management decisions.

---

## 55.3 Database Naming

Use consistent `snake_case` naming for PostgreSQL objects.

Example:

```text
users
course_modules
lesson_contents
quiz_questions
student_progress
created_at
updated_at
```

Avoid mixing:

```text
camelCase
PascalCase
snake_case
```

within the database schema.

---

## 55.4 Table Naming

Table names SHOULD:

* Be descriptive
* Represent the stored concept
* Follow a consistent pluralization strategy
* Avoid unnecessary abbreviations

Good:

```text
courses
lessons
quiz_attempts
student_progress
```

Avoid:

```text
crs
tblCourse
courseTbl
```

---

## 55.5 Primary Keys

Every persistent entity SHOULD have a clearly defined primary key.

For distributed systems, UUIDs may be preferable where appropriate.

Example:

```text
id UUID PRIMARY KEY
```

Do not introduce UUIDs merely because they are fashionable; consider indexing, storage, readability, and operational requirements.

---

## 55.6 Identifier Strategy

The identifier strategy must be consistent within a bounded context.

Possible strategies:

```text
UUID
BIGINT
Identity/sequence
```

Do not randomly mix identifier strategies without architectural justification.

---

## 55.7 Foreign Keys

Relationships that represent mandatory database integrity SHOULD use foreign keys.

Example:

```text
lesson.course_id
        ↓
courses.id
```

Foreign keys protect against orphaned records and invalid relationships.

---

## 55.8 Referential Integrity

Do not rely solely on Java code to maintain relational integrity.

Bad assumption:

```text
Application prevents invalid relation
        ↓
Therefore DB does not need constraint
```

The database should enforce critical invariants where practical.

---

## 55.9 Unique Constraints

Business-unique values SHOULD be protected at the database level.

Example:

```text
users.email UNIQUE
```

Application-level validation alone is insufficient because concurrent requests can bypass it.

---

## 55.10 NOT NULL

Use `NOT NULL` when a value is mandatory.

Avoid making every column nullable simply because the application currently permits nulls.

Nullability should represent an intentional domain decision.

---

## 55.11 Check Constraints

Use database check constraints where they provide meaningful protection.

Example:

```text
progress_percentage >= 0
AND progress_percentage <= 100
```

The application should also validate this, but the database provides a final integrity boundary.

---

## 55.12 Enum Strategy

Database enums SHOULD be introduced deliberately.

For values that change frequently, a lookup/reference table may be more flexible.

Example:

```text
course_status
lesson_type
user_status
```

The choice must consider:

```text
Schema evolution
Queryability
Application compatibility
Migration complexity
```

---

## 55.13 Timestamps

Persistent entities SHOULD generally track relevant lifecycle timestamps.

Common fields:

```text
created_at
updated_at
```

Additional timestamps may include:

```text
published_at
deleted_at
completed_at
last_login_at
```

only when meaningful.

---

## 55.14 Time Zone

Use a consistent time-handling strategy.

For PostgreSQL, timestamps representing real-world instants should generally be stored in a timezone-aware form such as:

```text
TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE
```

Application code should avoid silently mixing local times and UTC instants.

---

## 55.15 Soft Delete

Soft deletion may be appropriate for entities requiring recovery, auditing, or historical references.

Example:

```text
deleted_at
```

But do not add soft delete to every table automatically.

It complicates:

```text
Queries
Unique constraints
Indexes
Relationships
Storage
```

---

## 55.16 Hard Delete

Hard deletion is appropriate when:

```text
Data has no retention requirement
No historical relationship is required
Legal/privacy requirements permit deletion
```

Deletion policies must be documented.

---

# 55.17 Entity Design

JPA entities should represent persistence models rather than becoming giant business objects.

Avoid putting unrelated responsibilities inside entities.

---

## 55.18 Entity Example

Conceptually:

```java
@Entity
@Table(name = "courses")
public class Course {

    @Id
    private UUID id;

    private String title;

    private String description;
}
```

The exact implementation should follow the project's established conventions.

---

## 55.19 Entity Annotations

JPA annotations should be explicit where ambiguity could cause persistence problems.

Common annotations include:

```text
@Entity
@Table
@Id
@Column
@ManyToOne
@OneToMany
@OneToOne
@ManyToMany
@JoinColumn
```

Do not add annotations without understanding their database implications.

---

## 55.20 Column Mapping

Column names SHOULD be explicitly controlled when the Java naming strategy could become ambiguous.

Example:

```java
@Column(name = "created_at")
private Instant createdAt;
```

This makes the database contract obvious.

---

## 55.21 Entity Constructors

Entities SHOULD have an appropriate protected/package-private no-argument constructor when required by JPA.

Do not expose meaningless public constructors solely because Hibernate requires one.

---

## 55.22 Entity Identity

Entity equality requires careful consideration.

Do not blindly generate:

```text
equals()
hashCode()
```

from every mutable field.

Entity identity should remain stable.

---

## 55.23 Lombok and Entities

If Lombok is used, avoid blindly applying:

```text
@Data
```

to JPA entities.

Generated:

```text
equals
hashCode
toString
```

can cause problems with:

```text
Lazy loading
Bidirectional relationships
Proxy objects
Recursion
Performance
```

---

# 55.24 Relationships

Relationships should reflect actual domain ownership.

Example:

```text
Course
 ↓
Modules
 ↓
Lessons
```

should not automatically become deeply bidirectional JPA relationships everywhere.

---

## 55.25 Prefer Controlled Relationships

A common mistake is creating:

```text
Course → Modules
Module → Course
Module → Lessons
Lesson → Module
Lesson → Course
Course → Lessons
```

This creates unnecessary coupling.

Model only the navigations actually required.

---

## 55.26 Many-to-Many

Avoid direct `@ManyToMany` mappings when the relationship contains meaningful business data.

Example:

```text
Student
   ↕
Enrollment
   ↕
Course
```

If enrollment contains:

```text
enrolled_at
status
completion_percentage
completed_at
```

then `Enrollment` should be its own entity.

---

## 55.27 Join Entities

Prefer an explicit entity for relationships with attributes.

Example:

```text
student
   |
   | 1:N
   ↓
enrollment
   |
   | N:1
   ↓
course
```

This is more expressive and extensible.

---

# 55.28 Lazy Loading

Prefer lazy loading for large relationships where appropriate.

Avoid eagerly loading entire object graphs unnecessarily.

---

## 55.29 EAGER Loading

Do not use `EAGER` simply to solve:

```text
LazyInitializationException
```

That treats the symptom rather than fixing the query/service boundary.

---

## 55.30 N+1 Query Problem

Developers MUST watch for N+1 queries.

Bad:

```text
Load 100 courses
 ↓
100 separate instructor queries
```

Result:

```text
101 queries
```

Potential solutions include:

```text
JOIN FETCH
EntityGraph
DTO projection
Batch fetching
Purpose-built query
```

---

# 55.31 Fetch Joins

Use fetch joins deliberately when related data is required.

Example conceptual query:

```jpql
SELECT c
FROM Course c
JOIN FETCH c.instructor
WHERE c.id = :id
```

Do not blindly fetch every relationship.

---

# 55.32 DTO Projections

For read-heavy APIs, DTO projections SHOULD be considered.

Instead of:

```text
Database
 ↓
Huge Entity Graph
 ↓
JSON
```

prefer:

```text
Database
 ↓
Required projection
 ↓
DTO
 ↓
API response
```

This reduces unnecessary data loading.

---

# 55.33 Entity vs DTO

Do not expose JPA entities directly as API contracts.

Prefer:

```text
Entity
 ↓
Mapper
 ↓
Response DTO
```

This protects the API from persistence implementation details.

---

# 55.34 Request DTOs

Incoming API payloads SHOULD use request DTOs.

Example:

```text
CreateCourseRequest
UpdateCourseRequest
EnrollStudentRequest
SubmitQuizRequest
```

Do not bind arbitrary JSON directly to persistent entities.

---

# 55.35 Mass Assignment Protection

Never allow clients to modify protected fields merely because those fields exist on an entity.

A request such as:

```json
{
  "role": "ADMIN"
}
```

must not accidentally modify a user's role through a general user-update endpoint.

---

# 55.36 Repository Layer

Spring Data repositories SHOULD focus on persistence operations.

Example:

```java
public interface CourseRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Course, UUID> {
}
```

Do not place unrelated business workflows inside repositories.

---

# 55.37 Repository Naming

Repository names should correspond to the aggregate/entity.

Examples:

```text
CourseRepository
LessonRepository
EnrollmentRepository
QuizRepository
ProgressRepository
```

Avoid vague names such as:

```text
DataRepository
CommonRepository
GeneralRepository
```

---

# 55.38 Query Methods

Derived query methods are appropriate for simple queries.

Example:

```java
findByStatus(...)
findByCourseId(...)
findByEmail(...)
```

Do not create absurdly long method names.

---

# 55.39 Complex Queries

For complex queries use:

```text
JPQL
Native SQL
Specifications
QueryDSL
Criteria API
```

according to project standards.

Choose readability over cleverness.

---

# 55.40 Native SQL

Native SQL is acceptable when it provides a clear benefit.

Examples:

```text
Complex PostgreSQL feature
Performance-critical query
Database-specific operation
Advanced reporting
```

Document database-specific assumptions.

---

# 55.41 SQL Injection

Never concatenate untrusted user input into SQL.

Bad:

```java
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"
```

Use:

```text
Parameterized queries
JPA parameters
Prepared statements
```

---

# 55.42 Search Queries

User-entered search criteria must be handled safely.

Particular care is required for:

```text
LIKE
ORDER BY
Pagination
Sorting
Filters
```

Do not blindly inject user-provided column names into SQL.

---

# 55.43 Dynamic Sorting

Whitelist sortable fields.

Bad:

```text
sort = request.getParameter("sort")
```

directly inserted into SQL.

Prefer:

```text
title
createdAt
updatedAt
```

from a predefined allowed list.

---

# 55.44 Pagination

Collection endpoints SHOULD use pagination when datasets can grow significantly.

Example:

```text
GET /courses?page=0&size=20
```

---

# 55.45 Pagination Limits

The API should enforce a maximum page size.

Do not allow:

```text
size=1000000
```

to trigger massive database queries.

---

# 55.46 Offset vs Cursor Pagination

Offset pagination is suitable for many administrative and educational lists.

Cursor/keyset pagination may be preferable for:

```text
Large feeds
High-volume activity
Infinite scrolling
Frequently changing datasets
```

Choose based on actual access patterns.

---

# 55.47 Sorting

Paginated queries should have deterministic ordering.

For example:

```text
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
```

The secondary key prevents ambiguous ordering when timestamps match.

---

# 55.48 Transactions

Transactions MUST be used when multiple database operations must succeed or fail together.

Example:

```text
Enroll student
 ↓
Create enrollment
 ↓
Initialize progress
 ↓
Commit
```

If one required operation fails:

```text
Rollback
```

---

# 55.49 Transaction Boundary

Transactions SHOULD generally be defined at the service/use-case boundary rather than arbitrary repository calls.

Concept:

```text
Controller
 ↓
Service @Transactional
 ↓
Repositories
 ↓
Database
```

---

# 55.50 Read-Only Transactions

Read-only operations MAY use:

```java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
```

where appropriate.

This communicates intent and can provide optimization opportunities.

---

# 55.51 Transaction Size

Avoid unnecessarily long transactions.

Do not keep a database transaction open while performing:

```text
External API call
Large file upload
Long computation
User interaction
```

unless there is a compelling architectural reason.

---

# 55.52 External Calls Inside Transactions

Avoid:

```text
@Transactional
 ↓
Database
 ↓
HTTP call
 ↓
Another HTTP call
 ↓
Database
```

Long-running external operations can hold database resources unnecessarily.

Prefer an architecture using:

```text
Events
Outbox
Saga/workflow
Compensation
```

where appropriate.

---

# 55.53 Transaction Propagation

Transaction propagation should be intentional.

Do not add propagation options simply because they appear in examples.

Document non-default behavior.

---

# 55.54 Isolation Levels

Use the default transaction isolation level unless the use case requires something else.

Higher isolation can create:

```text
Lock contention
Reduced throughput
Deadlocks
```

---

# 55.55 Optimistic Locking

For concurrently modified entities, optimistic locking SHOULD be considered.

Example:

```java
@Version
private Long version;
```

This helps detect:

```text
User A edits
User B edits
User A saves
User B saves
```

without silently overwriting changes.

---

# 55.56 Pessimistic Locking

Use pessimistic locks only where justified.

Examples may include highly contention-sensitive operations where correctness requires serialized access.

Locks should be carefully reviewed for:

```text
Deadlocks
Throughput
Lock duration
Database impact
```

---

# 55.57 Concurrency

Never assume:

```text
if (not exists)
    insert
```

is safe under concurrent requests.

Two requests can both observe:

```text
not exists
```

and both insert.

Use:

```text
Unique constraint
Transaction
Upsert
Appropriate locking
```

as required.

---

# 55.58 Database Constraints as Concurrency Protection

If an enrollment must be unique:

```text
(student_id, course_id)
```

should have a unique constraint.

Do not rely solely on:

```text
repository.exists(...)
```

before insertion.

---

# 55.59 Bulk Operations

Bulk inserts/updates should be used carefully.

Consider:

```text
Batch size
Transaction size
Memory
Locking
Index overhead
```

---

# 55.60 JDBC Batching

For high-volume operations, Hibernate/JDBC batching may be enabled where appropriate.

Measure the actual improvement.

---

# 55.61 Bulk Updates and Persistence Context

Bulk JPQL/SQL updates may bypass normal entity state tracking.

After bulk operations, understand whether the persistence context needs to be cleared or refreshed.

---

# 55.62 Database Migrations

Schema changes MUST be version-controlled.

Use a migration framework such as:

```text
Flyway
Liquibase
```

according to the project's selected standard.

---

# 55.63 Never Manually Modify Production Schema

Avoid directly running ad-hoc schema changes in production.

Bad:

```text
ALTER TABLE ...
```

from an engineer's local terminal with no migration record.

Instead:

```text
Migration
 ↓
Code review
 ↓
CI validation
 ↓
Deployment
```

---

# 55.64 Migration Naming

Use consistent migration names.

Example:

```text
V1__create_users.sql
V2__create_courses.sql
V3__create_enrollments.sql
V4__add_course_status.sql
```

---

# 55.65 Immutable Migrations

Once a migration has been applied to a shared environment, do not casually edit it.

Create a new migration.

Bad:

```text
V5 already deployed
 ↓
Developer edits V5
```

Prefer:

```text
V5 deployed
 ↓
V6 corrects schema
```

---

# 55.66 Migration Review

Every database migration should be reviewed for:

```text
Correctness
Rollback implications
Performance
Locking
Data migration
Backward compatibility
```

---

# 55.67 Destructive Migrations

Operations such as:

```text
DROP COLUMN
DROP TABLE
DELETE large datasets
```

require special review.

Do not combine destructive changes with application changes that still depend on the old structure.

---

# 55.68 Expand-and-Contract

For production schema evolution, prefer:

```text
Expand
 ↓
Deploy compatible application
 ↓
Migrate data
 ↓
Switch application
 ↓
Contract
```

Example:

```text
Old column
+
New column
 ↓
Application writes both
 ↓
Backfill
 ↓
Application reads new
 ↓
Remove old column
```

---

# 55.69 Backward Compatibility

During rolling deployments, old and new application versions may coexist.

Database changes must therefore consider:

```text
Old application
+
New application
+
New schema
```

---

# 55.70 Data Backfills

Large data migrations SHOULD be:

```text
Chunked
Observable
Restartable
Idempotent where possible
```

Avoid one enormous transaction for millions of records.

---

# 55.71 Indexes

Indexes should be created based on query patterns.

Common candidates:

```text
Foreign keys
Frequently searched columns
Unique business identifiers
Sorting/filtering columns
```

---

# 55.72 Index Overuse

Every index has costs:

```text
Storage
Insert overhead
Update overhead
Maintenance
```

Do not create indexes on every column.

---

# 55.73 Composite Indexes

Composite indexes should reflect actual query patterns.

For example:

```text
(student_id, course_id)
```

may be useful for enrollment lookups.

Column ordering matters.

---

# 55.74 Index Validation

Before adding an index, understand the query.

Use PostgreSQL tooling such as:

```text
EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

when performance analysis is required.

---

# 55.75 Query Performance

Slow database operations should be investigated systematically:

```text
Application
 ↓
Generated SQL
 ↓
Query plan
 ↓
Indexes
 ↓
Data volume
 ↓
Locks
 ↓
Database resources
```

Do not automatically blame Hibernate.

---

# 55.76 Fetching Large Data

Do not load huge tables into Java memory.

Bad:

```java
courseRepository.findAll();
```

when millions of records may exist.

Prefer:

```text
Pagination
Streaming where appropriate
Projection
Batch processing
```

---

# 55.77 Database Connection Pool

Connection pooling SHOULD be configured appropriately.

Typical Spring Boot deployments use:

```text
HikariCP
```

The pool must account for:

```text
Application replicas
Database capacity
Concurrent workload
Connection limits
```

---

# 55.78 Connection Pool Sizing

More connections do not automatically mean more performance.

Example:

```text
10 application pods
×
50 DB connections
=
500 connections
```

If PostgreSQL cannot efficiently handle that workload, the application can make the system worse.

---

# 55.79 Connection Leak Prevention

Database connections must be returned to the pool.

Use framework-managed transactions and resources rather than manually managing connections unless required.

---

# 55.80 Query Timeout

Long-running queries SHOULD have appropriate timeout policies.

A runaway query should not consume database resources indefinitely.

---

# 55.81 Database Deadlocks

Applications should monitor for deadlocks.

Prevention includes:

```text
Consistent lock ordering
Short transactions
Appropriate indexes
Avoid unnecessary locks
```

Retry may be appropriate for certain transient deadlock scenarios.

---

# 55.82 Retry Strategy

Database retries MUST be selective.

Do not retry every SQL exception.

Retry only known transient failures where the operation is safe to retry.

---

# 55.83 Idempotency

Operations that may be retried should be designed for idempotency where possible.

This is especially important for:

```text
Enrollment
Progress updates
Payment-related operations
Event processing
Bulk imports
```

---

# 55.84 Data Integrity

Application logic and database constraints should work together.

Think of the layers as:

```text
Frontend validation
        ↓
Backend validation
        ↓
Business rules
        ↓
Database constraints
```

Each layer serves a different purpose.

---

# 55.85 Sensitive Data

Sensitive data stored in PostgreSQL SHOULD have appropriate protection.

Examples:

```text
Personal information
Authentication-related data
Private educational records
Audit information
```

Access should follow least privilege.

---

# 55.86 Encryption

Encryption requirements should be defined according to data classification and deployment environment.

At minimum, production database traffic SHOULD use encrypted transport where supported by the infrastructure.

---

# 55.87 Database Credentials

Database credentials MUST NOT be stored in:

```text
Source code
Git
application logs
Dockerfile
Frontend
```

Use appropriate secret-management mechanisms.

---

# 55.88 Database User Permissions

The application database user should have only the permissions required by the application.

Avoid running the application using a superuser.

Bad:

```text
application → postgres superuser
```

Prefer:

```text
application
 ↓
restricted application role
 ↓
required schema privileges
```

---

# 55.89 Read/Write Separation

Read replicas MAY be introduced when scale requires them.

Architecture:

```text
Write
 ↓
Primary DB

Read
 ↓
Replica
```

But replication lag must be considered.

---

# 55.90 Read-After-Write

If a user writes:

```text
Enroll course
```

and immediately reads:

```text
My courses
```

routing the read to a lagging replica can produce confusing results.

Critical read-after-write workflows may need to use the primary.

---

# 55.91 Caching and Database

Caching should not replace database correctness.

Example:

```text
Cache says:
Course available

Database says:
Course unpublished
```

The authoritative source and invalidation strategy must be clear.

---

# 55.92 Redis

If Redis is used for caching/session-related functionality:

```text
Cache
≠
Primary database
```

Critical persistent data must not exist only in an ephemeral cache unless explicitly designed as such.

---

# 55.93 Database Auditing

Important domain changes SHOULD be auditable.

Examples:

```text
Course published
Course unpublished
User role changed
Quiz configuration changed
Student progress modified
```

Audit design should distinguish:

```text
Who
What
When
Before
After
Why/context where appropriate
```

---

# 55.94 Audit Data

Audit records should be protected from ordinary application users.

Do not allow users to modify their own audit history through normal APIs.

---

# 55.95 PII

Personal information should be classified and handled according to Mediverse's privacy requirements.

Do not duplicate PII unnecessarily across tables/services.

---

# 55.96 Data Retention

Define retention policies for:

```text
User data
Learning progress
Audit records
Logs
Temporary uploads
Deleted accounts
```

Do not retain everything forever simply because storage is cheap.

---

# 55.97 Backup

Production PostgreSQL MUST have an appropriate backup strategy.

Backups should consider:

```text
Frequency
Retention
Encryption
Storage isolation
Recovery objectives
```

---

# 55.98 Restore Testing

A backup that has never been restored is not proven reliable.

Regularly test:

```text
Backup
 ↓
Restore
 ↓
Validation
```

---

# 55.99 Disaster Recovery

Database recovery planning should define:

```text
RPO
RTO
Backup strategy
Failover strategy
Recovery procedure
Ownership
```

---

# 55.100 Definition of Done

A Mediverse data-access implementation is production-ready when:

* [ ] Schema follows naming standards
* [ ] Primary keys are defined
* [ ] Foreign keys protect important relationships
* [ ] Unique constraints protect business uniqueness
* [ ] Required fields use appropriate `NOT NULL`
* [ ] Entity mappings are deliberate
* [ ] API DTOs are separated from entities
* [ ] Lazy/eager loading is intentional
* [ ] N+1 queries are checked
* [ ] Pagination exists for large collections
* [ ] Queries are parameterized
* [ ] Dynamic sorting/filtering is safely controlled
* [ ] Transactions have clear boundaries
* [ ] Concurrency has been considered
* [ ] Database migrations are version-controlled
* [ ] Destructive migrations receive additional review
* [ ] Indexes are justified
* [ ] Query performance has been evaluated
* [ ] Connection pooling is configured
* [ ] Database credentials are protected
* [ ] Application DB permissions follow least privilege
* [ ] Backups exist
* [ ] Restore procedures are tested
* [ ] Data retention is defined
* [ ] Sensitive data is appropriately protected
* [ ] Critical data changes are auditable

---

# 55.101 Core Principles

1. **The database is an integrity boundary.**
2. **Do not rely exclusively on application validation.**
3. **Do not expose JPA entities directly as API contracts.**
4. **Avoid unnecessary bidirectional relationships.**
5. **Do not solve lazy-loading problems with blanket EAGER loading.**
6. **Detect and eliminate N+1 queries.**
7. **Use transactions around business operations, not arbitrary repository calls.**
8. **Database constraints must protect important invariants.**
9. **Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL.**
10. **Pagination is mandatory for potentially large collections.**
11. **Indexes must be justified by access patterns.**
12. **Schema changes must be version-controlled.**
13. **Deployed migrations should be treated as immutable.**
14. **Production schema changes must support rolling deployments.**
15. **Concurrency must be explicitly considered.**
16. **Connection pools must be sized according to total application replicas.**
17. **The application must never use a database superuser.**
18. **Backups are useless if restoration has never been tested.**
19. **Caching must never silently replace authoritative persistence.**
20. **Database design must support correctness first, then performance, then convenience.**

> **For Mediverse, JPA/Hibernate is an implementation tool—not a substitute for understanding PostgreSQL. Developers must understand the SQL and data-access consequences of their entity mappings, queries, relationships, transactions, and indexes.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 56: API Design, REST, HTTP Semantics & Integration Standards.**

# CSDG — Chapter 56

## API Design, REST, HTTP Semantics & Integration Standards

### 56.1 Purpose

This chapter defines standards for designing, implementing, documenting, securing, versioning, testing, and consuming APIs within Mediverse.

It covers:

* REST API design
* HTTP semantics
* Resource modeling
* Request/response contracts
* Status codes
* Validation
* Pagination
* Filtering and sorting
* Error responses
* Idempotency
* API versioning
* Authentication and authorization
* Service-to-service communication
* API documentation
* Backward compatibility
* Observability

Core principle:

> **An API is a contract between systems. It must be predictable, explicit, versionable, secure, and independent of internal implementation details.**

---

# 56.2 API Architecture

Mediverse APIs SHOULD follow a layered architecture:

```text
Client
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Application / Service Layer
  ↓
Domain Logic
  ↓
Repository
  ↓
Database
```

The controller should not become the business-logic layer.

---

# 56.3 REST Resource Modeling

Model APIs around resources rather than implementation actions.

Prefer:

```text
GET    /api/v1/courses
GET    /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
POST   /api/v1/courses
PATCH  /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
DELETE /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
```

Avoid RPC-style endpoints where normal resource semantics are sufficient:

```text
/getAllCourses
/createNewCourse
/deleteCourseById
```

---

# 56.4 API Base Path

Mediverse APIs SHOULD use a consistent base path.

Example:

```text
/api/v1/...
```

Do not mix:

```text
/api/...
/v1/...
/service/api/...
```

without an architectural reason.

---

# 56.5 Resource Naming

Resource names SHOULD:

* Use nouns
* Be plural where the project convention requires it
* Use lowercase
* Use predictable hierarchy

Preferred:

```text
/courses
/lessons
/quizzes
/students
/enrollments
```

---

# 56.6 Nested Resources

Nested resources are appropriate when the relationship is meaningful.

Example:

```text
/courses/{courseId}/lessons
```

But avoid excessively deep URLs.

Bad:

```text
/courses/{courseId}/modules/{moduleId}/lessons/{lessonId}/questions/{questionId}/options
```

If the resource has an independent identity, a flatter endpoint may be clearer.

---

# 56.7 HTTP Methods

Use HTTP methods according to their intended semantics.

| Method | Typical purpose                           |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| GET    | Retrieve                                  |
| POST   | Create / execute non-idempotent operation |
| PUT    | Replace                                   |
| PATCH  | Partial update                            |
| DELETE | Delete                                    |

Do not use `POST` for everything.

---

# 56.8 GET

GET requests SHOULD:

* Retrieve data
* Be safe
* Not modify persistent state

Bad:

```text
GET /courses/{id}/enroll
```

if enrollment changes state.

Prefer:

```text
POST /courses/{id}/enrollments
```

---

# 56.9 POST

POST is appropriate for:

```text
Create resource
Submit operation
Trigger a non-idempotent domain action
```

Example:

```text
POST /courses/{courseId}/enrollments
POST /quizzes/{quizId}/attempts
```

---

# 56.10 PUT

PUT should represent replacement semantics where used.

Example:

```text
PUT /users/{userId}/preferences
```

The client provides the representation intended to replace the resource.

Do not casually use PUT and PATCH interchangeably.

---

# 56.11 PATCH

PATCH SHOULD be used for partial updates.

Example:

```text
PATCH /courses/{courseId}
```

Request:

```json
{
  "title": "Advanced Human Physiology"
}
```

Only the permitted field should change.

---

# 56.12 DELETE

DELETE should represent deletion or deactivation according to the resource's defined semantics.

For soft deletion, the API contract must make the behavior clear.

---

# 56.13 HTTP Status Codes

Use status codes consistently.

Common standards:

```text
200 OK
201 Created
202 Accepted
204 No Content
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
422 Unprocessable Entity
429 Too Many Requests
500 Internal Server Error
503 Service Unavailable
```

Do not return `200 OK` for every situation.

---

# 56.14 200 OK

Use when the request succeeded and a response body is returned.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses/123
→ 200 OK
```

---

# 56.15 201 Created

Use when a new resource has been successfully created.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/courses
→ 201 Created
```

The response SHOULD identify the newly created resource.

---

# 56.16 204 No Content

Use when the operation succeeds and no response body is required.

Example:

```text
DELETE /api/v1/courses/123
→ 204 No Content
```

---

# 56.17 400 Bad Request

Use for malformed requests or invalid request structure.

Examples:

```text
Malformed JSON
Invalid query parameter format
Invalid request syntax
```

---

# 56.18 401 Unauthorized

Use when authentication is required but missing or invalid.

Example:

```text
Missing/expired/invalid authentication
```

---

# 56.19 403 Forbidden

Use when the caller is authenticated but lacks permission.

Example:

```text
Student attempts faculty-only operation
```

---

# 56.20 404 Not Found

Use when the requested resource does not exist or should not be exposed as existing according to the security model.

Do not return `500` for a missing resource.

---

# 56.21 409 Conflict

Use when the request conflicts with the current state.

Examples:

```text
Duplicate enrollment
Concurrent modification
Invalid state transition
Unique constraint conflict
```

---

# 56.22 422 Unprocessable Entity

Where adopted by the project, use `422` for semantically invalid input that is structurally valid.

The project should choose a consistent convention between `400` and `422`.

---

# 56.23 429 Too Many Requests

Use when rate limiting has been triggered.

The response SHOULD provide enough information for a client to understand when retrying may be appropriate.

---

# 56.24 500 Internal Server Error

`500` represents an unexpected server-side failure.

Never use it as a generic replacement for:

```text
400
401
403
404
409
422
```

---

# 56.25 503 Service Unavailable

Use when the service is temporarily unable to process requests, such as during a dependency outage or controlled maintenance scenario.

---

# 56.26 Request DTOs

Every non-trivial write endpoint SHOULD have an explicit request contract.

Example:

```text
CreateCourseRequest
UpdateCourseRequest
CreateLessonRequest
SubmitQuizRequest
```

Avoid accepting arbitrary maps for normal application APIs.

---

# 56.27 Response DTOs

Responses SHOULD use explicit DTOs.

Example:

```text
CourseResponse
LessonResponse
QuizResponse
ProgressResponse
```

Do not expose internal JPA entities.

---

# 56.28 Response Consistency

Equivalent resources should have consistent response shapes.

If:

```text
CourseResponse
```

uses:

```json
{
  "id": "...",
  "title": "...",
  "description": "..."
}
```

do not create another endpoint returning:

```json
{
  "courseId": "...",
  "course_name": "..."
}
```

without a deliberate contract difference.

---

# 56.29 Resource Identifiers

Identifiers should be stable.

A resource ID should not change simply because:

```text
Title changed
Slug changed
Display name changed
```

---

# 56.30 Slugs

Slugs MAY be used for human-readable URLs.

Example:

```text
/courses/human-physiology
```

But do not treat mutable slugs as permanent database identity unless explicitly designed that way.

---

# 56.31 Request Validation

All externally supplied input MUST be validated.

Validation should include:

```text
Required fields
Length
Format
Range
Allowed values
Cross-field constraints
```

---

# 56.32 Validation Layers

Validation exists at multiple levels:

```text
Frontend
   ↓
API request validation
   ↓
Business validation
   ↓
Database constraints
```

These layers are complementary.

---

# 56.33 Business Validation

Business rules belong in the application/domain layer.

Example:

```text
Student cannot submit an attempt after the quiz is closed.
```

This is not merely a database validation problem.

---

# 56.34 Error Response Contract

Errors SHOULD use a consistent structure.

Example:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-09T10:30:00Z",
  "status": 400,
  "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
  "message": "Request validation failed",
  "path": "/api/v1/courses",
  "traceId": "abc123",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "code": "REQUIRED",
      "message": "Title is required"
    }
  ]
}
```

The exact contract must follow the project's canonical API specification.

---

# 56.35 Error Codes

Application error codes SHOULD be stable and machine-readable.

Examples:

```text
COURSE_NOT_FOUND
ENROLLMENT_ALREADY_EXISTS
QUIZ_CLOSED
ACCESS_DENIED
VALIDATION_ERROR
```

Do not make clients parse human-readable messages to determine behavior.

---

# 56.36 Error Messages

Messages should be:

```text
Clear
Useful
Non-sensitive
```

Never expose:

```text
SQL statements
Stack traces
Database credentials
Internal service details
```

to normal API consumers.

---

# 56.37 Global Exception Handling

Spring Boot APIs SHOULD use centralized exception handling.

Typical mechanism:

```java
@RestControllerAdvice
```

This prevents every controller from implementing its own inconsistent error handling.

---

# 56.38 Exception Mapping

Map known exceptions deliberately.

Example:

```text
ResourceNotFoundException → 404
ValidationException        → 400/422
AccessDeniedException      → 403
ConflictException          → 409
Unexpected exception       → 500
```

---

# 56.39 Internal Exceptions

Do not expose raw Java exception messages to clients.

Bad:

```json
{
  "message": "could not execute statement; SQL [insert into ...]"
}
```

---

# 56.40 Pagination Contract

Collection endpoints SHOULD have a consistent pagination model.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?page=0&size=20
```

Response may contain:

```json
{
  "content": [],
  "page": 0,
  "size": 20,
  "totalElements": 125,
  "totalPages": 7
}
```

The exact canonical response shape should remain consistent across the API.

---

# 56.41 Maximum Page Size

APIs MUST enforce a maximum page size.

Example:

```text
size <= 100
```

The actual limit should be selected according to workload.

---

# 56.42 Filtering

Filtering should use predictable query parameters.

Example:

```text
GET /courses?status=PUBLISHED
```

Avoid inventing endpoint variants for every filter combination.

---

# 56.43 Sorting

Example:

```text
GET /courses?sort=createdAt,desc
```

Only approved fields should be sortable.

---

# 56.44 Search

Search parameters should have clear semantics.

Example:

```text
GET /courses?search=physiology
```

The API must protect search functionality from:

```text
SQL injection
Excessive query cost
Unbounded result sets
```

---

# 56.45 API Idempotency

Idempotency matters for operations that may be retried.

Example:

```text
POST /payments
POST /enrollments
```

If duplicate processing is dangerous, an idempotency strategy should be considered.

---

# 56.46 Idempotency Keys

For appropriate operations:

```http
Idempotency-Key: <unique-request-id>
```

may be used.

The server must define:

```text
Key lifetime
Scope
Stored result
Conflict behavior
Retry semantics
```

---

# 56.47 Duplicate Requests

Never assume the client sends exactly one request.

Users can:

```text
Double-click
Refresh
Retry
Lose network response
```

Infrastructure can also retry requests.

The server must protect important operations against duplicate execution.

---

# 56.48 API Versioning

Breaking API changes MUST NOT silently replace an existing contract.

Preferred approach:

```text
/api/v1/...
/api/v2/...
```

or another explicitly adopted versioning mechanism.

---

# 56.49 Breaking Changes

Examples include:

```text
Removing response fields
Renaming fields
Changing field types
Changing semantics
Removing endpoints
Changing authorization requirements
```

These require explicit versioning or migration strategy.

---

# 56.50 Non-Breaking Changes

Generally safer changes include:

```text
Adding optional response fields
Adding new endpoints
Adding optional request fields
```

provided existing clients continue to function.

---

# 56.51 API Deprecation

Deprecated APIs SHOULD have:

```text
Deprecation notice
Migration documentation
Replacement endpoint
Expected removal timeline
```

Do not abruptly remove APIs used by active clients.

---

# 56.52 OpenAPI

All production APIs SHOULD be documented using OpenAPI/Swagger according to the project's canonical documentation strategy.

Documentation should describe:

```text
Endpoints
Parameters
Request bodies
Responses
Authentication
Errors
Examples
```

---

# 56.53 OpenAPI Accuracy

OpenAPI documentation must remain synchronized with actual behavior.

An API that says:

```text
201 Created
```

but actually returns:

```text
200 OK
```

has a broken contract.

---

# 56.54 API Examples

Important endpoints should have realistic request/response examples.

Examples should not contain:

```text
Real passwords
Real tokens
Personal information
Production secrets
```

---

# 56.55 Authentication

Protected APIs MUST enforce authentication according to Mediverse's security architecture.

Authentication answers:

> Who are you?

Authorization answers:

> What are you allowed to do?

Do not confuse the two.

---

# 56.56 Authorization

Every protected operation must enforce authorization server-side.

Example:

```text
Student
 ↓
POST /courses/{id}/publish
 ↓
403 Forbidden
```

if the student lacks the required permission.

---

# 56.57 Object-Level Authorization

Checking only:

```text
ROLE_FACULTY
```

may not be enough.

The backend may also need to verify:

```text
Does this faculty member own this course?
Is this user assigned to this institution?
Is this resource accessible to this student?
```

---

# 56.58 IDOR Protection

Never assume possession of an ID grants access.

Bad:

```text
GET /students/123/progress
```

simply because `123` exists.

The server must determine whether the requesting user is allowed to access that resource.

---

# 56.59 Authentication Tokens

Access tokens must be handled according to the project's security architecture.

Never log:

```text
Authorization: Bearer ...
```

or store tokens in application logs.

---

# 56.60 CORS

CORS should be explicitly configured.

Do not use:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

for protected production APIs unless there is a deliberate architectural reason.

---

# 56.61 CSRF

CSRF protection requirements depend on the authentication mechanism.

For cookie-based authentication, CSRF must be explicitly addressed.

Do not assume:

```text
JWT = automatically secure
```

Security depends on how the token is stored and transmitted.

---

# 56.62 Rate Limiting

Rate limiting SHOULD protect sensitive or expensive endpoints.

Examples:

```text
Login
Password reset
Search
File upload
Quiz submission
AI generation
```

---

# 56.63 Expensive APIs

Operations involving:

```text
AI generation
3D processing
Media processing
Large exports
Analytics
```

should not be allowed to consume unlimited resources from a single client.

---

# 56.64 Asynchronous APIs

Long-running operations SHOULD use asynchronous processing where appropriate.

Example:

```text
POST /exports
      ↓
202 Accepted
      ↓
background processing
      ↓
GET /exports/{id}
```

Do not keep an HTTP request open for several minutes if the operation can be modeled asynchronously.

---

# 56.65 202 Accepted

`202 Accepted` indicates that the request has been accepted for processing but has not necessarily completed.

The API should provide a way to determine the operation's state.

---

# 56.66 Webhooks

If Mediverse exposes webhooks:

```text
Authentication
Signature verification
Replay protection
Idempotency
Retry handling
Timeouts
```

must be addressed.

---

# 56.67 Service-to-Service APIs

Internal APIs should still have explicit contracts.

Do not assume:

```text
internal = trusted
```

Internal services can fail, misbehave, or be compromised.

---

# 56.68 Service Authentication

Service-to-service communication SHOULD use authenticated identities where required by the architecture.

Examples:

```text
mTLS
OAuth2 client credentials
Signed requests
Service identity
```

Use the project's approved mechanism.

---

# 56.69 Timeouts

Every outbound HTTP call SHOULD have an explicit timeout policy.

Never allow:

```text
Service A
 ↓
Service B
 ↓
wait forever
```

---

# 56.70 Retries

Retries should be:

```text
Limited
Backed off
Jittered where appropriate
Safe for the operation
```

Do not retry non-idempotent operations blindly.

---

# 56.71 Circuit Breaking

For unstable downstream services, circuit-breaking may be appropriate.

Concept:

```text
Healthy
 ↓
Failures
 ↓
Circuit Open
 ↓
Fail fast
 ↓
Recovery test
 ↓
Closed
```

---

# 56.72 Bulkheads

Critical services should not necessarily share unlimited resources.

Bulkhead strategies can isolate:

```text
AI requests
Media processing
Search
Notifications
Core learning APIs
```

so one subsystem cannot consume all resources.

---

# 56.73 Correlation IDs

Requests SHOULD carry a correlation/trace identifier.

Example:

```http
X-Request-ID: abc123
```

or the project's approved tracing mechanism.

This allows:

```text
Frontend
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Database
 ↓
Logs
```

to be correlated.

---

# 56.74 Distributed Tracing

Where Mediverse uses multiple services, distributed tracing SHOULD be considered.

Trace context should propagate across service boundaries.

---

# 56.75 API Logging

Log useful operational information such as:

```text
Request ID
Endpoint
HTTP method
Status
Latency
Service
```

Do not log sensitive request bodies indiscriminately.

---

# 56.76 API Metrics

Track useful metrics such as:

```text
Request count
Error rate
Latency
95th/99th percentile latency
Rate-limit events
Dependency failures
```

---

# 56.77 Health Endpoints

Health endpoints should distinguish:

```text
Liveness
Readiness
```

where applicable.

A service being alive does not necessarily mean it is ready to receive production traffic.

---

# 56.78 API Gateway

If Mediverse uses an API gateway:

```text
Client
 ↓
Gateway
 ↓
Services
```

the gateway may provide:

```text
Routing
Authentication integration
Rate limiting
TLS termination
Observability
```

But business authorization must not be assumed to exist only at the gateway.

---

# 56.79 File APIs

File upload/download endpoints must define:

```text
Allowed types
Maximum size
Authentication
Authorization
Storage strategy
Virus/malware scanning where required
Content-Disposition
Caching
```

---

# 56.80 Content-Type

APIs should use correct content types.

Typical examples:

```text
application/json
multipart/form-data
application/octet-stream
```

Do not accept arbitrary content types for sensitive endpoints.

---

# 56.81 API Security Headers

Security-related HTTP headers should be managed according to the project's security architecture and gateway configuration.

Do not duplicate conflicting policies across services.

---

# 56.82 API Contract Testing

Critical APIs SHOULD use contract testing where multiple independently deployed systems depend on them.

This helps detect:

```text
Provider changes
Consumer assumptions
Response schema drift
```

---

# 56.83 Backward Compatibility Testing

Before releasing API changes, test existing consumers where possible.

Especially for:

```text
Mobile
Web
Admin
External integrations
Other backend services
```

---

# 56.84 Integration Testing

Integration tests should verify:

```text
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Database / dependency
```

for important workflows.

Do not rely solely on mocked unit tests for API correctness.

---

# 56.85 API Documentation in Code

Endpoint documentation should explain:

```text
Purpose
Authorization
Request
Response
Errors
Important business constraints
```

Avoid comments that simply restate:

```java
// Get course
```

---

# 56.86 API Naming Consistency

The same domain concept must use the same terminology everywhere.

If the domain calls it:

```text
Course
```

do not alternate between:

```text
Course
Training
Subject
Program
CourseEntity
```

unless these represent genuinely different concepts.

---

# 56.87 Medical Domain Terminology

Mediverse APIs must preserve the project's canonical medical terminology.

For example, if the domain distinguishes:

```text
Subject
Chapter
Module
Lesson
Topic
```

do not collapse them into one generic API resource merely for convenience.

---

# 56.88 Educational Progress APIs

Progress APIs must clearly define what progress means.

For example:

```text
lesson completion
module completion
course completion
quiz score
learning time
```

These should not be conflated into a single ambiguous `progress` value.

---

# 56.89 Quiz Submission APIs

Quiz submission endpoints require particular attention to:

```text
Duplicate submissions
Attempt limits
Time limits
Authorization
Question version
Scoring consistency
Concurrency
```

The server must remain authoritative for scoring and attempt state.

---

# 56.90 AI APIs

Mediverse AI endpoints should clearly define:

```text
Input
Model/task type
Authorization
Usage limits
Response format
Timeout
Failure behavior
Audit requirements
```

AI-generated output must not automatically be treated as medically authoritative.

---

# 56.91 API Definition of Done

An API feature is production-ready when:

* [ ] Resource model is clear
* [ ] HTTP methods are semantically appropriate
* [ ] URL naming is consistent
* [ ] Request DTO exists
* [ ] Response DTO exists
* [ ] Validation exists
* [ ] Business rules are enforced server-side
* [ ] Authentication is enforced where required
* [ ] Authorization is enforced at resource level where required
* [ ] Correct HTTP status codes are returned
* [ ] Error contract is consistent
* [ ] Pagination exists where necessary
* [ ] Filtering/sorting is controlled
* [ ] Duplicate/retry behavior is understood
* [ ] API documentation is updated
* [ ] OpenAPI contract is accurate
* [ ] Sensitive information is not exposed
* [ ] Rate limiting exists where necessary
* [ ] Timeouts exist for downstream calls
* [ ] Retry behavior is safe
* [ ] Observability exists
* [ ] Integration tests exist
* [ ] Backward compatibility has been considered

---

# 56.92 Core Principles

1. **An API is a contract, not an implementation detail.**
2. **Use HTTP semantics correctly.**
3. **Model resources clearly.**
4. **Never expose persistence entities directly as public API contracts.**
5. **Use explicit request and response DTOs.**
6. **Return meaningful HTTP status codes.**
7. **Use consistent error responses.**
8. **Validate all external input.**
9. **Authorization must happen server-side.**
10. **Resource IDs do not imply permission.**
11. **Design for duplicate requests and retries.**
12. **Version breaking changes.**
13. **Keep OpenAPI documentation synchronized with reality.**
14. **Never expose secrets or internal stack traces.**
15. **Protect expensive APIs with appropriate limits.**
16. **Use timeouts on downstream calls.**
17. **Retries must be bounded and safe.**
18. **Long-running work should use asynchronous processing where appropriate.**
19. **Every production API should be observable.**
20. **API design must optimize for long-term compatibility, not just today's frontend.**

> **For Mediverse, APIs are the backbone connecting the web application, mobile clients, AI capabilities, administrative systems, and future services. An API that works today but is ambiguous, insecure, or impossible to evolve is not considered a successful implementation.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 57: Security Coding Standards, Authentication, Authorization & Application Security.**

# CSDG — Chapter 57

## Security Coding Standards, Authentication, Authorization & Application Security

### 57.1 Purpose

This chapter defines mandatory security coding standards for the Mediverse platform.

It covers:

* Authentication
* Authorization
* JWT/security tokens
* Password security
* RBAC and permissions
* Resource-level authorization
* Input validation
* Injection prevention
* XSS/CSRF/CORS
* Secrets management
* Session security
* API security
* File security
* AI security
* Logging and auditing
* Dependency security
* Security testing

Core principle:

> **Security must be enforced by design and at every trust boundary. The frontend, API gateway, service layer, and database must never blindly trust data originating outside their own security boundary.**

---

# 57.2 Security Principles

Mediverse MUST follow:

```text
Least Privilege
Defense in Depth
Secure by Default
Fail Securely
Zero Trust
Explicit Authorization
Input Validation
Output Encoding
Data Minimization
Secure Configuration
Auditability
```

---

# 57.3 Security Is Not a Frontend Responsibility

Frontend controls improve UX but do not provide authoritative security.

This is NOT security:

```text
if (user.role === "ADMIN") {
    showDeleteButton();
}
```

The backend must independently verify:

```text
Authentication
+
Authorization
+
Resource ownership/access
```

---

# 57.4 Trust Boundaries

Treat all external input as untrusted.

Sources include:

```text
Browser
Mobile application
Third-party API
Uploaded files
HTTP headers
Query parameters
Path variables
Request bodies
Cookies
Webhooks
AI-generated content
```

---

# 57.5 Authentication vs Authorization

Authentication:

> **Who is the caller?**

Authorization:

> **What is the caller allowed to do?**

Never use successful authentication as proof of authorization.

---

# 57.6 Authentication Architecture

The authentication architecture must have clearly defined:

```text
Identity provider
Credential verification
Token/session issuance
Token validation
Token expiration
Refresh strategy
Logout/revocation
Account recovery
```

---

# 57.7 Password Storage

Passwords MUST NEVER be stored as plaintext.

Never:

```text id="s9u1w8"
password = "MyPassword123"
```

or reversible encryption.

Use a modern password hashing algorithm such as the project's approved adaptive password hashing mechanism.

---

# 57.8 Password Hashing

Password hashing should be:

```text
One-way
Salted
Computationally expensive
Configurable
```

Do not invent a custom password-hashing algorithm.

---

# 57.9 Password Logging

Passwords MUST NEVER appear in:

```text
Application logs
Exception messages
Audit records
Metrics
Tracing
API responses
```

---

# 57.10 Password Requirements

Password policy should be defined centrally.

Consider:

```text
Minimum length
Common-password detection
Credential stuffing resistance
Rate limiting
Account lockout strategy
Password reset
```

Avoid unnecessarily complicated rules that encourage users to create predictable patterns.

---

# 57.11 Brute Force Protection

Authentication endpoints MUST be protected against excessive attempts.

Controls may include:

```text
Rate limiting
Progressive delays
Temporary lockout
CAPTCHA/risk controls
IP/device signals
```

Do not permanently lock accounts based solely on easily spoofed signals.

---

# 57.12 Credential Stuffing

Login protection must consider reused credentials obtained from external breaches.

Where appropriate, integrate:

```text
Compromised-password detection
Rate limiting
MFA
Risk-based controls
```

---

# 57.13 JWT

If JWT is used, tokens must have:

```text
Short, appropriate expiration
Strong signing algorithm
Issuer validation
Audience validation where applicable
Explicit claims
```

Do not accept arbitrary algorithms from the token header.

---

# 57.14 JWT Secret Management
