JWT signing secrets/private keys MUST NOT exist in:

```text
Git
Source code
Dockerfile
Frontend code
Application logs
README examples containing real values
```

Use secure secret management.

---

# 57.15 JWT Claims

Only include claims that are genuinely required.

Typical claims may include:

```text
sub
iss
aud
exp
iat
jti
scope/roles
```

Do not place sensitive personal information into tokens unnecessarily.

---

# 57.16 JWT Validation

The server must validate relevant token properties:

```text
Signature
Expiration
Issuer
Audience
Token type
Required claims
```

Do not merely decode a JWT and trust its contents.

---

# 57.17 JWT Storage

Token-storage strategy must be deliberately chosen.

Do not automatically assume:

```text
localStorage = secure
```

Browser-accessible storage can increase exposure if an XSS vulnerability exists.

---

# 57.18 Refresh Tokens

Refresh tokens require stronger protection than short-lived access tokens.

They should have:

```text
Limited lifetime
Rotation where appropriate
Revocation strategy
Secure storage
Reuse detection where appropriate
```

---

# 57.19 Token Revocation

The architecture must define how compromised or invalidated sessions are handled.

Possible mechanisms:

```text
Token blacklist
Refresh-token revocation
Session store
Token versioning
Short token lifetime
```

Choose according to the system architecture.

---

# 57.20 Logout

Logout must invalidate the relevant authentication state according to the chosen authentication model.

Deleting a frontend variable alone may not be sufficient.

---

# 57.21 Session Security

If server-side sessions are used:

```text
Secure cookies
HttpOnly
SameSite policy
Expiration
Session rotation
Session invalidation
```

must be appropriately configured.

---

# 57.22 Cookie Security

Authentication cookies should generally use:

```text
HttpOnly
Secure
Appropriate SameSite
```

according to the deployment architecture.

---

# 57.23 CSRF

If authentication relies on browser cookies, CSRF protection MUST be addressed.

Do not assume:

```text
HTTPS = CSRF protection
```

HTTPS protects transport confidentiality/integrity; it does not by itself prevent cross-site request forgery.

---

# 57.24 CORS

CORS must use explicit trusted origins in production.

Avoid:

```text
*
```

for authenticated applications unless there is a deliberate and reviewed reason.

---

# 57.25 Origin Validation

Do not treat the browser's `Origin` header as an authorization mechanism.

CORS is a browser enforcement mechanism, not a replacement for server-side access control.

---

# 57.26 RBAC

Mediverse may use Role-Based Access Control.

Example:

```text
STUDENT
FACULTY
ADMIN
```

Roles should represent meaningful authorization groupings.

---

# 57.27 Permission-Based Authorization

For complex systems, permissions should supplement roles.

Example:

```text
COURSE_READ
COURSE_CREATE
COURSE_EDIT
COURSE_PUBLISH
COURSE_DELETE
QUIZ_MANAGE
USER_MANAGE
```

Avoid embedding every authorization rule directly into role names.

---

# 57.28 Authorization Checks

Authorization should happen at the point where the protected action is executed.

Example:

```text
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Can this user modify this course?
 ↓
Business operation
```

---

# 57.29 Resource-Level Authorization

Role checks alone are insufficient.

Example:

```text
Faculty A
```

may have:

```text
COURSE_EDIT
```

but that does not automatically mean:

```text
Faculty A → Edit every course
```

The system may need to verify ownership or assignment.

---

# 57.30 IDOR Prevention

Never trust resource identifiers supplied by users.

Bad:

```text
GET /api/v1/students/123/progress
```

and automatically returning student `123`.

Verify:

```text
Authenticated user
+
Requested resource
+
Allowed relationship
```

---

# 57.31 Horizontal Privilege Escalation

Prevent users from accessing another user's data at the same privilege level.

Example:

```text
Student A
 ↓
Student B's private progress
```

must be rejected.

---

# 57.32 Vertical Privilege Escalation

Prevent lower-privileged users from invoking higher-privileged functionality.

Example:

```text
STUDENT
 ↓
POST /admin/users/{id}/roles
```

must fail authorization.

---

# 57.33 Administrative APIs

Administrative APIs require particularly strict controls.

Consider:

```text
Strong authentication
MFA
Fine-grained authorization
Audit logging
Rate limiting
Separate access policies
```

where appropriate.

---

# 57.34 Input Validation

Validate all external input.

Examples:

```text
Path parameters
Query parameters
JSON
Multipart forms
Headers
Cookies
Webhook payloads
```

---

# 57.35 Allowlisting

Where possible, prefer allowlists.

Example:

```text
Allowed sort fields:
title
createdAt
updatedAt
```

instead of attempting to blacklist dangerous values.

---

# 57.36 Injection Prevention

Prevent:

```text
SQL Injection
JPQL Injection
OS Command Injection
LDAP Injection
Expression Injection
Template Injection
NoSQL Injection
```

according to the technologies used.

---

# 57.37 SQL Injection

Always use:

```text
Prepared statements
Parameterized queries
JPA parameters
Safe query APIs
```

Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL.

---

# 57.38 Command Injection

Do not construct operating-system commands from user input.

Avoid:

```java
Runtime.getRuntime().exec(userInput);
```

If command execution is genuinely required:

```text
Allowlist executable
Allowlist arguments
Avoid shell interpretation
Apply least privilege
```

---

# 57.39 XSS

User-controlled content must not be rendered as executable HTML/JavaScript.

Avoid unsafe HTML injection.

If HTML is required:

```text
Sanitize
Allowlist tags
Allowlist attributes
Remove scripts
```

---

# 57.40 Output Encoding

Encode data according to its output context.

Different contexts include:

```text
HTML
JavaScript
URL
JSON
SQL
Shell
```

One generic escaping mechanism does not safely handle every context.

---

# 57.41 Content Security Policy

Production web applications SHOULD consider a strong Content Security Policy.

CSP should be designed around the actual application's requirements rather than copied blindly from examples.

---

# 57.42 Security Headers

Where applicable, configure security headers such as:

```text
Content-Security-Policy
X-Content-Type-Options
Referrer-Policy
Permissions-Policy
```

and appropriate transport-security controls.

---

# 57.43 HTTPS

Production traffic MUST use HTTPS.

Sensitive data must not travel over plaintext HTTP.

---

# 57.44 HSTS

Production HTTPS deployments SHOULD use HTTP Strict Transport Security where appropriate.

Be careful with preload-related settings because they can create long-lived browser behavior.

---

# 57.45 Secrets Management

Secrets must be externalized.

Examples:

```text
Database password
JWT private key
OAuth client secret
Cloud credentials
Encryption keys
Third-party API keys
```

should be managed using an approved secret-management system.

---

# 57.46 Environment Variables

Environment variables are useful for configuration, but they are not automatically a secure secret store.

Protect:

```text
CI logs
Container inspection
Process environments
Deployment manifests
```

accordingly.

---

# 57.47 Kubernetes Secrets

Kubernetes `Secret` objects are configuration mechanisms, not automatically equivalent to a dedicated secret vault.

Where required, integrate with:

```text
External Secrets
Cloud secret manager
Vault
```

according to the Mediverse infrastructure architecture.

---

# 57.48 Docker Secrets

Do not bake secrets into Docker images.

Bad:

```dockerfile
ENV DB_PASSWORD=myPassword
```

---

# 57.49 Git Security

Never commit:

```text
.env
private keys
password files
cloud credentials
JWT secrets
database dumps containing sensitive data
```

Use secret scanning in CI.

---

# 57.50 Secret Rotation

Security-sensitive credentials SHOULD support rotation.

Examples:

```text
Database credentials
API keys
Signing keys
OAuth secrets
Service credentials
```

The system should avoid requiring a complete outage for routine credential rotation where practical.

---

# 57.51 Encryption at Rest

Sensitive production data should use appropriate encryption-at-rest controls provided by the infrastructure/database/storage platform.

---

# 57.52 Encryption in Transit

Use TLS for:

```text
Browser → API
Service → Service
Application → Database
Application → External API
```

where supported and required.

---

# 57.53 File Upload Security

File uploads are untrusted.

Never trust:

```text
Filename
Extension
Content-Type header
Client-provided size
```

alone.

---

# 57.54 File Validation

Validate:

```text
Actual content type
File size
Extension
Filename
Content structure
```

according to the file type.

---

# 57.55 Malicious Files

Where appropriate, uploaded files should undergo malware/virus scanning before being made available to other users.

---

# 57.56 File Storage

Uploaded files should not automatically be placed into the application's executable/static resource directory.

Prefer controlled object/file storage.

---

# 57.57 Path Traversal

Never allow user-controlled filenames to directly determine filesystem paths.

Protect against:

```text
../
..\ 
absolute paths
encoded traversal
```

---

# 57.58 Download Authorization

A valid file ID does not automatically grant access.

The backend must verify:

```text
User
+
File
+
Access permission
```

before download.

---

# 57.59 Signed URLs

Signed URLs may be used for object storage access.

They should have:

```text
Short expiration
Restricted permissions
Appropriate scope
```

---

# 57.60 SSRF

Server-side requests based on user input can create SSRF vulnerabilities.

Do not allow arbitrary URLs to be fetched by backend services without controls.

Protect against access to:

```text
Internal services
Cloud metadata endpoints
Loopback addresses
Private networks
Sensitive administrative interfaces
```

---

# 57.61 URL Allowlisting

If Mediverse needs to fetch external resources, use approved domains/schemes and validate resolved destinations where necessary.

---

# 57.62 Open Redirect

Do not blindly redirect users to arbitrary URLs supplied by request parameters.

Bad:

```text
/login?redirect=https://attacker.example
```

unless the destination has been validated.

---

# 57.63 Deserialization

Do not deserialize untrusted data into arbitrary Java classes.

Avoid insecure polymorphic deserialization configurations.

---

# 57.64 Serialization

API serialization should expose only intended fields.

Do not accidentally serialize:

```text
Password hashes
Internal IDs
Security metadata
Tokens
Database internals
```

---

# 57.65 Sensitive DTO Fields

Sensitive properties should be explicitly excluded from API responses.

Example:

```text
UserResponse
```

should not contain:

```text
passwordHash
refreshToken
internalSecurityFlags
```

unless there is an extremely specific and reviewed reason.

---

# 57.66 Logging Security

Logs must never contain:

```text
Passwords
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
Private keys
Encryption keys
Full payment credentials
Sensitive medical information unnecessarily
```

---

# 57.67 Log Injection

Sanitize or structure user-controlled values before logging.

Attackers should not be able to inject misleading multiline log entries or control characters that obscure audit trails.

---

# 57.68 PII Minimization

Collect and log only information actually required.

Do not log:

```text
Full request bodies
Full user profiles
Medical learning records
```

just because debugging is convenient.

---

# 57.69 Medical Data Security

Mediverse may contain sensitive educational/user information.

The architecture must explicitly classify what constitutes:

```text
Personal data
Sensitive data
Educational records
Audit data
Authentication data
```

and apply appropriate controls.

Do not assume that "educational platform" means all stored data is harmless.

---

# 57.70 AI Security

AI-generated output must be treated as untrusted application data.

Do not allow AI output to automatically execute:

```text
SQL
Shell commands
Administrative operations
HTML/JavaScript
System configuration
```

---

# 57.71 Prompt Injection

If Mediverse AI features process user-controlled content, defend against prompt injection.

User content should not automatically override:

```text
System instructions
Security policies
Tool permissions
Data-access boundaries
```

---

# 57.72 AI Tool Authorization

An AI agent must not receive broad privileges simply because it needs to answer a question.

Use least privilege:

```text
AI
 ↓
Approved tool
 ↓
Approved operation
 ↓
Approved data scope
```

---

# 57.73 AI Data Leakage

Do not send unnecessary sensitive user information to external AI providers.

Define:

```text
Allowed data
Prohibited data
Retention expectations
Provider controls
Audit requirements
```

---

# 57.74 AI Output Validation

AI output must be validated before it enters:

```text
Database
API response
HTML
Medical content workflow
Administrative workflow
```

---

# 57.75 Dependency Security

Dependencies must be scanned for known vulnerabilities.

Use:

```text
Dependency scanning
SCA
SBOM
Container scanning
Secret scanning
```

according to the project's DevSecOps pipeline.

---

# 57.76 Dependency Updates

Critical vulnerabilities require prioritized remediation.

Do not blindly upgrade dependencies in production without compatibility testing.

---

# 57.77 SBOM

Production builds SHOULD generate a Software Bill of Materials where required by the project's security/compliance strategy.

The SBOM should identify relevant:

```text
Libraries
Versions
Transitive dependencies
Components
```

---

# 57.78 Container Security

Containers SHOULD:

```text
Run as non-root
Use minimal base images
Avoid unnecessary packages
Scan images
Avoid embedded secrets
Use read-only filesystems where practical
```

---

# 57.79 Kubernetes Security

Mediverse Kubernetes workloads should follow:

```text
Least privilege RBAC
Restricted service accounts
Network policies
Pod security controls
Resource limits
Secret protection
Image verification/scanning
```

---

# 57.80 Service Accounts

Do not use broad Kubernetes service-account permissions.

A service should receive only the permissions it requires.

---

# 57.81 Network Segmentation

Where appropriate, restrict network communication between services.

Example:

```text
Frontend
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Backend services
 ↓
Database
```

The database should not be directly accessible from arbitrary workloads.

---

# 57.82 Database Security

Database users should follow least privilege.

Do not run Mediverse application services using:

```text
postgres superuser
```

---

# 57.83 Security Misconfiguration

Production systems should not retain:

```text
Default passwords
Debug mode
Verbose error pages
Development credentials
Test endpoints
Swagger write access without protection
```

unless explicitly intended and secured.

---

# 57.84 Debug Endpoints

Never expose internal debugging endpoints publicly without strong controls.

Examples:

```text
Heap dumps
Environment endpoints
Thread dumps
Actuator internals
Debug consoles
```

---

# 57.85 Spring Actuator

If Spring Boot Actuator is enabled:

```text
Management endpoints
Health details
Metrics
Environment
Logs
```

must be deliberately exposed and protected.

Do not expose sensitive actuator endpoints to the public internet.

---

# 57.86 Security Testing

Security testing should include:

```text
SAST
DAST
Dependency scanning
Container scanning
Secret scanning
API security testing
Authorization testing
Penetration testing where appropriate
```

---

# 57.87 Authorization Testing

Tests must verify both:

```text
Allowed operation
Denied operation
```

Do not test only the happy path.

---

# 57.88 Negative Security Tests

Include tests for:

```text
Unauthenticated request
Wrong role
Wrong user
Expired token
Invalid token
Tampered token
Missing permission
Invalid input
Oversized request
Malformed file
```

---

# 57.89 Security Regression

Every discovered security vulnerability should result in:

```text
Fix
+
Regression test
```

where practical.

Otherwise the same vulnerability can return later.

---

# 57.90 Rate-Limit Testing

Security testing should verify that limits actually work for:

```text
Login
Password reset
AI generation
File upload
Search
Expensive endpoints
```

---

# 57.91 Security Incident Logging

Security-relevant events should be auditable.

Examples:

```text
Login failure
Login success
Password reset
Role change
Permission change
Account lock
Suspicious access
Administrative action
```

---

# 57.92 Audit Integrity

Audit records should not be freely mutable by ordinary application users.

Critical audit information should have stronger integrity protections where required.

---

# 57.93 Security Monitoring

Monitor for:

```text
Repeated login failures
Privilege escalation attempts
Unexpected 403/401 spikes
Token anomalies
Rate-limit abuse
Suspicious file uploads
Unusual API patterns
```

---

# 57.94 Incident Response

Mediverse security incidents should have a documented response process:

```text
Detect
 ↓
Contain
 ↓
Investigate
 ↓
Eradicate
 ↓
Recover
 ↓
Learn
```

---

# 57.95 Vulnerability Disclosure

The project should define how security vulnerabilities are reported internally and, where applicable, externally.

Security reports should not be handled through ordinary public issue discussions when they expose exploitable details.

---

# 57.96 Secure Coding Review

Security-sensitive code requires additional review.

Examples:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Token handling
File upload
Payment
AI tools
Encryption
Secrets
Administrative APIs
```

---

# 57.97 Definition of Done

A security-sensitive Mediverse feature is production-ready when:

* [ ] Authentication requirements are defined
* [ ] Authorization requirements are defined
* [ ] Resource-level access is checked
* [ ] Input validation exists
* [ ] Output handling is safe
* [ ] SQL injection protections exist
* [ ] XSS protections exist
* [ ] CSRF requirements are addressed
* [ ] CORS is explicitly configured
* [ ] Secrets are externalized
* [ ] Sensitive data is not logged
* [ ] File uploads are validated
* [ ] Rate limits exist where necessary
* [ ] API timeouts exist
* [ ] Retry behavior is safe
* [ ] Dependencies are scanned
* [ ] Container images are scanned
* [ ] Kubernetes permissions follow least privilege
* [ ] Security tests cover denial scenarios
* [ ] Audit requirements are implemented
* [ ] Monitoring exists for important security events
* [ ] Security regression tests exist
* [ ] Production configuration has been reviewed

---

# 57.98 Core Principles

1. **Never trust client-side security controls.**
2. **Authentication does not imply authorization.**
3. **Every protected resource requires explicit access control.**
4. **Never trust user-supplied IDs.**
5. **Passwords must only be stored using approved password hashing.**
6. **Never store secrets in source code.**
7. **Never log tokens, passwords, or private keys.**
8. **Validate input at every relevant trust boundary.**
9. **Use parameterized queries.**
10. **Treat uploaded files as hostile input.**
11. **Treat AI output as untrusted data.**
12. **Use least privilege everywhere.**
13. **Do not expose internal management/debugging endpoints publicly.**
14. **Security controls must be tested, not merely configured.**
15. **Every security vulnerability should result in a regression test where practical.**
16. **Defense in depth is mandatory for critical functionality.**
17. **Production configuration must be hardened independently from development configuration.**
18. **Sensitive data collection and retention should be minimized.**
19. **Security-sensitive operations must be auditable.**
20. **Security is a system property, not a feature added at the end of development.**

> **For Mediverse, security is especially important because the platform combines user identity, educational records, potentially sensitive information, AI capabilities, media, administrative functions, and distributed infrastructure. A vulnerable frontend, API, AI tool, Kubernetes service, or database can become a path into the entire platform.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 58: Testing Standards — Unit, Integration, API, E2E, Performance & Security Testing.**

# CSDG — Chapter 58

## Testing Standards — Unit, Integration, API, E2E, Performance & Security Testing

### 58.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the testing standards for Mediverse.

Testing MUST verify not only that individual components work, but that the complete platform behaves correctly across:

```text
Code
 ↓
Application
 ↓
API
 ↓
Database
 ↓
External Services
 ↓
Infrastructure
 ↓
User Workflow
```

Core principle:

> **A feature is not complete because the code compiles or the happy path works. It is complete when its expected behavior, failure behavior, security boundaries, integration points, and critical non-functional requirements have been verified.**

---

# 58.2 Testing Pyramid

Mediverse SHOULD follow a balanced testing strategy:

```text
                 /\
                /  \
               / E2E\
              /------\
             / API /  \
            /----------\
           / Integration \
          /--------------\
         /  Unit Tests    \
        /------------------\
```

The majority of tests should be fast, deterministic unit tests.

Fewer tests should exercise full integration.

E2E tests should focus on critical user journeys rather than every possible combination.

---

# 58.3 Testing Layers

Mediverse testing SHOULD include:

```text
1. Static analysis
2. Unit testing
3. Integration testing
4. API testing
5. Contract testing
6. Component testing
7. End-to-end testing
8. Security testing
9. Performance testing
10. Resilience testing
11. Infrastructure testing
12. Regression testing
```

---

# 58.4 Test Categories

Every feature should be considered against:

```text
Functional behavior
Validation
Authorization
Error handling
Boundary conditions
Concurrency
Performance
Security
Observability
Failure recovery
```

---

# 58.5 Test Naming

Test names should clearly describe behavior.

Prefer:

```java
shouldRejectEnrollmentWhenCourseIsAlreadyEnrolled()
```

over:

```java
testEnrollment()
```

A test name should explain:

```text
Given
When
Then
```

where practical.

---

# 58.6 Arrange–Act–Assert

Unit tests SHOULD follow:

```text
Arrange
   ↓
Act
   ↓
Assert
```

Example:

```java
// Arrange
Course course = ...

// Act
CourseResponse result = service.createCourse(request);

// Assert
assertThat(result.getTitle()).isEqualTo("Physiology");
```

---

# 58.7 Unit Testing

Unit tests verify isolated behavior.

Typical targets:

```text
Service methods
Domain logic
Validators
Mappers
Utility classes
Calculators
State transitions
```

---

# 58.8 Unit Test Isolation

Unit tests should avoid unnecessary:

```text
Database
Network
External API
Kafka
Redis
Filesystem
```

dependencies.

Mock or replace dependencies where appropriate.

---

# 58.9 What Not to Mock

Do not mock everything blindly.

Excessive mocking can create tests that verify the mocked architecture rather than actual behavior.

Mock external boundaries when isolation provides value.

---

# 58.10 Business Logic Coverage

Critical business rules MUST have tests.

Examples:

```text
Enrollment eligibility
Quiz scoring
Attempt limits
Progress calculation
Course publishing
Role transitions
Access rules
```

---

# 58.11 Boundary Testing

Test values around boundaries.

Example:

```text
Minimum allowed
Minimum - 1
Maximum allowed
Maximum + 1
Empty
Null
Very large
```

---

# 58.12 Null Testing

Where null is not valid:

```text
null → rejected
```

Where null is valid:

```text
null → defined behavior
```

Do not allow null behavior to remain accidental.

---

# 58.13 Collection Testing

Test:

```text
Empty collection
Single element
Multiple elements
Large collection
Duplicate elements
Unexpected ordering
```

where relevant.

---

# 58.14 Exception Testing

Tests should verify that expected exceptions are:

```text
Thrown
Mapped correctly
Handled correctly
Returned with the correct API contract
```

---

# 58.15 Unit Test Anti-Patterns

Avoid tests that:

```text
Depend on execution order
Use real external services unnecessarily
Contain random uncontrolled data
Sleep to wait for behavior
Assert implementation details instead of behavior
```

---

# 58.16 Integration Testing

Integration tests verify interactions between components.

Examples:

```text
Spring Boot
+
PostgreSQL
```

or:

```text
API
+
Security
+
Database
```

---

# 58.17 Database Integration Tests

Critical persistence behavior SHOULD be tested against a realistic database environment.

Where practical, use isolated test databases/containers.

Avoid relying exclusively on H2 when production uses PostgreSQL if SQL behavior differs materially.

---

# 58.18 Database Test Isolation

Each test should have predictable database state.

Possible approaches:

```text
Transactional rollback
Database cleanup
Testcontainers
Dedicated schema/database
```

Choose based on the test architecture.

---

# 58.19 Migration Testing

Database migrations MUST be tested.

Verify:

```text
Fresh installation
Upgrade from previous version
Data preservation
Rollback strategy where supported
Indexes
Constraints
```

---

# 58.20 Repository Testing

Repository tests should verify:

```text
Queries
Filters
Sorting
Pagination
Relationships
Constraints
```

especially for complex queries.

---

# 58.21 Integration Test Data

Test data should be:

```text
Deterministic
Minimal
Relevant
Isolated
```

Avoid massive uncontrolled fixtures unless required for realistic testing.

---

# 58.22 API Testing

Every important API endpoint should have tests for:

```text
Success
Validation failure
Authentication failure
Authorization failure
Not found
Conflict
Unexpected dependency failure
```

---

# 58.23 API Status-Code Testing

Tests MUST verify the intended status codes.

For example:

```text
POST valid       → 201
GET valid        → 200
DELETE valid     → 204
Unauthenticated  → 401
Unauthorized     → 403
Missing resource → 404
Conflict         → 409
```

---

# 58.24 API Contract Testing

API tests should verify:

```text
Request schema
Response schema
Required fields
Field types
Status codes
Error contract
```

---

# 58.25 OpenAPI Testing

Where OpenAPI is the source of API contracts, automated validation SHOULD detect divergence between:

```text
Implementation
        vs
OpenAPI specification
```

---

# 58.26 Consumer Contract Testing

For service-to-service APIs, contract tests SHOULD be used where independent deployments create compatibility risk.

Example:

```text
Service A
   ↓
API contract
   ↓
Service B
```

---

# 58.27 Authentication Testing

Test:

```text
Valid credentials
Invalid credentials
Missing credentials
Expired token
Malformed token
Tampered token
Revoked session/token
```

---

# 58.28 Authorization Testing

Every protected endpoint SHOULD have tests for:

```text
Allowed role
Disallowed role
Correct resource owner
Wrong resource owner
Missing permission
```

Authorization tests are mandatory for sensitive operations.

---

# 58.29 Horizontal Access Testing

Example:

```text
Student A → Student A progress → ALLOW
Student A → Student B progress → DENY
```

This should be explicitly tested.

---

# 58.30 Vertical Access Testing

Example:

```text
ADMIN → admin operation → ALLOW
FACULTY → admin operation → DENY
STUDENT → admin operation → DENY
```

---

# 58.31 File Upload Testing

Test:

```text
Valid file
Unsupported extension
Wrong MIME type
Oversized file
Empty file
Corrupted file
Malicious filename
Path traversal attempt
Unauthorized upload
Unauthorized download
```

---

# 58.32 Validation Testing

Every important validation rule should have at least:

```text
Valid input
Invalid input
Boundary input
```

---

# 58.33 Error Testing

The API must be tested for predictable failures.

Example:

```text
Database unavailable
External API timeout
Invalid resource ID
Malformed request
Duplicate request
Expired authentication
```

The system should fail safely and return the expected contract.

---

# 58.34 Frontend Component Testing

React components SHOULD be tested for behavior rather than implementation details.

Examples:

```text
Rendering
User interaction
Form validation
Loading state
Error state
Empty state
Permission-dependent UI
```

---

# 58.35 Frontend Form Testing

Forms should test:

```text
Required fields
Invalid values
Boundary values
Submission
Loading state
Server error
Success
Duplicate submission
```

---

# 58.36 Frontend API Failure Testing

The frontend must handle:

```text
400
401
403
404
409
429
500
503
Network failure
Timeout
```

appropriately.

---

# 58.37 E2E Testing

End-to-end testing validates real user journeys.

Examples:

```text
Student registration
 ↓
Login
 ↓
Browse course
 ↓
Enroll
 ↓
Study lesson
 ↓
Attempt quiz
 ↓
View progress
```

---

# 58.38 Critical E2E Journeys

Mediverse SHOULD prioritize E2E tests for:

```text
Authentication
Course discovery
Enrollment
Learning
Quiz attempt
Progress tracking
Faculty content management
Administrative workflows
Critical AI workflows
```

---

# 58.39 E2E Scope

Do not create E2E tests for every tiny UI state.

E2E tests are expensive and fragile.

Use them for business-critical workflows.

---

# 58.40 E2E Test Independence

E2E tests should not depend on another E2E test having run first.

Bad:

```text
Test 1 creates user
Test 2 assumes user exists
Test 3 assumes Test 2 completed
```

Each test should establish its required state.

---

# 58.41 Test Environment

Tests should run against controlled environments.

Environment-specific behavior must be explicit.

Avoid:

```text
Test
 ↓
Production database
```

unless specifically designed as a safe production verification mechanism.

---

# 58.42 Test Configuration

Never use production secrets in automated tests.

Use:

```text
Test credentials
Mock secrets
Ephemeral infrastructure
Dedicated test environments
```

---

# 58.43 Testcontainers

For Spring Boot integration testing, Testcontainers SHOULD be considered for dependencies such as:

```text
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka
Elasticsearch
```

when realistic integration behavior is required.

---

# 58.44 Mocking External Services

External services may be mocked when:

```text
Testing failure conditions
Testing deterministic behavior
Avoiding external cost
Preventing network dependency
Testing unavailable services
```

But important integrations should also have real integration coverage.

---

# 58.45 Test Doubles

Use the appropriate test double:

```text
Stub
Mock
Fake
Spy
```

Do not use mocks merely because the framework makes them convenient.

---

# 58.46 Deterministic Tests

Tests MUST be deterministic.

Avoid uncontrolled:

```text
Current time
Random IDs
Random ordering
External APIs
Network conditions
Thread scheduling
```

Use controlled clocks, seeded randomness, and deterministic fixtures where appropriate.

---

# 58.47 Time Testing

Time-dependent functionality should support controlled time.

Examples:

```text
Quiz expiration
JWT expiration
Course scheduling
Progress timestamps
Notifications
```

A test should not have to wait five real minutes to verify a five-minute timeout.

---

# 58.48 Concurrency Testing

Critical concurrent operations SHOULD be tested.

Examples:

```text
Two quiz submissions
Duplicate enrollment
Concurrent progress updates
Inventory-like resource limits
Simultaneous role changes
```

---

# 58.49 Race Conditions

Tests should attempt to expose:

```text
Lost updates
Duplicate records
Double processing
Inconsistent state
```

---

# 58.50 Transaction Testing

Verify transaction boundaries.

Examples:

```text
Operation succeeds → all changes committed
Operation fails → required changes rolled back
```

Do not assume `@Transactional` automatically solves every consistency problem.

---

# 58.51 Performance Testing

Performance tests should establish measurable targets.

Measure:

```text
Latency
Throughput
Error rate
CPU
Memory
Database load
Network usage
```

---

# 58.52 Load Testing

Load testing determines how the application behaves under expected traffic.

Example:

```text
100 users
500 users
1,000 users
5,000 users
```

The actual targets must come from the project's capacity requirements.

---

# 58.53 Stress Testing

Stress testing intentionally exceeds normal expected capacity.

Purpose:

```text
Find breaking point
Observe degradation
Validate recovery
Identify bottlenecks
```

---

# 58.54 Spike Testing

Spike testing verifies sudden traffic increases.

Example:

```text
Normal:
100 req/s

Sudden:
2,000 req/s
```

This is particularly relevant for:

```text
Exam results
Major course release
Popular learning content
Notifications
```

---

# 58.55 Soak Testing

Soak tests run workloads for extended periods to detect:

```text
Memory leaks
Connection leaks
Resource exhaustion
Performance degradation
Log growth
Queue buildup
```

---

# 58.56 API Performance Targets

Important APIs should have defined targets for:

```text
p50
p95
p99
Error rate
Throughput
```

Avoid relying only on average latency.

---

# 58.57 Database Performance Testing

Test:

```text
Slow queries
Indexes
Pagination
Large datasets
Concurrent access
Connection pool behavior
```

---

# 58.58 N+1 Detection

ORM-based applications MUST test for accidental N+1 query behavior.

Example:

```text
1 query for courses
+
N queries for lessons
```

may become unacceptable at scale.

---

# 58.59 Pagination Performance

Pagination tests should verify that large datasets do not cause:

```text
Huge memory usage
Slow response times
Unbounded database scans
```

---

# 58.60 Cache Testing

If Redis or another cache is used, test:

```text
Cache hit
Cache miss
Expiration
Invalidation
Stale data
Cache failure
```

The application must have defined behavior when the cache is unavailable.

---

# 58.61 Messaging Testing

For Kafka/RabbitMQ-style systems, test:

```text
Message publishing
Message consumption
Serialization
Retry
Duplicate delivery
Ordering where required
Dead-letter handling
Consumer failure
```

---

# 58.62 Eventual Consistency

Tests must account for eventual consistency where the architecture intentionally uses it.

Do not write tests that assume immediate consistency when the system explicitly provides asynchronous propagation.

---

# 58.63 Idempotent Consumer Testing

Consumers should be tested against duplicate messages.

Example:

```text
Event A
Event A
```

should not incorrectly produce:

```text
Duplicate side effect
```

---

# 58.64 Dead-Letter Testing

When messages cannot be processed:

```text
Message
 ↓
Retry
 ↓
Retry
 ↓
Dead Letter Queue
```

the system should preserve enough information for investigation and recovery.

---

# 58.65 AI Testing

AI features require specialized testing.

Test:

```text
Valid prompt
Invalid prompt
Adversarial prompt
Prompt injection
Unexpected model output
Empty output
Malformed structured output
Timeout
Provider failure
Rate limit
```

---

# 58.66 AI Determinism

Where AI behavior is inherently probabilistic, tests should focus on:

```text
Required structure
Safety constraints
Allowed content
Forbidden behavior
Schema validity
```

rather than exact natural-language equality.

---

# 58.67 AI Medical Content

AI-generated educational content must be tested for:

```text
Required structure
Source/reference requirements
Unsupported claims
Unsafe recommendations
Contradictory information
Hallucination indicators
```

AI output should not automatically become canonical medical content without the project's required review workflow.

---

# 58.68 Security Testing

Security testing should include:

```text
SAST
DAST
Dependency scanning
Container scanning
Secret scanning
API authorization tests
Authentication tests
Input fuzzing where appropriate
```

---

# 58.69 SAST

Static Application Security Testing should run in CI.

Examples of findings:

```text
Injection
Hardcoded secrets
Unsafe APIs
Weak cryptography
Security misconfiguration
```

---

# 58.70 DAST

Dynamic testing should exercise running applications to detect issues such as:

```text
Authentication weaknesses
Authorization problems
Injection
Security headers
Exposed endpoints
```

---

# 58.71 Dependency Scanning

CI SHOULD detect vulnerable dependencies before deployment.

Critical vulnerabilities should trigger appropriate release controls according to the project's security policy.

---

# 58.72 Secret Scanning

Repositories and CI pipelines should scan for accidental secrets.

Examples:

```text
AWS keys
Private keys
API tokens
Database passwords
JWT secrets
```

---

# 58.73 Fuzz Testing

Fuzzing should be considered for high-risk parsers and input-processing components.

Examples:

```text
JSON parsing
File processing
Image processing
Document processing
Complex query parameters
```

---

# 58.74 Regression Testing

Every fixed defect SHOULD receive a regression test where practical.

The goal:

```text
Bug found
 ↓
Bug fixed
 ↓
Test added
 ↓
Future builds prevent regression
```

---

# 58.75 Bug Classification

Defects should be categorized.

Example:

```text
Critical
High
Medium
Low
```

Severity and priority should be separate concepts where useful.

---

# 58.76 Critical Defects

Critical defects may include:

```text
Authentication bypass
Authorization bypass
Data corruption
Major data loss
Production outage
Severe security vulnerability
```

These require immediate attention according to the incident/release policy.

---

# 58.77 Test Coverage

Coverage metrics are useful but must not become the only quality metric.

For example:

```text
100% line coverage
```

does NOT prove:

```text
Correct behavior
Security
Concurrency safety
Performance
```

---

# 58.78 Coverage Expectations

Critical business logic SHOULD have high meaningful coverage.

Focus on:

```text
Business rules
Security rules
Error paths
Boundary conditions
```

rather than chasing arbitrary percentages.

---

# 58.79 Mutation Testing

Mutation testing MAY be used for critical logic to determine whether tests actually detect incorrect behavior.

---

# 58.80 Test Quality

A good test should fail when the behavior becomes incorrect.

A test that can pass while the feature is broken is low-value.

---

# 58.81 Flaky Tests

Flaky tests MUST NOT be ignored.

A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails is a reliability problem.

Investigate:

```text
Race conditions
Timing
External dependencies
Shared state
Randomness
Environment differences
```

---

# 58.82 Test Quarantine

Quarantining a flaky test may be temporarily necessary, but it must not become permanent.

Every quarantined test should have:

```text
Reason
Owner
Issue reference
Remediation plan
```

---

# 58.83 CI Testing Pipeline

The CI pipeline SHOULD progressively execute:

```text
Commit
 ↓
Compile
 ↓
Static analysis
 ↓
Unit tests
 ↓
Integration tests
 ↓
API/contract tests
 ↓
Security scans
 ↓
Build artifact
 ↓
E2E
 ↓
Performance/security gates where applicable
```

---

# 58.84 Fast Feedback

Fast tests should run early.

Expensive tests should run later or in appropriate pipeline stages.

Do not make every developer wait unnecessarily for a full E2E suite after every tiny change.

---

# 58.85 Pull Request Testing

A pull request should not be mergeable when mandatory quality gates fail.

Typical gates:

```text
Compilation
Unit tests
Integration tests
Static analysis
Security scanning
Coverage thresholds where defined
```

---

# 58.86 Branch Protection

Protected branches SHOULD require:

```text
Passing CI
Required reviews
No unresolved required checks
```

according to repository policy.

---

# 58.87 Test Reports

CI should preserve useful reports:

```text
Unit test results
Integration test results
Coverage
Security findings
Performance results
E2E results
```

---

# 58.88 Test Artifacts

Failures should retain enough information for debugging:

```text
Logs
Screenshots
Traces
Request/response metadata
Test reports
Container logs
```

Sensitive information must still be redacted.

---

# 58.89 Environment Parity

Testing environments should resemble production where practical.

Differences in:

```text
Database
JDK
Node version
OS
Container runtime
Configuration
Network
```

can produce production-only failures.

---

# 58.90 Release Testing

Before production release:

```text
Build verification
Regression suite
Security checks
Migration tests
Smoke tests
Critical E2E flows
```

must be completed according to release risk.

---

# 58.91 Smoke Testing

Smoke tests verify that the deployment is fundamentally operational.

Examples:

```text
Application starts
Health endpoint works
Login works
Primary API responds
Database connectivity works
Critical page loads
```

---

# 58.92 Post-Deployment Verification

After deployment, verify:

```text
Health
Error rate
Latency
Authentication
Critical workflows
Database migrations
Logs
Metrics
```

---

# 58.93 Rollback Testing

Critical deployments SHOULD have a tested rollback or recovery strategy.

A rollback plan that has never been tested is only an assumption.

---

# 58.94 Disaster Recovery Testing

Where required, test:

```text
Database restoration
Backup restoration
Service recovery
Queue recovery
Storage recovery
Infrastructure recreation
```

---

# 58.95 Chaos/Resilience Testing

For critical distributed components, resilience testing MAY simulate:

```text
Service unavailable
Network latency
Database failure
Redis failure
Kafka failure
Pod restart
Node failure
```

The goal is to verify graceful degradation and recovery.

---

# 58.96 Test Documentation

Each major feature should document:

```text
Test scope
Required environments
Test data
Critical scenarios
Known limitations
Performance expectations
Security expectations
```

---

# 58.97 Definition of Done

A Mediverse feature is considered tested when:

* [ ] Unit tests exist for important business logic
* [ ] Validation is tested
* [ ] Error paths are tested
* [ ] Authentication is tested
* [ ] Authorization is tested
* [ ] Resource-level access is tested
* [ ] API contract is tested
* [ ] Database integration is tested where required
* [ ] External integrations are tested where required
* [ ] Critical E2E workflow is covered
* [ ] Regression tests exist for fixed defects
* [ ] Security scanning passes
* [ ] Performance requirements are evaluated where applicable
* [ ] Concurrency is tested where applicable
* [ ] Messaging behavior is tested where applicable
* [ ] AI behavior is tested where applicable
* [ ] Tests are deterministic
* [ ] No known unexplained flaky tests remain
* [ ] CI executes required quality gates
* [ ] Test reports are available
* [ ] Production smoke tests are defined
* [ ] Rollback/recovery strategy is known for high-risk releases

---

# 58.98 Core Principles

1. **Test behavior, not implementation details.**
2. **Unit tests should be fast and numerous.**
3. **Integration tests verify real component boundaries.**
4. **Critical APIs require explicit contract testing.**
5. **Authentication and authorization failures must be tested.**
6. **Every security boundary needs negative tests.**
7. **Critical workflows require E2E coverage.**
8. **Performance must be measured, not guessed.**
9. **Concurrency bugs require concurrency-aware testing.**
10. **AI systems require behavior-oriented rather than exact-text testing.**
11. **Every important bug should become a regression test.**
12. **Flaky tests are defects, not harmless noise.**
13. **Coverage percentage is not equivalent to quality.**
14. **CI quality gates must prevent known-bad code from progressing.**
15. **Production readiness requires testing failure behavior, not only success behavior.**

> **For Mediverse, testing must prove that the platform remains correct when users behave unexpectedly, services fail, requests are duplicated, permissions are wrong, data is malformed, traffic increases, and AI produces unexpected output—not merely that the ideal workflow works on a developer laptop.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 59: Performance Engineering, Scalability, Caching & Resource Optimization.**
# CSDG — Chapter 59

## Performance Engineering, Scalability, Caching & Resource Optimization

### 59.1 Purpose

This chapter defines mandatory performance and scalability standards for Mediverse.

Performance engineering MUST be treated as an architectural concern, not as a final optimization activity.

The goal is to ensure Mediverse remains responsive and predictable as:

```text
Users increase
Content increases
Requests increase
AI usage increases
Concurrent learning sessions increase
Data volume increases
Services increase
```

Core principle:

> **Do not optimize based on assumptions. Measure the system, identify the bottleneck, fix the bottleneck, and verify the improvement.**

---

# 59.2 Performance Objectives

Performance requirements SHOULD be defined using measurable metrics:

```text
Latency
Throughput
Error rate
CPU utilization
Memory utilization
Database latency
Network latency
Queue depth
Cache hit ratio
```

Avoid vague requirements such as:

```text
"API should be fast."
```

Prefer:

```text
"95% of requests should complete within the defined SLA."
```

---

# 59.3 Performance Budget

Each major user-facing capability SHOULD have a performance budget.

Examples:

```text
Page load
API response
Database query
AI response
Search
File download
Quiz submission
```

A feature that consumes the entire performance budget of the application without justification should not be considered complete.

---

# 59.4 Measure Before Optimizing

Do not optimize code simply because it "looks slow."

Required process:

```text
Measure
   ↓
Profile
   ↓
Identify bottleneck
   ↓
Optimize
   ↓
Measure again
```

---

# 59.5 Performance Hierarchy

When investigating latency, analyze:

```text
Client
 ↓
Network
 ↓
Load Balancer
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Application
 ↓
Cache
 ↓
Database
 ↓
External Services
```

Do not assume the application code is always the bottleneck.

---

# 59.6 Latency Percentiles

Performance reports SHOULD use:

```text
p50
p95
p99
```

rather than relying only on averages.

Example:

```text
Average = 120 ms
p95     = 600 ms
p99     = 2.5 s
```

The average alone hides poor user experiences.

---

# 59.7 Throughput

Measure how much work the system can perform.

Examples:

```text
Requests/second
Events/second
Messages/second
Queries/second
AI requests/minute
```

---

# 59.8 Resource Utilization

Monitor:

```text
CPU
Memory
Disk I/O
Network I/O
Database connections
Thread pools
Connection pools
```

High utilization is not automatically bad, but unexpected saturation is a capacity problem.

---

# 59.9 Spring Boot Performance

Avoid unnecessary work inside request threads.

Do not perform expensive operations synchronously when they can safely be processed asynchronously.

Examples:

```text
Large report generation
Video processing
Bulk notifications
AI generation
Large document processing
```

---

# 59.10 Thread Pools

Thread pools MUST be deliberately configured.

Do not blindly increase thread counts.

Too many threads can cause:

```text
Context switching
Memory pressure
CPU contention
Database connection exhaustion
```

---

# 59.11 Blocking Operations

Avoid blocking operations inside highly concurrent request paths when the architecture expects non-blocking behavior.

Common examples:

```text
Slow HTTP calls
Large file processing
Long database operations
External AI calls
```

---

# 59.12 Database as a Bottleneck

The database is frequently the first scalability bottleneck.

Monitor:

```text
Query latency
Connection utilization
Locks
CPU
I/O
Index usage
Slow queries
```

---

# 59.13 Query Optimization

Queries MUST retrieve only the required data.

Avoid:

```sql
SELECT *
```

when only a few fields are required.

---

# 59.14 N+1 Queries

Avoid ORM patterns that produce:

```text
1 query
+
N additional queries
```

for a single API request.

Use appropriate:

```text
JOIN FETCH
Entity graphs
DTO projections
Batch fetching
```

according to the use case.

---

# 59.15 Database Indexing

Frequently queried columns SHOULD be indexed when justified by query patterns.

Typical candidates:

```text
Foreign keys
Search fields
Status fields
Timestamp fields
Unique identifiers
Composite query conditions
```

Do not create indexes blindly.

Every index introduces:

```text
Storage cost
Write overhead
Maintenance cost
```

---

# 59.16 Index Verification

An index should be justified using actual query behavior.

Use query execution analysis where appropriate.

Example:

```text
EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

---

# 59.17 Pagination

APIs returning collections MUST use pagination where result size can grow significantly.

Avoid:

```text
GET /courses
```

returning millions of records.

---

# 59.18 Pagination Strategy

For large datasets, consider:

```text
Offset pagination
Cursor pagination
Keyset pagination
```

Choose based on access patterns.

---

# 59.19 Pagination Limits

Clients MUST NOT be allowed to request unlimited page sizes.

Bad:

```text
?pageSize=100000000
```

Use server-enforced maximums.

---

# 59.20 Sorting

Sort fields should be allowlisted.

Do not allow arbitrary SQL expressions through request parameters.

---

# 59.21 Search Performance

Search functionality should define:

```text
Latency target
Index strategy
Pagination
Filtering
Sorting
Ranking
```

Large-scale search should not depend on inefficient wildcard database queries unless the dataset and workload justify it.

---

# 59.22 PostgreSQL Optimization

For PostgreSQL-backed functionality:

```text
Indexes
Query plans
Connection pooling
Vacuum behavior
Statistics
Partitioning where required
```

should be considered as data volume increases.

---

# 59.23 Connection Pooling

Database connections SHOULD use a properly configured connection pool.

Do not create a new database connection for every request.

---

# 59.24 Connection Pool Sizing

More connections do not automatically mean better performance.

An oversized pool can overwhelm the database.

Tune based on:

```text
Application concurrency
Database capacity
Query duration
Number of application instances
```

---

# 59.25 Distributed Connection Limits

If there are:

```text
10 application pods
```

and each allows:

```text
50 database connections
```

the database may receive up to:

```text
500 connections
```

before considering other workloads.

Capacity planning MUST account for total instances.

---

# 59.26 Transactions

Transactions should remain as short as practical.

Avoid holding database transactions open while waiting for:

```text
External API
AI model
User interaction
Long computation
```

---

# 59.27 Lazy vs Eager Loading

Do not globally choose eager loading simply to avoid lazy-loading errors.

Choose loading behavior based on the actual use case.

---

# 59.28 DTO Projections

Use DTO projections when retrieving large entities would unnecessarily load:

```text
Large object graphs
Unused fields
Relationships
Sensitive fields
```

---

# 59.29 Batch Operations

Use batch processing for large operations where appropriate.

Avoid:

```text
for each item:
    database.insert()
```

when the operation can safely use batching.

---

# 59.30 Bulk APIs

Bulk endpoints should have explicit limits.

Example:

```text
POST /courses/bulk-import
```

should not accept an unlimited number of records.

---

# 59.31 Caching

Caching SHOULD be used when:

```text
Data is frequently read
Data changes relatively infrequently
Computation is expensive
External calls are expensive
```

Caching is not automatically beneficial.

---

# 59.32 Cache-Aside Pattern

A common strategy:

```text
Request
  ↓
Cache lookup
  ↓
Hit ─────→ Return
  |
 Miss
  ↓
Database
  ↓
Update cache
  ↓
Return
```

---

# 59.33 Cache Key Design

Cache keys MUST be:

```text
Unique
Deterministic
Versionable where required
Free from sensitive information where possible
```

Example:

```text
course:v1:{courseId}
```

---

# 59.34 Cache TTL

Every cache entry SHOULD have an explicit expiration strategy unless persistent caching is intentionally required.

TTL should reflect:

```text
Data freshness
Update frequency
Business requirements
```

---

# 59.35 Cache Invalidation

Cache invalidation MUST be deliberately designed.

When data changes:

```text
Database updated
      ↓
Relevant cache invalidated/updated
```

---

# 59.36 Stale Data

Caching creates the possibility of stale information.

For each cached resource, define:

```text
Maximum acceptable staleness
Invalidation behavior
Fallback behavior
```

---

# 59.37 Cache Stampede

Prevent many concurrent requests from rebuilding the same expired cache entry.

Possible approaches:

```text
Request coalescing
Locking
Early refresh
Randomized TTL
```

---

# 59.38 Cache Penetration

Repeated requests for nonexistent resources can bypass the cache and overload the database.

Possible mitigation:

```text
Negative caching
Validation
Rate limiting
Bloom filters where appropriate
```

---

# 59.39 Cache Failure

The application should define what happens when Redis/cache infrastructure is unavailable.

For non-critical caches:

```text
Cache failure → database fallback
```

may be appropriate.

---

# 59.40 Distributed Cache

When multiple application instances are running, local in-memory caches can become inconsistent.

Use distributed caching when consistency and shared cache state require it.

---

# 59.41 Cache Security

Never cache sensitive data without considering:

```text
Access control
Tenant/user isolation
Expiration
Encryption requirements
Cache invalidation
```

---

# 59.42 Authorization-Aware Caching

A cached response for:

```text
Student A
```

must never accidentally be served to:

```text
Student B
```

Cache keys must incorporate relevant authorization scope where necessary.

---

# 59.43 HTTP Caching

Use HTTP caching headers where appropriate:

```text
Cache-Control
ETag
Last-Modified
```

Do not cache private or sensitive responses publicly.

---

# 59.44 CDN

Static or globally distributed content MAY use a CDN.

Potential candidates:

```text
Images
Videos
JavaScript
CSS
Public educational assets
```

---

# 59.45 CDN Cache Invalidation

Content publishing workflows should define how changed assets become visible.

Options include:

```text
Versioned filenames
Content hashes
Cache invalidation
Short TTL
```

Versioned assets are generally more predictable.

---

# 59.46 Image Optimization

Images SHOULD be optimized for:

```text
Resolution
Format
Compression
Responsive sizing
Lazy loading
```

Do not deliver a multi-megabyte original image when a smaller version is sufficient.

---

# 59.47 Video Optimization

Educational video delivery should consider:

```text
Adaptive bitrate
Streaming
Transcoding
CDN
Range requests
Caching
```

Do not make the application server stream every large video file directly if object storage/CDN architecture is more appropriate.

---

# 59.48 Lazy Loading

Frontend applications SHOULD lazy-load large features that are not immediately required.

Examples:

```text
3D module
Admin dashboard
Advanced analytics
Large course viewer
```

---

# 59.49 Code Splitting

React applications SHOULD use code splitting for large routes/features.

Example:

```text
Login
 ↓
Course
 ↓
Quiz
 ↓
Admin
```

should not necessarily load the entire application bundle at initial page load.

---

# 59.50 Frontend Rendering

Avoid unnecessary re-renders.

Use appropriate techniques such as:

```text
Memoization
Stable references
State locality
Virtualization
```

but only after identifying actual performance problems.

---

# 59.51 Large Lists

Large lists should use:

```text
Pagination
Virtualization
Incremental loading
```

rather than rendering thousands of DOM elements simultaneously.

---

# 59.52 Network Optimization

Avoid unnecessary API requests.

Bad:

```text
Page loads
 ↓
20 independent requests
 ↓
Same data repeatedly requested
```

Prefer appropriate aggregation, caching, batching, or API design.

---

# 59.53 API Payload Size

Responses should contain only necessary data.

Avoid returning huge objects when the UI requires only:

```text
id
title
thumbnail
status
```

---

# 59.54 Compression

HTTP compression SHOULD be enabled where beneficial.

Consider:

```text
Brotli
Gzip
```

depending on infrastructure support.

Do not compress already compressed media unnecessarily.

---

# 59.55 Serialization Performance

Use efficient serialization.

Avoid unnecessary transformations such as:

```text
Entity
 → JSON
 → Object
 → JSON
 → Object
```

inside the same request path.

---

# 59.56 Async Processing

Use asynchronous processing for operations that do not require immediate completion.

Examples:

```text
Notification
Email
Analytics event
Search indexing
Media processing
AI batch generation
```

---

# 59.57 Background Jobs

Background jobs MUST be:

```text
Retryable
Observable
Idempotent where necessary
Bounded
Failure-aware
```

---

# 59.58 Retry Strategy

Retries must not create retry storms.

Use:

```text
Exponential backoff
Jitter
Maximum attempts
Timeout
```

---

# 59.59 Retry Safety

Never blindly retry operations that are not idempotent.

Example:

```text
POST payment/create
```

should not be retried without appropriate idempotency controls.

---

# 59.60 Timeouts

Every external network call SHOULD have an explicit timeout.

Never rely indefinitely on:

```text
Default timeout
Infinite wait
```

---

# 59.61 Circuit Breakers

For critical external dependencies, circuit breakers MAY be used.

Pattern:

```text
Normal
 ↓
Failures increase
 ↓
OPEN
 ↓
Fast failure
 ↓
HALF-OPEN
 ↓
Recovery
```

---

# 59.62 Bulkheads

Separate resource pools for critical operations can prevent one workload from consuming everything.

Example:

```text
AI requests
Database requests
Notification workers
```

should not necessarily share unlimited resources.

---

# 59.63 Backpressure

When downstream systems cannot keep up, upstream systems must not continue producing unlimited work.

Controls include:

```text
Queue limits
Rate limiting
Concurrency limits
Load shedding
```

---

# 59.64 Rate Limiting

Rate limits should protect expensive endpoints.

Examples:

```text
Login
AI generation
Search
File upload
Quiz submission
Password reset
```

---

# 59.65 AI Performance

AI requests are often expensive and slow.

Optimize:

```text
Prompt size
Context size
Model selection
Token usage
Caching
Concurrency
Timeouts
Streaming
```

---

# 59.66 AI Cost and Performance

Performance optimization for AI must consider both:

```text
Latency
Cost
```

A faster model that costs dramatically more may not be the optimal architecture.

---

# 59.67 AI Streaming

For long AI responses, streaming MAY improve perceived latency.

Instead of:

```text
Request
 ↓
Wait 20 seconds
 ↓
Complete response
```

use:

```text
Request
 ↓
First token
 ↓
Streaming
 ↓
Complete response
```

where appropriate.

---

# 59.68 Queue-Based AI Workloads

Long-running AI operations may be processed asynchronously:

```text
User
 ↓
API
 ↓
Job Queue
 ↓
AI Worker
 ↓
Result
 ↓
Notification/UI
```

---

# 59.69 Search Performance

Search indexing should be asynchronous where immediate indexing is not required.

Example:

```text
Course updated
 ↓
Database commit
 ↓
Event
 ↓
Search indexing
```

---

# 59.70 Elasticsearch Performance

If Elasticsearch is used:

```text
Mappings
Shard count
Replica count
Query complexity
Index size
Refresh interval
```

must be deliberately configured.

Do not create excessive shards.

---

# 59.71 Observability

Performance problems cannot be solved reliably without observability.

Collect:

```text
Metrics
Logs
Traces
Profiles where required
```

---

# 59.72 Distributed Tracing

For microservices, trace requests across:

```text
Gateway
 ↓
Auth
 ↓
Course
 ↓
Progress
 ↓
Database
```

where applicable.

---

# 59.73 Correlation IDs

Requests SHOULD have a correlation/trace identifier that allows operators to follow a request across services.

Never use sensitive personal information as the correlation ID.

---

# 59.74 Performance Metrics

Monitor:

```text
Request latency
Request rate
Error rate
CPU
Memory
GC behavior
Database latency
Connection pool usage
Cache hit ratio
Queue depth
```

---

# 59.75 JVM Performance

For Spring Boot services, monitor:

```text
Heap
GC pauses
Thread count
CPU
Class loading
Connection pools
```

Do not tune JVM parameters without evidence.

---

# 59.76 Garbage Collection

Investigate:

```text
Frequent GC
Long GC pauses
Heap growth
OutOfMemoryError
```

before changing JVM configuration.

---

# 59.77 Memory Leaks

Potential sources include:

```text
Unbounded caches
Static collections
Thread-local misuse
Unclosed resources
Large object retention
```

---

# 59.78 Resource Lifecycle

Every acquired resource must have a defined lifecycle.

Examples:

```text
Database connection
File stream
HTTP connection
Thread
Executor
Temporary file
```

---

# 59.79 File Processing

Large files should not automatically be loaded completely into memory.

Prefer streaming where practical.

---

# 59.80 Request Size Limits

APIs should define limits for:

```text
Request body
Multipart uploads
Query length
Header size
Batch size
```

This protects both security and resource consumption.

---

# 59.81 Response Limits

Avoid endpoints capable of generating arbitrarily large responses.

Use:

```text
Pagination
Streaming
Limits
Async exports
```

where appropriate.

---

# 59.82 Export Operations

Large exports should generally be asynchronous.

Example:

```text
POST /exports
 ↓
202 Accepted
 ↓
Background processing
 ↓
GET /exports/{id}
 ↓
Download
```

rather than holding an HTTP request open indefinitely.

---

# 59.83 Scalability

The system should distinguish:

```text
Vertical scaling
Horizontal scaling
```

Vertical:

```text
More CPU/RAM
```

Horizontal:

```text
More application instances
```

---

# 59.84 Stateless Services

Application services SHOULD remain stateless where practical.

State should be externalized to:

```text
Database
Redis
Object storage
Message broker
```

where appropriate.

---

# 59.85 Horizontal Scaling

Services intended for horizontal scaling must avoid local-only state that creates incorrect behavior.

Examples:

```text
Local session
Local cache
Local file
In-memory job state
```

---

# 59.86 Kubernetes Autoscaling

Where Kubernetes autoscaling is used, scale based on meaningful signals.

Potential signals:

```text
CPU
Memory
Requests
Queue depth
Custom application metrics
```

---

# 59.87 Autoscaling Safety

Autoscaling must not cause:

```text
Database overload
Connection explosion
Cold-start storms
Queue oscillation
Cost explosion
```

---

# 59.88 Database Scalability

As Mediverse grows, consider:

```text
Read replicas
Partitioning
Archiving
Connection pooling
Query optimization
Caching
Database scaling
```

Do not introduce these prematurely without evidence.

---

# 59.89 Read/Write Separation

Read replicas may be useful for read-heavy workloads.

But developers must understand replication lag.

A recently written record may not immediately appear on a replica.

---

# 59.90 Data Partitioning

Partition large tables only when justified by:

```text
Dataset size
Query patterns
Write volume
Maintenance requirements
```

---

# 59.91 Archiving

Historical data that is rarely accessed MAY be archived.

Examples:

```text
Old audit records
Historical analytics
Old event data
Expired temporary records
```

---

# 59.92 Capacity Planning

Capacity planning should estimate:

```text
Users
Concurrent users
Requests/second
Storage growth
Database growth
AI usage
Media bandwidth
```

---

# 59.93 Performance Baselines

Every major release SHOULD be compared against an established baseline.

Example:

```text
Previous:
p95 = 420 ms

Current:
p95 = 710 ms
```

This represents a significant regression even if the API still "works."

---

# 59.94 Performance Regression

Performance regression tests SHOULD be introduced for critical endpoints.

Examples:

```text
Login
Course search
Course details
Enrollment
Quiz submission
Progress retrieval
AI generation
```

---

# 59.95 Performance Testing Environment

Performance tests should run in controlled environments.

Do not compare:

```text
Developer laptop
```

against:

```text
Production cluster
```

and treat the numbers as equivalent.

---

# 59.96 Performance Documentation

Each critical service SHOULD document:

```text
Expected throughput
Latency target
Resource requirements
Scaling behavior
Known bottlenecks
Caching strategy
Database dependencies
```

---

# 59.97 Definition of Done

A performance-sensitive feature is complete when:

* [ ] Performance requirements are defined
* [ ] Baseline metrics exist
* [ ] Important database queries are analyzed
* [ ] Pagination is implemented where required
* [ ] Database indexes are justified
* [ ] Connection pooling is configured
* [ ] External calls have timeouts
* [ ] Retry behavior is bounded
* [ ] Expensive operations are asynchronous where appropriate
* [ ] Cache strategy is documented where caching is used
* [ ] Cache invalidation is defined
* [ ] Large files are streamed where appropriate
* [ ] Request/response sizes are bounded
* [ ] Performance metrics are observable
* [ ] Critical APIs have latency targets
* [ ] Load testing is performed where required
* [ ] Performance regression is evaluated
* [ ] Horizontal scaling behavior is understood
* [ ] Database scalability is considered
* [ ] Resource consumption is acceptable

---

# 59.98 Core Principles

1. **Measure before optimizing.**
2. **Optimize bottlenecks, not code that merely looks inefficient.**
3. **Use p95/p99, not only averages.**
4. **Do not use unlimited database queries or API responses.**
5. **Pagination is mandatory for potentially large collections.**
6. **Database performance must be measured using real query behavior.**
7. **Caching requires an explicit invalidation strategy.**
8. **Cached data must respect authorization boundaries.**
9. **External calls require timeouts.**
10. **Retries must be bounded and safe.**
11. **Expensive operations should not unnecessarily block request threads.**
12. **Distributed systems require backpressure and resource isolation.**
13. **Horizontal scaling requires stateless application design where practical.**
14. **Autoscaling must consider downstream capacity.**
15. **AI performance must consider both latency and cost.**
16. **Performance regressions are defects when they violate defined budgets.**
17. **Every optimization must be validated with measurements.**
18. **Premature optimization is not a substitute for architecture.**

> **For Mediverse, performance engineering is particularly important because the platform combines conventional CRUD workloads with search, media, real-time learning interactions, analytics, distributed services, and potentially expensive AI operations. These workloads have very different performance characteristics and must not be treated as one generic request/response workload.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 60: Observability, Logging, Monitoring, Metrics, Tracing & Alerting.**

# CSDG — Chapter 60

## Observability, Logging, Monitoring, Metrics, Tracing & Alerting

### 60.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the standards for making Mediverse observable, diagnosable, and operationally measurable across:

```text
Frontend
Backend
Microservices
Database
Redis
Kafka / Messaging
AI services
File storage
Kubernetes
CI/CD
Infrastructure
External APIs
```

Core principle:

> **If the team cannot determine what happened, where it happened, why it happened, and what user impact it caused, the system is not sufficiently observable.**

---

# 60.2 Observability vs Monitoring

These terms MUST NOT be treated as identical.

**Monitoring** answers:

> "Is something wrong?"

**Observability** helps answer:

> "Why is it wrong?"

Mediverse SHOULD use:

```text
Metrics
+
Logs
+
Traces
+
Events
```

to provide operational visibility.

---

# 60.3 Three Primary Signals

The platform SHOULD treat these as the primary observability signals:

```text
Logs
Metrics
Traces
```

Conceptually:

```text
             Observability
                  |
       +----------+----------+
       |          |          |
      Logs      Metrics    Traces
       |          |          |
     Events     Health     Journey
```

---

# 60.4 Observability Architecture

A typical Mediverse flow:

```text
User
 ↓
Frontend
 ↓
Ingress / Load Balancer
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Microservice
 ↓
Database / Redis / Kafka / AI
 ↓
Observability Platform
 ↓
Logs + Metrics + Traces
 ↓
Dashboards + Alerts
```

---

# 60.5 Structured Logging

Application logs MUST be structured.

Prefer:

```json id="3l2j2h"
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-09T10:20:30Z",
  "level": "INFO",
  "service": "course-service",
  "event": "course_created",
  "requestId": "abc123",
  "courseId": "course-456"
}
```

over unstructured messages such as:

```text id="q0y1h2"
Course created successfully by user.
```

---

# 60.6 Log Levels

Use log levels intentionally:

```text id="wtx8yi"
TRACE
DEBUG
INFO
WARN
ERROR
```

Production logging SHOULD generally avoid excessive DEBUG/TRACE logging unless temporarily enabled for controlled troubleshooting.

---

# 60.7 TRACE

Use TRACE for extremely detailed diagnostic information.

It should generally not be enabled continuously in production.

---

# 60.8 DEBUG

DEBUG is intended for developer troubleshooting.

Do not rely on DEBUG logs as the only source of critical business/audit information.

---

# 60.9 INFO

INFO should describe meaningful application events.

Examples:

```text id="g0i9vu"
Service started
Course published
User authenticated
Message consumed
Job completed
```

---

# 60.10 WARN

WARN indicates an unusual condition that does not necessarily represent an application failure.

Examples:

```text id="p2i6m4"
Retry performed
Cache unavailable
Deprecated API used
Approaching resource limit
```

---

# 60.11 ERROR

ERROR indicates a failure requiring investigation or operational awareness.

Examples:

```text id="knw8r6"
Database failure
Unhandled exception
External service failure
Message processing failure
```

Do not log every expected 4xx response as ERROR.

---

# 60.12 Log Event Naming

Important application events SHOULD use stable event names.

Example:

```text id="ubp6t7"
course.created
course.updated
course.published
course.deleted
quiz.started
quiz.submitted
user.login.failed
```

Stable event names make searching and dashboards significantly easier.

---

# 60.13 Required Log Context

Where applicable, logs SHOULD include:

```text id="1g1m8r"
timestamp
service
environment
log level
event
request ID
trace ID
user/session reference where safe
resource ID
duration
error code
```

---

# 60.14 Correlation ID

Requests crossing service boundaries SHOULD carry a correlation identifier.

Example:

```text id="9k7z9f"
Frontend
  |
  | X-Correlation-ID
  ↓
Gateway
  |
  | X-Correlation-ID
  ↓
Course Service
  |
  | X-Correlation-ID
  ↓
Database / Worker
```

This allows operators to follow a request across services.

---

# 60.15 Trace ID

Distributed tracing SHOULD use a trace identifier that follows a request across service boundaries.

Do not invent incompatible trace IDs independently inside every service.

---

# 60.16 Sensitive Data

Logs MUST NOT expose:

```text id="3q8h7e"
Passwords
JWT tokens
Refresh tokens
Private keys
Encryption keys
Database passwords
OAuth secrets
```

---

# 60.17 Medical/Sensitive Information

Mediverse logs SHOULD minimize sensitive information.

Avoid logging entire:

```text id="x7y8o4"
User profiles
Learning records
Uploaded documents
AI prompts
AI responses
```

unless explicitly required and appropriately protected.

---

# 60.18 Request Logging

Do not blindly log complete HTTP requests.

Avoid logging:

```text id="m6b2hz"
Authorization headers
Cookies
Passwords
Full request bodies
```

Use selective fields.

---

# 60.19 Response Logging

Do not automatically log complete responses.

For large or sensitive responses, log metadata such as:

```text id="9cl3wr"
status
duration
response size
resource ID
```

---

# 60.20 Exception Logging

Exceptions should contain enough information to diagnose the failure.

Include:

```text id="7sy5bf"
Exception type
Error code
Trace ID
Relevant resource
Stack trace where appropriate
```

Do not expose internal stack traces to end users.

---

# 60.21 Error Codes

Application errors SHOULD have stable machine-readable error codes.

Example:

```json id="6x1i9h"
{
  "code": "COURSE_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "Course could not be found",
  "traceId": "abc123"
}
```

---

# 60.22 User-Facing Error Messages

User-facing messages should be:

```text id="pzhk6j"
Clear
Safe
Actionable
Non-sensitive
```

Do not expose:

```text id="c4gq0h"
SQL errors
Stack traces
Internal hostnames
Database structure
Secrets
```

---

# 60.23 Logging Cardinality

Avoid creating metrics or log dimensions with uncontrolled cardinality.

Bad metric labels:

```text id="2a3l1g"
userId
requestId
full URL
AI prompt
```

These can generate enormous metric volumes.

---

# 60.24 Metrics

Metrics SHOULD measure system behavior using numerical time-series data.

Core categories:

```text id="4b7o9v"
Traffic
Errors
Latency
Saturation
Business metrics
Infrastructure metrics
```

---

# 60.25 RED Metrics

For request-driven services, monitor:

```text id="e2a7w9"
Rate
Errors
Duration
```

Example:

```text id="b8p1fs"
HTTP requests/sec
HTTP error rate
HTTP latency
```

---

# 60.26 USE Metrics

For infrastructure resources, consider:

```text id="1hj9s0"
Utilization
Saturation
Errors
```

for:

```text id="9e5w8a"
CPU
Memory
Disk
Network
```

---

# 60.27 Application Metrics

Important application metrics may include:

```text id="0ah4i6"
Active users
Course enrollments
Quiz submissions
Failed logins
AI requests
AI failures
Notification failures
Search requests
File uploads
```

Business metrics must not replace technical metrics; both are required.

---

# 60.28 Counter Metrics

Use counters for monotonically increasing events.

Examples:

```text id="ndp9dd"
http_requests_total
login_failures_total
quiz_submissions_total
ai_requests_total
```

---

# 60.29 Gauge Metrics

Use gauges for values that increase and decrease.

Examples:

```text id="q8q5ir"
Active users
Queue depth
Memory usage
Database connections
```

---

# 60.30 Histogram Metrics

Histograms SHOULD be used for distributions such as:

```text id="r8z9k2"
Request latency
Database query duration
AI response duration
File-processing duration
```

---

# 60.31 Metric Naming

Metric names MUST follow a consistent convention.

Example:

```text id="u5c5ak"
mediverse_http_requests_total
mediverse_course_creation_duration_seconds
mediverse_ai_requests_total
```

Avoid inconsistent naming between services.

---

# 60.32 Metric Labels

Labels SHOULD represent bounded dimensions.

Good:

```text id="k8v6c9"
method
status
service
endpoint
environment
```

Avoid:

```text id="0tq8k6"
userId
email
requestId
```

---

# 60.33 Endpoint Metrics

HTTP metrics SHOULD distinguish important dimensions such as:

```text id="e7v9a1"
HTTP method
route
status
duration
```

Use normalized routes.

Prefer:

```text id="r1z4g2"
/courses/{courseId}
```

rather than generating a unique metric series for:

```text id="6xw3b9"
/courses/123
/courses/124
/courses/125
```

---

# 60.34 Database Metrics

Monitor:

```text id="q3w2p9"
Query latency
Connection count
Connection pool exhaustion
Locks
Slow queries
Transaction failures
CPU
Storage
```

---

# 60.35 Redis Metrics

Where Redis is used, monitor:

```text id="k2v9y6"
Memory
Hit ratio
Miss ratio
Evictions
Connections
Command latency
Failures
```

---

# 60.36 Kafka/Messaging Metrics

Monitor:

```text id="n9z4j8"
Messages published
Messages consumed
Consumer lag
Processing latency
Retries
Dead-letter messages
Failed consumers
```

---

# 60.37 Queue Lag

Consumer lag MUST be monitored for asynchronous systems.

Increasing lag can indicate:

```text id="m0q1d7"
Insufficient consumers
Slow processing
Downstream dependency failure
Traffic spike
```

---

# 60.38 AI Metrics

AI functionality SHOULD expose metrics such as:

```text id="8h4w1m"
Requests
Success rate
Failure rate
Latency
Token usage where available
Timeouts
Rate-limit events
Provider errors
Estimated cost where available
```

---

# 60.39 AI Observability

Do not blindly log complete AI prompts/responses.

Instead consider safe metadata:

```text id="4c7p5x"
Model
Request type
Duration
Token counts
Status
Error code
Trace ID
```

---

# 60.40 AI Cost Monitoring

Where applicable, track AI consumption by:

```text id="n2r7y4"
Feature
Model
Environment
Tenant/user scope where safe
Time period
```

This allows abnormal consumption to be detected.

---

# 60.41 Frontend Monitoring

Frontend observability SHOULD include:

```text id="q6v1m9"
JavaScript errors
Failed API requests
Page-load performance
Route performance
Core user journeys
```

---

# 60.42 Frontend Error Reporting

Capture enough context to reproduce failures without collecting unnecessary sensitive information.

Useful information includes:

```text id="6w1z8e"
Browser
OS
Application version
Route
Error type
Trace/correlation ID
```

---

# 60.43 Synthetic Monitoring

Critical user journeys SHOULD be monitored synthetically where appropriate.

Examples:

```text id="2a6m8h"
Login
Course search
Course opening
Quiz submission
```

---

# 60.44 Health Checks

Services SHOULD expose appropriate health information.

Distinguish:

```text id="w3z7f0"
Liveness
Readiness
Startup
```

---

# 60.45 Liveness

Liveness answers:

> "Should this process be restarted?"

Do not make liveness depend on every external dependency.

A temporary database outage should not necessarily cause Kubernetes to endlessly restart a service.

---

# 60.46 Readiness

Readiness answers:

> "Should this instance receive traffic?"

Readiness can consider critical dependencies required to serve requests.

---

# 60.47 Startup Checks

Slow-starting services SHOULD use startup checks so Kubernetes does not incorrectly kill them during initialization.

---

# 60.48 Health Endpoint Security

Health endpoints should not expose sensitive infrastructure information publicly.

Avoid returning:

```text id="2g5r9m"
Database credentials
Internal topology
Environment secrets
Detailed exception information
```

---

# 60.49 Distributed Tracing

Tracing SHOULD be used for cross-service request analysis.

Example:

```text id="p4o2f6"
Trace
 |
 +-- Gateway
 |
 +-- Auth Service
 |
 +-- Course Service
 |     |
 |     +-- PostgreSQL
 |
 +-- Redis
```

---

# 60.50 Trace Spans

A span should represent a meaningful operation.

Examples:

```text id="c8k6m0"
HTTP request
Database query
Redis operation
Kafka publish
External API call
AI generation
```

---

# 60.51 Trace Attributes

Trace attributes SHOULD provide diagnostic context without exposing sensitive information.

Examples:

```text id="0g8x6w"
service
route
status
duration
dependency
operation
```

---

# 60.52 Trace Sampling

Tracing every request at full detail may become expensive.

Use appropriate sampling strategies.

Critical error traces SHOULD remain discoverable.

---

# 60.53 External Service Tracing

Where supported, propagate trace context across service boundaries.

This makes failures such as:

```text id="2h8s4v"
Mediverse
 ↓
External AI provider
```

easier to diagnose.

---

# 60.54 Database Tracing
