# CSDG — Chapter 66

## Java & Spring Boot Backend Engineering Standards — Project Structure, Layers, Services, Dependency Injection, Exception Handling & Coding Practices

### 66.1 Purpose

This chapter defines backend engineering standards for Mediverse services built with Java and Spring Boot.

The backend MUST prioritize:

```text
Correctness
Maintainability
Testability
Security
Performance
Observability
Separation of concerns
```

Core principle:

> **Spring Boot makes it easy to build an API quickly. CSDG exists to prevent that API from becoming an unmaintainable collection of controllers, services, repositories, entities, and business rules.**

---

# 66.2 Technology Baseline

The Mediverse backend SHOULD follow the approved technology baseline:

```text
Java 17+
Spring Boot
Spring Web
Spring Data JPA
Hibernate
Spring Security
Bean Validation
PostgreSQL
OpenAPI
JUnit
Mockito
```

Additional technologies such as Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch, or WebSocket SHOULD only be introduced when an actual architectural requirement exists.

---

# 66.3 Java Version

The project MUST define one supported Java version for each release line.

Example:

```text
Java 17
```

or:

```text
Java 21
```

Developers MUST NOT casually compile with one JDK and run with another incompatible runtime.

---

# 66.4 Spring Boot Version

Spring Boot versions MUST be centrally managed.

Do not allow individual services to independently select unrelated Spring Boot versions without architectural justification.

---

# 66.5 Maven/Gradle

The project MUST standardize on one primary build system.

Example:

```text
Maven
```

or:

```text
Gradle
```

Do not mix build systems arbitrarily across services.

---

# 66.6 Package Naming

Java packages SHOULD follow reverse-domain naming.

Example:

```text
com.mediverse
```

Feature/domain packages SHOULD remain organized.

Example:

```text
com.mediverse.course
com.mediverse.assessment
com.mediverse.user
```

---

# 66.7 Backend Package Structure

For a modular Spring Boot service:

```text
src/main/java/com/mediverse/
├── config/
├── controller/
├── dto/
├── entity/
├── repository/
├── service/
├── exception/
├── mapper/
├── security/
└── util/
```

For larger services, feature-oriented organization SHOULD be considered:

```text
course/
├── controller/
├── dto/
├── entity/
├── repository/
└── service/
```

The project SHOULD avoid creating a single massive package containing hundreds of unrelated classes.

---

# 66.8 Layered Architecture

A conventional Mediverse backend SHOULD follow:

```text
Controller
    ↓
Service
    ↓
Repository
    ↓
Database
```

Supporting layers may include:

```text
DTO
Mapper
Security
Configuration
Exception
Domain
```

---

# 66.9 Controller Responsibility

Controllers SHOULD handle:

```text
HTTP request
Input binding
Validation trigger
Authentication context
Calling application/service layer
HTTP response
```

Controllers SHOULD NOT contain complex business logic.

---

# 66.10 Controller Anti-Pattern

Avoid:

```java
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<?> createCourse(...) {

    // validate
    // calculate business rules
    // manipulate entities
    // save multiple repositories
    // send Kafka event
    // format response
}
```

This is not a controller's responsibility.

---

# 66.11 Service Responsibility

Services SHOULD contain application/business orchestration.

Example:

```text
CourseService
EnrollmentService
QuizService
ProgressService
```

A service may coordinate:

```text
Validation
Business rules
Repositories
External services
Transactions
Events
```

---

# 66.12 Repository Responsibility

Repositories SHOULD primarily handle persistence operations.

They SHOULD NOT contain business workflows.

Example:

```java
courseRepository.findById(id);
```

is appropriate.

A repository deciding:

```text
whether a student is eligible to take an exam
```

is generally not.

---

# 66.13 Entity Responsibility

JPA entities represent persistent domain state.

Entities SHOULD NOT become giant containers for unrelated application workflows.

---

# 66.14 DTO Responsibility

DTOs define API boundaries.

Examples:

```text
CreateCourseRequest
UpdateCourseRequest
CourseResponse
CourseSummaryResponse
```

---

# 66.15 Entity vs DTO

Never assume:

```text
Entity == API Response
```

They serve different purposes.

```text
Entity
 ↓
Persistence model

DTO
 ↓
External contract
```

---

# 66.16 Mapper

Mapping between:

```text
Entity ↔ DTO
```

SHOULD be explicit and testable.

For complex projects, a mapping framework MAY be used.

---

# 66.17 Dependency Injection

Use Spring dependency injection rather than manually constructing managed dependencies.

Prefer constructor injection.

Example:

```java
@Service
public class CourseService {

    private final CourseRepository courseRepository;

    public CourseService(CourseRepository courseRepository) {
        this.courseRepository = courseRepository;
    }
}
```

---

# 66.18 Field Injection

Avoid:

```java
@Autowired
private CourseRepository courseRepository;
```

Constructor injection is preferred because dependencies become explicit and the class is easier to test.

---

# 66.19 Dependency Direction

Dependencies SHOULD flow toward lower-level implementation details.

A controller should depend on a service abstraction/application layer rather than directly implementing persistence logic.

---

# 66.20 Circular Dependencies

Circular dependencies MUST be avoided.

Example:

```text
Service A
 ↓
Service B
 ↓
Service A
```

A circular dependency is usually a design smell rather than something to solve with lazy injection.

---

# 66.21 Service Size

Services SHOULD remain cohesive.

Avoid:

```text
MegaService
```

containing unrelated responsibilities such as:

```text
Authentication
Courses
Payments
Notifications
Analytics
File processing
```

---

# 66.22 Transaction Boundaries

Transactions SHOULD normally be defined around application/service use cases.

Example:

```java
@Transactional
public EnrollmentResponse enroll(...) {
    ...
}
```

---

# 66.23 Read Transactions

Read-only transactions MAY be used where appropriate.

Example:

```java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
```

This communicates intent and may provide optimization opportunities.

---

# 66.24 Transaction Anti-Pattern

Avoid putting a transaction around an operation that performs slow external communication:

```text
@Transactional
 ↓
Database
 ↓
External AI API
 ↓
Kafka
 ↓
Database
```

unless there is a deliberate reason.

---

# 66.25 Business Rules

Business rules MUST have a clear location.

Example:

```text
Student can attempt quiz
```

belongs in the appropriate application/domain service rather than:

```text
React
Controller
Repository
```

---

# 66.26 Validation

Use Bean Validation for structural input validation.

Example:

```java
@NotBlank
private String title;
```

and:

```java
@Size(max = 200)
private String description;
```

---

# 66.27 Validation vs Business Rules

Distinguish:

```text
Input validation
```

from:

```text
Business validation
```

Example:

```text
title cannot be blank
```

is input validation.

```text
student cannot submit an expired quiz
```

is a business rule.

---

# 66.28 Exception Handling

Backend services MUST use consistent exception handling.

Prefer centralized handling using:

```text
@RestControllerAdvice
```

---

# 66.29 Custom Exceptions

Create meaningful exceptions for important business failures.

Examples:

```text
CourseNotFoundException
LessonNotFoundException
QuizClosedException
DuplicateEnrollmentException
AccessDeniedException
```

---

# 66.30 Exception Naming

Exception names SHOULD clearly communicate the failure.

Avoid:

```text
SomethingWentWrongException
GeneralException
CommonException
MyException
```

---

# 66.31 HTTP Exception Mapping

Map exceptions to appropriate HTTP responses.

Example:

```text
ResourceNotFoundException
        ↓
404

ValidationException
        ↓
400 / 422

AccessDenied
        ↓
403

Conflict
        ↓
409
```

---

# 66.32 Internal Errors

Unexpected internal exceptions MUST NOT expose implementation details.

Do not return:

```text
java.lang.NullPointerException...
org.hibernate...
SQL...
```

to the client.

---

# 66.33 Logging Exceptions

Unexpected exceptions SHOULD be logged with sufficient context and trace identifiers.

---

# 66.34 Logging Levels

Use appropriate logging levels:

```text
ERROR
WARN
INFO
DEBUG
TRACE
```

Do not log everything at `ERROR`.

---

# 66.35 Logging Sensitive Data

Never log:

```text
Passwords
JWTs
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
Database passwords
Private keys
Sensitive personal information
```

---

# 66.36 Structured Logging

Production logs SHOULD preferably use structured formats such as JSON.

Useful fields may include:

```text
timestamp
service
environment
traceId
requestId
level
event
```

---

# 66.37 Correlation IDs

Requests SHOULD carry a correlation identifier across service boundaries.

Example:

```text
Frontend
 ↓
Gateway
 ↓
Course Service
 ↓
Database
```

All relevant logs should be traceable to the same request/trace.

---

# 66.38 Configuration

Application configuration MUST be externalized.

Avoid hardcoding:

```text
Database URLs
Passwords
API keys
Environment-specific URLs
```

inside Java source.

---

# 66.39 Configuration Profiles

Use environment-specific configuration appropriately.

Example:

```text
application.yml
application-dev.yml
application-uat.yml
application-prod.yml
```

Do not duplicate large amounts of configuration between files.

---

# 66.40 Secrets

Secrets MUST be provided through secure mechanisms such as:

```text
Environment variables
Secret managers
Kubernetes Secrets
External secret systems
```

depending on deployment architecture.

---

# 66.41 Configuration Validation

Critical configuration SHOULD fail fast when missing or invalid.

A service should not start successfully with an unusable database configuration.

---

# 66.42 Database Access

Use Spring Data JPA/repositories where appropriate.

For complex SQL, explicit queries MAY be used.

Do not force every query through an ORM abstraction when it produces poor performance or incorrect semantics.

---

# 66.43 JPA Relationships

JPA relationships MUST be designed intentionally.

Be careful with:

```text
@OneToMany
@ManyToMany
@ManyToOne
@OneToOne
```

because relationship mappings can create:

```text
N+1 queries
Large object graphs
Serialization loops
Unexpected deletes
```

---

# 66.44 Fetch Strategy

Do not blindly use eager fetching.

Prefer explicit loading based on the use case.

---

# 66.45 LazyInitializationException

Do not solve:

```text
LazyInitializationException
```

by simply changing everything to `EAGER`.

Instead determine:

```text
Which data does the use case actually require?
Where should it be fetched?
```

---

# 66.46 Entity Serialization

Avoid serializing JPA entities directly through REST.

This can trigger:

```text
Lazy loading
Circular references
Large payloads
Sensitive fields
```

Use DTOs.

---

# 66.47 Repository Query Design

Repository methods SHOULD communicate intent.

Good:

```java
findByCourseIdAndStatus(...)
```

Avoid unreadable methods containing enormous derived query names.

For complex queries, use:

```text
JPQL
Native SQL
Specifications
QueryDSL
```

as appropriate.

---

# 66.48 Query Performance

Every important query SHOULD be evaluated for:

```text
Execution time
Index usage
Returned rows
Join behavior
```

Use:

```text
EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

when diagnosing performance.

---

# 66.49 Pagination

Repositories MUST support pagination for potentially large datasets.

Example:

```java
Page<Course> findAll(Pageable pageable);
```

---

# 66.50 Unbounded Queries

Avoid:

```java
repository.findAll();
```

on large production tables unless the dataset is demonstrably small and bounded.

---

# 66.51 Entity Mutability

Be careful with exposing mutable entities across application layers.

Business operations SHOULD modify state deliberately.

---

# 66.52 Immutable DTOs

Request/response DTOs MAY use immutable structures where practical.

For modern Java, records are suitable for many simple DTOs.

Example:

```java
public record CourseResponse(
    Long id,
    String name
) {}
```

---

# 66.53 Java Records

Records SHOULD be considered for immutable data-transfer structures.

Do not force records into cases requiring substantial mutable behavior.

---

# 66.54 Optional

Use `Optional` appropriately.

For repository results:

```java
Optional<Course>
```

can clearly express absence.

Avoid using `Optional` indiscriminately for every field, parameter, or internal variable.

---

# 66.55 Null Handling

Null behavior SHOULD be explicit.

Avoid methods whose null semantics are unclear.

---

# 66.56 Collections

Return empty collections rather than unnecessary null values where appropriate.

Prefer:

```java
List<Course>
```

returning:

```text
[]
```

rather than:

```text
null
```

---

# 66.57 String Handling

Avoid magic strings for domain-critical values.

Prefer:

```text
Enum
Constant
Value object
```

where appropriate.

---

# 66.58 Constants

Constants SHOULD have meaningful names.

Bad:

```java
static final int X = 10;
```

Prefer:

```java
static final int MAX_QUIZ_ATTEMPTS = 10;
```

---

# 66.59 Magic Numbers

Avoid unexplained numbers in business logic.

Bad:

```java
if (attempts > 3) ...
```

Prefer:

```java
if (attempts > MAX_ALLOWED_ATTEMPTS) ...
```

---

# 66.60 Utility Classes

Do not create giant:

```text
Utils
Helper
Common
```

classes containing unrelated functionality.

---

# 66.61 Domain Utilities

Utilities SHOULD have one clear purpose.

Examples:

```text
DateTimeUtils
SecurityUtils
FileNameUtils
```

---

# 66.62 Service Interfaces

Do not automatically create an interface for every service.

Use interfaces where they provide:

```text
Abstraction
Multiple implementations
Architectural boundary
Testing value
```

Otherwise a concrete service can be sufficient.

---

# 66.63 Repository Interfaces

Spring Data repository interfaces SHOULD remain focused on persistence operations.

---

# 66.64 Dependency Scope

Keep dependencies at the narrowest appropriate scope.

Avoid exposing unnecessary dependencies through public APIs.

---

# 66.65 Method Size

Methods SHOULD be short enough to understand without reconstructing an entire system mentally.

If a method performs:

```text
Validation
Database operations
External calls
Mapping
Notifications
Logging
```

it likely needs decomposition.

---

# 66.66 Method Naming

Method names MUST communicate intent.

Good:

```text
enrollStudent()
submitQuiz()
calculateProgress()
publishCourse()
```

Bad:

```text
process()
handle()
doStuff()
execute()
```

unless the abstraction genuinely warrants it.

---

# 66.67 Boolean Naming

Boolean methods SHOULD read naturally.

Examples:

```text
isPublished()
isEligible()
hasCompletedLesson()
canAttemptQuiz()
```

---

# 66.68 Class Naming

Classes SHOULD represent meaningful concepts.

Examples:

```text
CourseService
QuizSubmissionService
ProgressCalculator
EnrollmentPolicy
```

---

# 66.69 Comments

Comments SHOULD explain **why**, not merely repeat **what** the code does.

Bad:

```java
// increment count
count++;
```

Useful:

```java
// We increment only after successful submission because
// failed attempts must not consume the student's attempt quota.
```

---

# 66.70 TODO Comments

TODOs SHOULD contain enough context to be actionable.

Bad:

```text
TODO fix
```

Better:

```text
TODO: Replace temporary polling with event-driven progress updates.
```

---

# 66.71 Dead Code

Unused classes, methods, imports, configurations, and commented-out code SHOULD be removed.

Git already stores historical versions.

---

# 66.72 Copy-Paste Code

Repeated business logic SHOULD be consolidated when duplication creates maintenance risk.

Do not abstract tiny coincidental similarities merely to eliminate a few lines.

---

# 66.73 Code Duplication

Repeated rules such as:

```text
Eligibility calculation
Progress calculation
Permission checks
Quiz scoring
```

SHOULD have a single authoritative implementation.

---

# 66.74 Domain Logic

Domain rules SHOULD be placed close to the domain they govern.

For example:

```text
Quiz scoring
```

should not be implemented independently in:

```text
Controller
Frontend
Reporting service
```

without a clear source of truth.

---

# 66.75 Source of Truth

Every critical business calculation MUST have an authoritative implementation.

Examples:

```text
Quiz score
Course completion
Learning progress
Eligibility
```

---

# 66.76 Monetary/Precise Calculations

Where financial or precision-sensitive calculations exist, avoid floating-point arithmetic where inappropriate.

Use suitable types such as:

```text
BigDecimal
```

when exact decimal semantics are required.

---

# 66.77 Date and Time

Use modern Java time APIs:

```text
java.time.*
```

Avoid legacy:

```text
java.util.Date
java.util.Calendar
```

for new code unless interoperability requires them.

---

# 66.78 Time Zone

Store/operate on timestamps consistently, preferably UTC at system boundaries.

Convert to user-local time at presentation.

---

# 66.79 UUIDs and IDs

Identifier generation SHOULD be centralized.

Do not generate inconsistent identifiers across different layers.

---

# 66.80 File Processing

File operations SHOULD be isolated from ordinary business services where they become complex.

For example:

```text
MediaService
FileStorageService
DocumentProcessingService
```

---

# 66.81 External APIs

External integrations SHOULD be wrapped behind dedicated clients/services.

Avoid calling external APIs directly from controllers.

---

# 66.82 External API Client

External clients SHOULD define:

```text
Timeout
Authentication
Retry
Error mapping
Logging policy
Circuit breaker where needed
```

---

# 66.83 Resilience

External dependencies SHOULD have controlled failure behavior.

Potential mechanisms:

```text
Timeout
Retry
Circuit breaker
Bulkhead
Fallback
```

Use only where appropriate.

---

# 66.84 Retry Safety

Never blindly retry every operation.

A retry of:

```text
GET
```

is usually safer than blindly retrying:

```text
POST
```

that triggers an external side effect.

---

# 66.85 Async Processing

Long-running workflows SHOULD use asynchronous processing when appropriate.

Examples:

```text
AI content generation
Video processing
Large document processing
Bulk notifications
Report generation
```

---

# 66.86 Messaging

If Kafka/RabbitMQ is used, message publishing/consumption MUST have clear:

```text
Event schema
Versioning
Retry
Dead-letter handling
Idempotency
Observability
```

---

# 66.87 Consumer Idempotency

Message consumers MUST assume that duplicate delivery can happen.

Example:

```text
Same event
    ↓
received twice
```

must not corrupt application state.

---

# 66.88 Scheduled Jobs

Scheduled jobs SHOULD be:

```text
Idempotent
Observable
Recoverable
Bounded
```

---

# 66.89 Distributed Locks

If a scheduled job can run on multiple service replicas, consider whether duplicate execution is possible.

Do not assume:

```text
@Scheduled
```

runs only once across a Kubernetes deployment.

---

# 66.90 Background Jobs

Background workers SHOULD expose enough metrics/logging to answer:

```text
How many jobs?
How many succeeded?
How many failed?
How many retried?
How long did they take?
```

---

# 66.91 Thread Pools

Do not create unbounded thread pools.

Thread pool sizes SHOULD reflect workload characteristics.

---

# 66.92 Async Methods

Use Spring asynchronous execution deliberately.

Avoid turning every method into asynchronous execution merely to "increase performance."

---

# 66.93 Performance

Performance optimization SHOULD follow measurement.

Process:

```text
Measure
 ↓
Identify bottleneck
 ↓
Optimize
 ↓
Measure again
```

---

# 66.94 Premature Optimization

Do not optimize code based on assumptions.

A complicated optimization that saves 2 ms but makes the system unmaintainable is usually a bad trade.

---

# 66.95 Caching

Use caching for demonstrated performance needs.

Possible candidates:

```text
Course catalog
Reference data
Frequently accessed public educational content
```

Do not cache mutable data without an invalidation strategy.

---

# 66.96 Cache Consistency

Every cache MUST have a defined:

```text
TTL
Invalidation strategy
Fallback behavior
Ownership
```

---

# 66.97 Security

Backend code MUST follow the security architecture defined by Mediverse.

At minimum:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Input validation
Secure password handling
Secret management
Auditability
```

---

# 66.98 Authorization

Authorization MUST happen at the backend/domain boundary.

Example:

```text
Student
 ↓
Request course content
 ↓
Service verifies access
 ↓
Return data
```

---

# 66.99 Security Checks

Security-sensitive operations SHOULD have explicit tests.

Examples:

```text
Student cannot access admin API
Student cannot modify another user's progress
Teacher cannot modify unrelated courses
Unauthorized user cannot access private content
```

---

# 66.100 API Security

Controllers SHOULD never assume that a request is trustworthy because it came from the Mediverse frontend.

Every request is untrusted input.

---

# 66.101 Database Security

Application users SHOULD have only required database privileges.

Do not run the application as PostgreSQL superuser.

---

# 66.102 Testing Structure

Backend tests SHOULD mirror application responsibilities.

Example:

```text
src/test/
├── controller/
├── service/
├── repository/
├── integration/
└── security/
```

---

# 66.103 Unit Tests

Unit tests SHOULD focus on isolated business behavior.

Examples:

```text
Quiz scoring
Progress calculation
Eligibility rules
Validation logic
```

---

# 66.104 Service Tests

Service tests SHOULD verify:

```text
Business rules
Repository interactions
Failure conditions
Transactions where relevant
```

---

# 66.105 Controller Tests

Controller tests SHOULD verify:

```text
HTTP status
Request validation
Response contract
Authorization
Error mapping
```

---

# 66.106 Repository Tests

Repository tests SHOULD verify important queries against a realistic database environment when query behavior is non-trivial.

---

# 66.107 Integration Tests

Integration tests SHOULD verify collaboration between components.

Example:

```text
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
PostgreSQL
```

---

# 66.108 Testcontainers

Where appropriate, Testcontainers SHOULD be considered for realistic integration testing with:

```text
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka
```

rather than relying exclusively on mocks.

---

# 66.109 Mocking

Mock external boundaries deliberately.

Do not mock everything.

If the behavior being tested is fundamentally about database interaction, a real test database may be more valuable than a mocked repository.

---

# 66.110 Test Naming

Test names SHOULD describe behavior.

Good:

```text
shouldRejectEnrollmentWhenStudentAlreadyEnrolled()
```

Bad:

```text
test1()
```

---

# 66.111 Test Data

Test data SHOULD be deterministic and isolated.

Tests MUST NOT depend on another test having run first.

---

# 66.112 Test Isolation

Tests SHOULD be independent.

Avoid:

```text
Test A creates data
Test B expects Test A's data
```

---

# 66.113 Test Coverage

Coverage metrics SHOULD be used as indicators, not the sole measure of quality.

100% coverage does not guarantee correct software.

---

# 66.114 Static Analysis

Backend code SHOULD be checked with tools such as:

```text
SonarQube
Checkstyle
SpotBugs
PMD
```

according to the project's approved tooling.

---

# 66.115 Quality Gates

CI SHOULD reject builds when critical quality gates fail.

Examples:

```text
Compilation failure
Critical security issue
Severe code smell
Test failure
Coverage threshold failure
```

---

# 66.116 Build Reproducibility

Builds SHOULD be reproducible.

Dependencies and plugin versions SHOULD be controlled.

---

# 66.117 Dependency Management

Dependencies SHOULD be:

```text
Necessary
Supported
Version-controlled
Security-scanned
```

---

# 66.118 Dependency Vulnerabilities

Critical dependency vulnerabilities SHOULD be addressed according to the project's security SLA.

---

# 66.119 Actuator

Spring Boot Actuator MAY be used for operational observability.

Exposed endpoints MUST be secured.

Do not expose sensitive management endpoints publicly.

---

# 66.120 Health Checks

Services SHOULD expose appropriate health information for orchestration.

Distinguish between:

```text
Liveness
Readiness
```

---

# 66.121 Kubernetes Readiness

A service should not receive traffic before critical dependencies required for serving requests are ready.

---

# 66.122 Kubernetes Liveness

Liveness checks should identify whether the application process is fundamentally unhealthy.

Do not configure liveness checks so aggressively that normal temporary dependency failures cause unnecessary restarts.

---

# 66.123 Graceful Shutdown

Spring Boot services SHOULD support graceful shutdown.

On shutdown:

```text
Stop accepting new work
 ↓
Finish safe in-flight work
 ↓
Close resources
 ↓
Exit
```

---

# 66.124 Database Migration Startup

Do not allow uncontrolled production migration behavior merely because the application starts.

Migration strategy should be explicitly defined.

---

# 66.125 API Documentation

Every public service endpoint SHOULD have OpenAPI documentation.

Documentation should include:

```text
Description
Parameters
Request schema
Response schema
Errors
Authentication
Examples
```

---

# 66.126 Code Review

Backend PRs SHOULD review:

```text
Architecture
Business logic
Security
Database impact
Transactions
Performance
Testing
Logging
Observability
```

---

# 66.127 Pull Request Size

Avoid giant backend PRs containing unrelated changes.

Prefer focused changes that are easier to review and revert.

---

# 66.128 Commit Discipline

Commits SHOULD represent coherent changes.

Avoid:

```text
fix everything
final changes
some updates
working now
```

as meaningless commit messages.

---

# 66.129 Backward Compatibility

Backend changes MUST consider:

```text
Frontend consumers
Other services
Mobile clients
External integrations
Existing database versions
```

---

# 66.130 Feature Flags

Feature flags MAY be used for gradual rollout.

They MUST have:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Default behavior
Removal plan
```

A permanent feature flag is technical debt.

---

# 66.131 Production Debugging

Production debugging SHOULD use:

```text
Logs
Metrics
Traces
Database metrics
Application health
```

rather than adding random debug code directly to production.

---

# 66.132 Emergency Changes

Emergency production changes MUST still be documented and followed by proper review.

"Production emergency" is not a permanent exemption from engineering standards.

---

# 66.133 Definition of Done

A backend feature is production-ready when:

* [ ] Package structure is appropriate
* [ ] Layer responsibilities are clear
* [ ] Constructor injection is used
* [ ] Controllers contain minimal logic
* [ ] Business logic is properly located
* [ ] DTOs are used
* [ ] Validation exists
* [ ] Exception handling is centralized
* [ ] Error responses follow API standards
* [ ] Transactions are correctly defined
* [ ] Database queries are reviewed
* [ ] Pagination exists where required
* [ ] Security checks exist
* [ ] Logging is safe
* [ ] Trace/correlation support exists
* [ ] Configuration is externalized
* [ ] Secrets are protected
* [ ] Tests exist
* [ ] Integration tests exist where appropriate
* [ ] Static analysis passes
* [ ] Dependencies are secure
* [ ] Health checks are configured
* [ ] Graceful shutdown is supported
* [ ] OpenAPI is updated
* [ ] Documentation is updated

---

# 66.134 Core Principles

1. **Controllers coordinate HTTP; they do not contain the business system.**
2. **Services implement application/business workflows.**
3. **Repositories handle persistence, not business decisions.**
4. **DTOs protect API contracts from persistence models.**
5. **Constructor injection should be the default.**
6. **Transactions should represent meaningful business operations.**
7. **Do not solve ORM problems by blindly making everything eager.**
8. **Never expose internal exceptions to clients.**
9. **Every critical business rule needs one authoritative implementation.**
10. **External integrations require timeout and failure strategies.**
11. **Retries must consider idempotency.**
12. **Distributed jobs must account for duplicate execution.**
13. **Performance optimization must be measurement-driven.**
14. **Security must be enforced on the backend, not merely represented in the UI.**
15. **Observability is part of backend engineering, not an afterthought.**
16. **Tests should verify behavior, not merely increase coverage numbers.**
17. **Production readiness includes operational behavior, not just successful compilation.**

> **For Mediverse, the backend will eventually contain the rules governing authentication, courses, learning progression, assessments, content, AI-assisted functionality, notifications, and potentially multiple independent services. If those rules are allowed to leak into controllers, repositories, or frontend code, the system will become difficult to change and even harder to trust. The backend architecture must therefore make business ownership explicit.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 67: Security Engineering Standards — Authentication, Authorization, JWT/OAuth2, Secrets, OWASP, Data Protection & Secure Development.**

# CSDG — Chapter 67

## Security Engineering Standards — Authentication, Authorization, JWT/OAuth2, Secrets, OWASP, Data Protection & Secure Development

### 67.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the security engineering standards for Mediverse.

Security MUST be treated as a **system-wide architectural concern**, covering:

```text
Identity
Authentication
Authorization
Session/token management
API security
Data protection
Secrets
Input validation
Dependency security
Logging
Auditing
Infrastructure
Frontend
Backend
Database
```

Core principle:

> **Never trust the client. Never treat UI restrictions as security. Every security-sensitive decision must ultimately be enforced by a trusted backend boundary.**

---

# 67.2 Security Objectives

Mediverse security engineering MUST protect:

```text
Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authenticity
Authorization
Accountability
Privacy
```

---

# 67.3 Security by Design

Security MUST be considered during:

```text
Requirements
 ↓
Architecture
 ↓
Design
 ↓
Implementation
 ↓
Testing
 ↓
Deployment
 ↓
Operations
```

Security reviews SHOULD NOT be postponed until production deployment.

---

# 67.4 Threat Modeling

Security-sensitive features SHOULD undergo threat modeling.

At minimum identify:

```text
Asset
Threat actor
Attack surface
Threat
Impact
Likelihood
Mitigation
Residual risk
```

---

# 67.5 Trust Boundaries

The architecture MUST explicitly identify trust boundaries.

Example:

```text
Browser
   ↓
API Gateway
   ↓
Backend Service
   ↓
Database
```

Every boundary should be treated as potentially hostile.

---

# 67.6 Zero Trust Principle

Internal network location MUST NOT automatically imply trust.

For example:

```text
Service A → Service B
```

should not be considered secure merely because both services run inside the same Kubernetes cluster.

---

# 67.7 Authentication vs Authorization

These MUST remain conceptually separate.

```text
Authentication
    ↓
Who are you?

Authorization
    ↓
What are you allowed to do?
```

Successful authentication does not imply permission to perform every operation.

---

# 67.8 Identity

Every authenticated user SHOULD have a stable unique identity.

Example:

```text
userId
```

should be the authoritative identity reference rather than relying on mutable attributes such as email address.

---

# 67.9 User Roles

Mediverse MAY use roles such as:

```text
STUDENT
TEACHER
ADMIN
CONTENT_AUTHOR
```

Actual roles MUST come from the approved authorization model.

Do not invent ad-hoc roles inside individual services.

---

# 67.10 Permissions

Where role-based access control becomes insufficient, permissions SHOULD be modeled explicitly.

Example:

```text
COURSE_READ
COURSE_CREATE
COURSE_UPDATE
COURSE_PUBLISH
QUIZ_CREATE
QUIZ_SUBMIT
USER_MANAGE
```

---

# 67.11 RBAC

Role-Based Access Control SHOULD be centralized.

Example:

```text
STUDENT
   ↓
COURSE_READ
QUIZ_SUBMIT
PROGRESS_READ

TEACHER
   ↓
COURSE_CREATE
COURSE_UPDATE
QUIZ_MANAGE

ADMIN
   ↓
Administrative permissions
```

---

# 67.12 Authorization Must Be Server-Side

The frontend MAY hide:

```text
Admin menu
Teacher controls
Restricted actions
```

but this provides **zero security by itself**.

The backend MUST independently validate authorization.

---

# 67.13 Object-Level Authorization

Authorization MUST consider the resource being accessed.

Example:

```text
GET /api/users/123/progress
```

must not assume that any authenticated user may access user `123`.

The backend MUST verify ownership or explicit permission.

---

# 67.14 Broken Object-Level Authorization

The following is a critical security risk:

```text
User A
 ↓
changes
 ↓
/users/123 → /users/124
 ↓
sees User B's data
```

Every resource access MUST be authorized.

---

# 67.15 Function-Level Authorization

Users must not gain privileged operations simply by manually calling hidden endpoints.

Example:

```text
POST /api/admin/users
```

must enforce admin authorization regardless of whether the UI exposes the operation.

---

# 67.16 Authentication Mechanism

Mediverse authentication SHOULD use an approved identity mechanism such as:

```text
OAuth2 / OpenID Connect
```

or:

```text
JWT-based authentication
```

according to the system architecture.

Do not implement a custom cryptographic authentication mechanism.

---

# 67.17 Password Storage

Passwords MUST NEVER be stored as plaintext.

Do not use:

```text
MD5
SHA-1
SHA-256(password)
Base64
```

as password hashing mechanisms.

Use a password hashing algorithm designed for password storage, such as:

```text
Argon2
bcrypt
scrypt
```

according to the approved security architecture.

---

# 67.18 Password Policy

Password requirements SHOULD balance security and usability.

Do not create arbitrary requirements such as:

```text
exactly 8 characters
must change every 30 days
```

without a documented security reason.

---

# 67.19 Password Reset

Password reset mechanisms MUST:

```text
Use unpredictable tokens
Expire tokens
Invalidate used tokens
Avoid revealing account existence
```

---

# 67.20 Account Enumeration

Authentication endpoints SHOULD avoid revealing whether a specific account exists.

Avoid responses such as:

```text
"Email does not exist"
```

when that information can be used for enumeration.

---

# 67.21 Login Protection

Authentication endpoints SHOULD implement appropriate defenses against:

```text
Brute force
Credential stuffing
Automated attacks
```

Potential mechanisms include:

```text
Rate limiting
Progressive delays
Account protection
CAPTCHA where justified
Monitoring
```

---

# 67.22 JWT

If JWT is used, tokens MUST be validated correctly.

Validation SHOULD include relevant claims such as:

```text
Signature
Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Not-before
Algorithm
```

as applicable to the architecture.

---

# 67.23 JWT Signing Secret

JWT signing secrets MUST NOT be:

```text
Hardcoded
Committed to Git
Stored in frontend code
Shared through source files
```

---

# 67.24 JWT Algorithm

The accepted signing algorithm MUST be explicitly configured.

Do not blindly trust the algorithm specified by an untrusted token.

---

# 67.25 JWT Expiration

Access tokens SHOULD have a controlled expiration period.

Long-lived access tokens increase the impact of token theft.

---

# 67.26 Refresh Tokens

If refresh tokens are used, they MUST have stronger lifecycle controls.

Consider:

```text
Expiration
Rotation
Revocation
Reuse detection
Secure storage
```

---

# 67.27 Token Storage

Token storage MUST be selected based on the threat model.

Avoid automatically storing sensitive authentication tokens in browser `localStorage` merely because it is convenient.

---

# 67.28 Logout

Logout behavior MUST be explicitly defined.

For systems using refresh tokens, logout SHOULD invalidate the relevant refresh-token/session state.

---

# 67.29 Session Management

Sessions MUST have controlled:

```text
Creation
Expiration
Renewal
Revocation
Logout
```

---

# 67.30 OAuth2

If OAuth2/OIDC is adopted, use standard flows rather than creating custom OAuth behavior.

The identity provider SHOULD remain responsible for authentication.

---

# 67.31 OAuth2 Authorization Code

For browser-based applications, an appropriate modern OAuth2/OIDC flow such as Authorization Code with PKCE SHOULD be considered.

---

# 67.32 Service-to-Service Authentication

Internal services SHOULD authenticate when accessing protected services.

Do not rely solely on:

```text
Private IP
Kubernetes namespace
Internal DNS
```

as proof of identity.

---

# 67.33 API Gateway

If Mediverse uses an API gateway, security responsibilities MUST be clearly defined.

Gateway MAY handle:

```text
TLS termination
Authentication
Rate limiting
Request filtering
Routing
```

but services MUST still enforce resource-level authorization where required.

---

# 67.34 TLS

Production traffic containing sensitive information MUST use encrypted transport.

Use HTTPS/TLS.

Avoid transmitting authentication credentials over plaintext HTTP.

---

# 67.35 Internal TLS

For highly sensitive deployments, service-to-service TLS SHOULD be considered.

---

# 67.36 Certificate Management

Certificates MUST have:

```text
Expiration monitoring
Rotation strategy
Secure private-key storage
```

---

# 67.37 Secrets Management

Secrets MUST be stored in approved secret-management systems.

Examples:

```text
Kubernetes Secrets
Vault
Cloud secret manager
CI/CD secret store
```

---

# 67.38 Secrets in Git

Never commit:

```text
Passwords
Private keys
JWT secrets
Cloud credentials
Database credentials
API keys
```

into source control.

---

# 67.39 `.env` Files

Local `.env` files containing secrets MUST be excluded from source control.

Example:

```text
.env
.env.local
```

should be handled appropriately.

---

# 67.40 Secret Rotation

Important secrets SHOULD support rotation without requiring uncontrolled application changes.

Examples:

```text
Database credentials
API keys
JWT signing keys
Cloud credentials
```

---

# 67.41 Secret Exposure Response

If a secret is accidentally committed:

```text
1. Revoke it
2. Rotate it
3. Investigate usage
4. Remove it from active source
5. Review repository history if necessary
```

Simply deleting the file in a later commit does NOT make the secret safe.

---

# 67.42 Input Validation

All external input MUST be treated as untrusted.

Sources include:

```text
HTTP body
Query parameters
Path variables
Headers
Uploaded files
WebSocket messages
Events
External APIs
```

---

# 67.43 Input Validation Location

Validation SHOULD happen at multiple appropriate boundaries.

Example:

```text
Request
 ↓
Structural validation
 ↓
Business validation
 ↓
Persistence
```

---

# 67.44 SQL Injection

Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL.

Bad:

```java
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"
```

Prefer parameterized queries / ORM mechanisms.

---

# 67.45 JPA Query Safety

Use parameter binding for dynamic values.

---

# 67.46 Command Injection

Never pass untrusted user input directly to operating-system commands.

If command execution is unavoidable:

```text
Validate
Allowlist
Escape appropriately
Restrict privileges
```

---

# 67.47 Cross-Site Scripting

Untrusted content MUST NOT be rendered as executable HTML/JavaScript.

Where rich educational content requires HTML:

```text
Sanitize
Allowlist
Encode
```

as appropriate.

---

# 67.48 HTML Content

Mediverse may eventually support rich educational content.

Therefore, content-authoring functionality MUST define:

```text
Allowed HTML
Allowed attributes
Allowed URLs
Allowed embeds
Sanitization rules
```

---

# 67.49 File Upload Security

Uploaded files MUST be treated as untrusted.

Validate:

```text
File size
Content type
Extension
Actual file signature
Filename
Storage path
```

---

# 67.50 File Extension

Do not trust the filename extension alone.

Example:

```text
malicious.exe
```

renamed to:

```text
image.jpg
```

must not automatically be treated as an image.

---

# 67.51 File Names

Never use raw user-provided filenames as filesystem paths.

Generate safe storage identifiers.

---

# 67.52 File Storage

Uploaded files SHOULD be stored outside executable application directories.

Cloud/object storage MAY be preferred for scalable media.

---

# 67.53 File Download Authorization

A valid file URL does not automatically mean every user should access the file.

Private educational/media assets MUST enforce authorization.

---

# 67.54 Path Traversal

Never allow user-controlled path fragments to directly determine filesystem locations.

Protect against patterns such as:

```text
../
```

and equivalent traversal techniques.

---

# 67.55 SSRF

Server-side requests to user-supplied URLs MUST be carefully controlled.

Do not blindly allow:

```text
POST /fetch?url=<user-url>
```

without SSRF protections.

---

# 67.56 URL Allowlisting

For systems that fetch remote resources, prefer explicit allowlists where feasible.

---

# 67.57 Deserialization

Do not deserialize untrusted data using unsafe mechanisms.

Prefer well-defined formats such as JSON with validated schemas.

---

# 67.58 API Rate Limiting

Public and sensitive endpoints SHOULD have rate limits appropriate to their risk.

High-risk endpoints include:

```text
Login
Password reset
OTP
Search
AI generation
File upload
Expensive queries
```

---

# 67.59 Rate Limit Response

Rate-limited clients SHOULD receive a consistent response such as:

```text
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
```

where appropriate.

---

# 67.60 Abuse Prevention

Mediverse should consider abuse scenarios such as:

```text
Automated quiz submission
Course scraping
AI endpoint abuse
Credential stuffing
File upload abuse
Spam notifications
```

---

# 67.61 CORS

CORS MUST be explicitly configured.

Avoid:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

for authenticated sensitive applications unless there is a documented reason.

---

# 67.62 CSRF

CSRF protection MUST be determined based on the authentication mechanism.

Cookie-based authentication requires particular attention to CSRF.

---

# 67.63 Security Headers

Production applications SHOULD use appropriate security headers.

Examples include controls for:

```text
Content Security Policy
Frame protection
MIME sniffing
Referrer policy
Transport security
```

---

# 67.64 Content Security Policy

CSP SHOULD be introduced carefully and tightened over time.

Avoid unnecessarily broad policies such as unrestricted:

```text
script-src *
```

---

# 67.65 Clickjacking

Sensitive application pages SHOULD be protected against unauthorized framing.

---

# 67.66 Browser Storage

Do not store sensitive information in browser storage without evaluating:

```text
XSS risk
Persistence
Access scope
Expiration
```

---

# 67.67 PII

Mediverse may process personally identifiable information.

Examples:

```text
Name
Email
Phone number
Date of birth
Profile information
Learning activity
```

Such data MUST be handled according to applicable privacy requirements.

---

# 67.68 Data Minimization

Collect only data that the application actually needs.

Do not collect personal information simply because it might become useful someday.

---

# 67.69 Data Classification

Data SHOULD be classified according to sensitivity.

Example:

```text
PUBLIC
INTERNAL
CONFIDENTIAL
SENSITIVE
```

Actual classifications MUST follow the project's approved data classification model.

---

# 67.70 Sensitive Educational Data

Learning records may reveal:

```text
Courses taken
Quiz performance
Learning weaknesses
Academic progress
```

Access to such information MUST be controlled.

---

# 67.71 Passwords in Logs

Passwords MUST NEVER appear in:

```text
Application logs
Audit logs
Error messages
Analytics
Monitoring
```

---

# 67.72 Tokens in Logs

Authentication tokens MUST NEVER be logged.

---

# 67.73 Database Encryption

Sensitive data protection SHOULD consider:

```text
Encryption at rest
Encryption in transit
Key management
Access controls
```

---

# 67.74 Encryption

Do not implement custom cryptography.

Use well-reviewed standard libraries and algorithms.

---

# 67.75 Encryption Keys

Encryption keys MUST be managed separately from encrypted data where appropriate.

---

# 67.76 Password Reset Tokens

Reset tokens MUST be:

```text
Unpredictable
Short-lived
Single-use
Revocable
```

---

# 67.77 Email Verification

Email verification links SHOULD contain unpredictable, time-limited tokens.

---

# 67.78 Account Recovery

Account recovery MUST NOT bypass the security guarantees of normal authentication.

---

# 67.79 Audit Logging

Security-sensitive actions SHOULD be auditable.

Examples:

```text
Login
Logout
Password reset
Role change
Permission change
Course publication
Administrative changes
Sensitive data access
```

---

# 67.80 Audit Log Integrity

Audit logs SHOULD be protected against unauthorized modification.

---

# 67.81 Audit Log Content

Audit logs SHOULD capture enough information to answer:

```text
Who?
What?
When?
Where/from which system?
What resource?
Was it successful?
```

Avoid logging unnecessary sensitive payloads.

---

# 67.82 Failed Authentication Logging

Repeated authentication failures SHOULD be observable for security monitoring.

---

# 67.83 Privileged Activity

Administrative actions SHOULD receive stronger auditing.

Example:

```text
Admin
 ↓
changes student role
```

should be traceable.

---

# 67.84 Security Monitoring

Security monitoring SHOULD detect suspicious patterns such as:

```text
Repeated login failures
Impossible access patterns
Privilege escalation
Mass downloads
Abnormal API usage
```

---

# 67.85 Dependency Security

All backend dependencies SHOULD be continuously or regularly scanned.

---

# 67.86 Vulnerability Management

Vulnerabilities SHOULD be prioritized based on:

```text
Severity
Exploitability
Exposure
Business impact
Availability of fix
```

---

# 67.87 Vulnerable Dependencies

Do not blindly upgrade dependencies in production without testing compatibility.

But also do not indefinitely ignore known critical vulnerabilities.

---

# 67.88 Secure CI/CD

Security checks SHOULD be integrated into CI/CD.

Example:

```text
Commit
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Unit tests
 ↓
Static analysis
 ↓
Dependency scan
 ↓
Container scan
 ↓
Security gates
 ↓
Deploy
```

---

# 67.89 Secret Scanning

Repositories SHOULD use automated secret scanning.

---

# 67.90 SAST

Static Application Security Testing SHOULD be used where appropriate.

---

# 67.91 DAST

Dynamic security testing SHOULD be incorporated for suitable environments and APIs.

---

# 67.92 Container Security

Container images SHOULD be scanned for:

```text
OS vulnerabilities
Dependency vulnerabilities
Misconfiguration
Secrets
```

---

# 67.93 Container User

Applications SHOULD avoid running as root inside containers unless there is a justified requirement.

---

# 67.94 Kubernetes Security

Kubernetes deployments SHOULD follow least privilege.

Avoid:

```yaml
privileged: true
```

unless absolutely required.

---

# 67.95 Kubernetes RBAC

Kubernetes service accounts MUST receive only required permissions.

Avoid giving:

```text
cluster-admin
```

to ordinary application workloads.

---

# 67.96 Network Policies

Sensitive Mediverse services SHOULD use Kubernetes NetworkPolicies where appropriate.

Example:

```text
Frontend
   ↓
Gateway
   ↓
Course Service

Course Service
   ↓
PostgreSQL
```

Services should not automatically communicate with everything.

---

# 67.97 Database Credentials

Application services SHOULD use dedicated database accounts with least privilege.

---

# 67.98 Database Access

A service should only have the database permissions it needs.

For example, a read-only reporting service should not automatically have:

```text
DROP
ALTER
CREATE
```

privileges.

---

# 67.99 Backup Security

Database backups MUST be protected with appropriate:

```text
Access controls
Encryption
Retention
Monitoring
```

---

# 67.100 Backup Testing

A backup that has never been restored is only an assumption.

Restore procedures MUST be tested periodically.

---

# 67.101 Security Testing

Security testing SHOULD include:

```text
Authentication testing
Authorization testing
Input validation
API abuse
File upload testing
Dependency scanning
Container scanning
Penetration testing
```

according to project risk.

---

# 67.102 OWASP Alignment

The Mediverse security program SHOULD align with the OWASP application-security guidance, particularly risks involving:

```text
Broken access control
Cryptographic failures
Injection
Security misconfiguration
Vulnerable components
Authentication failures
Logging/monitoring failures
```

---

# 67.103 Security Code Review

Security-sensitive code SHOULD receive additional review.

Examples:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Password handling
Cryptography
File uploads
Payment functionality
Admin operations
Personal data
```

---

# 67.104 Security Regression Tests

Once a security vulnerability is fixed, add a regression test where practical.

Example:

```text
Vulnerability found
       ↓
Fix
       ↓
Security regression test
       ↓
Prevent recurrence
```

---

# 67.105 Vulnerability Disclosure

The project SHOULD define a mechanism for reporting security vulnerabilities.

Security reports SHOULD NOT be handled through ordinary public issue trackers when they expose exploitable details.

---

# 67.106 Security Incident Response

A security incident process SHOULD define:

```text
Detection
Containment
Investigation
Eradication
Recovery
Communication
Post-incident review
```

---

# 67.107 Compromised Account

If an account is suspected to be compromised:

```text
Invalidate sessions/tokens
Reset credentials
Review activity
Investigate affected resources
Notify according to policy
```

---

# 67.108 Compromised Secret

If an application secret is exposed:

```text
Revoke
Rotate
Identify affected systems
Review logs
Deploy replacement
Document incident
```

---

# 67.109 Security Documentation

Security-sensitive architectural decisions MUST be documented.

Examples:

```text
Authentication architecture
Token strategy
Role model
Secret management
Encryption strategy
Data classification
Threat model
```

---

# 67.110 Security Review Checklist

Every major security-sensitive feature SHOULD answer:

```text
Who can access it?
What happens if the user modifies the request?
What happens if the token is stolen?
What happens if the request is repeated?
What data can be exposed?
What happens when dependencies fail?
What happens when authentication expires?
What is logged?
Can the action be audited?
```

---

# 67.111 Definition of Done

A security-sensitive feature is NOT complete until:

* [ ] Authentication requirements are defined
* [ ] Authorization rules are defined
* [ ] Object-level access is checked
* [ ] Input validation exists
* [ ] Sensitive data is protected
* [ ] Secrets are externalized
* [ ] Tokens are handled securely
* [ ] Rate limiting is considered
* [ ] Audit logging is implemented where required
* [ ] Security headers are appropriate
* [ ] CORS is restricted
* [ ] File uploads are validated where applicable
* [ ] Dependencies are scanned
* [ ] Security tests exist
* [ ] Relevant threats have been considered
* [ ] Production configuration is secure
* [ ] Documentation is updated

---

# 67.112 Core Principles

1. **Never trust the frontend.**
2. **Authentication does not equal authorization.**
3. **Every resource access must be authorized.**
4. **Never store passwords in plaintext.**
5. **Never commit secrets to Git.**
6. **Never log passwords, tokens, or secrets.**
7. **Do not implement custom cryptography.**
8. **Treat every external input as untrusted.**
9. **Validate uploaded files instead of trusting extensions.**
10. **Protect against injection attacks.**
11. **Use least privilege everywhere.**
12. **Internal services are not automatically trusted.**
13. **JWTs require proper validation and lifecycle management.**
14. **Security vulnerabilities require regression tests where practical.**
15. **Audit sensitive operations.**
16. **Security must exist in CI/CD, infrastructure, application code, and operations.**
17. **A security control that exists only in documentation does not protect the system.**

> **For Mediverse, security is especially important because the platform may eventually hold identity data, academic performance, private learning records, teacher/admin capabilities, uploaded educational content, and AI-related functionality. A compromised account must therefore not automatically become a compromised platform. The architecture must contain the blast radius through authentication, authorization, least privilege, isolation, auditing, and secure defaults.**

# CSDG — Chapter 68

## API Engineering Standards — REST Design, HTTP Methods, Status Codes, DTOs, Pagination, Filtering, Versioning, Idempotency & Error Contracts

### 68.1 Purpose

This chapter defines how Mediverse APIs MUST be designed, implemented, documented, secured, tested, and evolved.

The objective is to ensure that APIs are:

```text
Consistent
Predictable
Secure
Discoverable
Backward-compatible
Observable
Testable
```

Core principle:

> **An API is a contract, not merely a URL that returns JSON. Once consumers depend on it, changing it carelessly becomes a system-wide breaking change.**

---

# 68.2 API Architecture

The standard request flow SHOULD be:

```text
Client
   ↓
API Gateway / Ingress
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Application / Service Layer
   ↓
Domain Logic
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
Database
```

Controllers MUST NOT bypass the application/service layer for business operations.

---

# 68.3 REST Principles

Where REST is selected, APIs SHOULD model resources rather than actions.

Prefer:

```text
GET    /api/v1/courses
GET    /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
POST   /api/v1/courses
PUT    /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
PATCH  /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
DELETE /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
```

Avoid action-heavy designs such as:

```text
POST /api/createCourse
POST /api/getCourse
POST /api/deleteCourse
```

---

# 68.4 Resource Naming

Resource names SHOULD be nouns.

Good:

```text
/courses
/students
/lessons
/quizzes
/submissions
/enrollments
```

Avoid:

```text
/getCourses
/createStudent
/deleteLesson
```

---

# 68.5 Plural Resource Names

Collection resources SHOULD normally use plural nouns:

```text
/courses
/users
/lessons
/quizzes
```

Consistency is more important than personal preference.

---

# 68.6 URL Naming

URLs SHOULD use lowercase characters.

Prefer:

```text
/api/v1/course-progress
```

over:

```text
/api/v1/CourseProgress
```

---

# 68.7 URL Separators

Use hyphens for multi-word resource names where appropriate.

Example:

```text
/course-progress
/quiz-attempts
/learning-paths
```

---

# 68.8 Avoid File Extensions

Do not expose unnecessary extensions:

```text
/courses.json
/courses.xml
```

unless content negotiation explicitly requires them.

---

# 68.9 API Base Path

Mediverse APIs SHOULD use a consistent base namespace.

Example:

```text
/api/v1
```

---

# 68.10 API Versioning

Versioning MUST be planned before the API becomes widely consumed.

Example:

```text
/api/v1/courses
/api/v2/courses
```

---

# 68.11 Versioning Strategy

The project MUST select one primary versioning strategy.

Possible approaches:

```text
URI versioning
Header versioning
Media-type versioning
```

Do not randomly mix strategies across services.

---

# 68.12 Breaking Changes

The following MAY constitute breaking changes:

```text
Removing fields
Renaming fields
Changing field types
Changing required parameters
Changing authentication requirements
Changing semantics
Removing endpoints
Changing error contracts
```

---

# 68.13 Backward Compatibility

When possible, prefer additive API evolution.

Example:

```text
Existing:
{
  "id": 10,
  "title": "Physiology"
}
```

Adding:

```text
"description"
```

is generally safer than renaming:

```text
"title"
```

to:

```text
"name"
```

---

# 68.14 HTTP GET

GET SHOULD retrieve resources.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses/101
```

GET MUST NOT intentionally perform destructive side effects.

---

# 68.15 HTTP POST

POST SHOULD be used for:

```text
Resource creation
Non-idempotent operations
Commands that do not naturally map to replacement/update semantics
```

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/courses
POST /api/v1/quizzes/{quizId}/submissions
```

---

# 68.16 HTTP PUT

PUT SHOULD represent replacement of a resource when the API semantics require full replacement.

Example:

```text
PUT /api/v1/courses/101
```

The exact semantics MUST be documented.

---

# 68.17 HTTP PATCH

PATCH SHOULD be used for partial updates.

Example:

```text
PATCH /api/v1/courses/101
```

Request:

```json
{
  "title": "Advanced Human Physiology"
}
```

---

# 68.18 HTTP DELETE

DELETE SHOULD remove or logically delete a resource according to the system's deletion model.

Example:

```text
DELETE /api/v1/courses/101
```

---

# 68.19 HTTP HEAD

HEAD MAY be supported when clients need metadata without the response body.

---

# 68.20 HTTP OPTIONS

OPTIONS MAY be used for capability discovery and CORS preflight handling.

---

# 68.21 Safe Methods

GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS SHOULD remain safe according to HTTP semantics.

---

# 68.22 Idempotency

An operation is idempotent when repeating the same operation produces the same intended resulting state.

Examples:

```text
PUT
DELETE
```

are generally designed to be idempotent.

POST is generally not inherently idempotent.

---

# 68.23 Idempotency Keys

For important non-idempotent operations, support idempotency keys where duplicate requests could cause serious problems.

Example:

```text
Idempotency-Key: 7b8c...
```

Potential use cases:

```text
Enrollment
Payment
Submission
AI generation request
Bulk operation
```

---

# 68.24 Duplicate Requests

Backend systems MUST assume clients can retry requests.

A timeout does not necessarily mean the server did not process the request.

---

# 68.25 HTTP Status Codes

Use HTTP status codes consistently.

Common mapping:

```text
200 OK
201 Created
202 Accepted
204 No Content
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
422 Unprocessable Content
429 Too Many Requests
500 Internal Server Error
502 Bad Gateway
503 Service Unavailable
504 Gateway Timeout
```

---

# 68.26 200 OK

Use when a request succeeds and a response body is returned.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses/101
```

---

# 68.27 201 Created

Use when a new resource has been successfully created.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/courses
```

Response:

```text
201 Created
```

The response SHOULD provide the created resource or appropriate resource identification.

---

# 68.28 202 Accepted

Use when a request has been accepted for asynchronous processing.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/ai/content-generation
```

when generation occurs asynchronously.

---

# 68.29 204 No Content

Use when the operation succeeds but no response body is required.

Example:

```text
DELETE /api/v1/courses/101
```

---

# 68.30 400 Bad Request

Use for malformed requests or invalid request structure.

Examples:

```text
Malformed JSON
Invalid parameter syntax
Invalid request format
```

---

# 68.31 401 Unauthorized

Use when authentication is missing or invalid.

Important distinction:

```text
401
=
Authentication problem
```

---

# 68.32 403 Forbidden

Use when the requester is authenticated but lacks permission.

```text
403
=
Authorization problem
```

---

# 68.33 404 Not Found

Use when the requested resource does not exist or should not be revealed according to the security model.

---

# 68.34 409 Conflict

Use when the request conflicts with the current resource state.

Examples:

```text
Duplicate enrollment
Duplicate username
Course already published
Conflicting state transition
```

---

# 68.35 422 Unprocessable Content

MAY be used when the request is syntactically valid but violates semantic validation rules.

The project SHOULD standardize whether semantic validation errors use:

```text
400
```

or:

```text
422
```

rather than mixing them inconsistently.

---

# 68.36 429 Too Many Requests

Use when rate limits are exceeded.

---

# 68.37 500 Internal Server Error

Use for unexpected server failures.

Never expose stack traces or internal implementation details.

---

# 68.38 502 Bad Gateway

Use when a gateway/proxy receives an invalid response from an upstream service.

---

# 68.39 503 Service Unavailable

Use when a service is temporarily unable to handle requests.

---

# 68.40 504 Gateway Timeout

Use when an intermediary does not receive a timely upstream response.

---

# 68.41 Response Contract

API responses MUST follow consistent structures.

For example:

```json
{
  "data": {},
  "meta": {},
  "errors": []
}
```

The exact Mediverse response envelope MUST be standardized rather than invented independently by each service.

---

# 68.42 Single Resource Response

Example:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "id": 101,
    "title": "Human Physiology"
  }
}
```

---

# 68.43 Collection Response

Example:

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": 101,
      "title": "Human Physiology"
    },
    {
      "id": 102,
      "title": "Anatomy"
    }
  ],
  "meta": {
    "page": 0,
    "size": 20,
    "totalElements": 2,
    "totalPages": 1
  }
}
```

The exact structure MUST remain consistent across APIs.

---

# 68.44 Error Contract

Errors MUST have a predictable schema.

Example:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "COURSE_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Course was not found.",
    "timestamp": "2026-08-09T10:30:00Z",
    "traceId": "abc-123"
  }
}
```

---

# 68.45 Error Codes

Machine-readable error codes SHOULD be stable.

Example:

```text
COURSE_NOT_FOUND
INVALID_COURSE_STATUS
DUPLICATE_ENROLLMENT
QUIZ_ALREADY_SUBMITTED
ACCESS_DENIED
```

Do not make clients parse human-readable messages to determine behavior.

---

# 68.46 Error Messages

Messages SHOULD be understandable to clients but MUST NOT expose:

```text
Stack traces
SQL queries
Internal class names
Database structure
Secrets
Infrastructure details
```

---

# 68.47 Validation Errors

Validation responses SHOULD identify which fields failed.

Example:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
    "message": "Request validation failed.",
    "fields": [
      {
        "field": "title",
        "message": "Title is required."
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

---

# 68.48 Trace IDs

Responses SHOULD include a trace/correlation identifier when appropriate.

This allows:

```text
Client error
    ↓
traceId
    ↓
API logs
    ↓
Service logs
    ↓
Database / downstream traces
```

---

# 68.49 DTOs

API contracts MUST use DTOs rather than exposing persistence entities directly.

Example:

```text
CourseEntity
      ↓
CourseResponse
```

---

# 68.50 Request DTOs

Create/update requests SHOULD use dedicated DTOs.

Examples:

```text
CreateCourseRequest
UpdateCourseRequest
PublishCourseRequest
```

---

# 68.51 Response DTOs

Responses SHOULD expose only the fields required by consumers.

Do not return entire entities merely because serialization makes it convenient.

---

# 68.52 Sensitive Fields

Sensitive internal fields MUST never accidentally appear in API responses.

Examples:

```text
passwordHash
internalToken
securityMetadata
internalAuditFields
```

---

# 68.53 DTO Naming

Use descriptive names.

Good:

```text
CourseResponse
CourseSummaryResponse
CreateCourseRequest
UpdateCourseRequest
```

Avoid:

```text
CourseDTO1
CourseData
CommonResponse
```

when those names provide no useful semantic distinction.

---

# 68.54 Nested DTOs

Nested DTOs MAY be used when they clearly represent the response contract.

Avoid enormous deeply nested response objects.

---

# 68.55 API Payload Size

Responses SHOULD contain only necessary data.

Large responses increase:

```text
Latency
Memory consumption
Network usage
Frontend processing
```

---

# 68.56 N+1 API Calls

Avoid APIs that force clients to perform excessive sequential calls.

Bad:

```text
GET /courses
GET /course/1
GET /course/2
GET /course/3
...
```

when the use case clearly requires a summarized collection response.

---

# 68.57 Batching

Where appropriate, provide batch APIs.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/progress/batch
```

instead of hundreds of individual calls.

Batch APIs MUST still have controlled limits.

---

# 68.58 Pagination

Collection endpoints that can grow significantly MUST support pagination.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?page=0&size=20
```

---

# 68.59 Pagination Defaults

APIs SHOULD define safe defaults.

Do not allow:

```text
size=1000000
```

to trigger an uncontrolled database query.

---

# 68.60 Maximum Page Size

Every paginated endpoint SHOULD define a maximum allowed page size.

Example:

```text
default = 20
maximum = 100
```

The actual limits MUST be based on workload requirements.

---

# 68.61 Pagination Metadata

Paginated responses SHOULD expose enough metadata for clients to navigate results.

Example:

```text
page
size
totalElements
totalPages
```

---

# 68.62 Cursor Pagination

Cursor-based pagination SHOULD be considered for:

```text
Very large datasets
High-frequency feeds
Time-ordered events
Real-time activity
```

---

# 68.63 Offset Pagination

Offset pagination is suitable for many ordinary administrative and educational datasets.

---

# 68.64 Sorting

Sorting parameters MUST be validated against an allowlist.

Do not blindly convert user-provided strings into arbitrary SQL ordering clauses.

Example:

```text
?sort=title
?sort=createdAt
```

---

# 68.65 Filtering

Filtering SHOULD use predictable query parameters.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?status=PUBLISHED
```

---

# 68.66 Search

Search parameters SHOULD be clearly distinguished from filters.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?search=physiology
```

---

# 68.67 Filtering Combinations

The API SHOULD document how filters combine:

```text
AND
OR
```

Do not make clients guess.

---

# 68.68 Date Filtering

Date filters SHOULD use standardized ISO-8601 representations.

Example:

```text
?from=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
&to=2026-02-01T00:00:00Z
```

---

# 68.69 Enum Parameters

Enums SHOULD be validated.

Example:

```text
status=PUBLISHED
```

should reject unknown values rather than silently interpreting them incorrectly.

---

# 68.70 Field Selection

Field-selection APIs MAY be introduced for large payloads.

Example:

```text
?fields=id,title,status
```

Only introduce this complexity when there is a real need.

---

# 68.71 Expansion

Nested resource expansion MAY be supported where useful.

Example:

```text
?include=lessons
```

It MUST be controlled to prevent huge payloads.

---

# 68.72 Resource Relationships

Related resources SHOULD be represented consistently.

Example:

```text
GET /courses/{courseId}/lessons
```

may be appropriate when lessons are strongly scoped to a course.

---

# 68.73 Nested Resource Depth

Avoid excessively deep URLs.

Bad:

```text
/courses/1/modules/2/lessons/3/topics/4/questions/5
```

unless the hierarchy genuinely requires this representation.

---

# 68.74 Resource Ownership

Where resources belong to users, the API SHOULD make ownership semantics clear.

Example:

```text
/users/{userId}/progress
```

or:

```text
/me/progress
```

---

# 68.75 `/me`

A `/me` endpoint MAY be used for current-user operations.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/me
GET /api/v1/me/progress
GET /api/v1/me/enrollments
```

---

# 68.76 HTTP Headers

Security and tracing headers SHOULD follow standardized conventions.

Examples:

```text
Authorization
Content-Type
Accept
Traceparent
X-Request-ID
```

The project SHOULD avoid inventing unnecessary custom headers.

---

# 68.77 Content-Type

Request and response content types MUST be explicit.

Typical JSON API:

```text
Content-Type: application/json
```

---

# 68.78 Accept Header

Clients MAY specify expected response representations through `Accept`.

---

# 68.79 JSON Naming Convention

The project MUST choose a consistent JSON naming convention.

Example:

```json
{
  "courseId": 101,
  "createdAt": "..."
}
```

Do not mix:

```text
camelCase
snake_case
PascalCase
```

randomly.

---

# 68.80 Null Handling

API contracts MUST define how null values are handled.

Do not allow every endpoint to make independent decisions.

---

# 68.81 Empty Collections

Collection responses SHOULD return:

```json
[]
```

rather than:

```json
null
```

when no items exist.

---

# 68.82 Dates

Dates and timestamps SHOULD use ISO-8601 formats.

Example:

```text
2026-08-09T10:30:00Z
```

---

# 68.83 Time Zone

API timestamps SHOULD use UTC unless the contract explicitly requires another representation.

---

# 68.84 Large Numbers

APIs MUST consider whether numeric identifiers or values can exceed JavaScript's safe integer range when consumed by browser clients.

---

# 68.85 File APIs

File upload endpoints SHOULD define:

```text
Maximum size
Allowed types
Authentication
Authorization
Virus/malware scanning requirements
Storage behavior
Error responses
```

---

# 68.86 Multipart APIs

Multipart requests MUST document:

```text
File field
Metadata fields
Allowed MIME types
Maximum size
```

---

# 68.87 Download APIs

Downloads SHOULD correctly set:

```text
Content-Type
Content-Disposition
Cache-Control
```

according to the resource sensitivity.

---

# 68.88 Streaming

Streaming SHOULD be used where payload size or real-time requirements justify it.

Do not load extremely large resources completely into application memory.

---

# 68.89 Long-Running APIs

Long-running operations SHOULD NOT hold HTTP connections unnecessarily.

Prefer:

```text
POST
 ↓
202 Accepted
 ↓
jobId
 ↓
GET /jobs/{jobId}
```

when appropriate.

---

# 68.90 Async Job Response

Example:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "jobId": "job-123",
    "status": "PROCESSING"
  }
}
```

---

# 68.91 API Timeouts

Every downstream API call MUST have explicit timeout behavior.

Never allow external calls to hang indefinitely.

---

# 68.92 Retry Behavior

API clients MAY retry transient failures.

Retries MUST use:

```text
Bounded attempts
Backoff
Jitter
Idempotency awareness
```

---

# 68.93 API Gateway Timeout

Gateway and service timeout values MUST be compatible.

Avoid:

```text
Gateway timeout = 30s
Service timeout = 120s
```

if the service cannot possibly return before the gateway terminates the request.

---

# 68.94 API Contract Testing

Important APIs SHOULD have contract tests.

Contract testing helps verify:

```text
Producer
    ↕
Consumer
```

remain compatible.

---

# 68.95 OpenAPI

All public APIs SHOULD be described through OpenAPI.

The specification SHOULD define:

```text
Paths
Parameters
Request bodies
Responses
Schemas
Security requirements
Errors
Examples
```

---

# 68.96 OpenAPI Accuracy

OpenAPI MUST reflect actual runtime behavior.

A beautiful but inaccurate OpenAPI specification is worse than incomplete documentation because it creates false expectations.

---

# 68.97 API Examples

Important endpoints SHOULD contain realistic request/response examples.

---

# 68.98 API Deprecation

Deprecated endpoints MUST be explicitly marked.

Deprecation SHOULD include:

```text
Replacement endpoint
Migration guidance
Expected removal date
```

where applicable.

---

# 68.99 API Sunset

Before removing an API version:

```text
Announce
 ↓
Measure consumers
 ↓
Provide migration path
 ↓
Deprecate
 ↓
Monitor usage
 ↓
Remove
```

---

# 68.100 API Observability

Every important API SHOULD expose:

```text
Request count
Error count
Latency
Status-code distribution
```

and appropriate tracing.

---

# 68.101 API Metrics

Useful metrics include:

```text
HTTP request rate
P50 latency
P95 latency
P99 latency
4xx rate
5xx rate
Timeout rate
Rate-limit count
```

---

# 68.102 API Logging

Logs SHOULD include:

```text
Method
Route
Status
Latency
Trace ID
Request ID
Authenticated principal where appropriate
```

Never log sensitive payloads indiscriminately.

---

# 68.103 API Security

Every endpoint MUST answer:

```text
Who can call it?
What can they access?
What can they modify?
What happens if they modify IDs?
What happens if they repeat the request?
What happens if authentication expires?
```

---

# 68.104 API Performance

Performance requirements SHOULD be defined for important endpoints.

Example:

```text
Course listing:
P95 < agreed threshold
```

The actual SLA/SLO MUST be determined from system requirements rather than arbitrary numbers.

---

# 68.105 Database Protection

APIs MUST prevent users from indirectly forcing uncontrolled database operations.

Examples:

```text
Huge page size
Unrestricted sorting
Unbounded search
Expensive filters
Mass export
```

---

# 68.106 Bulk Operations

Bulk endpoints MUST impose safe limits.

Example:

```text
POST /courses/bulk-import
```

should define:

```text
Maximum records
Maximum file size
Processing timeout
Failure behavior
```

---

# 68.107 Partial Failure

Bulk APIs MUST define what happens when some records fail.

Possible models:

```text
All-or-nothing
Partial success
Asynchronous processing
```

The behavior MUST be documented.

---

# 68.108 API Transactions

If an API performs multiple database operations that must succeed or fail together, transaction boundaries MUST be explicitly defined.

---

# 68.109 API Concurrency

APIs modifying shared resources SHOULD consider concurrent updates.

Example:

```text
Teacher A
 ↓
updates course

Teacher B
 ↓
updates same course
```

Potential solutions:

```text
Optimistic locking
Version fields
Conflict detection
```

---

# 68.110 Optimistic Locking

For resources with concurrent modification risk, versioning MAY be used.

Example:

```text
version: 7
```

If the client submits an outdated version:

```text
409 Conflict
```

may be appropriate.

---

# 68.111 API Caching

Cache behavior MUST be explicit.

For public/read-heavy resources, appropriate HTTP caching MAY be used.

Sensitive personalized responses require careful cache controls.

---

# 68.112 Cache-Control

Responses containing private user information SHOULD prevent unintended shared caching.

---

# 68.113 ETags

ETags MAY be used for:

```text
Conditional requests
Optimistic concurrency
Bandwidth optimization
```

---

# 68.114 API Security Headers

Production APIs SHOULD apply appropriate security controls at gateway/service boundaries.

---

# 68.115 API Contract Ownership

Every important API MUST have an owning team/service.

Ownership SHOULD define:

```text
Business owner
Technical owner
Documentation owner
Support responsibility
```

---

# 68.116 API Change Review

API changes MUST be reviewed for:

```text
Backward compatibility
Security
Performance
Database impact
Consumer impact
Documentation
Testing
Observability
```

---

# 68.117 API Naming Consistency

The same domain concept MUST use the same name across APIs.

Do not call the same concept:

```text
studentId
learnerId
userId
candidateId
```

in unrelated endpoints unless these represent genuinely different concepts.

---

# 68.118 Domain Terminology

Mediverse API terminology SHOULD follow the approved domain glossary.

Example:

```text
Student
Course
Module
Lesson
Quiz
Question
Attempt
Submission
Progress
Enrollment
```

---

# 68.119 API Anti-Patterns

The following SHOULD be rejected during review:

```text
POST for every operation
```

```text
Entities returned directly
```

```text
Inconsistent error structures
```

```text
Unbounded collection queries
```

```text
Missing authorization checks
```

```text
Business logic in controllers
```

```text
Stack traces returned to clients
```

```text
Arbitrary SQL sort parameters
```

```text
Inconsistent naming
```

```text
Breaking changes without versioning
```

---

# 68.120 Definition of Done

An API endpoint is production-ready when:

* [ ] Resource/action semantics are clear
* [ ] HTTP method is appropriate
* [ ] URL follows naming conventions
* [ ] Authentication is defined
* [ ] Authorization is defined
* [ ] Object-level authorization is verified
* [ ] Request DTO exists
* [ ] Response DTO exists
* [ ] Validation exists
* [ ] Error contract is implemented
* [ ] Correct HTTP status codes are used
* [ ] Pagination exists where required
* [ ] Filtering/sorting is safely implemented
* [ ] Maximum request size is defined
* [ ] Idempotency is considered
* [ ] Concurrency is considered
* [ ] API documentation exists
* [ ] OpenAPI is updated
* [ ] Tests exist
* [ ] Security tests exist
* [ ] Logging/traceability exists
* [ ] Metrics exist where appropriate
* [ ] Performance characteristics are understood
* [ ] Backward compatibility has been reviewed

---

# 68.121 Core Principles

1. **APIs are contracts.**
2. **Use resources and HTTP semantics consistently.**
3. **Do not use POST for everything.**
4. **Never expose JPA entities directly.**
5. **Use stable machine-readable error codes.**
6. **Never make clients parse human-readable error messages.**
7. **Every collection endpoint needs a scalability strategy.**
8. **Never allow unbounded queries.**
9. **Validate sorting and filtering parameters.**
10. **Every endpoint requires explicit authorization reasoning.**
11. **Design for retries and duplicate requests.**
12. **Use idempotency mechanisms where duplicate side effects matter.**
13. **Version breaking API changes.**
14. **Document actual behavior, not intended behavior.**
15. **Measure API performance using real metrics.**
16. **Treat API security and API design as inseparable.**
17. **Consistency across Mediverse APIs is more valuable than individual developer preference.**

> **For Mediverse, API consistency will become increasingly important as the platform grows into multiple modules and potentially multiple services. A student-facing frontend, teacher portal, admin portal, mobile client, AI services, notification services, and analytics systems cannot safely depend on APIs whose conventions change from one service to another. The API contract must therefore be treated as a first-class product artifact.**
