Avoid unnecessarily RPC-style endpoints such as:

```http
POST /api/createCourse
POST /api/getCourse
POST /api/deleteCourse
```

---

# 72.4 Endpoint Naming

Resource names SHOULD generally be plural nouns.

Good:

```text
/courses
/students
/lessons
/quizzes
/enrollments
```

Avoid:

```text
/course
/getCourses
/createLesson
```

---

# 72.5 URL Naming

URLs SHOULD use lowercase naming.

Prefer:

```text
/api/v1/course-progress
```

rather than:

```text
/api/v1/courseProgress
/api/v1/CourseProgress
```

---

# 72.6 URL Structure

A typical Mediverse API structure SHOULD follow:

```text
/api/v1/{resource}
```

Example:

```text
/api/v1/courses
/api/v1/lessons
/api/v1/quizzes
/api/v1/progress
```

---

# 72.7 API Versioning

Production APIs SHOULD be versioned.

Example:

```text
/api/v1/courses
/api/v2/courses
```

Versioning strategy MUST be consistent across the platform.

---

# 72.8 Versioning Principle

Do not create a new API version for every small change.

A new version should generally be considered when backward compatibility cannot reasonably be preserved.

---

# 72.9 Backward Compatibility

Existing consumers SHOULD NOT break unexpectedly.

Potential breaking changes include:

```text
Removing fields
Renaming fields
Changing field types
Changing required fields
Changing response structure
Changing authentication requirements
Changing HTTP semantics
```

---

# 72.10 HTTP Methods

Use HTTP methods according to their intended semantics.

```text
GET
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE
```

---

# 72.11 GET

`GET` MUST be used for retrieval.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses/101
```

GET requests SHOULD NOT modify server state.

---

# 72.12 POST

`POST` SHOULD be used for:

```text
Resource creation
Non-idempotent operations
Operations where the server determines the resulting resource
```

Example:

```http
POST /api/v1/courses
```

---

# 72.13 PUT

`PUT` SHOULD represent replacement semantics where appropriate.

Example:

```http
PUT /api/v1/courses/101
```

The API contract MUST clearly define whether omitted fields are replaced, rejected, or otherwise handled.

---

# 72.14 PATCH

`PATCH` SHOULD be used for partial updates.

Example:

```http
PATCH /api/v1/users/101
```

---

# 72.15 DELETE

`DELETE` SHOULD remove or logically deactivate a resource according to the domain model.

Example:

```http
DELETE /api/v1/courses/101
```

---

# 72.16 Idempotency

API operations MUST clearly define idempotency behavior.

`GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` SHOULD generally be idempotent.

`POST` is not inherently idempotent.

---

# 72.17 Idempotency Keys

For operations where duplicate requests could create serious problems, idempotency keys SHOULD be considered.

Potential examples:

```text
Enrollment
Payment
Certificate generation
Important submission operations
```

---

# 72.18 HTTP Status Codes

APIs MUST use meaningful HTTP status codes.

Common examples:

```text
200 OK
201 Created
202 Accepted
204 No Content
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
422 Unprocessable Entity
429 Too Many Requests
500 Internal Server Error
503 Service Unavailable
```

Only statuses appropriate to the actual API contract should be used.

---

# 72.19 `401 Unauthorized`

`401` SHOULD indicate that authentication is missing or invalid.

Example:

```text
No valid authentication credentials.
```

---

# 72.20 `403 Forbidden`

`403` SHOULD indicate that the user is authenticated but does not have permission to perform the requested operation.

---

# 72.21 `404 Not Found`

Use `404` when the requested resource does not exist or when the API contract intentionally hides resource existence.

---

# 72.22 `409 Conflict`

`409` SHOULD be considered for domain conflicts.

Examples:

```text
Duplicate enrollment
Duplicate resource
Invalid state transition
Concurrent update conflict
```

---

# 72.23 Validation Errors

Validation failures MUST return a consistent structure.

Example:

```json
{
  "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
  "message": "Request validation failed",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "message": "Title is required"
    }
  ]
}
```

The exact structure MUST be standardized across Mediverse APIs.

---

# 72.24 Error Response Contract

Error responses SHOULD contain machine-readable information.

Recommended conceptual structure:

```text
code
message
details/errors
timestamp
requestId
path
```

Do not expose internal stack traces.

---

# 72.25 Error Codes

Business/API errors SHOULD have stable machine-readable codes.

Example:

```text
COURSE_NOT_FOUND
DUPLICATE_ENROLLMENT
QUIZ_ATTEMPT_EXPIRED
INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSION
VALIDATION_ERROR
```

Frontend applications SHOULD rely on error codes rather than parsing human-readable messages.

---

# 72.26 Human-Readable Messages

Messages SHOULD be understandable to developers/operators.

They SHOULD NOT contain:

```text
Database stack traces
SQL queries
Internal class names
Server filesystem paths
Secrets
Tokens
```

---

# 72.27 DTOs

Controllers SHOULD expose DTOs rather than directly exposing persistence entities.

Example:

```text
CourseEntity
      ↓
CourseResponse
```

---

# 72.28 Why DTOs

DTOs provide protection against:

```text
Database schema leakage
Accidental field exposure
Over-posting
Unstable API contracts
Entity serialization problems
```

---

# 72.29 Request DTOs

Input requests SHOULD use dedicated request DTOs.

Example:

```text
CreateCourseRequest
UpdateCourseRequest
CreateLessonRequest
SubmitQuizRequest
```

---

# 72.30 Response DTOs

Responses SHOULD use explicit response models.

Example:

```text
CourseResponse
LessonResponse
QuizResultResponse
ProgressResponse
```

---

# 72.31 Entity Exposure

JPA entities MUST NOT be casually returned directly from controllers.

Avoid:

```java
return courseRepository.findById(id).get();
```

as the public API contract.

---

# 72.32 DTO Mapping

Mapping SHOULD happen through a consistent mechanism.

Depending on project needs:

```text
Manual mapper
MapStruct
Dedicated mapper classes
```

---

# 72.33 DTO Naming

Recommended:

```text
CreateCourseRequest
UpdateCourseRequest
CourseResponse
CourseSummaryResponse
```

Avoid ambiguous names such as:

```text
CourseDTO
CourseData
CourseObject
```

when multiple DTO types exist.

---

# 72.34 Request Validation

Incoming requests MUST be validated at the API boundary.

Examples:

```text
@NotNull
@NotBlank
@Size
@Email
@Positive
@Min
@Max
```

where appropriate.

---

# 72.35 Business Validation

Bean validation is not sufficient for all business rules.

Example:

```text
Course must contain at least one lesson before publication.
```

This belongs to business/service validation.

---

# 72.36 Validation Layers

Use:

```text
Request validation
       ↓
Business validation
       ↓
Persistence constraints
```

All three serve different purposes.

---

# 72.37 Pagination

Collection endpoints SHOULD support pagination when datasets can become large.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?page=0&size=20
```

---

# 72.38 Pagination Response

A standardized pagination structure SHOULD be used.

Example:

```json
{
  "content": [],
  "page": 0,
  "size": 20,
  "totalElements": 245,
  "totalPages": 13
}
```

The actual project contract MAY differ, but it MUST remain consistent.

---

# 72.39 Maximum Page Size

APIs MUST enforce a maximum page size.

Do not allow:

```text
?page=0&size=1000000
```

to trigger uncontrolled database retrieval.

---

# 72.40 Sorting

Collection APIs MAY support sorting.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?sort=createdAt,desc
```

Allowed sort fields SHOULD be explicitly controlled.

Do not allow arbitrary SQL fragments through query parameters.

---

# 72.41 Filtering

Filtering SHOULD use predictable query parameters.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses?status=PUBLISHED&category=PHYSIOLOGY
```

---

# 72.42 Search

Search APIs SHOULD define:

```text
Search fields
Case sensitivity
Pagination
Sorting
Minimum query length
Special characters
```

---

# 72.43 Search Input

Search input MUST be validated and safely parameterized.

Never concatenate user input directly into SQL.

---

# 72.44 Nested Resources

Nested resources SHOULD be used when the relationship is meaningful and bounded.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/courses/{courseId}/lessons
```

---

# 72.45 Excessive Nesting

Avoid deeply nested URLs.

Bad:

```text
/courses/{courseId}/modules/{moduleId}/lessons/{lessonId}/questions/{questionId}
```

when the resource can be addressed more simply.

---

# 72.46 Resource Identity

Every resource MUST have a stable identifier.

Example:

```text
courseId
lessonId
quizId
userId
```

---

# 72.47 IDs

The identifier strategy MUST be consistent.

Possible approaches:

```text
UUID
Long
String identifier
```

The project MUST avoid arbitrary mixing unless there is a clear domain reason.

---

# 72.48 UUIDs

UUIDs MAY be preferred where external exposure of sequential identifiers is undesirable.

The choice MUST consider:

```text
Database performance
Index size
Debugging
Distributed systems
Security
```

---

# 72.49 Date and Time

API date/time formats MUST be standardized.

ISO 8601 SHOULD be preferred.

Example:

```text
2026-08-09T10:30:00Z
```

---

# 72.50 Time Zones

Server-side APIs SHOULD store timestamps in a consistent timezone strategy, generally UTC.

User-facing timezone conversion SHOULD happen at the presentation boundary where appropriate.

---

# 72.51 Boolean Fields

Boolean fields SHOULD have clear names.

Good:

```text
isPublished
isActive
hasCertificate
```

Avoid ambiguous fields such as:

```text
statusFlag
enabledValue
```

unless they have a documented meaning.

---

# 72.52 Enum Values

Enum values exposed through APIs SHOULD be stable and documented.

Example:

```text
DRAFT
PUBLISHED
ARCHIVED
```

Do not casually rename enum values because frontend clients may depend on them.

---

# 72.53 Null Handling

The API contract MUST define whether fields can be:

```text
null
missing
empty
```

These are not automatically equivalent.

---

# 72.54 Optional Fields

Optional request fields SHOULD have explicit semantics.

For example:

```text
missing → leave unchanged
null → clear value
```

if PATCH semantics require that distinction.

---

# 72.55 Response Consistency

Similar endpoints SHOULD return similarly structured responses.

Do not make one API return:

```json
{
  "data": []
}
```

and another:

```json
{
  "results": []
}
```

without a deliberate contract reason.

---

# 72.56 API Envelope

The project SHOULD decide whether APIs use an envelope such as:

```json
{
  "data": {},
  "meta": {}
}
```

or direct resource responses.

The choice MUST be consistent.

---

# 72.57 API Documentation

Every public/internal application API SHOULD be documented using OpenAPI.

Documentation SHOULD describe:

```text
Endpoint
Method
Parameters
Request body
Response
Status codes
Authentication
Authorization
Validation errors
```

---

# 72.58 OpenAPI

OpenAPI documentation SHOULD be generated from the actual application contract where practical.

Documentation MUST NOT become a manually maintained document that diverges from the implementation.

---

# 72.59 Swagger UI

Swagger UI MAY be exposed in development/UAT.

Production exposure MUST be evaluated from a security perspective.

---

# 72.60 Authentication Documentation

Protected APIs MUST clearly indicate required authentication.

Example:

```text
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

where bearer-token authentication is the approved mechanism.

---

# 72.61 Authorization Documentation

API documentation SHOULD identify role/permission requirements.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/courses
Required role: TEACHER
```

---

# 72.62 API Security

All production APIs MUST use HTTPS.

Never send authentication credentials over plain HTTP in production.

---

# 72.63 Input Sanitization

All external input MUST be considered untrusted.

Validate:

```text
Path variables
Query parameters
Headers where applicable
Request bodies
File metadata
```

---

# 72.64 SQL Injection

Parameterized queries MUST be used.

Never construct SQL by concatenating untrusted user input.

---

# 72.65 Mass Assignment

Request DTOs MUST prevent users from modifying fields they are not authorized to control.

For example, a student request should not be able to submit:

```json
{
  "role": "ADMIN"
}
```

and have the backend blindly persist it.

---

# 72.66 Object-Level Authorization

Every resource access MUST verify that the authenticated user has permission to access that resource.

Do not assume:

```text
authenticated = authorized
```

---

# 72.67 File Upload APIs

File-upload endpoints MUST define:

```text
Allowed MIME types
Maximum file size
Filename rules
Storage strategy
Virus/malware scanning where required
Authorization
Content validation
```

---

# 72.68 File Download APIs

Download endpoints MUST verify authorization before returning protected educational assets.

---

# 72.69 Media URLs

Do not expose internal storage paths unnecessarily.

Prefer controlled URLs or signed URLs where appropriate.

---

# 72.70 Rate Limiting

Sensitive and expensive APIs SHOULD have rate limiting.

Candidates include:

```text
Login
Password reset
Search
Quiz submission
File upload
AI-assisted features
```

---

# 72.71 Authentication Rate Limiting

Authentication endpoints MUST be protected against brute-force abuse.

---

# 72.72 Request Size Limits

APIs MUST enforce request-size limits.

This is especially important for:

```text
File uploads
Rich text
Bulk imports
Large JSON requests
```

---

# 72.73 Timeout Handling

External service calls MUST have explicit timeouts.

Never allow a request to wait indefinitely for:

```text
AI service
Email service
Storage service
External API
```

---

# 72.74 External API Failures

External failures SHOULD be translated into controlled application behavior.

Do not expose raw external service errors directly to clients.

---

# 72.75 Retry Strategy

Retries SHOULD only be used for failures that are safe to retry.

Avoid blindly retrying non-idempotent operations.

---

# 72.76 Circuit Breaking

For important external dependencies, circuit breaking MAY be used.

Example:

```text
Mediverse
    ↓
External AI Service
    ↓
Failure
    ↓
Circuit Open
    ↓
Fast controlled failure
```

---

# 72.77 Asynchronous Operations

Long-running operations SHOULD NOT block synchronous HTTP requests unnecessarily.

Examples:

```text
Video processing
Large file processing
Certificate generation
Bulk imports
Complex analytics
AI content generation
```

These MAY use:

```text
Queue
Event
Background worker
Job
```

---

# 72.78 `202 Accepted`

`202 Accepted` MAY be used when a request has been accepted for asynchronous processing.

Example:

```http
POST /api/v1/certificates/generate
```

Response:

```json
{
  "jobId": "..."
}
```

---

# 72.79 Job Status

Long-running jobs SHOULD expose controlled status tracking where required.

Example:

```http
GET /api/v1/jobs/{jobId}
```

---

# 72.80 API Transactions

Business operations requiring atomicity MUST use appropriate transaction boundaries.

Example:

```text
Quiz submission
 ↓
Save attempt
 ↓
Calculate score
 ↓
Update progress
```

If these operations must be atomic, they should be handled within an appropriate transactional boundary.

---

# 72.81 Partial Failure

APIs MUST define behavior when multi-step operations partially fail.

Do not leave ambiguous states such as:

```text
Quiz submitted
but
Progress not updated
```

without a defined recovery strategy.

---

# 72.82 Concurrency

APIs modifying shared resources SHOULD consider concurrent requests.

Potential strategies:

```text
Optimistic locking
Pessimistic locking
Idempotency
Unique constraints
Version fields
```

---

# 72.83 Optimistic Locking

Where appropriate, entities MAY use version-based concurrency control.

This is particularly relevant to:

```text
Course editing
Content editing
Administrative configuration
```

---

# 72.84 Duplicate Requests

Critical operations SHOULD be protected from accidental duplicate requests.

Example:

```text
Student clicks "Submit Quiz"
        ↓
Network delay
        ↓
Student clicks again
```

The backend must safely handle this scenario according to the operation's semantics.

---

# 72.85 Bulk APIs

Bulk APIs SHOULD only be introduced when they solve a real performance or workflow problem.

They MUST define:

```text
Maximum batch size
Partial failure behavior
Validation
Authorization
Transaction behavior
```

---

# 72.86 Bulk Error Handling

If some records succeed and others fail, the API MUST clearly communicate the result.

---

# 72.87 API Logging

Important API requests SHOULD produce structured logs.

Logs SHOULD contain identifiers such as:

```text
requestId
userId where appropriate
endpoint
HTTP method
status
duration
```

Avoid logging sensitive request bodies indiscriminately.

---

# 72.88 Correlation IDs

Distributed requests SHOULD support correlation/request IDs.

Example:

```text
Frontend
 ↓ requestId
API Gateway
 ↓
Course Service
 ↓
Database
```

This allows troubleshooting across system boundaries.

---

# 72.89 Sensitive Logging

Never log:

```text
Passwords
JWTs
Refresh tokens
API secrets
Private keys
Sensitive personal data
```

unless there is an exceptional, approved security/debugging mechanism.

---

# 72.90 API Metrics

Production APIs SHOULD expose metrics such as:

```text
Request count
Error count
Latency
Throughput
Status-code distribution
```

---

# 72.91 Health APIs

Health endpoints SHOULD distinguish between:

```text
Liveness
Readiness
```

where the deployment platform requires them.

---

# 72.92 Health Endpoint Security

Detailed infrastructure information SHOULD NOT be unnecessarily exposed publicly.

---

# 72.93 API Deprecation

Deprecated APIs MUST be clearly documented.

A deprecation strategy SHOULD define:

```text
Deprecated date
Replacement API
Migration guidance
Removal timeline
```

---

# 72.94 Breaking Changes

Breaking API changes SHOULD be introduced through:

```text
Versioning
Migration period
Compatibility layer
```

where appropriate.

---

# 72.95 API Consumer Communication

Changes affecting frontend or other consumers SHOULD be communicated through:

```text
API documentation
Release notes
Migration guides
Pull request documentation
```

---

# 72.96 Frontend Integration

Frontend services SHOULD map closely to API resources.

Example:

```text
courseService
quizService
progressService
enrollmentService
```

---

# 72.97 Frontend API Types

Frontend request/response types SHOULD be derived from or aligned with the backend API specification where practical.

---

# 72.98 Generated API Clients

For sufficiently large APIs, generated clients MAY be used.

The project SHOULD avoid manually duplicating hundreds of API contracts when code generation provides meaningful reliability benefits.

---

# 72.99 API Mocking

Frontend development SHOULD support API mocking where useful.

This allows UI development without requiring every backend service to be running.

---

# 72.100 API Contract Testing

Frontend and backend CI SHOULD detect incompatible contract changes before deployment.

---

# 72.101 API Documentation Quality

An endpoint is not considered complete if:

```text
Implementation exists
```

but:

```text
Contract is undocumented
```

Documentation is part of API implementation.

---

# 72.102 Definition of Done

An API feature is complete when:

* [ ] Endpoint follows REST conventions
* [ ] Resource naming is consistent
* [ ] HTTP method is appropriate
* [ ] HTTP status codes are defined
* [ ] Request DTO exists
* [ ] Response DTO exists
* [ ] Validation exists
* [ ] Authorization exists
* [ ] Error contract is defined
* [ ] Pagination exists where required
* [ ] Sorting/filtering are controlled
* [ ] API documentation exists
* [ ] OpenAPI is updated
* [ ] Unit tests exist
* [ ] Integration/API tests exist
* [ ] Security tests exist where required
* [ ] Rate limiting is considered
* [ ] Logging/metrics are considered
* [ ] Backward compatibility is considered
* [ ] Frontend integration is verified
* [ ] CI passes

---

# 72.103 Core Principles

1. **APIs are contracts, not implementation details.**
2. **Design around resources and business capabilities.**
3. **Use HTTP semantics correctly.**
4. **Keep controllers thin.**
5. **Never expose persistence entities directly as public contracts.**
6. **Validate all external input.**
7. **Authorization must happen server-side.**
8. **Pagination is mandatory for potentially large collections.**
9. **Error responses must be predictable and machine-readable.**
10. **API changes must consider backward compatibility.**
11. **Critical operations must consider idempotency and concurrency.**
12. **External dependencies require timeouts and controlled failure behavior.**
13. **Sensitive information must never leak through API responses or logs.**
14. **OpenAPI documentation is part of the API implementation.**
15. **Frontend and backend must evolve against an explicit API contract.**

> **For Mediverse, API design becomes particularly important because the platform will eventually support Student, Teacher, Admin, content-management, quiz, progress, multimedia, notification, analytics, and potentially AI capabilities. A poorly designed API will create coupling across all of these areas. The API contract must therefore be treated as a first-class architectural boundary rather than as a thin layer over Spring Boot controllers.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 73: Database Coding & Data Access Standards — PostgreSQL, JPA/Hibernate, entities, relationships, repositories, transactions, migrations, indexing, query optimization, locking, auditing, soft delete and data integrity.**

# CSDG — Chapter 73

## Database Coding & Data Access Standards

### 73.1 Purpose

This chapter defines database and data-access standards for Mediverse.

The objective is to ensure that persistence code remains:

```text
Consistent
Reliable
Performant
Transaction-safe
Secure
Maintainable
Auditable
Scalable
```

Core principle:

> **The database is part of the application's architecture, not merely a storage layer. Data integrity must be protected at the database, application, and transaction boundaries.**

---

# 73.2 Approved Database

Mediverse SHOULD use **PostgreSQL** as the primary relational database.

The application MUST NOT depend on database-specific behavior without documenting the dependency.

---

# 73.3 Database Responsibilities

The database SHOULD be responsible for enforcing structural integrity such as:

```text
Primary keys
Foreign keys
Unique constraints
Not-null constraints
Check constraints
Indexes
```

Business workflows SHOULD remain primarily in the application/domain layer.

---

# 73.4 Database Naming

Database naming MUST follow one consistent convention.

Recommended:

```text
snake_case
```

Examples:

```text
users
course_modules
quiz_questions
student_progress
created_at
updated_at
```

Avoid mixing:

```text
camelCase
PascalCase
snake_case
```

within the same schema.

---

# 73.5 Table Naming

Tables SHOULD generally use plural nouns.

Good:

```text
users
courses
lessons
quizzes
enrollments
```

---

# 73.6 Column Naming

Columns SHOULD use descriptive names.

Good:

```text
created_at
published_at
course_id
student_id
is_active
```

Avoid vague names:

```text
value
data
info
flag
type
```

unless their meaning is unambiguous.

---

# 73.7 Primary Keys

Every persistent entity MUST have a stable primary key.

---

# 73.8 Primary Key Strategy

The project MUST establish a consistent identifier strategy.

Possible strategies include:

```text
BIGINT
UUID
```

The decision SHOULD consider:

```text
Database performance
Distributed architecture
Security
Index size
External exposure
Operational simplicity
```

---

# 73.9 Foreign Keys

Relationships between persistent records SHOULD use foreign keys unless there is a deliberate architectural reason not to.

Example:

```text id="n2d0j3"
courses
   ↑
course_modules
   ↑
lessons
```

---

# 73.10 Referential Integrity

The database MUST prevent invalid relationships where appropriate.

Example:

A lesson referencing a nonexistent course SHOULD NOT be possible.

---

# 73.11 Unique Constraints

Uniqueness requirements SHOULD be enforced at the database level.

Example:

```text id="7ce5rj"
A student cannot have duplicate enrollment
```

A unique constraint SHOULD support this requirement rather than relying only on application checks.

---

# 73.12 Application + Database Validation

Important constraints SHOULD be enforced at both levels when appropriate.

```text id="j1l6wq"
Application
   ↓
Friendly validation
   ↓
Database
   ↓
Final integrity protection
```

---

# 73.13 NOT NULL

Columns that are logically mandatory SHOULD use `NOT NULL`.

Do not allow nullable columns merely because it is convenient for the ORM.

---

# 73.14 Default Values

Database defaults SHOULD be used for appropriate infrastructure fields.

Examples:

```text id="lq8v9h"
created_at
updated_at
is_active
```

But defaults MUST be documented when their behavior affects application semantics.

---

# 73.15 Boolean Columns

Boolean fields SHOULD use clear names.

Examples:

```text id="f4g9xn"
is_active
is_published
is_deleted
```

---

# 73.16 Timestamp Columns

Important entities SHOULD generally contain:

```text id="f7z1js"
created_at
updated_at
```

where auditability requires them.

---

# 73.17 Time Zone

Timestamps SHOULD follow a consistent UTC-based strategy.

The application SHOULD convert timestamps to the user's timezone only at the presentation boundary.

---

# 73.18 JPA Entities

Spring Data JPA/Hibernate MAY be used as the primary persistence framework.

Entities MUST represent persistence concerns clearly.

Do not turn entities into massive objects containing unrelated application behavior.

---

# 73.19 Entity Naming

Entity classes SHOULD use singular domain names.

Example:

```java id="3g3aq1"
User
Course
Lesson
Quiz
Enrollment
Progress
```

---

# 73.20 Entity-to-Table Mapping

Explicit mapping SHOULD be used where naming conventions could create ambiguity.

Example:

```java id="f5x0s4"
@Entity
@Table(name = "courses")
public class Course {
}
```

---

# 73.21 Entity Exposure

JPA entities MUST NOT be directly exposed through REST APIs.

Use DTOs.

```text id="vmyh0x"
Entity
 ↓
Mapper
 ↓
Response DTO
 ↓
API
```

---

# 73.22 Entity Relationships

Relationships MUST be designed intentionally.

Examples:

```text id="6z7d6e"
Course
 ├── Modules
 │    └── Lessons
 └── Quizzes
```

---

# 73.23 `@OneToMany`

`@OneToMany` relationships MUST be used carefully.

Large collections SHOULD NOT automatically be loaded whenever the parent entity is retrieved.

---

# 73.24 Lazy Loading

Large relationships SHOULD generally use lazy loading unless eager loading is clearly justified.

---

# 73.25 Eager Loading

Avoid defaulting everything to:

```java id="j9mt7c"
FetchType.EAGER
```

This can cause:

```text id="g7w4p9"
Large queries
Unexpected joins
Memory consumption
N+1 queries
Slow APIs
```

---

# 73.26 N+1 Query Problem

Developers MUST actively watch for N+1 query behavior.

Example:

```text id="s2o3k8"
1 query → courses
N queries → lessons for each course
```

This can become catastrophic with larger datasets.

---

# 73.27 Fetch Strategies

Appropriate solutions MAY include:

```text id="c9h7hx"
JOIN FETCH
EntityGraph
Projection
Batch fetching
Dedicated queries
```

Use the solution appropriate to the actual access pattern.

---

# 73.28 Repository Layer

Spring Data repositories SHOULD focus on persistence operations.

Avoid placing business workflows directly inside repositories.

---

# 73.29 Repository Naming

Repositories SHOULD use consistent names:

```text id="v8y3da"
UserRepository
CourseRepository
LessonRepository
QuizRepository
EnrollmentRepository
```

---

# 73.30 Query Methods

Simple query methods MAY use Spring Data derived queries.

Example:

```java id="3r0q7m"
findByStatus(...)
findByCourseId(...)
findByStudentId(...)
```

---

# 73.31 Complex Queries

Complex queries SHOULD use:

```text id="5r8jup"
JPQL
Native SQL
Specifications
Criteria APIs
QueryDSL
```

according to project standards.

Do not force extremely complicated business queries into unreadable method names.

---

# 73.32 Query Method Naming

Avoid absurdly long repository methods such as:

```text id="lq0zj3"
findByCourseIdAndStatusAndPublishedAtBeforeAndTeacherIdAnd...
```

If a query becomes difficult to understand, use a dedicated query.

---

# 73.33 Projections

Use projections when only a subset of columns is required.

Example:

```text id="8m4xzz"
CourseSummary
    id
    title
    thumbnail
```

There is no reason to load an entire entity graph for a small card displayed on the dashboard.

---

# 73.34 Database Indexes

Indexes MUST be created based on actual query patterns.

Common candidates:

```text id="b1h7wx"
Foreign keys
Frequently searched columns
Frequently filtered columns
Frequently sorted columns
Unique business identifiers
```

---

# 73.35 Index Overuse

Do not create indexes on every column.

Indexes have costs:

```text id="8v1t4x"
Storage
Write overhead
Maintenance
Memory
```

---

# 73.36 Composite Indexes

Composite indexes SHOULD match common query patterns.

Example:

```text id="9w8t0e"
WHERE course_id = ?
AND status = ?
```

may justify an index involving:

```text id="f4b4qs"
(course_id, status)
```

depending on actual workload.

---

# 73.37 Index Validation

Important indexes SHOULD be validated using realistic query plans.

Use PostgreSQL tools such as:

```text id="g17p0d"
EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

when diagnosing query performance.

---

# 73.38 Query Performance

Never assume a query is fast because it is syntactically simple.

Performance MUST be evaluated against realistic data volumes.

---

# 73.39 Pagination

Large datasets MUST use pagination.

Avoid loading entire tables into memory.

Bad:

```text id="6y8k2q"
findAll()
```

for potentially millions of records.

Prefer:

```text id="h4l0y1"
Pageable
```

or another bounded retrieval strategy.

---

# 73.40 Sorting

Database sorting SHOULD be used when data needs to be ordered.

Avoid retrieving thousands of rows just to sort them in Java.

---

# 73.41 Filtering

Filtering SHOULD happen at the database layer.

Bad:

```text id="x1q5h3"
findAll()
 ↓
filter in Java
```

for large datasets.

Prefer database predicates.

---

# 73.42 Search

Search behavior SHOULD be designed around actual requirements.

Potential PostgreSQL strategies include:

```text id="x1v5ma"
B-tree indexes
GIN indexes
Full-text search
Trigram indexes
```

Use the simplest strategy that satisfies the requirement.

---

# 73.43 Transactions

Business operations that require atomicity MUST execute inside appropriate transactions.

Example:

```text id="g5v5n0"
Submit quiz
 ↓
Persist attempt
 ↓
Calculate score
 ↓
Update progress
 ↓
Commit
```

---

# 73.44 Transaction Boundary

Transactions SHOULD generally be defined at the service/application boundary rather than arbitrary repository methods.

---

# 73.45 Transaction Size

Transactions SHOULD be kept as short as practical.

Do not hold database transactions open while waiting for:

```text id="k4a6f2"
External HTTP APIs
AI services
File uploads
User interaction
Long-running computation
```

---

# 73.46 External Calls Inside Transactions

Avoid:

```text id="y1zzq5"
BEGIN TRANSACTION
 ↓
Call external API
 ↓
Wait 10 seconds
 ↓
Database update
 ↓
COMMIT
```

This unnecessarily holds database resources.

---

# 73.47 Transaction Rollback

Failure scenarios MUST be considered.

Developers SHOULD know which exceptions trigger rollback and configure transactional behavior intentionally.

---

# 73.48 Read-Only Transactions

Read-only transactions MAY be used where they provide meaningful optimization or semantic clarity.

---

# 73.49 Isolation Levels

The default transaction isolation level SHOULD generally be used unless a specific business requirement demands otherwise.

Changing isolation levels MUST be justified.

---

# 73.50 Concurrency

Concurrent updates MUST be considered for shared data.

Examples:

```text id="8aqg4x"
Course editing
Quiz attempts
Progress updates
Enrollment
Administrative changes
```

---

# 73.51 Optimistic Locking

Optimistic locking SHOULD be considered for resources where simultaneous editing is possible.

Example:

```text id="5ptnq2"
Course version = 12

Teacher A edits
Teacher B edits

Only compatible version can be saved.
```

---

# 73.52 Pessimistic Locking

Pessimistic locking MAY be used when strong serialization is required.

It MUST be used carefully because it can reduce concurrency and create contention.

---

# 73.53 Deadlocks

The application MUST handle the possibility of database deadlocks in high-concurrency operations.

---

# 73.54 Retry on Deadlock

Safe transaction retries MAY be implemented where appropriate.

Retries MUST NOT blindly repeat non-idempotent operations.

---

# 73.55 Soft Delete

Soft deletion MAY be used where data retention or auditability requires it.

Example:

```text id="l7w3qk"
deleted_at
```

---

# 73.56 Soft Delete Risks

Soft delete creates complexity.

Developers MUST consider:

```text id="p3n7ms"
Unique constraints
Queries
Relationships
Indexes
Restore behavior
Data retention
Reporting
```

Do not implement soft delete simply because it "sounds safer."

---

# 73.57 Hard Delete

Hard deletion MAY be used where:

```text id="k3grd8"
Data has no retention requirement
Legal/privacy requirements permit deletion
Relationships are safely handled
```

---

# 73.58 Data Retention

The project SHOULD define retention policies for:

```text id="1sg8rc"
User data
Quiz attempts
Audit records
Logs
Uploaded media
Notifications
Archived courses
```

---

# 73.59 Audit Fields

Important domain entities SHOULD support appropriate audit information.

Examples:

```text id="j2i4p7"
created_at
created_by
updated_at
updated_by
```

where required by the domain.

---

# 73.60 Audit Logs

Sensitive operations SHOULD produce audit records.

Examples:

```text id="7fj6x2"
Course publication
Course deletion
User role changes
Medical-content changes
Quiz answer changes
Administrative actions
```

---

# 73.61 Audit Integrity

Audit records SHOULD be protected against ordinary users modifying or deleting them.

---

# 73.62 Data Ownership

The application MUST clearly define ownership relationships.

Example:

```text id="f6o4a9"
Student
 ↓
Enrollment
 ↓
Course
```

Authorization logic SHOULD use these relationships where appropriate.

---

# 73.63 Cascading Deletes

Cascade behavior MUST be explicitly designed.

Do not blindly apply:

```java id="9n7h0z"
CascadeType.ALL
```

to every relationship.

---

# 73.64 Cascade Risks

Uncontrolled cascading can delete large portions of the data model unintentionally.

---

# 73.65 Orphan Removal

`orphanRemoval = true` MUST be used only when the child lifecycle is genuinely owned by the parent.

---

# 73.66 Database Constraints

Important business invariants SHOULD be backed by database constraints when possible.

Examples:

```text id="z7n7c4"
Unique enrollment
Non-null course title
Valid foreign key
Unique email
```

---

# 73.67 Business Rules

Not every business rule belongs in the database.

Example:

```text id="w2p7f1"
"A course requires review before publication."
```

This generally belongs in the application/domain layer.

---

# 73.68 Migration Tool

Database schema changes MUST be version-controlled.

Use an approved migration tool such as:

```text id="3z8tqf"
Flyway
Liquibase
```

The project MUST select one standard.

---

# 73.69 No Manual Production Schema Changes

Developers MUST NOT manually alter production schema as a normal deployment practice.

Schema changes MUST go through controlled migrations.

---

# 73.70 Migration Naming

Migration filenames MUST follow the selected migration tool's conventions.

Example for Flyway:

```text id="7t3h1f"
V1__create_users.sql
V2__create_courses.sql
V3__create_enrollments.sql
```

---

# 73.71 Migration Immutability

Applied migrations SHOULD NOT be modified.

Create a new migration to correct the schema.

---

# 73.72 Migration Testing

Every migration MUST be tested against a representative database.

---

# 73.73 Backward-Compatible Migrations

For zero/minimal-downtime deployments, schema changes SHOULD follow an expand-and-contract strategy.

Example:

```text id="qk8k2y"
Phase 1
Add new column

Phase 2
Deploy application using both

Phase 3
Backfill data

Phase 4
Switch reads/writes

Phase 5
Remove old column
```

---

# 73.74 Destructive Migrations

Destructive migrations require additional review.

Examples:

```text id="l0j3v4"
DROP COLUMN
DROP TABLE
Changing data type
Deleting large datasets
```

---

# 73.75 Backup Before Destructive Changes

Production backup/recovery procedures MUST be verified before high-risk migrations.

---

# 73.76 Seed Data

Development seed data MAY be provided.

Production seed data MUST be handled deliberately.

---

# 73.77 Reference Data

Stable reference data MAY be inserted through controlled migrations.

Examples:

```text id="z8o3v7"
Roles
Permissions
Course categories
Supported languages
System configuration
```

---

# 73.78 Secrets

Database credentials MUST NOT be committed to source control.

Use approved secret-management mechanisms.

---

# 73.79 Database Connection Pool

Connection pools MUST be configured intentionally.

Important parameters include:

```text id="1lcb7e"
Maximum pool size
Minimum idle
Connection timeout
Idle timeout
Max lifetime
```

Do not simply increase the pool size whenever performance problems occur.

---

# 73.80 Connection Pool Sizing

A large connection pool is not automatically faster.

Too many connections can overload PostgreSQL.

Pool sizing MUST consider:

```text id="x3b1jm"
Application instances
Database capacity
Concurrent workloads
Query duration
CPU
Memory
```

---

# 73.81 Connection Leaks

Database connections MUST always be released properly.

Framework-managed transactions and repositories SHOULD be preferred over manual connection handling where possible.

---

# 73.82 Lazy Initialization

Lazy relationships MUST be accessed within appropriate persistence boundaries.

Do not rely on accidental Open Session in View behavior to hide architectural problems.

---

# 73.83 Open Session in View

The project SHOULD explicitly decide whether Open Session in View is enabled.

It MUST NOT be used as a workaround for poorly designed data-access boundaries.

---

# 73.84 Entity Serialization

Never serialize entities containing large lazy collections directly.

This can cause:

```text id="rx2o6j"
Unexpected queries
Recursive serialization
Huge responses
LazyInitializationException
```

DTOs eliminate much of this risk.

---

# 73.85 Database Transactions and Events

When database changes trigger asynchronous events, transaction/event consistency MUST be considered.

For important workflows, patterns such as an outbox may be appropriate.

---

# 73.86 Outbox Pattern

For reliable event publication:

```text id="4l2vgr"
Database transaction
      ↓
Business record + Outbox event
      ↓
Commit
      ↓
Event publisher
      ↓
Message broker
```

This MAY be used where eventual consistency and reliable messaging are required.

---

# 73.87 Caching

Caching SHOULD only be introduced where profiling or workload characteristics justify it.

Potential candidates:

```text id="7a0xjy"
Course catalog
Reference data
Frequently accessed metadata
```

---

# 73.88 Cache Invalidation

Every cache MUST have a defined invalidation strategy.

> **There are few things more dangerous than a cache with no clear ownership or invalidation policy.**

---

# 73.89 Redis

If Redis is used, it SHOULD be treated as a cache/temporary state store according to the approved architecture.

Do not assume Redis automatically replaces PostgreSQL persistence.

---

# 73.90 Database Security

Production database access MUST be restricted.

Applications SHOULD use least-privilege database users.

---

# 73.91 Database Users

Do not run the application with PostgreSQL superuser privileges.

---

# 73.92 Read/Write Separation

Read replicas MAY be introduced when justified by workload.

The application architecture MUST clearly define:

```text id="9plcyn"
Read source
Write source
Replication lag
Consistency expectations
```

---

# 73.93 Replication Lag

If read replicas are introduced, developers MUST account for eventual consistency.

Example:

```text id="j3qz0b"
Write enrollment
 ↓
Immediately read replica
 ↓
Enrollment may not appear yet
```

---

# 73.94 Reporting Queries

Heavy analytics/reporting queries SHOULD NOT unnecessarily compete with transactional workloads.

Potential strategies:

```text id="3ft4d2"
Read replica
Materialized views
Dedicated analytics store
Batch processing
```

---

# 73.95 Large Data Operations

Bulk updates/deletes MUST be designed carefully.

Avoid loading millions of entities into application memory just to modify them.

---

# 73.96 Batch Processing

Batch operations SHOULD use controlled batch sizes.

---

# 73.97 Database Monitoring

Production database monitoring SHOULD track:

```text id="k70gzo"
CPU
Memory
Connections
Query latency
Locks
Deadlocks
Cache hit ratio
Disk usage
Replication lag
Slow queries
```

---

# 73.98 Slow Query Monitoring

Slow queries MUST be investigated rather than ignored.

---

# 73.99 Database Documentation

The project SHOULD maintain a current data model/ERD covering major entities and relationships.

---

# 73.100 Definition of Done

A database-related feature is complete when:

* [ ] Entity model is defined
* [ ] Table naming follows standards
* [ ] Primary/foreign keys are defined
* [ ] Constraints are defined
* [ ] Indexes are justified
* [ ] DTO boundaries are maintained
* [ ] Repository methods are appropriate
* [ ] Query performance is considered
* [ ] Pagination is implemented where required
* [ ] Transaction boundary is defined
* [ ] Concurrency is considered
* [ ] Migration is created
* [ ] Migration is tested
* [ ] Audit requirements are satisfied
* [ ] Security requirements are satisfied
* [ ] Tests cover important persistence behavior
* [ ] No N+1 query problem exists
* [ ] No unnecessary eager loading exists
* [ ] Documentation/ERD is updated where required

---

# 73.101 Core Principles

1. **PostgreSQL is a critical architectural component.**
2. **Database constraints protect data integrity.**
3. **JPA entities must not become API contracts.**
4. **DTOs define external boundaries.**
5. **Avoid uncontrolled eager loading.**
6. **N+1 queries must be actively prevented.**
7. **Pagination is mandatory for large datasets.**
8. **Indexes must be driven by query patterns.**
9. **Transactions belong around business operations.**
10. **Do not hold database transactions during slow external calls.**
11. **Concurrency must be explicitly considered.**
12. **Schema changes must be version-controlled through migrations.**
13. **Applied migrations must not be rewritten.**
14. **Database credentials must never be committed.**
15. **Caching requires an explicit invalidation strategy.**
16. **Production databases require least-privilege access.**
17. **Auditability is essential for sensitive administrative and educational-content changes.**
18. **Database performance must be evaluated using realistic data volumes.**
19. **The database should enforce structural integrity; application code should enforce domain workflows.**
20. **Never optimize database code based on assumptions when query plans and measurements can provide evidence.**

> **For Mediverse, database design is especially critical because the platform will accumulate relationships among users, courses, chapters, lessons, multimedia content, questions, answers, attempts, enrollments, progress, assessments, notifications, and audit records. Poor persistence design will eventually surface as slow course pages, incorrect progress, duplicate enrollments, inconsistent quiz results, N+1 queries, database contention, and difficult migrations. The database model therefore needs to be designed for both current correctness and future scale.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 74: Security Coding Standards — Spring Security, authentication, authorization, JWT/OAuth2, passwords, RBAC, object-level access control, secrets, OWASP, input security, file security, API security, session management and security testing.**

# CSDG — Chapter 74

## Security Coding Standards

### 74.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the mandatory security coding standards for Mediverse.

Security MUST be treated as a cross-cutting concern across:

```text
Frontend
   ↓
API
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Business Logic
   ↓
Database
   ↓
Infrastructure
   ↓
External Services
```

Core principle:

> **Never trust the client. Every security-sensitive decision must ultimately be enforced by the backend.**

---

# 74.2 Security Objectives

Mediverse security controls MUST protect:

```text
Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authentication
Authorization
Account security
Personal data
Educational content
Assessment data
Auditability
```

---

# 74.3 Security-by-Design

Security MUST be considered during design rather than added after implementation.

Every security-sensitive feature SHOULD answer:

```text
Who can access it?
What can they do?
What data can they see?
What happens if the request is modified?
What happens if the request is repeated?
What happens if the user is malicious?
What happens if a dependency fails?
```

---

# 74.4 Zero Trust Principle

The backend MUST NOT trust:

```text
Frontend validation
Hidden UI controls
Request origin alone
Client-provided roles
Client-provided ownership
Client-provided prices/statuses
```

Example:

```json
{
  "role": "ADMIN"
}
```

MUST NOT cause the backend to grant administrative privileges.

---

# 74.5 Authentication vs Authorization

These MUST remain conceptually separate.

```text
Authentication
    ↓
Who are you?

Authorization
    ↓
What are you allowed to do?
```

A valid login does not automatically grant access to every resource.

---

# 74.6 Authentication

Mediverse SHOULD use an approved centralized authentication mechanism such as:

```text
Spring Security
JWT
OAuth2/OIDC
```

depending on the final architecture.

Authentication logic MUST NOT be duplicated across controllers.

---

# 74.7 Password Storage

Passwords MUST NEVER be stored as plaintext.

Do not store:

```text
password123
```

or reversible encrypted passwords.

Passwords SHOULD be stored using an adaptive password hashing algorithm such as:

```text
Argon2
BCrypt
```

according to the project's selected security standard.

---

# 74.8 Password Hashing

Passwords MUST be hashed using a strong, intentionally configured work factor.

The application MUST NOT implement custom password hashing algorithms.

Avoid:

```text
MD5
SHA-1
Plain SHA-256
```

for password storage.

---

# 74.9 Password Verification

Password comparison MUST be performed through the approved password encoder.

Never manually compare hashes using insecure string logic.

---

# 74.10 Password Policy

Password requirements SHOULD balance security and usability.

The project SHOULD define:

```text
Minimum length
Maximum length
Allowed characters
Compromised-password handling
Password reset behavior
```

Avoid arbitrary complexity requirements that encourage predictable passwords.

---

# 74.11 Password Reset

Password-reset mechanisms MUST use short-lived, single-use tokens.

Reset tokens MUST NOT be reusable indefinitely.

---

# 74.12 Password Reset Response

Password-reset endpoints SHOULD avoid revealing whether an email/account exists.

Bad:

```text
User does not exist.
```

Prefer a response that does not enable account enumeration.

---

# 74.13 Account Enumeration

Authentication and recovery endpoints SHOULD avoid exposing whether a particular user exists.

---

# 74.14 Brute-Force Protection

Authentication endpoints MUST have protections against repeated credential attacks.

Controls MAY include:

```text
Rate limiting
Progressive delays
Temporary account protection
IP-based controls
Risk-based controls
```

---

# 74.15 JWT

If JWT is used, tokens MUST be:

```text
Short-lived where appropriate
Cryptographically signed
Validated on every protected request
```

---

# 74.16 JWT Claims

JWT claims MUST contain only information necessary for authentication/authorization.

Avoid placing sensitive information inside tokens.

JWT payloads are encoded, not inherently secret.

---

# 74.17 JWT Validation

The backend MUST validate:

```text
Signature
Expiration
Issuer where applicable
Audience where applicable
Token type where applicable
```

---

# 74.18 JWT Algorithm

The accepted JWT signing algorithm MUST be explicitly configured.

The application MUST NOT blindly trust the algorithm specified by an untrusted token.

---

# 74.19 Token Expiration

Access tokens SHOULD have controlled expiration.

Long-lived access tokens increase the impact of token theft.

---

# 74.20 Refresh Tokens

If refresh tokens are used:

```text
Rotation
Expiration
Revocation
Secure storage
Reuse detection
```

MUST be considered.

---

# 74.21 Token Storage

Browser token storage MUST be selected based on the application's threat model.

Sensitive authentication tokens SHOULD NOT be exposed unnecessarily to JavaScript.

Where cookies are used, security attributes such as:

```text
HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite
```

MUST be configured appropriately.

---

# 74.22 Logout

Logout MUST invalidate the relevant authentication state according to the chosen token/session architecture.

Simply deleting a frontend variable is not sufficient for every authentication architecture.

---

# 74.23 Session Management

If server-side sessions are used, sessions MUST have:

```text
Expiration
Secure identifiers
Session invalidation
Session fixation protection
```

---

# 74.24 Session Fixation

Authentication MUST prevent attackers from forcing users to authenticate using an attacker-controlled session identifier.

---

# 74.25 Spring Security

Spring Security configuration SHOULD be centralized and explicit.

Avoid scattering authorization rules across unrelated controllers.

---

# 74.26 Security Filter Chain

The security filter chain MUST be reviewed whenever authentication or authorization behavior changes.

Developers MUST understand:

```text
Request
 ↓
Security filters
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Controller
```

---

# 74.27 Public Endpoints

Public endpoints MUST be explicitly identified.

Do not accidentally expose sensitive endpoints because of overly broad rules.

---

# 74.28 Default Deny

Security configuration SHOULD follow a default-deny approach.

Conceptually:

```text
Unknown endpoint
      ↓
DENY
```

rather than:

```text
Unknown endpoint
      ↓
ALLOW
```

---

# 74.29 Role-Based Access Control

Mediverse SHOULD use RBAC where appropriate.

Potential roles:

```text
STUDENT
TEACHER
CONTENT_AUTHOR
REVIEWER
ADMIN
SUPER_ADMIN
```

The actual roles MUST be defined by the approved authorization model.

---

# 74.30 Least Privilege

Users MUST receive only the permissions required for their responsibilities.

Example:

```text
Student
  → View course
  → Attempt quiz

Teacher
  → Manage assigned content

Admin
  → Manage platform configuration
```

---

# 74.31 Role Checks

Authorization SHOULD preferably use explicit permissions rather than scattered string comparisons.

Avoid:

```java
if (user.getRole().equals("ADMIN")) {
```

throughout business code.

---

# 74.32 Permission-Based Authorization

For complex systems, permissions MAY provide greater flexibility.

Example:

```text
COURSE_READ
COURSE_CREATE
COURSE_UPDATE
COURSE_PUBLISH
COURSE_DELETE
QUIZ_MANAGE
USER_MANAGE
```

---

# 74.33 Method-Level Security

Spring Security method-level authorization MAY be used for sensitive service operations.

Example conceptually:

```text
@PreAuthorize(...)
```

Authorization MUST still reflect actual domain rules.

---

# 74.34 Object-Level Authorization

Role-based authorization alone is insufficient.

Example:

```text
Teacher A
```

may have permission to edit courses, but not necessarily:

```text
Teacher B's course
```

The backend MUST verify resource ownership or permitted scope.

---

# 74.35 IDOR Prevention

APIs MUST protect against Insecure Direct Object Reference vulnerabilities.

A request such as:

```text
GET /api/v1/students/1001/progress
```

MUST NOT expose another student's data merely because the attacker changed:

```text
1001 → 1002
```

---

# 74.36 Ownership Checks

Sensitive resource access SHOULD verify relationships such as:

```text
Current user
   ↓
Enrollment
   ↓
Course
   ↓
Lesson
```

rather than trusting IDs supplied by the client.

---

# 74.37 Administrative APIs

Administrative endpoints MUST have stronger authorization controls.

Examples:

```text
User management
Role management
Course publication
Content deletion
Audit access
System configuration
```

---

# 74.38 Privilege Escalation

The application MUST prevent horizontal and vertical privilege escalation.

```text
Horizontal:
Student A → Student B's data

Vertical:
Student → Admin functionality
```

---

# 74.39 CORS

CORS MUST be explicitly configured.

Avoid:

```text
allow all origins
```

for production security-sensitive APIs.

---

# 74.40 CORS Credentials

If credentials are used, origin and credential configuration MUST be carefully controlled.

---

# 74.41 CSRF

CSRF protections MUST match the authentication architecture.

Cookie-based authentication generally requires strong CSRF consideration.

Stateless bearer-token architectures have different CSRF characteristics, but other token-theft risks remain.

---

# 74.42 HTTPS

All production authentication and application traffic MUST use HTTPS.

HTTP MUST NOT be used to transmit:

```text
Passwords
JWTs
Session identifiers
Personal data
Sensitive educational records
```

---

# 74.43 TLS

TLS configuration SHOULD use modern secure protocols and configurations.

Deprecated protocols and weak cryptographic configurations MUST NOT be used.

---

# 74.44 HTTP Security Headers

The application SHOULD configure appropriate security headers.

Potential controls include:

```text
Content-Security-Policy
X-Content-Type-Options
Referrer-Policy
Strict-Transport-Security
```

according to the deployment architecture.

---

# 74.45 Content Security Policy

CSP SHOULD be configured to reduce the impact of XSS.

Do not blindly use:

```text
unsafe-inline
unsafe-eval
```

without understanding the security implications.

---

# 74.46 Input Validation

All external input MUST be treated as untrusted.

Validate:

```text
Request bodies
Query parameters
Path parameters
Headers
File uploads
Search input
Rich text
```

---

# 74.47 Input Validation Is Not Authorization

Validating that:

```text
courseId = 101
```

is syntactically valid does NOT mean the user is authorized to access course 101.

---

# 74.48 Output Encoding

User-generated content MUST be safely encoded before being rendered in contexts where injection is possible.

---

# 74.49 Cross-Site Scripting

The application MUST protect against:

```text
Stored XSS
Reflected XSS
DOM-based XSS
```

This is especially important for:

```text
Course descriptions
Teacher content
Discussion posts
Comments
Rich-text educational content
```

---

# 74.50 Rich Text

If Mediverse supports rich-text educational content, HTML MUST be sanitized before being stored/rendered according to an approved sanitization strategy.

Do not trust HTML supplied by users.

---

# 74.51 SQL Injection

All database queries MUST use parameterized mechanisms.

Never construct SQL like:

```text
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"
```

---

# 74.52 JPA/ORM Security

JPA does not automatically make every query safe.

Developers MUST still avoid unsafe dynamic query construction.

---

# 74.53 Command Injection

User-controlled input MUST NOT be passed directly to operating-system commands.

---

# 74.54 Path Traversal

File paths derived from user input MUST be validated.

Never blindly accept:

```text
../../../../etc/passwd
```

or equivalent path traversal attempts.

---

# 74.55 File Upload Security

File uploads MUST be treated as untrusted.

Controls SHOULD include:

```text
Maximum size
Allowed content types
Extension validation
Content inspection
Safe filename handling
Authorization
Storage isolation
Malware scanning where appropriate
```

---

# 74.56 File Extension Validation

Do not rely solely on filename extensions.

An attacker may rename:

```text
malicious.exe
```

to:

```text
image.jpg
```

Content type and actual content SHOULD also be evaluated.

---

# 74.57 Uploaded File Names

Original filenames SHOULD NOT be used directly as storage paths.

Generate controlled internal identifiers.

---

# 74.58 File Storage

User-uploaded files SHOULD be stored outside executable application directories.

---

# 74.59 File Download Authorization

Every protected download MUST verify authorization.

Knowing the URL MUST NOT automatically grant access.

---

# 74.60 Malware Scanning

High-risk uploads SHOULD be scanned using an approved malware-scanning mechanism where required.

---

# 74.61 Secrets Management

Secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code.

Never commit:

```text
Passwords
JWT secrets
Private keys
API keys
Database credentials
Cloud credentials
```

---

# 74.62 Environment Variables

Environment variables MAY be used for configuration/secrets, but production environments SHOULD use a dedicated secret-management solution where appropriate.

---

# 74.63 Git Security

Before committing code, developers MUST ensure secrets are not present in:

```text
Java files
application.yml
application.properties
.env
Dockerfiles
Kubernetes manifests
Terraform files
Scripts
Documentation
```

---

# 74.64 Secret Rotation

Production secrets SHOULD support controlled rotation.

Security-sensitive credentials MUST NOT remain unchanged indefinitely.

---

# 74.65 Logging Security

Logs MUST NOT contain:

```text
Passwords
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
Authorization headers
Private keys
Database passwords
Sensitive personal data
```

---

# 74.66 Error Security

Production error responses MUST NOT expose:

```text
Stack traces
Class names
SQL statements
Database details
Filesystem paths
Internal service topology
```

---

# 74.67 Exception Handling

Security-related exceptions MUST be handled consistently.

The external response SHOULD provide enough information for the consumer without exposing internal details.

---

# 74.68 Account Lockout

Account lockout policies MUST be carefully designed.

Permanent lockout based only on failed login attempts can itself become a denial-of-service mechanism.

---

# 74.69 Rate Limiting

Rate limiting SHOULD protect:

```text
Login
Registration
Password reset
Search
File upload
Quiz submission
AI endpoints
Expensive APIs
```

---

# 74.70 API Abuse

The backend MUST assume that attackers can bypass the frontend and directly invoke APIs.

Therefore:

```text
Frontend restrictions ≠ security controls
```

---

# 74.71 Sensitive Data

Mediverse may handle sensitive user and educational information.

The application MUST minimize unnecessary collection and exposure of personal data.

---

# 74.72 Data Minimization

Only collect data required for the business purpose.

Avoid storing unnecessary personal information simply because the database can store it.

---

# 74.73 Data Exposure

API responses MUST return only fields required by the consumer.

Do not return:

```text
passwordHash
security tokens
internal permissions
private administrative data
```

unless explicitly required and appropriately protected.

---

# 74.74 PII

Personally identifiable information SHOULD be classified and handled according to the project's privacy requirements.

---

# 74.75 Encryption at Rest

Sensitive production data SHOULD use appropriate encryption-at-rest mechanisms provided by the infrastructure/database/storage architecture.

---

# 74.76 Encryption in Transit

Sensitive communication between:

```text
Frontend ↔ API
API ↔ Database
Service ↔ Service
API ↔ External Service
```

SHOULD use encrypted transport where applicable.

---

# 74.77 Service-to-Service Security

If Mediverse uses microservices, internal services MUST NOT automatically trust every caller.

Authentication and authorization between services SHOULD be designed explicitly.

---

# 74.78 Internal APIs

"Internal" does not mean "trusted."

Internal endpoints MUST still have appropriate access controls.

---

# 74.79 Service Identity

Where required, services SHOULD authenticate using dedicated identities rather than shared credentials.

---

# 74.80 API Gateway

If an API gateway is used, security MUST NOT exist exclusively at the gateway.

Critical authorization MUST still be enforced by the responsible service.

---

# 74.81 Security Dependency Management

Dependencies MUST be regularly checked for known vulnerabilities.

Tools MAY include:

```text
OWASP Dependency-Check
Snyk
Dependabot
Trivy
Maven security scanning
```

The project SHOULD standardize its selected tools.

---

# 74.82 Vulnerable Dependencies

Known critical vulnerabilities MUST be evaluated promptly.

Do not ignore security scanner findings simply because the application currently works.

---

# 74.83 Dependency Pinning

Production dependency versions MUST be controlled.

Avoid uncontrolled version ranges.

---

# 74.84 Container Security

Docker images MUST:

```text
Use trusted base images
Avoid unnecessary packages
Run as non-root where practical
Avoid embedding secrets
Be scanned for vulnerabilities
```

---

# 74.85 Kubernetes Security

Kubernetes workloads SHOULD follow:

```text
Least privilege
Non-root containers
Restricted capabilities
Read-only filesystem where practical
Resource limits
Network policies where required
Secret management
```

---

# 74.86 Database Security

Application database accounts MUST use least privilege.

Do not run the application as a PostgreSQL superuser.

---

# 74.87 Security Testing

Security-sensitive features MUST have automated tests.

Test categories SHOULD include:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Role boundaries
Object ownership
Input validation
Injection
File upload
Token handling
```

---

# 74.88 Negative Testing

Security tests MUST test what users **cannot** do.

Example:

```text
Student attempts admin endpoint
        ↓
403
```

and:

```text
Student A accesses Student B's progress
        ↓
Denied
```

---

# 74.89 Security Test Cases

Every protected endpoint SHOULD have at least:

```text
Unauthenticated test
Authorized-user test
Unauthorized-role test
Unauthorized-resource test
```

where applicable.

---

# 74.90 Penetration Testing

Before major production releases, security testing SHOULD include appropriate penetration/security assessment based on project risk.

---

# 74.91 OWASP

The project SHOULD use the OWASP Top 10 and relevant OWASP guidance as a baseline for application-security review.

---

# 74.92 Threat Modeling

High-risk features SHOULD undergo threat modeling.

Potential targets:

```text
Authentication
Payments if introduced
File uploads
Admin APIs
AI integrations
User-generated content
Medical/educational records
```

---

# 74.93 Security Review

Security-sensitive pull requests SHOULD receive additional review.

Examples:

```text
Authentication changes
Authorization changes
JWT changes
Password handling
Database permissions
File handling
Secrets/configuration
External integrations
```

---

# 74.94 Security Incident Handling

The system SHOULD support investigation through:

```text
Audit logs
Correlation IDs
Security logs
Authentication events
Administrative activity
```

---

# 74.95 Security Monitoring

Production monitoring SHOULD detect suspicious behavior such as:

```text
Repeated login failures
Unusual request rates
Repeated authorization failures
Unexpected administrative actions
Large-scale data access
```

---

# 74.96 Security Configuration

Security-sensitive configuration MUST be externalized where appropriate.

Avoid hardcoding:

```text
JWT secret
Database password
OAuth client secret
Cloud credentials
Encryption keys
```

---

# 74.97 Secure Defaults

The application SHOULD choose secure defaults.

Example:

```text
Unknown endpoint → deny
Unknown role → deny
Missing permission → deny
Invalid token → deny
Invalid input → reject
```

---

# 74.98 Fail Securely

When security verification fails, the system MUST fail closed rather than accidentally granting access.

---

# 74.99 Security Definition of Done

A security-sensitive feature is complete only when:

* [ ] Authentication requirements are defined
* [ ] Authorization requirements are defined
* [ ] Object-level authorization is verified
* [ ] Input validation exists
* [ ] Output exposure is reviewed
* [ ] Sensitive data is protected
* [ ] Secrets are externalized
* [ ] Error responses do not leak internals
* [ ] Logs do not leak secrets
* [ ] Rate limiting is considered
* [ ] File security is addressed where applicable
* [ ] Security tests exist
* [ ] Negative authorization tests exist
* [ ] Dependency vulnerabilities are checked
* [ ] Documentation is updated
* [ ] Security review is completed where required

---

# 74.100 Core Principles

1. **Never trust the client.**
2. **Authentication does not equal authorization.**
3. **Every protected resource requires server-side authorization.**
4. **Object-level authorization is mandatory for user-owned resources.**
5. **Passwords must never be stored in plaintext.**
6. **Tokens must be short-lived and properly validated.**
7. **Secrets must never enter source control.**
8. **All external input is untrusted.**
9. **Frontend validation is a usability feature, not a security boundary.**
10. **Sensitive data must be minimized and protected.**
11. **Errors must fail safely without exposing internals.**
12. **Security controls must exist at the appropriate architectural layer.**
13. **Internal APIs are not automatically trusted.**
14. **Security-sensitive changes require testing and review.**
15. **Secure defaults must be the normal behavior.**

> **For Mediverse, security is not merely about protecting the login endpoint. The dangerous attack surface is much larger: student progress, assessments, course ownership, teacher content, administrative APIs, uploaded media, JWT/session handling, user-generated content, and potentially AI integrations. The most important rule is therefore simple: every request must be treated as potentially malicious, and every authorization decision must be enforced server-side.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 75: Testing & Quality Assurance Standards — unit testing, integration testing, API testing, security testing, Testcontainers, MockMvc, frontend testing, E2E, test data, coverage, mocking strategy, CI quality gates and Definition of Done.**


# CSDG — Chapter 75

## Testing & Quality Assurance Standards

### 75.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the testing and quality-assurance standards for Mediverse.

The objective is to ensure that every feature is:

```text
Correct
Secure
Reliable
Maintainable
Regression-safe
Performant
Deployable
```

Core principle:

> **A feature is not complete because the code compiles. It is complete when its expected behavior and important failure modes are verified automatically.**

---

# 75.2 Testing Pyramid

Mediverse SHOULD follow a balanced testing strategy:

```text
                 E2E Tests
                    ▲
                   / \
              API / Integration
                 /     \
                /       \
           Unit Tests
```

The majority of tests SHOULD be fast unit tests.

Integration and E2E tests SHOULD be used where real component interaction matters.

---

# 75.3 Test Categories

The platform SHOULD contain:

```text
Unit Tests
Integration Tests
Repository Tests
API Tests
Security Tests
Contract Tests
End-to-End Tests
Performance Tests
```

Not every feature requires every category, but critical workflows require broader coverage.

---

# 75.4 Unit Tests

Unit tests MUST verify isolated business behavior.

Examples:

```text
CourseService
QuizScoringService
ProgressService
EnrollmentService
```

---

# 75.5 Unit Test Characteristics

Good unit tests should be:

```text
Fast
Deterministic
Isolated
Repeatable
Focused
```

A unit test SHOULD NOT require:

```text
Real PostgreSQL
Real Redis
Real Kafka
Real external API
```

unless the test is intentionally an integration test.

---

# 75.6 Unit Test Naming

Test names SHOULD clearly describe behavior.

Example:

```text
shouldCalculateQuizScoreWhenAllAnswersAreCorrect()
```

rather than:

```text
test1()
```

---

# 75.7 Given / When / Then

Tests SHOULD follow a clear behavioral structure:

```text
Given
 ↓
When
 ↓
Then
```

Example:

```text
Given a published course
When a student enrolls
Then enrollment should be created
```

---

# 75.8 Arrange / Act / Assert

The equivalent structure MAY be expressed as:

```text
Arrange
Act
Assert
```

The project SHOULD use one consistent style.

---

# 75.9 Test One Behavior

A test SHOULD focus on one meaningful behavior.

Avoid tests that simultaneously verify:

```text
Enrollment
Payment
Notification
Progress
Certificate
```

unless the test is intentionally an end-to-end workflow.

---

# 75.10 Mocking

Mocks SHOULD be used to isolate external dependencies.

Example:

```text
CourseService
   ↓
Mock CourseRepository
```

---

# 75.11 Mocking Abuse

Do not mock everything.

If the test becomes mostly:

```text
when(...)
verify(...)
when(...)
verify(...)
```

with almost no real behavior, the test may be testing implementation details rather than behavior.

---

# 75.12 Mockito

Mockito MAY be used for Spring Boot unit testing where appropriate.

---

# 75.13 Mock Verification

Use verification when interaction itself is important.

Avoid excessive verification of internal implementation details.

---

# 75.14 Service Tests

Service-layer tests SHOULD cover:

```text
Successful operation
Invalid input
Not-found conditions
Authorization failures
Business rule violations
Duplicate operations
Boundary conditions
```

---

# 75.15 Business Rules

Every significant business rule SHOULD have automated tests.

Example:

```text
A student cannot submit an expired quiz.
```

Test:

```text
Given quiz is expired
When student submits answers
Then submission is rejected
```

---

# 75.16 Edge Cases

Tests MUST consider boundary conditions.

Examples:

```text
Empty collection
Single item
Maximum allowed value
Minimum allowed value
Null/optional value
Expired resource
Duplicate request
Concurrent request
```

---

# 75.17 Exception Testing

Expected exceptions MUST be explicitly tested.

Example:

```text
CourseNotFoundException
UnauthorizedException
ValidationException
DuplicateEnrollmentException
```

---

# 75.18 Repository Tests

Database access SHOULD be tested separately from business logic.

Repository tests MAY use:

```text
Spring Boot Test
Testcontainers
```

---

# 75.19 Real Database Testing

For PostgreSQL-specific behavior, tests SHOULD preferably use a real PostgreSQL instance rather than relying exclusively on an in-memory replacement.

---

# 75.20 Testcontainers

**Testcontainers** SHOULD be considered the preferred mechanism for integration tests involving:

```text
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka
Other infrastructure dependencies
```

This reduces the gap between test and production infrastructure.

---

# 75.21 H2 Database

H2 MAY be used for simple tests where PostgreSQL-specific behavior is irrelevant.

However:

> **Passing H2 tests does not prove PostgreSQL compatibility.**

---

# 75.22 Integration Tests

Integration tests MUST verify that multiple application components work correctly together.

Example:

```text
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
PostgreSQL
```

---

# 75.23 Spring Boot Integration Tests

Integration tests MAY use:

```java
@SpringBootTest
```

where the full application context is required.

Do not use full-context tests for every small service method because they are slower and harder to diagnose.

---

# 75.24 API Tests

Every important REST API SHOULD have automated API tests.

API tests MUST verify:

```text
HTTP method
URL
Authentication
Authorization
Request validation
Response status
Response body
Error response
```

---

# 75.25 MockMvc

For Spring MVC APIs, **MockMvc** SHOULD be used for controller/API testing where an actual HTTP server is unnecessary.

---

# 75.26 API Success Tests

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/enrollments
```

Test:

```text
Valid student
Valid course
Valid authentication
        ↓
201 Created
```

---

# 75.27 API Failure Tests

Test at minimum where applicable:

```text
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
400 Bad Request
409 Conflict
422 Unprocessable Entity
```

---

# 75.28 Validation Tests

Invalid requests MUST be tested.

Examples:

```text
Missing title
Invalid email
Negative duration
Invalid enum
Oversized field
Malformed ID
```

---

# 75.29 Authorization Tests

Authorization tests MUST verify role boundaries.

Example:

```text
Student
   ↓
POST /api/v1/courses
   ↓
403 Forbidden
```

---

# 75.30 Object-Level Authorization Tests

This is mandatory for resources belonging to individual users.

Example:

```text
Student A
   ↓
GET Student B's progress
   ↓
DENIED
```

---

# 75.31 Authentication Tests

Authentication tests SHOULD cover:

```text
Valid credentials
Invalid password
Unknown user
Expired token
Malformed token
Missing token
Revoked token where applicable
```

---

# 75.32 JWT Tests

If JWT is used, tests SHOULD cover:

```text
Valid signature
Invalid signature
Expired token
Incorrect issuer
Incorrect audience where applicable
Missing required claims
```

---

# 75.33 Security Regression Tests

Security bugs that are fixed MUST receive regression tests.

Example:

```text
Bug:
Student could access another student's progress.

Fix:
Authorization added.

Required:
Regression test proving unauthorized access remains blocked.
```

---

# 75.34 Repository Query Tests

Custom repository queries MUST be tested against realistic database behavior.

Especially important for:

```text
JOIN queries
Pagination
Sorting
Filtering
Aggregations
Native SQL
```

---

# 75.35 Pagination Tests

Pagination tests SHOULD verify:

```text
First page
Middle page
Last page
Empty page
Maximum page size
Invalid page size
Sorting
```

---

# 75.36 Database Constraint Tests

Important constraints SHOULD have integration tests.

Examples:

```text
Duplicate email
Duplicate enrollment
Invalid foreign key
Required field missing
```

---

# 75.37 Transaction Tests

Critical transactional workflows SHOULD test rollback behavior.

Example:

```text
Create enrollment
 ↓
Update progress
 ↓
Failure
 ↓
Rollback
```

The test should verify that partial state was not persisted.

---

# 75.38 Concurrency Tests

Concurrency-sensitive operations SHOULD have appropriate tests.

Examples:

```text
Duplicate enrollment
Quiz submission
Concurrent course editing
Progress updates
```

---

# 75.39 Idempotency Tests

Operations designed to be idempotent MUST verify repeated requests.

Example:

```text
Request 1 → success
Request 2 → no duplicate side effect
```

---

# 75.40 File Upload Tests

File-upload APIs MUST test:

```text
Valid file
Unsupported extension
Invalid MIME type
Oversized file
Empty file
Malicious filename
Unauthorized upload
```

---

# 75.41 File Download Tests

Protected downloads MUST test:

```text
Authorized user → allowed
Unauthorized user → denied
Nonexistent file → correct response
```

---

# 75.42 External Service Tests

External integrations SHOULD be tested using controlled mocks/stubs rather than depending on live external services during normal CI.

Examples:

```text
Email provider
AI provider
Object storage
Payment provider
Notification service
```

---

# 75.43 Contract Testing

Where multiple services or independently deployed components communicate, contract testing SHOULD be considered.

The objective is to catch:

```text
Backend changes
        ↓
Frontend/service breaks
```

before deployment.

---

# 75.44 OpenAPI Contract

OpenAPI SHOULD act as an explicit API contract.

Changes to:

```text
Request fields
Response fields
Status codes
Authentication
```

SHOULD be reviewed for compatibility.

---

# 75.45 End-to-End Testing

E2E tests SHOULD validate critical user journeys through the actual application.

Examples:

```text
Register
 ↓
Login
 ↓
Browse course
 ↓
Enroll
 ↓
Study lesson
 ↓
Attempt quiz
 ↓
View result
 ↓
View progress
```

---

# 75.46 E2E Scope

Do not turn every unit test into an E2E test.

E2E tests are:

```text
Slower
More fragile
More expensive
Harder to diagnose
```

Use them for high-value workflows.

---

# 75.47 Frontend E2E

A browser automation framework such as Playwright MAY be used.

---

# 75.48 Critical User Journeys

At minimum, important Mediverse workflows SHOULD have E2E coverage.

Potential examples:

```text
Student login
Course discovery
Course enrollment
Lesson completion
Quiz submission
Progress tracking
Teacher content management
Admin authorization
```

---

# 75.49 Test Data

Test data MUST be deterministic.

Tests SHOULD NOT depend on:

```text
Random production data
External live APIs
Current date without control
Shared mutable state
Developer-specific local configuration
```

---

# 75.50 Test Isolation

Tests SHOULD be isolated from each other.

One test MUST NOT depend on another test running first.

---

# 75.51 Test Cleanup

Integration tests MUST clean up their state appropriately.

---

# 75.52 Database Reset

Integration tests MAY use:

```text
Transaction rollback
Database cleanup
Container recreation
Test fixtures
```

depending on the test architecture.

---

# 75.53 Test Fixtures

Reusable fixtures SHOULD be created for common domain objects.

Example:

```text
StudentFixture
CourseFixture
LessonFixture
QuizFixture
```

---

# 75.54 Test Builders

Builders MAY improve readability for complex test objects.

Example concept:

```text
CourseBuilder
    .withTitle(...)
    .published()
    .withLessons(...)
    .build()
```

---

# 75.55 Avoid Giant Fixtures

Do not create one enormous fixture containing every possible field.

Tests should define only the data relevant to the behavior.

---

# 75.56 Test Environment

CI tests SHOULD execute in an environment that resembles production where practical.

Differences MUST be understood.

---

# 75.57 CI Test Stages

Recommended pipeline:

```text
Checkout
   ↓
Compile
   ↓
Unit Tests
   ↓
Integration Tests
   ↓
Security Checks
   ↓
Static Analysis
   ↓
Build Artifact
   ↓
E2E / Deployment Validation
```

---

# 75.58 Fast Feedback

Fast tests SHOULD execute early in the pipeline.

Slow tests SHOULD run later.

---

# 75.59 Test Parallelization

Independent tests MAY run in parallel.

Tests MUST NOT rely on shared mutable state if parallel execution is enabled.

---

# 75.60 Flaky Tests

Flaky tests MUST be treated as defects.

Do not solve flaky tests by blindly adding retries.

---

# 75.61 Test Retries

Retries MAY be used only for genuinely transient infrastructure conditions.

A retry MUST NOT hide deterministic application failures.

---

# 75.62 Code Coverage

Code coverage SHOULD be tracked.

Coverage is a signal, not the definition of quality.

---

# 75.63 Coverage Targets

The project MAY establish targets such as:

```text
Unit tests: high coverage of business logic
Critical security code: very high coverage
Integration tests: critical persistence/API paths
```

Avoid blindly requiring 100% coverage.
