# 87.50 Session Fixation

Session identifiers SHOULD be regenerated when privilege level changes, particularly after successful authentication.

---

# 87.51 Concurrent Sessions

The system MAY support session/device management.

Example:

```text id="qg3a0x"
My Account
 ├── Chrome / Windows
 ├── Android
 └── Edge / Windows
```

Users MAY be given the ability to revoke individual sessions.

---

# 87.52 Authorization Middleware

Spring Security SHOULD perform common authentication/authorization checks before business logic.

Example flow:

```text id="v0g3ai"
HTTP Request
 ↓
Security Filter Chain
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Service
```

---

# 87.53 Method Security

Spring method-level authorization MAY be used where useful.

Conceptually:

```java id="8s4q21"
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('COURSE_UPDATE')")
```

But expressions should remain understandable and maintainable.

---

# 87.54 Domain Authorization

Complex authorization rules SHOULD NOT become giant annotations.

Example:

```text id="l15z6w"
"User can modify course only if:
user is instructor AND
user owns course AND
course is not locked"
```

Such business rules belong in an appropriate authorization/domain service.

---

# 87.55 Authorization Order

Recommended:

```text id="5v3p1t"
Authenticate
   ↓
Check account state
   ↓
Check role/permission
   ↓
Load resource
   ↓
Check resource ownership/policy
   ↓
Execute operation
```

---

# 87.56 Information Leakage

Authorization failures should not unnecessarily reveal sensitive information.

Example:

If a student requests:

```text id="q4v9ha"
/courses/999
```

and the course is private, returning a detailed message about its existence may leak information.

Security policy should determine whether the correct response is:

```text id="yupwqn"
404
```

or:

```text id="n3m7yo"
403
```

---

# 87.57 Audit Logging

Security-sensitive actions MUST be auditable.

Examples:

```text id="p2b2l4"
Login success
Login failure
Password reset
MFA change
Role change
Permission change
Account disable
Admin action
```

---

# 87.58 Audit Content

Security audit records SHOULD include:

```text id="c0hrw2"
Timestamp
Actor
Action
Target
Result
IP/device context where appropriate
Trace ID
```

Avoid storing raw passwords or tokens.

---

# 87.59 Failed Authentication Monitoring

Repeated failures SHOULD generate monitoring signals.

Example:

```text id="x0v7gk"
100 failed login attempts
        ↓
same IP
        ↓
security alert
```

---

# 87.60 Credential Stuffing

The system SHOULD account for attackers using leaked username/password combinations from other services.

Controls MAY include:

```text id="r5z1yd"
Rate limiting
MFA
Risk detection
Breached-password screening
Login anomaly detection
```

---

# 87.61 API Keys

API keys MAY be used for machine-to-machine or external integrations where appropriate.

API keys SHOULD have:

```text id="yn9zq6"
Identity
Scope
Expiration/rotation strategy
Revocation
Usage monitoring
```

Never treat an API key as equivalent to a user's unrestricted administrator credential.

---

# 87.62 OAuth Scopes

External clients MAY receive limited scopes.

Example:

```text id="0x0h2p"
courses:read
progress:read
profile:read
```

Do not issue unnecessarily broad scopes.

---

# 87.63 Refresh Token Protection

Refresh tokens SHOULD:

```text id="8n3p1a"
Be protected from theft
Be rotated where appropriate
Be revocable
Have bounded lifetime
Be associated with client/session context where useful
```

---

# 87.64 Token Logging

Never log:

```text id="2r4r9k"
Authorization header
Access token
Refresh token
Session secret
Password reset token
```

Even debug logs can leak into centralized logging systems.

---

# 87.65 Secret Rotation

Cryptographic signing keys SHOULD support rotation.

Conceptually:

```text id="k9j8l7"
Key A
 ↓
Key B introduced
 ↓
New tokens signed with B
 ↓
Old tokens validated with A temporarily
 ↓
A retired
```

Key rotation strategy should be planned before production.

---

# 87.66 Key Management

Production signing keys SHOULD be stored in secure key/secret management infrastructure.

Do not place private signing keys in Git.

---

# 87.67 Identity Data Separation

Identity information and business profile information MAY be separated.

Example:

```text id="r6f1k0"
Identity Service
 ├── authentication
 ├── credentials
 └── identity

User Service
 ├── profile
 ├── preferences
 └── application data
```

This reduces coupling.

---

# 87.68 Authorization Service

A dedicated authorization service MAY be introduced when authorization rules become sufficiently complex.

Do not create one prematurely.

A centralized authorization service introduces:

```text id="p0g8y2"
Network dependency
Latency
Availability concerns
Caching complexity
Policy-management complexity
```

---

# 87.69 Policy-Based Authorization

For complex systems, policy-based access control MAY complement RBAC.

Conceptually:

```text id="3f6j2v"
Subject
 +
Action
 +
Resource
 +
Context
 ↓
Policy Decision
```

Example:

```text id="x7j1b4"
Instructor A
ACTION = UPDATE
RESOURCE = Course 101
OWNER = Instructor A
STATUS = DRAFT
 ↓
ALLOW
```

---

# 87.70 Authorization Caching

Authorization decisions MAY be cached carefully.

But cache invalidation becomes critical when:

```text id="9a1f2e"
Role changes
Permission revoked
Account disabled
Resource ownership changes
```

Do not cache authorization decisions for long periods without a clear revocation strategy.

---

# 87.71 Multi-Tenancy Authorization

If Mediverse becomes multi-tenant:

```text id="g1t5l9"
Tenant A
Tenant B
Tenant C
```

authorization MUST include tenant context.

A user belonging to Tenant A must not access Tenant B data merely because the resource ID is known.

---

# 87.72 Tenant Context

Every relevant request should establish:

```text id="5f0x1z"
User
Tenant
Roles
Permissions
```

before accessing tenant-scoped resources.

---

# 87.73 API Gateway vs Service Authorization

The gateway MAY perform coarse authentication.

But services SHOULD enforce authorization for resources they own.

Do not rely entirely on:

```text id="u9b8c2"
Gateway says authenticated
```

as proof that:

```text
Course Service
```

should allow the operation.

---

# 87.74 Defense in Depth

Security should exist at multiple layers:

```text id="p8z3vn"
Network
 ↓
Gateway
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Database
```

No single layer should be the only defense for critical operations.

---

# 87.75 Authentication Failure Handling

Authentication errors SHOULD be generic enough to avoid unnecessary information leakage.

Do not expose internal authentication implementation details.

---

# 87.76 Authorization Failure Handling

Authorization failures SHOULD be consistent and auditable.

The API should not accidentally return:

```text id="1p7t9q"
500 Internal Server Error
```

when the actual condition is:

```text id="j2k5w4"
403 Forbidden
```

---

# 87.77 Testing Authentication

Test at least:

```text id="0x2n4q"
Valid login
Invalid password
Unknown user
Expired token
Malformed token
Wrong issuer
Wrong audience
Invalid signature
Disabled account
```

---

# 87.78 Testing Authorization

Test:

```text id="d7v1n6"
Student → student resource
Student → instructor resource
Instructor → own course
Instructor → another instructor's course
Admin → administrative endpoint
Unauthenticated → protected endpoint
```

The second category is especially important.

Many applications test "can access" but fail to test "cannot access."

---

# 87.79 Security Regression Tests

Authorization rules SHOULD have automated regression tests.

If a developer accidentally removes:

```text id="l2b5x7"
@PreAuthorize(...)
```

or equivalent service-level checks, CI should catch the regression.

---

# 87.80 Definition of Done

Authentication/authorization is production-ready when:

* [ ] Authentication architecture is documented
* [ ] OIDC/OAuth2/JWT strategy is defined
* [ ] Access-token lifetime is defined
* [ ] Refresh-token strategy is defined
* [ ] Token revocation strategy exists
* [ ] Signing keys are securely managed
* [ ] Passwords are securely hashed
* [ ] Password reset is secure
* [ ] MFA strategy exists for privileged users
* [ ] Roles are defined
* [ ] Permissions are defined where required
* [ ] Resource ownership checks exist
* [ ] Object-level authorization is tested
* [ ] Service-to-service authentication exists
* [ ] Least privilege is enforced
* [ ] Sensitive fields are protected
* [ ] Tokens are not logged
* [ ] Audit logging exists
* [ ] Rate limiting exists for sensitive endpoints
* [ ] CORS is controlled
* [ ] CSRF requirements are understood
* [ ] Security regression tests exist
* [ ] Key rotation strategy exists

---

# 87.81 Core Principles

1. **Authentication ≠ authorization.**
2. **The backend is the security boundary.**
3. **Frontend authorization is not security.**
4. **Never trust role claims without validating the token.**
5. **Never trust resource IDs without checking authorization.**
6. **Use least privilege everywhere.**
7. **Keep access tokens short-lived.**
8. **Protect refresh tokens aggressively.**
9. **Never store plaintext passwords.**
10. **Never log tokens or passwords.**
11. **Privileged accounts need stronger protection.**
12. **Resource ownership matters as much as role membership.**
13. **Internal services must not automatically trust each other.**
14. **Authorization decisions need automated tests, especially negative tests.**
15. **Security architecture must account for revocation, not just initial login.**
16. **Do not build a custom identity platform unless there is a compelling reason.**

> **For Mediverse, the biggest security mistake would be implementing JWT login and assuming authentication is finished. It isn't. The dangerous part starts after login: resource-level authorization, role escalation, token lifecycle, refresh-token theft, disabled-account behavior, service-to-service trust, and tenant isolation. Build those rules explicitly and test the cases where access must be denied—not just the happy path.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 88: Frontend Architecture & React Standards — React structure, component architecture, state management, routing, API integration, forms, error handling, performance, accessibility, security, design system, and frontend observability.**


# CSDG — Chapter 88

## Frontend Architecture & React Standards

### 88.1 Purpose

This chapter defines standards for the Mediverse frontend: React architecture, component design, state management, routing, API communication, forms, error handling, performance, accessibility, security, and maintainability.

Core principle:

> **The frontend is not merely a collection of screens. It is a client application with its own architecture, state model, security constraints, performance requirements, and contracts with backend APIs.**

---

## 88.2 Recommended Frontend Architecture

Mediverse SHOULD use a feature-oriented structure rather than organizing the entire application only by technical type.

Recommended:

```text
src/
├── app/
│   ├── router/
│   ├── providers/
│   ├── store/
│   └── config/
│
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   ├── courses/
│   ├── modules/
│   ├── lessons/
│   ├── quizzes/
│   ├── progress/
│   ├── users/
│   └── admin/
│
├── components/
│   ├── ui/
│   ├── layout/
│   └── common/
│
├── services/
│   ├── api/
│   └── storage/
│
├── hooks/
├── utils/
├── types/
├── constants/
└── assets/
```

The exact structure may evolve, but ownership of code should remain obvious.

---

# 88.3 Feature-Based Organization

Instead of:

```text
components/
controllers/
services/
pages/
```

for the entire application, prefer:

```text
features/
└── courses/
    ├── components/
    ├── pages/
    ├── hooks/
    ├── api/
    ├── types/
    └── store/
```

This makes large applications easier to maintain.

---

# 88.4 Component Responsibilities

A React component SHOULD have a clear responsibility.

Bad:

```text
CoursePage
 ├── API calls
 ├── authentication logic
 ├── database-shaped data manipulation
 ├── 1000 lines of UI
 ├── business rules
 └── navigation logic
```

Prefer:

```text
CoursePage
   ↓
CourseHeader
CourseOverview
CourseModules
CourseProgress
```

with business/API logic separated appropriately.

---

# 88.5 Component Size

There is no magical line-count limit for React components.

However, a component should be considered for decomposition when:

* It has multiple unrelated responsibilities.
* Logic becomes difficult to test.
* Conditional rendering becomes deeply nested.
* The same UI logic is repeated.
* Changes to one feature repeatedly risk breaking another.

Do not split components merely to reduce line count.

---

# 88.6 Presentational vs Container Logic

Where useful, separate:

```text
Data/state logic
       ↓
Container / hook
       ↓
Presentation
```

But do not turn this into unnecessary abstraction.

Modern React can comfortably colocate related logic when the component remains understandable.

---

# 88.7 Reusable UI Components

Common UI components SHOULD be centralized.

Examples:

```text
Button
Input
Modal
Dialog
Card
Table
Pagination
LoadingSpinner
EmptyState
ErrorState
Toast
ConfirmDialog
```

---

# 88.8 Design System

Mediverse SHOULD maintain a consistent design system.

Define:

```text
Typography
Spacing
Colors
Borders
Elevation
Breakpoints
Buttons
Forms
Cards
Navigation
Feedback states
```

Avoid every feature inventing its own visual language.

---

# 88.9 Material UI / Tailwind

If the project uses MUI and/or Tailwind, establish clear ownership.

Do not randomly mix:

```text
MUI
Tailwind
plain CSS
CSS modules
styled-components
```

without architectural rules.

A hybrid system can become difficult to maintain.

---

# 88.10 Routing

Routes SHOULD represent application navigation and user intent.

Example:

```text
/login
/register
/dashboard
/courses
/courses/:courseId
/courses/:courseId/modules
/courses/:courseId/lessons/:lessonId
/quizzes/:quizId
/profile
/admin
```

---

# 88.11 Route Protection

Protected routes SHOULD verify authentication state.

Conceptually:

```text
Route
 ↓
Authentication check
 ↓
Authorization check
 ↓
Page
```

But remember:

> Route protection is not backend authorization.

The API must independently enforce access.

---

# 88.12 Role-Based Routes

Administrative pages MAY be protected based on roles/permissions.

Example:

```text
/admin
    ↓
ADMIN permission?
    ↓
Yes → render
No  → access denied
```

---

# 88.13 Route-Level Code Splitting

Large features SHOULD use lazy loading where beneficial.

Conceptually:

```text
Dashboard
Courses
Quiz
Admin
```

need not all be downloaded immediately on initial page load.

---

# 88.14 State Categories

Not all state belongs in Redux.

Distinguish:

### Local UI state

```text
Modal open/closed
Selected tab
Input value
Dropdown state
```

### Server state

```text
Courses
Lessons
Quiz data
Progress
User profile
```

### Global client state

```text
Authentication context
Theme
Global preferences
Application configuration
```

---

# 88.15 Server State

Server state SHOULD generally be managed using a data-fetching/cache solution where appropriate.

Examples include:

```text
TanStack Query
RTK Query
```

Do not automatically put every API response into a giant Redux store.

---

# 88.16 Redux

Redux Toolkit MAY be used for genuine application-wide client state.

Prefer:

```text
Redux Toolkit
```

over manually implementing Redux patterns.

---

# 88.17 Avoid Redux Abuse

Do not put:

```text
isModalOpen
temporaryInput
hoveredElement
localDropdownValue
```

into global Redux state unless there is a concrete reason.

---

# 88.18 API Layer

Frontend API calls SHOULD be centralized.

Example:

```text
services/api/
    authApi
    courseApi
    quizApi
    progressApi
```

Avoid scattering raw Axios/fetch calls throughout UI components.

Bad:

```javascript
useEffect(() => {
  axios.get(...)
}, [])
```

in dozens of unrelated components.

---

# 88.19 API Client

Create a consistent HTTP client abstraction.

Conceptually:

```text
React
 ↓
API Client
 ↓
HTTP
 ↓
Backend
```

The client can centralize:

```text
Base URL
Headers
Authentication
Timeout
Error normalization
Request IDs
```

---

# 88.20 Authentication Handling

The frontend SHOULD NOT implement authentication rules independently from the backend.

It should consume the authentication contract.

Example:

```text
Login
 ↓
Authentication system
 ↓
Authenticated session
 ↓
Frontend state
```

---

# 88.21 Token Handling

Token storage must follow the chosen authentication architecture.

Do not blindly use:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("token", token)
```

for every authentication design.

The security implications must be understood.

---

# 88.22 API Error Handling

The frontend SHOULD normalize backend errors.

Example backend:

```json
{
  "code": "COURSE_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "Course was not found"
}
```

Frontend:

```text
API Error
   ↓
Error normalization
   ↓
UI-specific handling
```

---

# 88.23 Error Categories

Frontend should distinguish:

```text
Validation error
Authentication error
Authorization error
Not found
Conflict
Rate limited
Server failure
Network failure
Timeout
```

Do not display:

```text
"Something went wrong"
```

for every possible failure.

---

# 88.24 User-Friendly Errors

Technical errors should be translated into appropriate user-facing messages.

Bad:

```text
HibernateLazyInitializationException
```

Good:

```text
"We couldn't load the course right now. Please try again."
```

---

# 88.25 Retry UI

Retry SHOULD be offered when the error is likely temporary.

Example:

```text
Unable to load course.

[Try Again]
```

Do not offer retry for every authorization failure.

---

# 88.26 Loading States

Every asynchronous UI SHOULD define its loading state.

Example:

```text
Loading
   ↓
Success
```

or:

```text
Loading
   ↓
Error
```

---

# 88.27 Skeleton Loading

Skeletons MAY be used for content-heavy pages.

Example:

```text
████████████
████████
████████████████
```

They should represent the approximate final layout.

---

# 88.28 Empty States

Empty data is not necessarily an error.

Example:

```text
No courses enrolled yet.

[Explore Courses]
```

Do not display:

```text
Error loading courses
```

when the API successfully returned an empty list.

---

# 88.29 Forms

Forms SHOULD have:

```text
Validation
Clear labels
Error messages
Loading state
Submission feedback
Accessible controls
```

---

# 88.30 Client vs Server Validation

Frontend validation improves UX.

Backend validation provides security and correctness.

Therefore:

```text
Frontend validation
+
Backend validation
```

are both required.

Never rely only on React validation.

---

# 88.31 Form Submission

During submission:

```text
Idle
 ↓
Submitting
 ↓
Success / Error
```

The submit button SHOULD prevent accidental duplicate submissions where appropriate.

---

# 88.32 Optimistic Updates

Optimistic updates MAY be used when:

```text
Operation is highly likely to succeed
Rollback is straightforward
User experience benefits significantly
```

Example:

```text
Like lesson
 ↓
UI immediately updates
 ↓
API request
```

But avoid optimistic updates for operations where incorrect temporary state could cause serious confusion.

---

# 88.33 Pagination

Large datasets SHOULD use pagination or incremental loading.

Examples:

```text
Courses
Questions
Users
Audit logs
Notifications
```

Do not load thousands of records into the browser unnecessarily.

---

# 88.34 Infinite Scrolling

Infinite scrolling MAY be used for feeds or content exploration.

It should not be used automatically.

For administrative tables, traditional pagination is often easier to operate.

---

# 88.35 Search Debouncing

Search inputs that trigger API calls SHOULD use debouncing.

Example:

```text
User types:
cardio

Instead of:
c
ca
car
card
cardi
cardio

send one request after a short delay.
```

---

# 88.36 Request Cancellation

The frontend SHOULD cancel or ignore stale requests where appropriate.

Example:

```text
Search: cardio
Search: cardiovascular
```

The response for the older request must not overwrite the newer result.

---

# 88.37 Race Conditions

Frontend asynchronous operations can race.

Bad:

```text
Request A
Request B
Response B
Response A
```

If A overwrites B, the UI displays stale data.

Use cancellation, request IDs, or a proper server-state library.

---

# 88.38 Caching

Cache data that benefits from reuse.

Examples:

```text
Course metadata
User profile
Reference data
```

But avoid caching data indefinitely.

Define:

```text
Cache lifetime
Invalidation strategy
Refetch behavior
```

---

# 88.39 Cache Invalidation

After mutations, stale cached data must be invalidated or updated.

Example:

```text
Update Course
   ↓
Invalidate courses query
   ↓
Refetch
```

---

# 88.40 Accessibility

Accessibility MUST be considered from the beginning.

The application SHOULD support:

```text
Keyboard navigation
Screen readers
Focus management
Semantic HTML
Accessible labels
Sufficient contrast
Reduced-motion preferences
```

---

# 88.41 Semantic HTML

Prefer:

```html
<button>
<nav>
<main>
<header>
<footer>
<form>
<label>
```

over using:

```html
<div onClick="...">
```

for everything.

---

# 88.42 Keyboard Navigation

Users must be able to perform important workflows without relying entirely on a mouse.

Test:

```text
Tab
Shift + Tab
Enter
Space
Escape
Arrow keys
```

where appropriate.

---

# 88.43 Focus Management

Dialogs and route transitions should manage focus appropriately.

When a modal opens:

```text
Focus → modal
```

When it closes:

```text
Focus → triggering element
```

---

# 88.44 Images

Images SHOULD have meaningful alternative text when they convey information.

Decorative images SHOULD be treated as decorative.

---

# 88.45 Medical Educational Content

Because Mediverse is an educational platform, accessibility is especially important for:

```text
Anatomy diagrams
Physiology diagrams
Flowcharts
3D models
Medical illustrations
Videos
Audio
```

Important information contained only in a visual should have an accessible textual equivalent where practical.

---

# 88.46 3D Content

3D visualization SHOULD NOT become the only way to understand educational material.

For example:

```text
3D Heart
+
2D diagram
+
Text explanation
+
Labels
+
Audio narration
```

This provides multiple learning modalities.

---

# 88.47 Responsive Design

The frontend SHOULD support:

```text
Mobile
Tablet
Desktop
Large displays
```

Do not design desktop first and simply shrink it.

Important interactions should remain usable on small screens.

---

# 88.48 Mobile Navigation

Mobile navigation SHOULD prioritize the most important tasks.

Avoid forcing desktop navigation patterns into narrow screens.

---

# 88.49 Performance Budget

The frontend SHOULD define measurable performance targets.

Monitor:

```text
LCP
INP
CLS
TTFB
JavaScript bundle size
Image size
API latency
```

---

# 88.50 Bundle Optimization

Avoid shipping unnecessary code.

Use:

```text
Code splitting
Tree shaking
Lazy loading
Dependency analysis
Image optimization
```

---

# 88.51 Images

Large images SHOULD be optimized.

Use:

```text
WebP
AVIF
Responsive images
Lazy loading
Appropriate dimensions
```

where supported by the platform and requirements.

---

# 88.52 Video

Educational videos can dominate bandwidth.

Use:

```text
Adaptive streaming where required
Poster images
Lazy loading
Appropriate resolutions
CDN delivery
```

Do not load full high-resolution videos on initial page load.

---

# 88.53 Audio

Audio lessons SHOULD support:

```text
Play/pause
Seek
Volume
Playback speed
Progress
Accessible controls
```

---

# 88.54 3D Performance

3D modules SHOULD consider:

```text
Model complexity
Texture size
GPU usage
Memory usage
Device capability
Lazy loading
Level of detail
```

A medical 3D model that crashes mobile browsers is not a successful feature.

---

# 88.55 WebGL Fallback

If a device cannot support the intended 3D experience, provide an alternative.

Example:

```text
3D unavailable
     ↓
2D interactive diagram
     ↓
Text explanation
```

---

# 88.56 Security

Frontend security SHOULD address:

```text
XSS
CSRF where applicable
Dependency vulnerabilities
Sensitive data exposure
Unsafe HTML rendering
Insecure storage
Clickjacking
Content Security Policy
```

---

# 88.57 Dangerous HTML

Avoid rendering arbitrary HTML from users.

If HTML must be rendered:

```text
sanitize
+
validate
+
restrict allowed content
```

---

# 88.58 Dependency Management

Frontend dependencies SHOULD be:

```text
Tracked
Updated
Scanned
Removed when unused
```

Do not accumulate packages merely because they solve a tiny problem.

---

# 88.59 Environment Configuration

Frontend configuration SHOULD distinguish:

```text
Development
UAT
Production
```

Never embed production secrets into a browser bundle.

Important:

> **Anything shipped to the browser should be considered public.**

---

# 88.60 API URLs

Environment-specific API endpoints SHOULD be configurable.

Example:

```text
Development
→ http://localhost:8080

UAT
→ UAT API

Production
→ Production API
```

Do not hardcode environment-specific URLs throughout components.

---

# 88.61 Logging

Frontend logs SHOULD be controlled.

Do not leave verbose debugging enabled in production.

Never log:

```text
Passwords
Tokens
Sensitive medical/user data
Private information
```

---

# 88.62 Error Monitoring

Production frontend SHOULD use error monitoring.

Useful information:

```text
Error
Stack
Browser
OS
Application version
Route
Release
Trace ID
```

Sensitive information should be filtered.

---

# 88.63 Frontend Observability

Frontend observability should connect with backend observability where practical.

Conceptually:

```text
Browser
 traceId = ABC
   ↓
API Gateway
 traceId = ABC
   ↓
Course Service
 traceId = ABC
```

This dramatically simplifies debugging.

---

# 88.64 API Contract Types

Frontend SHOULD derive or maintain typed API contracts where practical.

For TypeScript:

```text
Course
CourseResponse
CourseCreateRequest
CourseUpdateRequest
ApiError
```

Avoid using:

```typescript
any
```

as the default escape hatch.

---

# 88.65 Type Safety

TypeScript SHOULD be preferred for a large production React application.

Use types to detect:

```text
Missing fields
Wrong response assumptions
Invalid component props
Incorrect API usage
```

before runtime.

---

# 88.66 Component Props

Props should be explicit and meaningful.

Bad:

```text
<Component data={everything} />
```

Prefer:

```text
<CourseCard
  title={course.title}
  duration={course.duration}
  progress={course.progress}
/>
```

when that improves clarity.

---

# 88.67 Prop Drilling

If data passes through many unrelated components:

```text
A
 ↓
B
 ↓
C
 ↓
D
 ↓
E
```

consider:

```text
Context
State management
Custom hook
Server-state library
```

But do not introduce global state merely because props passed through two components.

---

# 88.68 Context API

Context is appropriate for relatively stable cross-cutting concerns such as:

```text
Theme
Localization
Authentication context
```

Avoid putting rapidly changing large datasets into a single global context.

---

# 88.69 Custom Hooks

Custom hooks SHOULD encapsulate reusable behavior.

Examples:

```text
useAuth()
useCourses()
useDebounce()
usePagination()
useMediaQuery()
useQuiz()
```

---

# 88.70 Business Logic

Complex business rules SHOULD NOT be scattered across JSX.

Bad:

```text
{user.role === "ADMIN" &&
 course.status === "DRAFT" &&
 user.department === course.department &&
 ... && ...}
```

across dozens of components.

Centralize important rules.

---

# 88.71 Internationalization

If Mediverse is expected to support multiple languages, internationalization SHOULD be designed early.

Potential languages may include:

```text
English
Marathi
Hindi
```

depending on product requirements.

Do not hardcode every user-facing string directly into components if localization is a committed requirement.

---

# 88.72 Date and Time

Dates SHOULD be represented using consistent backend/frontend contracts.

Avoid manually parsing ambiguous strings.

Prefer standardized formats such as ISO 8601.

---

# 88.73 Time Zones

The application SHOULD explicitly define whether a date/time represents:

```text
UTC
User local time
Institution local time
```

This matters for:

```text
Exam schedules
Deadlines
Notifications
Learning sessions
Certificates
```

---

# 88.74 State Machines

Complex workflows MAY benefit from explicit state modeling.

Example quiz:

```text
NOT_STARTED
   ↓
IN_PROGRESS
   ↓
SUBMITTING
   ↓
SUBMITTED
   ↓
EVALUATED
```

Avoid representing complex workflows with dozens of unrelated booleans.

Bad:

```text
isStarted
isSubmitting
isSubmitted
isEvaluated
isLoading
```

which can accidentally create impossible combinations.

---

# 88.75 Feature Flags

Feature flags MAY be used for controlled rollout.

Example:

```text
ENABLE_3D_HEART_V2
```

Useful for:

```text
Beta features
A/B testing
Gradual rollout
Emergency disablement
```

Do not let feature flags become permanent undocumented architecture.

---

# 88.76 Testing Pyramid

Frontend testing SHOULD include:

```text
Unit tests
Integration/component tests
End-to-end tests
```

---

# 88.77 Unit Tests

Use unit tests for isolated logic.

Examples:

```text
Utility functions
Validation
Transformations
Business calculations
```

---

# 88.78 Component Tests

Test important UI behavior.

Example:

```text
Course page
 ↓
loads course
 ↓
renders modules
 ↓
handles loading
 ↓
handles API error
```

---

# 88.79 End-to-End Tests

Critical user journeys SHOULD have E2E tests.

Examples:

```text
Register
Login
Browse course
Open lesson
Take quiz
Submit quiz
View progress
```

---

# 88.80 Negative Testing

Do not test only:

```text
Everything works
```

Also test:

```text
Unauthorized user
Expired authentication
Network failure
Empty response
Invalid input
Slow API
Duplicate submission
Mobile viewport
```

---

# 88.81 Frontend Definition of Done

A feature is not complete until:

* [ ] Responsive UI exists
* [ ] Loading state exists
* [ ] Empty state exists
* [ ] Error state exists
* [ ] API integration is centralized
* [ ] Validation exists
* [ ] Authorization behavior is handled
* [ ] Accessibility is considered
* [ ] Keyboard navigation works
* [ ] Mobile layout works
* [ ] Tests exist
* [ ] Performance impact is understood
* [ ] Sensitive data is protected
* [ ] Production logging is safe
* [ ] Documentation exists where required

---

# 88.82 Recommended Mediverse Frontend Flow

A typical course page should follow:

```text
User
 ↓
React Router
 ↓
Course Page
 ↓
Course Hook / Server-State Layer
 ↓
API Client
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Course Service
 ↓
Response DTO
 ↓
API Client
 ↓
Cache / State
 ↓
React Components
 ↓
User
```

Not:

```text
Component
 ↓
Random Axios call
 ↓
JPA entity
 ↓
Some global state
 ↓
Another component modifies it
```

---

# 88.83 Core Principles

1. **Organize around features, not only file types.**
2. **Keep components focused.**
3. **Do not put every piece of state into Redux.**
4. **Treat server state differently from UI state.**
5. **Centralize API communication.**
6. **Frontend validation improves UX; backend validation enforces correctness.**
7. **Never treat frontend authorization as security.**
8. **Every asynchronous operation needs loading/error/success handling.**
9. **Design for accessibility from the beginning.**
10. **3D, video, and audio must have performance and accessibility strategies.**
11. **Anything delivered to the browser is potentially visible to the user.**
12. **Never ship secrets in frontend code.**
13. **Use TypeScript for a large production React application.**
14. **Test failure paths, not just successful paths.**
15. **Do not introduce abstractions until they solve a real problem.**
16. **A visually impressive frontend with poor loading, error handling, accessibility, and mobile behavior is not production quality.**

> **For Mediverse, the frontend must be treated as a serious application architecture, not just a UI layer. The biggest mistake would be building beautiful medical-learning screens while allowing API calls, authentication, state, 3D assets, errors, and business rules to become scattered across components. Establish the architecture first, then build features inside it.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 89: Database Architecture & Data Management Standards — PostgreSQL, schema design, normalization, indexing, transactions, constraints, migrations, JPA/Hibernate, query optimization, connection pooling, partitioning, backups, and data lifecycle.**


# CSDG — Chapter 89

## Database Architecture & Data Management Standards

### 89.1 Purpose

This chapter defines standards for PostgreSQL database architecture, schema design, relationships, constraints, indexing, transactions, JPA/Hibernate usage, migrations, performance, backup, recovery, and data lifecycle within Mediverse.

Core principle:

> **The database is not merely persistent storage. It is part of the system's correctness boundary.**

Application code can contain bugs. The database should prevent invalid states wherever practical.

---

## 89.2 Primary Database

For the core Mediverse transactional platform:

```text
PostgreSQL
     ↓
Primary transactional database
```

PostgreSQL SHOULD be the authoritative source for structured transactional data such as:

```text
Users
Courses
Modules
Lessons
Questions
Quizzes
Enrollments
Progress
Assessments
Certificates
```

---

# 89.3 Database Ownership

Each service SHOULD have clearly defined ownership of its data.

Example:

```text
User Service
   ↓
User data

Course Service
   ↓
Course data

Quiz Service
   ↓
Quiz data

Progress Service
   ↓
Progress data
```

A service should not directly modify another service's tables.

---

# 89.4 Database-per-Service

For a true microservices architecture:

```text
User Service
   ↓
User DB

Course Service
   ↓
Course DB

Quiz Service
   ↓
Quiz DB
```

This provides strong ownership boundaries.

However:

> Do not introduce database-per-service merely because "microservices require it."

For an early-stage Mediverse system, a modular monolith with PostgreSQL may be significantly simpler.

---

# 89.5 Modular Monolith Option

A modular architecture can initially use:

```text
Mediverse Application
       ↓
PostgreSQL
       ├── user
       ├── course
       ├── quiz
       ├── progress
       └── notification
```

while keeping module boundaries clear.

This allows future extraction into services.

---

# 89.6 Schema Ownership

Database schemas MAY represent bounded domains.

Example:

```text
user_schema
course_schema
quiz_schema
progress_schema
```

The important requirement is clear ownership.

---

# 89.7 Naming Convention

Use consistent naming.

Recommended:

```text
snake_case
```

Example:

```text
course_id
created_at
updated_at
published_at
course_status
```

Avoid inconsistent combinations such as:

```text
courseId
course_id
CourseID
COURSE_ID
```

within the same database.

---

# 89.8 Table Naming

Use consistent table names.

Example:

```text
users
courses
modules
lessons
quizzes
questions
enrollments
progress_records
```

Avoid unnecessary abbreviations.

Bad:

```text
usr
crs
mdl
```

---

# 89.9 Primary Keys

Every major entity SHOULD have a stable primary key.

Example:

```text
users
------
id
```

The identifier should not depend on mutable business information.

---

# 89.10 UUID vs Numeric IDs

Both are valid.

### Numeric

```text
BIGINT
```

Advantages:

```text
Compact
Fast indexing
Simple
```

### UUID

```text
UUID
```

Advantages:

```text
Globally unique
Harder to guess
Useful across distributed systems
```

The choice should be architectural, not fashionable.

---

# 89.11 Do Not Use Business Fields as IDs

Avoid:

```text
email → primary key
course_name → primary key
mobile_number → primary key
```

Business values can change.

---

# 89.12 Foreign Keys

Relationships SHOULD normally be enforced with foreign keys when the database boundary allows it.

Example:

```text
courses
   |
   └── instructor_id
          ↓
       users.id
```

---

# 89.13 Referential Integrity

The database should prevent invalid relationships.

Example:

```text
Enrollment
   ↓
student_id = 999999
```

must not reference a nonexistent student if a foreign-key relationship is intended.

---

# 89.14 NOT NULL

Fields required for a valid entity SHOULD be declared `NOT NULL`.

Bad:

```text
course.name
```

allowing:

```text
NULL
```

when every course must have a name.

---

# 89.15 UNIQUE Constraints

Business uniqueness should be enforced at the database level.

Example:

```text
users.email UNIQUE
```

Do not rely only on:

```text
SELECT → check exists → INSERT
```

because concurrent requests can bypass the application check.

---

# 89.16 Check Constraints

Use database constraints for simple invariants.

Example:

```sql
CHECK (duration_minutes > 0)
```

Another:

```sql
CHECK (passing_score >= 0 AND passing_score <= 100)
```

---

# 89.17 Database Constraints vs Application Validation

Use both.

```text
Frontend
   ↓
Backend validation
   ↓
Database constraints
```

Each layer has a different responsibility.

---

# 89.18 Normalization

Transactional data SHOULD generally follow normalized relational design.

Typical target:

```text
1NF
2NF
3NF
```

Avoid unnecessary duplication.

Example:

Bad:

```text
enrollment
--------------------------------
student_name
student_email
course_name
course_description
```

Better:

```text
students
courses
enrollments
```

---

# 89.19 Denormalization

Denormalization MAY be introduced when there is a demonstrated performance or reporting requirement.

Do not denormalize prematurely.

You are trading:

```text
Read performance
```

for:

```text
Data duplication
Consistency complexity
Update complexity
```

---

# 89.20 Core Mediverse Relationships

A simplified model:

```text
User
 │
 ├── Enrollment ── Course
 │                    │
 │                    └── Module
 │                          │
 │                          └── Lesson
 │
 └── Progress
```

Quiz:

```text
Course
  ↓
Quiz
  ↓
Question
  ↓
Answer Option
```

---

# 89.21 Enrollment

Enrollment SHOULD be modeled independently.

Example:

```text
enrollments
-----------
id
student_id
course_id
enrolled_at
status
completed_at
```

---

# 89.22 Enrollment Uniqueness

A student should not accidentally receive duplicate active enrollments for the same course.

A suitable uniqueness rule MAY be:

```text
(student_id, course_id)
```

depending on the product's re-enrollment requirements.

---

# 89.23 Course Hierarchy

Recommended:

```text
Course
 ↓
Module
 ↓
Lesson
 ↓
Content
```

Do not store an entire course hierarchy inside one giant JSON field unless there is a compelling reason.

---

# 89.24 Lesson Content

Structured lesson metadata SHOULD be relational.

Large or flexible educational content MAY use JSONB where appropriate.

Example:

```text
lessons
-------
id
module_id
title
content_type
duration
sequence_number
status
```

---

# 89.25 JSONB

PostgreSQL JSONB is useful for flexible structures.

Examples:

```text
Interactive configuration
3D model metadata
Quiz configuration
UI configuration
Flexible content metadata
```

But:

> JSONB is not a substitute for relational modeling.

Do not put the entire application database into one JSONB column.

---

# 89.26 JSONB Indexing

If JSONB fields are queried frequently, appropriate indexes SHOULD be considered.

Potentially:

```text
GIN index
```

depending on query patterns.

---

# 89.27 Timestamps

Major tables SHOULD track lifecycle timestamps where useful.

Typical:

```text
created_at
updated_at
deleted_at
published_at
```

Do not add timestamps blindly to every table if they have no semantic value.

---

# 89.28 UTC

Persist timestamps consistently, preferably in UTC.

Convert to user/institution timezone at presentation boundaries.

This avoids major problems with:

```text
Daylight saving
International users
Distributed services
```

---

# 89.29 Soft Delete

Soft deletion MAY be appropriate for important business records.

Example:

```text
deleted_at
```

But soft delete is not automatically better.

It creates complications around:

```text
Unique constraints
Queries
Indexes
Storage growth
Referential integrity
```

Use it intentionally.

---

# 89.30 Hard Delete

Hard deletion SHOULD be used when legally and architecturally appropriate.

Examples may include:

```text
Temporary records
Expired tokens
Short-lived sessions
Temporary processing data
```

---

# 89.31 Data Retention

Every major data category SHOULD have a retention policy.

Example:

```text
Authentication logs → defined retention
Audit logs → defined retention
Temporary files → short retention
Learning progress → long-term retention
```

Retention must align with applicable legal and institutional requirements.

---

# 89.32 Database Migrations

Schema changes MUST be version-controlled.

Use a migration tool such as:

```text
Flyway
Liquibase
```

Do not manually modify production schemas as the normal deployment mechanism.

---

# 89.33 Migration Example

Conceptually:

```text
V1__create_users.sql
V2__create_courses.sql
V3__add_course_status.sql
V4__create_enrollments.sql
```

Every environment should be reproducible from migration history.

---

# 89.34 Migration Immutability

Applied migrations SHOULD NOT be modified casually.

If a migration is already deployed:

```text
V4
```

do not rewrite V4 to produce a different schema.

Create:

```text
V5
```

for the new change.

---

# 89.35 Zero-Downtime Migration

Production schema changes SHOULD consider compatibility between:

```text
Old application version
New application version
```

Prefer:

```text
Expand
 ↓
Deploy compatible application
 ↓
Migrate data
 ↓
Remove old structure
```

rather than destructive one-step changes.

---

# 89.36 Example

Do not immediately:

```text
DROP old_column
```

if the currently running application still reads it.

Prefer:

```text
Add new column
 ↓
Deploy code supporting both
 ↓
Migrate data
 ↓
Switch reads/writes
 ↓
Remove old column later
```

---

# 89.37 Transactions

Operations requiring atomicity MUST use database transactions.

Example enrollment:

```text
Create enrollment
+
Initialize progress
+
Create audit record
```

If one required operation fails:

```text
ROLLBACK
```

---

# 89.38 Transaction Boundaries

Transactions SHOULD be as short as practical.

Avoid:

```text
BEGIN
 ↓
API call
 ↓
Wait 10 seconds
 ↓
external service
 ↓
database update
 ↓
COMMIT
```

Long transactions create locking and scalability problems.

---

# 89.39 External Calls and Transactions

Do not assume a database transaction can atomically include:

```text
PostgreSQL
+
Kafka
+
S3
+
External API
```

These are separate systems.

Use appropriate patterns such as:

```text
Outbox
Saga
Idempotency
Compensation
```

where required.

---

# 89.40 Isolation Levels

The application should understand PostgreSQL transaction isolation.

Typical levels include:

```text
READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
SERIALIZABLE
```

Use the weakest level that correctly satisfies the business requirement.

Do not select `SERIALIZABLE` everywhere just because it sounds safer.

---

# 89.41 Optimistic Locking

For concurrently modified entities, optimistic locking SHOULD be considered.

JPA example:

```java
@Version
private Long version;
```

This can prevent silent overwrites.

---

# 89.42 Pessimistic Locking

Pessimistic locking MAY be appropriate for highly contention-sensitive operations.

Example:

```text
Seat allocation
Limited resource allocation
Critical inventory-like operations
```

But it can reduce concurrency.

---

# 89.43 Indexes

Indexes SHOULD be based on actual query patterns.

Common candidates:

```text
Foreign keys
Search fields
Frequently filtered columns
Sort columns
Unique business identifiers
```

---

# 89.44 Index Cost

Indexes are not free.

Every index increases:

```text
Storage
INSERT cost
UPDATE cost
DELETE cost
Maintenance
```

Therefore:

> **Do not index every column.**

---

# 89.45 Composite Indexes

Composite indexes SHOULD follow actual query patterns.

Example query:

```sql
WHERE course_id = ?
AND status = ?
ORDER BY created_at DESC
```

may benefit from an appropriately designed composite index.

---

# 89.46 Column Order

For composite indexes, column order matters.

Do not blindly create:

```text
(course_id, status, created_at)
```

without understanding the application's query patterns and selectivity.

---

# 89.47 Query Plans

Slow queries SHOULD be investigated using:

```sql
EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

Do not optimize database queries based purely on intuition.

---

# 89.48 N+1 Query Problem

Hibernate/JPA applications MUST actively monitor for N+1 queries.

Example:

```text
SELECT courses
       ↓
SELECT modules for course 1
SELECT modules for course 2
SELECT modules for course 3
...
```

A single page can accidentally generate hundreds of queries.

---

# 89.49 Fetch Strategy

Do not solve every N+1 problem with:

```text
FetchType.EAGER
```

This can create different performance problems.

Prefer explicit fetching strategies appropriate to the use case.

---

# 89.50 DTO Projections

For read-heavy APIs, DTO projections MAY be preferable to loading entire entity graphs.

Example:

```text
CourseSummaryDTO
```

instead of:

```text
Course
 + instructor
 + modules
 + lessons
 + quizzes
 + progress
```

when the screen only needs five fields.

---

# 89.51 Pagination

Database queries returning potentially large datasets MUST use pagination.

Bad:

```text
SELECT * FROM audit_logs;
```

for an admin UI.

Better:

```text
LIMIT
OFFSET
```

or keyset/cursor pagination where appropriate.

---

# 89.52 Keyset Pagination

For very large datasets, keyset pagination MAY outperform offset pagination.

Conceptually:

```text
WHERE id > last_seen_id
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 50
```

This is particularly useful for:

```text
Feeds
Audit logs
Large event tables
```

---

# 89.53 Connection Pooling

Spring Boot applications SHOULD use a database connection pool such as:

```text
HikariCP
```

Connection pool size must be tuned based on:

```text
Application concurrency
Database capacity
Query duration
Number of application instances
```

---

# 89.54 Connection Pool Misconfiguration

Do not configure:

```text
100 connections
```

for every service simply because the server has 16 CPU cores.

If ten application instances each open 100 connections:

```text
10 × 100 = 1000 connections
```

The database may collapse under the load.

---

# 89.55 Database Capacity

Database sizing must consider:

```text
CPU
RAM
IOPS
Storage
Connections
Query patterns
Replication
Backup workload
```

---

# 89.56 Read Replicas

Read replicas MAY be introduced when read workload justifies them.

Example:

```text
Primary
 ├── Writes
 └── Critical reads

Replica
 └── Read-heavy workloads
```

But replicas introduce replication lag.

---

# 89.57 Replication Lag

Never assume:

```text
WRITE → immediately visible on replica
```

For workflows requiring read-after-write consistency, route the relevant read appropriately.

---

# 89.58 Caching

Redis MAY be used for frequently accessed data.

Example:

```text
Course metadata
Reference data
Session information
Rate-limit counters
```

But PostgreSQL remains the authoritative transactional store unless explicitly designed otherwise.

---

# 89.59 Cache Invalidation

Cache invalidation MUST be designed.

Example:

```text
Update Course
 ↓
Update database
 ↓
Invalidate/update Redis
```

Otherwise users may see stale educational content.

---

# 89.60 Distributed Cache

When multiple application instances exist:

```text
App 1
App 2
App 3
```

a local in-memory cache on each instance can become inconsistent.

Use shared cache infrastructure where necessary.

---

# 89.61 Database Transactions and Cache

Do not blindly assume:

```text
DB commit
+
cache update
```

are atomic.

For critical workflows, carefully design the consistency model.

---

# 89.62 Outbox Pattern

For reliable database-to-event publishing:

```text
Business transaction
      ↓
PostgreSQL
 ├── business record
 └── outbox event
      ↓
Outbox processor
      ↓
Kafka
```

This avoids the classic problem:

```text
DB commit succeeded
Kafka publish failed
```

---

# 89.63 Idempotency

Operations that may be retried SHOULD be idempotent.

Example:

```text
POST /enrollments
Idempotency-Key: abc123
```

If the same request is repeated, the system should not create duplicate enrollments.

---

# 89.64 Duplicate Prevention

Use database constraints as the final defense.

Example:

```text
UNIQUE(student_id, course_id)
```

The application can check first, but the database should enforce the invariant.

---

# 89.65 JPA Entity Design

JPA entities SHOULD represent persistence models, not automatically become API contracts.

Avoid returning entities directly from controllers.

Prefer:

```text
Entity
 ↓
Mapper
 ↓
DTO
 ↓
API response
```

---

# 89.66 Why Not Return Entities?

Returning entities directly can expose:

```text
Internal fields
Relationships
Sensitive data
Lazy-loading behavior
Database structure
```

It can also create serialization problems.

---

# 89.67 DTOs

Separate:

```text
Create DTO
Read DTO
Update DTO
```

where their responsibilities differ.

Example:

```text
CourseCreateRequest
CourseUpdateRequest
CourseResponse
```

---

# 89.68 Lazy Loading

JPA relationships should generally avoid indiscriminate eager loading.

Prefer explicit data fetching based on use case.

---

# 89.69 Entity Graphs

JPA `EntityGraph` or fetch joins MAY be used for specific read paths.

Example:

```text
Course details page
 ↓
Course
 + Modules
 + Instructor summary
```

Load what the endpoint actually needs.

---

# 89.70 Repository Layer

Repositories SHOULD remain focused on persistence concerns.

Avoid placing complex business workflows directly into repository classes.

Recommended:

```text
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
Database
```

---

# 89.71 Service Layer

The service layer SHOULD coordinate:

```text
Business rules
Transactions
Authorization decisions
Repositories
Domain operations
```

---

# 89.72 Database Exceptions

Database-specific exceptions SHOULD be translated into meaningful application-level errors.

For example:

```text
Unique constraint violation
        ↓
Course code already exists
```

rather than exposing raw PostgreSQL errors to API clients.

---

# 89.73 SQL Injection

Never construct SQL by concatenating untrusted input.

Bad:

```text
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"
```

Use parameterized queries.

JPA and prepared statements should be used correctly.

---

# 89.74 Dynamic Queries

When dynamic filtering is required, use safe mechanisms such as:

```text
Specifications
Criteria API
QueryDSL
Parameterized SQL
```

depending on the architecture.

---

# 89.75 Full-Text Search

PostgreSQL full-text search MAY be sufficient for some early Mediverse search requirements.

For larger search workloads, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch MAY be introduced.

Do not introduce Elasticsearch simply because it exists in the technology stack.

---

# 89.76 Search Data

Search indexes should generally be treated as derived data.

Conceptually:

```text
PostgreSQL
   ↓
source of truth

Search index
   ↓
derived representation
```

---

# 89.77 Large Files

Do not store large videos and 3D models directly in ordinary PostgreSQL rows unless there is a deliberate architectural reason.

Prefer:

```text
Object Storage
   ↓
S3-compatible storage
   ↓
CDN
```

Database stores metadata:

```text
file_id
storage_key
content_type
size
checksum
```

---

# 89.78 Medical Content Metadata

For educational media:

```text
3D model
 ↓
metadata
 ├── model_id
 ├── version
 ├── anatomy_region
 ├── storage_key
 ├── license
 └── checksum
```

This keeps large binary content outside the transactional database.

---

# 89.79 Checksums

Important uploaded assets SHOULD have integrity metadata such as checksums.

This helps detect:

```text
Corruption
Unexpected changes
Duplicate content
```

---

# 89.80 Backup

Production PostgreSQL MUST have a backup strategy.

Backups should address:

```text
Full backup
Incremental/WAL strategy
Retention
Encryption
Off-site storage
Restore testing
```

---

# 89.81 Backup Is Not Recovery

Having:

```text
backup_2026_08_09.sql
```

does not prove the system is recoverable.

The restore process must be tested.

---

# 89.82 Recovery Testing

Regularly test:

```text
Backup
 ↓
Restore
 ↓
Application starts
 ↓
Data integrity verified
```

---

# 89.83 Recovery Objectives

Define:

### RPO

How much data can be lost?

```text
RPO = 5 minutes
```

means the architecture should target no more than roughly five minutes of data loss under the defined failure scenario.

### RTO

How quickly must service recover?

```text
RTO = 30 minutes
```

means recovery should target restoring service within that window.

---

# 89.84 Database Monitoring

Monitor:

```text
Connections
CPU
Memory
Disk
IOPS
Replication lag
Slow queries
Locks
Deadlocks
Cache hit ratio
Transaction rate
```

---

# 89.85 Slow Query Monitoring

Production should identify queries exceeding defined latency thresholds.

Example:

```text
query > 500ms
```

may trigger investigation depending on the workload.

Do not use one universal threshold for every query.

---

# 89.86 Deadlocks

The application SHOULD be designed to handle transient deadlocks appropriately.

Possible strategy:

```text
Detect
 ↓
Rollback
 ↓
Retry safely
```

Only retry operations that are actually safe to retry.

---

# 89.87 Database Security

Database access MUST use:

```text
Strong authentication
TLS where required
Least-privilege accounts
Network restrictions
Secret management
Audit controls
```

---

# 89.88 Application DB User

The application should not connect as:

```text
postgres
```

or another superuser in production.

Use a restricted application role.

---

# 89.89 Migration User

Migration privileges MAY be separated from normal application privileges.

Example:

```text
migration_user
application_user
readonly_user
```

This reduces blast radius.

---

# 89.90 Read-Only Access

Analytics/reporting systems SHOULD use read-only credentials where possible.

Never give reporting workloads write access simply because it is convenient.

---

# 89.91 Sensitive Data

Sensitive information should be minimized.

Do not store information merely because:

```text
"We might need it someday."
```

Every stored data field creates:

```text
Security responsibility
Privacy responsibility
Retention responsibility
Backup responsibility
```

---

# 89.92 Data Encryption

Sensitive data MAY require encryption:

```text
At rest
In transit
At application level
```

depending on threat model and regulatory requirements.

Do not assume database disk encryption solves every data-protection requirement.

---

# 89.93 Audit Data

Audit records SHOULD be append-oriented.

Important audit information should not be casually overwritten.

Example:

```text
Who
What
When
Target
Previous state
New state
```

where appropriate.

---

# 89.94 Database Testing

Database behavior SHOULD be tested against a real PostgreSQL-compatible environment for important integration scenarios.

Do not assume:

```text
H2
```

behaves exactly like PostgreSQL.

---

# 89.95 Testcontainers

For Spring Boot integration testing, Testcontainers MAY be used:

```text
JUnit
 ↓
Testcontainers
 ↓
PostgreSQL
 ↓
Spring Boot
```

This provides significantly more realistic database testing than relying exclusively on H2.

---

# 89.96 Production-Like Testing

Critical database behavior SHOULD be tested using production-like:

```text
Schema
Indexes
Constraints
Queries
Database engine
```

where practical.

---

# 89.97 Load Testing

Before major production launches, test realistic workloads.

Examples:

```text
100 concurrent users
1,000 concurrent users
10,000 concurrent requests
```

The actual target must come from expected traffic.

Measure:

```text
API latency
DB CPU
Connections
Query latency
Lock contention
Error rate
```

---

# 89.98 Database Scaling

Scaling options include:

```text
Vertical scaling
Read replicas
Partitioning
Caching
Query optimization
Connection tuning
Archival
Sharding
```

Use them in increasing order of complexity where practical.

---

# 89.99 Partitioning

PostgreSQL partitioning MAY be useful for very large tables.

Potential candidates:

```text
Audit logs
Events
Activity history
Time-series records
```

Do not partition small tables just because partitioning exists.

---

# 89.100 Archival

Large historical data MAY be moved to cheaper storage.

Example:

```text
Active audit records
       ↓
PostgreSQL

Old audit records
       ↓
Archive storage
```

Define retrieval requirements before implementing archival.

---

# 89.101 Database Disaster Recovery

The disaster recovery architecture should define:

```text
Primary database failure
Backup restoration
Replica promotion
Application reconnection
DNS/service routing
Data verification
```

---

# 89.102 Schema Evolution

Database evolution should be treated as part of application versioning.

Conceptually:

```text
Git commit
+
Application version
+
Database migration
=
Deployable release
```

---

# 89.103 Data Integrity Principle

The strongest invariant should exist as close to the data as practical.

For example:

```text
Requirement:
One student cannot enroll twice.

Application:
checks enrollment

Database:
UNIQUE(student_id, course_id)
```

The database provides the final protection.

---

# 89.104 Definition of Done

Database architecture is production-ready when:

* [ ] Ownership boundaries are documented
* [ ] Schema naming conventions exist
* [ ] Primary keys are defined
* [ ] Foreign keys are defined
* [ ] Required fields use NOT NULL
* [ ] Business uniqueness uses UNIQUE constraints
* [ ] Important invariants use CHECK constraints
* [ ] Migrations are version controlled
* [ ] Transaction boundaries are defined
* [ ] N+1 queries are checked
* [ ] Query indexes are based on real access patterns
* [ ] Slow queries are monitored
* [ ] Connection pools are configured
* [ ] Backup strategy exists
* [ ] Restore has been tested
* [ ] RPO/RTO are defined
* [ ] Database credentials use least privilege
* [ ] Secrets are externally managed
* [ ] Sensitive data is protected
* [ ] Large media is stored outside PostgreSQL where appropriate
* [ ] Production-like integration tests exist
* [ ] Disaster recovery is documented

---

# 89.105 Core Principles

1. **PostgreSQL should enforce important invariants.**
2. **Do not let application code be the only line of defense for data integrity.**
3. **Do not use business fields as primary keys.**
4. **Do not index everything.**
5. **Do not use `EAGER` loading as a lazy solution to JPA problems.**
6. **Do not return JPA entities directly from APIs.**
7. **Do not use H2 as proof that PostgreSQL behavior is correct.**
8. **Do not manually modify production schemas.**
9. **Do not treat backups as proof of recoverability.**
10. **Do not introduce Redis, Elasticsearch, partitioning, or sharding without a demonstrated need.**
11. **Keep large binary media outside the transactional database where appropriate.**
12. **Use transactions for atomic business operations.**
13. **Design explicitly for retries and idempotency.**
14. **Measure database performance instead of guessing.**
15. **Treat data lifecycle, retention, security, and recovery as architecture concerns.**

> **For Mediverse, the biggest database mistake would be designing tables around Java entities and then discovering production requirements later. Start from business invariants and access patterns: what must always be true, who owns the data, how it will be queried, what happens under concurrency, and how the system recovers after failure. PostgreSQL should actively protect those invariants rather than merely store whatever the application sends it.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 90: Caching & Distributed Data Standards — Redis architecture, cache-aside, TTL, invalidation, distributed locks, rate limiting, session storage, cache stampede, consistency, and failure handling.**

# CSDG — Chapter 90

## Caching & Distributed Data Standards

Caching is useful, but it is also one of the easiest ways to create subtle production bugs.

Core principle:

> **A cache is an optimization, not the source of truth, unless the architecture explicitly makes it one.**

For Mediverse, PostgreSQL should remain authoritative for transactional data, while Redis can reduce latency and database load.

---

## 90.1 Why Caching Exists

Without caching:

```text
User
 ↓
React
 ↓
API
 ↓
PostgreSQL
 ↓
Response
```

With caching:

```text
User
 ↓
React
 ↓
API
 ↓
Redis
 ├── HIT → Response
 └── MISS
       ↓
   PostgreSQL
       ↓
     Redis
       ↓
    Response
```

The goal is to reduce:

* Database load
* API latency
* Repeated computation
* Network traffic
* Expensive queries

---

# 90.2 Recommended Technology

For Mediverse:

```text
Redis 7+
```

can be used for:

```text
Caching
Session-related state
Rate limiting
Temporary data
Distributed coordination
Counters
Short-lived tokens
```

But Redis should not automatically become a second PostgreSQL.

---

# 90.3 What Should Be Cached?

Good candidates:

```text
Course metadata
Popular courses
Reference data
Frequently accessed configuration
Public educational content metadata
Computed summaries
Rate-limit counters
```

Poor candidates:

```text
Highly sensitive transactional state
Data requiring strict immediate consistency
Rarely accessed records
Huge objects with little reuse
```

---

# 90.4 Cache-Aside Pattern

The default pattern SHOULD generally be:

```text
Application
    ↓
Check Redis
    ↓
 HIT ───────→ Return
    │
 MISS
    ↓
PostgreSQL
    ↓
Store in Redis
    ↓
Return
```

Example:

```text
GET /courses/123
```

Flow:

```text
Redis:
course:123
```

If missing:

```text
PostgreSQL
 ↓
Course
 ↓
Redis SET
```

---

# 90.5 Cache Key Design

Keys must be predictable and namespaced.

Recommended:

```text
course:123
course:123:summary
user:456:profile
quiz:789:metadata
progress:456:course:123
```

Avoid meaningless keys:

```text
data1
temp123
cache_xyz
```

---

# 90.6 Key Namespaces

Use a logical hierarchy:

```text
mediverse:
    course:
    user:
    quiz:
    progress:
```

Example:

```text
mediverse:course:123
mediverse:user:456
```

This makes operational inspection easier.

---

# 90.7 TTL

Cached data SHOULD generally have an expiration policy.

Example:

```text
course:123
TTL = 10 minutes
```

TTL should be based on how frequently the data changes.

---

# 90.8 TTL Examples

Potential strategy:

```text
Reference data
→ hours

Course catalog
→ minutes

User dashboard
→ short TTL

Rate-limit counters
→ seconds/minutes

Temporary verification state
→ very short TTL
```

These are starting points, not universal values.

---

# 90.9 No TTL Cache

Avoid permanent caching unless there is an explicit invalidation strategy.

Otherwise:

```text
Database:
Course version 5

Redis:
Course version 2
```

can persist indefinitely.

---

# 90.10 Cache Invalidation

The classic problem:

```text
Database updated
      ↓
Cache still contains old value
```

Therefore every cached dataset needs an invalidation strategy.

Common approaches:

```text
TTL
Explicit invalidation
Write-through
Event-driven invalidation
Versioned keys
```

---

# 90.11 Explicit Invalidation

Example:

```text
UPDATE course
      ↓
DELETE Redis course:123
```

Next request:

```text
Redis MISS
 ↓
PostgreSQL
 ↓
Redis populated
```

This is simple and often effective.

---

# 90.12 Update-Then-Delete

For many cache-aside workflows:

```text
1. Update database
2. Commit transaction
3. Invalidate cache
```

This is safer than deleting the cache first and then attempting the database update.

---

# 90.13 The Race Condition

Consider:

```text
Request A → DB update
Request B → DB read
```

combined with cache invalidation.

Poorly designed cache flows can result in stale values being written back into Redis.

Therefore concurrency behavior must be considered.

---

# 90.14 Cache Stampede

Suppose:

```text
course:123
TTL expires
```

and suddenly:

```text
10,000 users
```

request it simultaneously.

All see:

```text
CACHE MISS
```

All query PostgreSQL.

Result:

```text
Redis miss
 ↓
10,000 DB queries
 ↓
Database overload
```

This is a cache stampede.

---

# 90.15 Preventing Stampede

Possible techniques:

```text
Request coalescing
Distributed locking
Jittered TTL
Background refresh
Prewarming
```

Do not use distributed locks blindly.

---

# 90.16 TTL Jitter

Instead of:

```text
TTL = 600 seconds
```

for every key, use slight randomness:

```text
TTL = 570–630 seconds
```

This prevents huge numbers of keys from expiring simultaneously.

---

# 90.17 Cache Warming

Important data MAY be preloaded.

Example:

```text
Popular courses
 ↓
Application startup / scheduled job
 ↓
Redis
```

But don't preload millions of records without evidence that it helps.

---

# 90.18 Cache Size

Redis memory is finite.

Monitor:

```text
Memory usage
Evictions
Hit ratio
Key count
Fragmentation
```

---

# 90.19 Eviction Policy

Redis can evict data when memory limits are reached.

The chosen policy should match the workload.

Do not assume:

```text
"Redis will automatically handle memory."
```

It will follow configured behavior, which may not match your business expectations.

---

# 90.20 Cache Hit Ratio

Track:

```text
Cache hits
Cache misses
```

Example:

```text
1,000 requests
900 hits
100 misses
```

Hit ratio:

```text
90%
```

But:

> A high hit ratio does not automatically mean the cache is useful.

A cache could have a 99% hit ratio while caching insignificant data.

Measure latency and database load too.

---

# 90.21 Cache Observability

Monitor:

```text
Hit rate
Miss rate
Latency
Memory
Evictions
Connections
Commands/sec
Errors
```

---

# 90.22 Redis Failure

Your application must define what happens if Redis becomes unavailable.

Recommended for non-critical caching:

```text
Redis unavailable
      ↓
Log / metric
      ↓
Fallback to PostgreSQL
```

The application should remain functional if the cache is only an optimization.

---

# 90.23 Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed

For ordinary caching:

```text
Redis failure
 ↓
Fallback to database
```

is generally preferable.

For security-sensitive mechanisms such as:

```text
Rate limiting
Distributed authorization state
Session state
```

the correct behavior may be different.

Define it explicitly.

---

# 90.24 Redis Must Not Become a Hidden Dependency

Bad architecture:

```text
PostgreSQL
+
Redis

Application cannot function without Redis
```

when Redis was originally introduced only for caching.

That creates unnecessary operational coupling.

---

# 90.25 Cache Serialization

Objects stored in Redis need a stable serialization format.

Possible:

```text
JSON
Binary serialization
String values
Hash structures
```

Choose based on compatibility, performance, and operational needs.

---

# 90.26 Cache Versioning

When the structure of cached data changes, version keys.

Example:

```text
course:v1:123
course:v2:123
```

This can prevent incompatible old cached objects from breaking newer application versions.

---

# 90.27 Cache Key Versioning

This is particularly useful during deployments.

```text
v1:user:123
v2:user:123
```

New application instances can use the new namespace without depending on old serialized structures.

---

# 90.28 Cache Security

Never assume Redis data is harmless.

Protect Redis with:

```text
Authentication
Network restrictions
TLS where required
Private networking
Least privilege
Firewall rules
```

Never expose Redis directly to the public internet.

---

# 90.29 Sensitive Data

Avoid caching highly sensitive information unless absolutely necessary.

Examples:

```text
Passwords
Raw authentication secrets
Sensitive personal information
Sensitive educational records
```

If sensitive data must be cached, define:

```text
Encryption
TTL
Access control
Deletion
Audit
```

---

# 90.30 Session Storage

Redis MAY be used for distributed session state.

Example:

```text
Browser
 ↓
Load Balancer
 ├── App 1
 ├── App 2
 └── App 3
       ↓
     Redis
```

This avoids relying on one application instance's memory.

---

# 90.31 Stateless Authentication

If Mediverse uses stateless JWT access tokens:

```text
Request
 ↓
JWT
 ↓
Application validates
```

Redis may not need to store every access token.

It can still be useful for:

```text
Refresh token state
Revocation
Rate limiting
Session metadata
```

depending on the security design.

---

# 90.32 Rate Limiting

Redis is well suited for distributed rate limiting.

Example:

```text
User
 ↓
100 requests / minute
```

Across:

```text
App 1
App 2
App 3
```

Redis provides shared counters.

---

# 90.33 Rate-Limit Key

Example:

```text
rate:user:123
```

or:

```text
rate:ip:192.0.2.1
```

depending on the policy.

Do not rely exclusively on IP addresses for user-level controls because many users can share an IP.

---

# 90.34 Rate-Limit Algorithm

Possible algorithms:

```text
Fixed window
Sliding window
Token bucket
Leaky bucket
```

Select based on the requirement.

---

# 90.35 Distributed Locks

Redis MAY support distributed locking.

Example use case:

```text
Only one worker should process a specific expensive job.
```

But distributed locking is dangerous if implemented incorrectly.

Use a well-understood library/pattern rather than inventing:

```text
SET lock = true
sleep()
delete lock
```

---

# 90.36 Lock TTL

A distributed lock SHOULD have an expiration mechanism.

Otherwise:

```text
Worker crashes
 ↓
Lock remains forever
 ↓
Job never runs
```

---

# 90.37 Lock Ownership

A worker should only release the lock it owns.

Do not blindly:

```text
DEL lock
```

if another worker may have acquired the lock after expiration.

---

# 90.38 Distributed Locks Are Not Transactions

A Redis lock does not magically provide:

```text
PostgreSQL transaction
+
Redis atomicity
```

Treat these as separate consistency mechanisms.

---

# 90.39 Counters

Redis atomic counters can be useful for:

```text
Views
Rate limits
Temporary counters
Attempts
Metrics
```

But if a counter represents authoritative business data, ensure eventual persistence and failure handling are designed.

---

# 90.40 Quiz Attempt Counters

For example:

```text
quiz_attempts:user:123:quiz:456
```

could be cached temporarily.

But the authoritative attempt record should generally live in PostgreSQL.

---

# 90.41 Distributed Data Consistency

With:

```text
PostgreSQL
+
Redis
```

you now have two representations of data.

Therefore you must define:

```text
Source of truth
Consistency model
Invalidation
Recovery
Failure behavior
```

---

# 90.42 Strong vs Eventual Consistency

For some data:

```text
Course title
```

a few seconds of staleness may be acceptable.

For:

```text
Exam submission
Quiz score
Certificate issuance
```

stale state may be unacceptable.

The cache strategy must reflect the business consequence.

---

# 90.43 Never Cache Everything

This is a common bad architecture:

```text
Every PostgreSQL query
 ↓
Redis
```

Caching should answer:

> **Which repeated expensive operations benefit from caching enough to justify the complexity?**

---

# 90.44 Cache Database Queries vs Domain Objects

Prefer caching meaningful domain results:

```text
course:123:summary
```

rather than blindly caching arbitrary SQL results.

Domain-level cache keys are easier to invalidate and reason about.

---

# 90.45 Cache Dependencies

Suppose:

```text
Course
 ├── Modules
 └── Lessons
```

and you cache:

```text
course:123
course:123:modules
course:123:lessons
```

Updating a course may require invalidating multiple keys.

Cache dependency design must therefore be explicit.

---

# 90.46 Hierarchical Invalidation

One approach:

```text
course:123:*
```

with a strategy for deleting all related keys.

Another:

```text
course:v2:123
```

with version changes invalidating the entire logical namespace.

The right solution depends on scale.

---

# 90.47 Event-Driven Invalidation

For larger systems:

```text
Course Service
   ↓
CourseUpdated event
   ↓
Kafka
   ↓
Cache consumers
   ↓
Invalidate relevant keys
```

This can decouple cache invalidation across services.

---

# 90.48 Cache and Kafka

Do not assume Kafka guarantees Redis consistency automatically.

You still need to handle:

```text
Event duplication
Event ordering
Consumer failure
Retry
Out-of-order events
```

---

# 90.49 Idempotent Cache Consumers

Cache invalidation consumers SHOULD be idempotent.

Receiving:

```text
CourseUpdated
CourseUpdated
CourseUpdated
```

should not cause corruption.

---

# 90.50 Cache Warm-Up After Restart

After Redis restart:

```text
Redis = empty
```

The application should tolerate this.

Possible behavior:

```text
First request
 ↓
DB
 ↓
Redis repopulated
```

For high-traffic systems, selective warm-up may be useful.

---

# 90.51 Redis Persistence

If Redis is being used strictly as a cache:

```text
Redis data loss
 ↓
Rebuild from PostgreSQL
```

may be acceptable.

If Redis stores important state:

```text
Sessions
Queues
Critical workflow state
```

then persistence and recovery requirements change.

---

# 90.52 Do Not Treat Cache Data as Permanent

A restart, eviction, failover, or flush can remove cache data.

Therefore application correctness should not depend on cached data unless Redis is intentionally part of the authoritative state architecture.

---

# 90.53 Cache Stampede vs Thundering Herd

These are related but not identical problems.

### Cache stampede

Many requests regenerate the same expired cache entry.

### Thundering herd

Many requests simultaneously hit an overloaded dependency.

Caching can reduce the second problem, but poorly designed caching can create the first.

---

# 90.54 Negative Caching

Sometimes cache the fact that something does not exist.

Example:

```text
course:999999 = NOT_FOUND
```

This prevents repeated database queries for nonexistent resources.

But negative entries MUST have short TTLs.

Otherwise newly created resources may remain invisible until expiration.

---

# 90.55 Null Caching

If implemented, null/negative cache values should be distinguishable from:

```text
Redis key doesn't exist
```

Use explicit representation rather than ambiguous null behavior.

---

# 90.56 Cache Poisoning

Never allow untrusted input to arbitrarily control cache keys or stored objects.

Validate:

```text
Keys
Serialized content
Authorization context
Tenant boundaries
```

---

# 90.57 Multi-Tenant Systems

If Mediverse eventually supports institutions/tenants, cache keys MUST include tenant context where relevant.

Bad:

```text
course:123
```

Potentially dangerous if course IDs overlap between tenants.

Better:

```text
tenant:456:course:123
```

---

# 90.58 Authorization and Cache

This is critical.

Suppose:

```text
User A
 ↓
GET /courses/123
 ↓
Redis caches response
```

Then:

```text
User B
 ↓
GET /courses/123
 ↓
Redis HIT
```

If the cached response contains user-specific authorization-sensitive information, User B may receive User A's data.

Therefore:

> **Never cache personalized responses without including the correct authorization/user dimensions in the cache key.**

---

# 90.59 Personalized Cache Keys

For user-specific data:

```text
progress:user:123:course:456
```

not:

```text
progress:course:456
```

unless the content is genuinely identical for every user.

---

# 90.60 Cache-Control

HTTP caching and Redis caching are different layers.

Architecture may contain:

```text
Browser cache
 ↓
CDN cache
 ↓
Application Redis
 ↓
PostgreSQL
```

Each layer needs an explicit policy.

---

# 90.61 CDN Caching

Static educational assets such as:

```text
Images
Videos
3D models
JavaScript
CSS
```

may be better cached through a CDN rather than Redis.

Redis is not a replacement for a CDN.

---

# 90.62 Cache Hierarchy

A mature Mediverse architecture might look like:

```text
Browser
   ↓
CDN
   ↓
API
   ↓
Redis
   ↓
PostgreSQL
```

Each layer solves a different problem.

---

# 90.63 Cache Invalidation Strategy Matrix

| Data               | Cache?     | Typical strategy       |
| ------------------ | ---------- | ---------------------- |
| Course catalog     | Yes        | TTL + invalidation     |
| Course metadata    | Yes        | TTL                    |
| User profile       | Maybe      | Short TTL/invalidation |
| Quiz configuration | Maybe      | Versioned/invalidation |
| Quiz submission    | No         | PostgreSQL             |
| Exam score         | Usually no | PostgreSQL             |
| Rate limits        | Yes        | Redis                  |
| Static images      | CDN        | CDN                    |
| 3D models          | CDN        | CDN                    |
| Videos             | CDN        | CDN                    |

---

# 90.64 Caching Anti-Patterns

### Anti-pattern 1

```text
Cache everything
```

### Anti-pattern 2

```text
No TTL
```

### Anti-pattern 3

```text
Cache without invalidation
```

### Anti-pattern 4

```text
Redis is required for every request
```

### Anti-pattern 5

```text
Personalized data under shared cache keys
```

### Anti-pattern 6

```text
Redis used as primary database without explicit architecture
```

### Anti-pattern 7

```text
Distributed locks implemented manually
```

---

# 90.65 Testing

Caching behavior SHOULD be tested.

Test:

```text
Cache hit
Cache miss
Expiration
Invalidation
Redis unavailable
Stale data
Concurrent requests
Serialization failure
Authorization isolation
```

---

# 90.66 Failure Testing

Simulate:

```text
Redis down
Redis restart
Network latency
Memory pressure
Evictions
Connection exhaustion
```

The application should behave according to its defined failure strategy.

---

# 90.67 Observability

Expose metrics such as:

```text
redis_cache_hits_total
redis_cache_misses_total
redis_operation_latency
redis_errors_total
redis_evictions_total
redis_memory_usage
```

These metrics can feed:

```text
Prometheus
 ↓
Grafana
```

---

# 90.68 Alerts

Potential alerts:

```text
Cache hit ratio suddenly drops
Redis memory critically high
Eviction rate spikes
Redis unavailable
Latency increases
Connection pool exhausted
```

Alert thresholds should be based on actual operational baselines.

---

# 90.69 Security Checklist

* [ ] Redis is not publicly exposed
* [ ] Authentication configured
* [ ] Network access restricted
* [ ] TLS used where required
* [ ] Sensitive data minimized
* [ ] User/tenant boundaries included in keys
* [ ] Cache poisoning risks addressed
* [ ] Secrets are not stored in source code
* [ ] Logs do not expose cached sensitive values

---

# 90.70 Definition of Done

Caching architecture is production-ready when:

* [ ] Every cache has a defined purpose
* [ ] PostgreSQL remains source of truth where appropriate
* [ ] Cache keys are standardized
* [ ] TTL strategy exists
* [ ] Invalidation strategy exists
* [ ] Stampede behavior is addressed
* [ ] Redis failure behavior is defined
* [ ] Sensitive data is protected
* [ ] Personalized cache keys are isolated
* [ ] Memory limits are configured
* [ ] Eviction behavior is understood
* [ ] Metrics exist
* [ ] Alerts exist
* [ ] Integration tests exist
* [ ] Failure scenarios have been tested

---

# 90.71 Core Principles

1. **Cache for a measured reason.**
