2. **PostgreSQL remains authoritative for transactional data unless explicitly designed otherwise.**
3. **Every cache requires a lifecycle strategy.**
4. **Every cached dataset needs an invalidation or expiration strategy.**
5. **Never expose one user's cached data to another user.**
6. **Use tenant-aware keys in multi-tenant systems.**
7. **Redis failure should not destroy application correctness when Redis is merely a cache.**
8. **Do not use Redis as a replacement for PostgreSQL.**
9. **Do not use Redis locks casually.**
10. **Measure cache effectiveness using latency and backend load, not hit ratio alone.**
11. **Use CDN for large static media rather than turning Redis into a media cache.**
12. **Design for cache stampedes and stale data before production.**
13. **Treat cache invalidation as part of the feature design, not an afterthought.**

> **The brutal truth about caching: most systems don't fail because they lack Redis. They fail because developers add Redis without defining consistency, invalidation, ownership, failure behavior, and authorization boundaries. A slower but correct system is far better than a fast system that occasionally shows a student's private progress to the wrong user.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 91: API Architecture & REST Standards — resource design, HTTP semantics, URI conventions, DTOs, pagination, filtering, sorting, versioning, idempotency, errors, HATEOAS considerations, API contracts, and backward compatibility.**


# CSDG — Chapter 91

## API Architecture & REST Standards

This chapter defines how Mediverse APIs should be designed, structured, secured, versioned, documented, tested, and evolved.

Core principle:

> **An API is a long-term contract, not just a collection of controller methods.**

---

## 91.1 API Architecture

Recommended flow:

```text
React / Mobile / External Client
              ↓
         API Gateway
              ↓
        Spring Boot API
              ↓
       Service Layer
              ↓
       Domain / Repository
              ↓
          PostgreSQL
```

Supporting infrastructure:

```text
Redis
Kafka
Object Storage
Search
Observability
```

---

# 91.2 REST Resource Design

Design APIs around **resources**, not implementation methods.

Good:

```text
GET    /api/v1/courses
GET    /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
POST   /api/v1/courses
PATCH  /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
DELETE /api/v1/courses/{courseId}
```

Avoid:

```text
/getCourse
/createCourse
/updateCourse
/deleteCourse
```

The HTTP method already communicates the operation.

---

# 91.3 Resource Naming

Use plural nouns.

Recommended:

```text
/courses
/users
/modules
/lessons
/quizzes
/questions
/enrollments
```

Avoid:

```text
/course
/getCourses
/courseList
```

---

# 91.4 URI Naming

Use lowercase paths.

Recommended:

```text
/api/v1/course-categories
```

Avoid:

```text
/api/v1/CourseCategories
/api/v1/courseCategories
/api/v1/course_categories
```

Hyphenated resource names are generally easier to read.

---

# 91.5 API Versioning

Mediverse APIs SHOULD be explicitly versioned.

Recommended:

```text
/api/v1/courses
```

Later:

```text
/api/v2/courses
```

Do not break existing consumers silently.

---

# 91.6 Versioning Strategy

Possible approaches include:

```text
URI versioning
Header versioning
Content negotiation
```

For Mediverse, URI versioning is simple and operationally obvious:

```text
/api/v1/...
```

---

# 91.7 HTTP Methods

Use HTTP semantics correctly.

| Method | Purpose          |
| ------ | ---------------- |
| GET    | Read             |
| POST   | Create/action    |
| PUT    | Full replacement |
| PATCH  | Partial update   |
| DELETE | Delete           |

---

# 91.8 GET

GET SHOULD be safe and should not modify business state.

Good:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses/123
```

Bad:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses/123/delete
```

---

# 91.9 POST

POST is commonly used to create resources.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/courses
```

Request:

```json
{
  "title": "Human Physiology",
  "description": "..."
}
```

---

# 91.10 POST for Commands

POST MAY also be appropriate for explicit business actions that don't map cleanly to CRUD.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/quizzes/123/submit
```

This represents an operation/command rather than simple resource creation.

---

# 91.11 PUT

PUT generally represents replacement of a resource representation.

Example:

```text
PUT /api/v1/courses/123
```

Request:

```json
{
  "title": "Updated Course",
  "description": "Updated description",
  "status": "PUBLISHED"
}
```

---

# 91.12 PATCH

PATCH is appropriate for partial changes.

Example:

```text
PATCH /api/v1/courses/123
```

```json
{
  "status": "PUBLISHED"
}
```

---

# 91.13 DELETE

DELETE should remove or logically remove the resource according to the system's deletion policy.

Example:

```text
DELETE /api/v1/courses/123
```

Do not automatically assume every DELETE must physically remove database data.

---

# 91.14 HTTP Status Codes

Use meaningful status codes.

Common:

```text
200 OK
201 Created
202 Accepted
204 No Content

400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
409 Conflict
422 Unprocessable Content
429 Too Many Requests

500 Internal Server Error
502 Bad Gateway
503 Service Unavailable
```

---

# 91.15 200 OK

Use when the request succeeded and a response body is returned.

Example:

```text
GET /courses/123
→ 200
```

---

# 91.16 201 Created

Use when a resource has been created.

Example:

```text
POST /courses
→ 201 Created
```

The response SHOULD identify the created resource.

---

# 91.17 204 No Content

Useful when the operation succeeds without requiring a response body.

Example:

```text
DELETE /courses/123
→ 204
```

---

# 91.18 400 Bad Request

Use when the request itself is malformed or invalid.

Examples:

```text
Malformed JSON
Invalid query syntax
Invalid request structure
```

---

# 91.19 401 Unauthorized

Use when authentication is missing or invalid.

```text
No valid authentication
```

Do not use 401 simply because the user lacks permission to perform a specific operation.

---

# 91.20 403 Forbidden

Use when the user is authenticated but not permitted.

Example:

```text
Student
 ↓
PATCH /courses/123
 ↓
403 Forbidden
```

---

# 91.21 404 Not Found

Use when the requested resource does not exist or should not be revealed as existing under the security policy.

Example:

```text
GET /courses/999999
→ 404
```

---

# 91.22 409 Conflict

Useful for business/state conflicts.

Examples:

```text
Duplicate enrollment
Course already published
Version conflict
Username already exists
```

---

# 91.23 422 Unprocessable Content

Can be useful when the request structure is valid but business validation fails.

Example:

```text
passingScore = 150
```

The exact distinction between 400 and 422 should be standardized across the platform rather than decided randomly by each developer.

---

# 91.24 429 Too Many Requests

Use for rate limiting.

Example:

```text
User exceeded login attempts
```

Response SHOULD communicate retry information where appropriate.

---

# 91.25 500 Internal Server Error

Do not expose internal exception details.

Bad:

```json
{
  "error": "NullPointerException at CourseService.java:123"
}
```

Good:

```json
{
  "code": "INTERNAL_ERROR",
  "message": "An unexpected error occurred."
}
```

Log the technical details internally.

---

# 91.26 Standard Response Envelope

You may standardize response structures.

Example:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "id": 123,
    "title": "Human Physiology"
  },
  "meta": {}
}
```

But do not create envelopes merely because every API design article recommends them.

If the envelope adds no value, simple JSON is fine.

The important requirement is **consistency**.

---

# 91.27 Error Response Contract

Mediverse SHOULD use a consistent error format.

Example:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-09T10:30:00Z",
  "status": 409,
  "code": "COURSE_ALREADY_EXISTS",
  "message": "A course with this code already exists.",
  "path": "/api/v1/courses"
}
```

---

# 91.28 Validation Errors

Validation errors SHOULD identify the problematic fields.

Example:

```json
{
  "status": 400,
  "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "message": "Request validation failed.",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "message": "Title is required."
    },
    {
      "field": "duration",
      "message": "Duration must be greater than zero."
    }
  ]
}
```

---

# 91.29 Never Leak Internal Details

Do not expose:

```text
SQL
Stack traces
Database usernames
Internal hostnames
File paths
JWT secrets
Infrastructure details
```

through API errors.

---

# 91.30 Request DTOs

Use dedicated request models.

Example:

```java
public record CreateCourseRequest(
    String title,
    String description
) {}
```

Do not bind arbitrary entity fields directly from client requests.

---

# 91.31 Response DTOs

Use response DTOs to control API contracts.

Example:

```java
public record CourseResponse(
    UUID id,
    String title,
    String status
) {}
```

---

# 91.32 Never Trust Client Fields

A client should not be able to send:

```json
{
  "role": "ADMIN",
  "createdAt": "2020-01-01",
  "approved": true
}
```

and expect the backend to accept them simply because the fields exist in the entity.

Authorization and server-owned fields must be controlled by the backend.

---

# 91.33 Pagination

Collection APIs SHOULD support pagination when datasets can become large.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?page=0&size=20
```

---

# 91.34 Pagination Response

Example:

```json
{
  "data": [
    {}
  ],
  "page": {
    "number": 0,
    "size": 20,
    "totalElements": 150,
    "totalPages": 8
  }
}
```

---

# 91.35 Pagination Limits

Never allow:

```text
?page=0&size=1000000
```

Set a server-side maximum.

Example:

```text
maximum size = 100
```

The exact value should be based on workload.

---

# 91.36 Sorting

Support controlled sorting.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?sort=createdAt,desc
```

Never blindly concatenate arbitrary client-provided column names into SQL.

Maintain an allowlist:

```text
createdAt
title
updatedAt
```

---

# 91.37 Filtering

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?status=PUBLISHED
```

Multiple filters:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?status=PUBLISHED&category=PHYSIOLOGY
```

Filters should be explicitly defined.

---

# 91.38 Search

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses?search=cardiology
```

For complex search:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses/search?q=cardiology
```

Choose one consistent convention.

---

# 91.39 API Query Parameters

Document:

```text
name
type
allowed values
default
maximum
behavior
```

Example:

```text
size
type: integer
default: 20
maximum: 100
```

---

# 91.40 Nested Resources

Nested resources can express relationships.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/courses/123/modules
```

This is useful when the relationship is meaningful.

But avoid excessive nesting:

```text
/courses/123/modules/456/lessons/789/questions/999/options
```

Such APIs become difficult to use and maintain.

---

# 91.41 Resource Depth

Prefer shallow URLs.

Instead of:

```text
/courses/123/modules/456/lessons/789
```

you can often expose:

```text
/courses/123/modules/456
/lessons/789
```

with relationships represented in the response.

---

# 91.42 API Idempotency

Idempotency is critical for operations that may be retried.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/enrollments
Idempotency-Key: 9c1...
```

If the same request is accidentally submitted twice, the backend should avoid creating duplicate business records.

---

# 91.43 Retry Safety

Consider:

```text
Client
 ↓
POST enrollment
 ↓
Server creates enrollment
 ↓
Network timeout
 ↓
Client retries
```

Without idempotency:

```text
Enrollment #1
Enrollment #2
```

This is a real production failure mode.

---

# 91.44 Idempotency Storage

The server may store:

```text
idempotency_key
user_id
request_hash
response
status
expires_at
```

in a suitable persistence mechanism.

---

# 91.45 Authentication

Protected APIs SHOULD require authentication.

Example:

```text
Authorization: Bearer <access-token>
```

Authentication establishes:

```text
Who are you?
```

Authorization establishes:

```text
What are you allowed to do?
```

Do not confuse the two.

---

# 91.46 Authorization

Example:

```text
Student
 ├── View courses
 ├── Submit quizzes
 └── View own progress

Instructor
 ├── Create lessons
 ├── Update course content
 └── View student analytics

Admin
 └── Platform administration
```

---

# 91.47 Object-Level Authorization

This is more important than simply checking roles.

Bad:

```text
if role == STUDENT
    allow GET /progress/{id}
```

A student might then request:

```text
/progress/another-student-id
```

Correct authorization must verify ownership:

```text
Authenticated user
        ↓
Requested resource
        ↓
Does user have access?
```

---

# 91.48 BOLA / IDOR Protection

Never assume that knowing an ID grants access.

Example:

```text
GET /api/v1/users/123/progress
```

must verify that the caller is allowed to access user `123`.

This is one of the most important API security controls.

---

# 91.49 API Gateway

A gateway MAY handle cross-cutting concerns:

```text
Authentication
Routing
Rate limiting
TLS termination
Request correlation
```

But business authorization should remain appropriately enforced by backend services.

---

# 91.50 Gateway Does Not Replace Service Security

Do not assume:

```text
Gateway authenticated request
```

means:

```text
Every internal service can trust every request.
```

Internal services still need appropriate authorization and trust boundaries.

---

# 91.51 Correlation ID

Each request SHOULD have a correlation/request ID.

Example:

```text
X-Request-ID: 7f8a9c...
```

Flow:

```text
React
 ↓
Gateway
 ↓
Course Service
 ↓
PostgreSQL
```

The same correlation ID can help trace the request.

---

# 91.52 Distributed Tracing

For distributed systems, propagate trace context.

Example:

```text
Request
 ↓
Gateway
 ↓
Course Service
 ↓
Kafka
 ↓
Notification Service
```

Use OpenTelemetry-compatible tracing where appropriate.

---

# 91.53 API Timeouts

Every downstream request SHOULD have a timeout.

Never allow:

```text
Service A
 ↓
wait indefinitely for Service B
```

Timeouts prevent resource exhaustion.

---

# 91.54 Retries

Retries should be:

```text
Limited
Exponential backoff
Jittered
Idempotency-aware
```

Do not retry every error.

For example:

```text
400 Bad Request
```

should not normally be retried.

---

# 91.55 Circuit Breaker

For unstable downstream services:

```text
Service A
 ↓
Service B
```

a circuit breaker can prevent Service A from repeatedly overwhelming a failing Service B.

Typical states:

```text
CLOSED
 ↓
OPEN
 ↓
HALF-OPEN
 ↓
CLOSED
```

---

# 91.56 Bulkheads

Separate resource pools can prevent one dependency from consuming everything.

Example:

```text
Course API
 ↓
Database pool

Search API
 ↓
Search connection pool
```

A failing search system should not necessarily exhaust all application resources.

---

# 91.57 API Rate Limiting

Apply rate limits based on risk and workload.

Examples:

```text
Login
Password reset
Search
Public APIs
Quiz submission
Admin APIs
```

High-risk endpoints generally need stronger controls.

---

# 91.58 Request Size Limits

Set limits for:

```text
JSON body
File upload
Query parameters
Header size
```

This protects against accidental and malicious resource exhaustion.

---

# 91.59 File Upload APIs

Do not send huge medical videos through ordinary JSON APIs.

Use:

```text
Client
 ↓
API requests upload authorization
 ↓
Object Storage
```

Potentially with pre-signed URLs.

---

# 91.60 API Documentation

All public/internal APIs SHOULD be documented using:

```text
OpenAPI
Swagger UI
```

Documentation should include:

```text
Endpoints
Parameters
Request bodies
Responses
Authentication
Errors
Examples
```

---

# 91.61 OpenAPI as Contract

OpenAPI should not be generated and forgotten.

It should be treated as an evolving API contract.

CI SHOULD validate:

```text
Implementation
 ↓
OpenAPI
```

for important services.

---

# 91.62 Contract Testing

For service-to-service communication:

```text
Consumer
 ↓
Expected contract
 ↓
Provider
```

contract testing MAY prevent accidental breaking changes.

---

# 91.63 Backward Compatibility

Avoid breaking existing clients.

Dangerous changes:

```text
Rename response field
Remove field
Change field type
Change meaning
Change enum unexpectedly
```

Prefer additive changes.

---

# 91.64 Example

Existing:

```json
{
  "title": "Physiology"
}
```

Safe:

```json
{
  "title": "Physiology",
  "shortDescription": "..."
}
```

Potentially breaking:

```json
{
  "courseTitle": "Physiology"
}
```

if clients still expect `title`.

---

# 91.65 Enum Evolution

Be careful with enums.

Suppose:

```text
DRAFT
PUBLISHED
ARCHIVED
```

A client may fail if the server introduces:

```text
UNDER_REVIEW
```

Clients should handle unknown values defensively where appropriate.

---

# 91.66 API Deprecation

When an API version becomes obsolete:

```text
v1
 ↓
Deprecated
 ↓
Migration period
 ↓
v2
 ↓
Retire v1
```

Do not remove APIs without understanding who consumes them.

---

# 91.67 API Gateway Routing

Example:

```text
/api/v1/auth/**       → Auth Service
/api/v1/users/**      → User Service
/api/v1/courses/**    → Course Service
/api/v1/quizzes/**    → Quiz Service
/api/v1/progress/**   → Progress Service
```

---

# 91.68 Internal vs External APIs

Not every internal endpoint needs to be exposed publicly.

Separate:

```text
External API
Internal API
Admin API
Service-to-service API
```

---

# 91.69 Admin APIs

Administrative APIs require stronger controls.

Example:

```text
/api/v1/admin/users
/api/v1/admin/courses
/api/v1/admin/audit-logs
```

Use explicit authorization.

---

# 91.70 Service-to-Service APIs

Internal APIs SHOULD use authenticated service identities where appropriate.

Do not rely solely on:

```text
"it's inside Kubernetes."
```

Network location is not a security boundary.

---

# 91.71 API Secrets

Never place secrets in:

```text
Source code
Git
OpenAPI examples
Logs
Client-side JavaScript
```

Use:

```text
Kubernetes Secrets
External Secret Manager
Vault
Cloud secret services
```

as appropriate.

---

# 91.72 CORS

CORS should be explicitly configured.

Avoid production:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

for authenticated applications unless the security model explicitly supports it.

---

# 91.73 CSRF

The CSRF strategy depends on the authentication mechanism.

Cookie-based authentication needs appropriate CSRF protection.

Bearer-token APIs have a different threat model.

Do not blindly enable or disable CSRF without understanding the authentication architecture.

---

# 91.74 API Logging

Log useful metadata:

```text
Request ID
Method
Path
Status
Latency
Authenticated principal
Service
```

Do not log:

```text
Passwords
JWTs
Refresh tokens
Sensitive personal data
```

---

# 91.75 API Metrics

Track:

```text
Request count
Error rate
Latency
Status code distribution
Endpoint throughput
Rate-limit events
Dependency latency
```

Useful metrics:

```text
p50
p95
p99
```

Average latency alone is not enough.

---

# 91.76 API Performance

Do not optimize only for average response time.

Example:

```text
Average = 100ms
p99 = 8 seconds
```

That API has a serious tail-latency problem.

---

# 91.77 API Caching

Public or safe read APIs MAY use:

```text
Cache-Control
ETag
Last-Modified
```

where appropriate.

Do not cache personalized responses publicly.

---

# 91.78 ETags

For resources that change infrequently, ETags can reduce unnecessary payload transfer.

Conceptually:

```text
GET /courses/123
ETag: "abc123"
```

Later:

```text
If-None-Match: "abc123"
```

Server:

```text
304 Not Modified
```

---

# 91.79 Bulk APIs

If clients need many resources, avoid:

```text
GET /courses/1
GET /courses/2
GET /courses/3
...
GET /courses/1000
```

Consider appropriate batch APIs.

But bulk APIs require:

```text
Limits
Authorization
Payload constraints
Error semantics
```

---

# 91.80 API Composition

A dashboard may require:

```text
User
Course
Progress
Notifications
```

Instead of making the frontend call six services, an API composition/BFF layer MAY aggregate them.

Example:

```text
React
 ↓
BFF
 ├── User Service
 ├── Course Service
 ├── Progress Service
 └── Notification Service
```

---

# 91.81 Backend-for-Frontend

A BFF can provide client-specific responses.

For example:

```text
Web BFF
Mobile BFF
Admin BFF
```

But don't create BFFs just to hide poor backend architecture.

---

# 91.82 API Aggregation Risks

Aggregation can introduce:

```text
Latency
Dependency failures
Complex error handling
Large payloads
```

Use timeouts and graceful degradation.

---

# 91.83 API Error Propagation

Do not blindly forward downstream errors.

Bad:

```text
Service B → 500 + internal database error
Service A → forwards exact error to client
```

Service A should translate it into an appropriate external contract.

---

# 91.84 Async APIs

Some operations should not block the client until completion.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/reports
→ 202 Accepted
```

Then:

```text
GET /api/v1/reports/{id}
```

can retrieve status.

Useful for:

```text
Large report generation
Video processing
3D asset processing
Bulk imports
Analytics jobs
```

---

# 91.85 API Jobs

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/reports
```

Response:

```json
{
  "jobId": "abc123",
  "status": "QUEUED"
}
```

Client can poll or receive an event.

---

# 91.86 Webhooks

When external integrations need notifications:

```text
Event
 ↓
Webhook
 ↓
External system
```

Webhook delivery SHOULD support:

```text
Retries
Signing
Idempotency
Timeouts
Dead-letter handling
```

---

# 91.87 API Security Checklist

* [ ] Authentication implemented
* [ ] Authorization implemented
* [ ] Object-level authorization verified
* [ ] Input validation enabled
* [ ] Request size limits configured
* [ ] Rate limiting configured
* [ ] CORS restricted
* [ ] Sensitive errors hidden
* [ ] Secrets protected
* [ ] SQL injection prevented
* [ ] IDOR/BOLA protection implemented
* [ ] Audit logging for sensitive actions
* [ ] TLS enforced
* [ ] API documentation maintained

---

# 91.88 API Testing

Every important endpoint SHOULD have tests for:

```text
Happy path
Validation failure
Authentication failure
Authorization failure
Not found
Conflict
Concurrency
Rate limiting
Malformed input
Downstream failure
```

---

# 91.89 Example API Test Matrix

For:

```text
POST /api/v1/enrollments
```

test:

```text
Valid student
Invalid token
Nonexistent course
Already enrolled
Suspended student
Duplicate request
Missing course ID
Invalid course ID
Database failure
```

---

# 91.90 API Contract Definition of Done

An API is production-ready when:

* [ ] Resource names are consistent
* [ ] HTTP methods are semantically correct
* [ ] HTTP status codes are standardized
* [ ] API versioning exists
* [ ] DTOs are used
* [ ] Validation exists
* [ ] Error contract exists
* [ ] Pagination is implemented where needed
* [ ] Filtering/sorting is controlled
* [ ] Authorization is enforced
* [ ] Object-level access is checked
* [ ] Rate limits exist where needed
* [ ] Timeouts exist
* [ ] Retries are controlled
* [ ] API documentation exists
* [ ] Metrics exist
* [ ] Logs exist
* [ ] Tracing exists where appropriate
* [ ] Contract compatibility is considered
* [ ] Automated tests exist

---

# 91.91 Core Principles

1. **Design APIs as contracts, not controller methods.**
2. **Use nouns for resources and HTTP methods for standard CRUD operations.**
3. **Version APIs deliberately.**
4. **Never trust client-supplied authorization fields.**
5. **Authentication and authorization are different problems.**
6. **Always perform object-level authorization where resources are user-owned.**
7. **Make retryable operations idempotent.**
8. **Never expose internal exceptions to clients.**
9. **Paginate large collections.**
10. **Control sorting and filtering through allowlists.**
11. **Set timeouts for downstream calls.**
12. **Do not blindly retry failures.**
13. **Measure p95/p99 latency, not just averages.**
14. **Treat OpenAPI as a contract.**
15. **Prefer backward-compatible API evolution.**
16. **Do not put business logic in controllers.**
17. **Do not make the API Gateway your only security boundary.**
18. **Do not expose internal infrastructure details through API responses.**

> **The biggest API mistake is thinking REST means "make CRUD endpoints." A production API is a contract between independently changing systems. Its real engineering difficulty is not `GET /courses`; it is handling authorization, retries, duplicate requests, partial failures, backward compatibility, concurrency, observability, and malformed input without corrupting business state.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 92: Authentication, Authorization & Identity Standards — OAuth2, JWT, refresh tokens, RBAC, ABAC, permissions, service identities, token lifecycle, session security, MFA, password security, and identity architecture.**


# CSDG — Chapter 92

## Authentication, Authorization & Identity Standards

This chapter defines how Mediverse should establish **who a user is**, determine **what they are allowed to do**, and securely propagate identity across the platform.

Core principle:

> **Authentication answers "Who are you?" Authorization answers "What are you allowed to do?" Identity architecture defines how that information is created, propagated, trusted, and revoked.**

---

## 92.1 Identity Architecture

Recommended high-level architecture:

```text
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │     React     │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            │
                            ▼
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │  API Gateway  │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            │
                            ▼
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │ Auth Service  │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            │
              ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
              ▼                           ▼
        Identity Store               Token Service
              │
              ▼
        User / Roles / Permissions
```

Other services consume authenticated identity:

```text
Course Service
Quiz Service
Progress Service
Notification Service
Admin Service
```

---

# 92.2 Authentication

Authentication establishes identity.

Typical flow:

```text
User
 ↓
Username / Email + Password
 ↓
Auth Service
 ↓
Verify credentials
 ↓
Issue tokens
 ↓
Client
```

---

# 92.3 Authorization

Authorization happens after authentication.

```text
User authenticated
        ↓
Who is this?
        ↓
Student
        ↓
What can Student do?
        ↓
Allowed / Denied
```

Never treat authentication as authorization.

---

# 92.4 Identity Model

A user identity should have a stable identifier.

Example:

```text
User
 ├── id
 ├── username
 ├── email
 ├── status
 ├── roles
 ├── createdAt
 └── updatedAt
```

Use an immutable internal identifier where possible.

Do not use email as the primary identity key if emails can change.

---

# 92.5 User ID

Prefer:

```text
UUID
```

or another non-guessable identifier where appropriate.

Example:

```text
userId = 7e2a... 
```

Avoid exposing sequential IDs when enumeration creates unnecessary risk.

This is not a substitute for authorization.

Even with UUIDs:

```text
GET /users/{uuid}
```

still requires access control.

---

# 92.6 Password Storage

Never store plaintext passwords.

Never store reversible encrypted passwords merely so the system can "decrypt" them later.

Use a password hashing algorithm designed for password storage.

Examples:

```text
Argon2id
bcrypt
scrypt
```

For Spring Security, use an appropriate `PasswordEncoder`.

---

# 92.7 Password Hashing

Conceptually:

```text
Password
   ↓
Password Hashing Algorithm
   ↓
Password Hash
   ↓
Database
```

During login:

```text
Password
   ↓
Password verification
   ↓
Stored hash
```

The original password should never be recoverable from the stored value.

---

# 92.8 Password Policy

Define requirements for:

```text
Minimum length
Compromised-password protection
Rate limiting
Reset procedure
Account lockout strategy
Password history where justified
```

Do not create ridiculous composition rules such as forcing six different character classes if they provide little practical benefit.

Length and resistance to credential stuffing matter more.

---

# 92.9 Credential Stuffing

Attackers may reuse leaked credentials from other sites.

Protection:

```text
Rate limiting
MFA
Breached-password detection
Suspicious-login detection
Credential monitoring
```

---

# 92.10 Brute-Force Protection

Authentication endpoints are high-risk.

Example:

```text
POST /api/v1/auth/login
```

Apply controls such as:

```text
Rate limiting
Progressive delays
Risk-based controls
MFA
Monitoring
```

Be careful with permanent account lockouts because attackers can intentionally lock other users out.

---

# 92.11 JWT

JWT can carry claims about an authenticated identity.

Example conceptual payload:

```json
{
  "sub": "user-123",
  "iss": "mediverse-auth",
  "aud": "mediverse-api",
  "exp": 1780000000
}
```

A JWT is **not encrypted merely because it is encoded**.

Do not put secrets inside it.

---

# 92.12 JWT Claims

Common claims:

```text
sub
iss
aud
exp
iat
nbf
jti
```

Use only claims that are actually required.

Do not stuff the entire user profile into the JWT.

---

# 92.13 `sub`

`sub` identifies the subject.

Example:

```text
sub = user-123
```

The application should use a stable identity identifier.

---

# 92.14 `iss`

`iss` identifies the issuer.

Example:

```text
iss = https://auth.mediverse.example
```

Services should validate that the token was issued by a trusted issuer.

---

# 92.15 `aud`

`aud` identifies intended recipients.

Example:

```text
aud = mediverse-api
```

Services should validate the audience where applicable.

---

# 92.16 `exp`

`exp` defines expiration.

Example:

```text
exp = current time + short lifetime
```

Access tokens should generally be short-lived.

---

# 92.17 `iat`

`iat` represents token issuance time.

Useful for:

```text
Auditing
Token-age policies
Debugging
Security analysis
```

---

# 92.18 `jti`

`jti` can uniquely identify a token.

Useful for:

```text
Revocation lists
Incident response
Token tracking
```

Use it only when needed.

---

# 92.19 Access Token

An access token authorizes API access.

Flow:

```text
Login
 ↓
Access Token
 ↓
API request
 ↓
Authorization
```

Example:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <access-token>
```

---

# 92.20 Access Token Lifetime

Do not make access tokens unnecessarily long-lived.

A long-lived token means:

```text
Token stolen
 ↓
Attacker has access
 ↓
Longer exploitation window
```

Choose lifetime according to risk and usability requirements.

---

# 92.21 Refresh Token

A refresh token allows the client to obtain a new access token without forcing the user to enter credentials again.

Conceptually:

```text
Access Token
   ↓
Expires
   ↓
Refresh Token
   ↓
New Access Token
```

---

# 92.22 Refresh Token Rotation

A stronger design uses rotation:

```text
Refresh Token A
      ↓
Refresh
      ↓
Refresh Token B
      ↓
Invalidate A
```

If an old refresh token is reused unexpectedly, the system can detect possible token theft.

---

# 92.23 Refresh Token Storage

Refresh tokens require stronger protection than ordinary access tokens.

For browser applications, carefully evaluate secure cookie-based approaches rather than exposing long-lived refresh credentials to JavaScript unnecessarily.

Typical cookie protections include:

```text
HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite
```

The exact configuration depends on the deployment architecture.

---

# 92.24 JWT Revocation

JWT access tokens are often difficult to revoke immediately because they are self-contained.

Options include:

```text
Short access-token lifetime
Refresh-token revocation
Token denylist
Session versioning
User security-version changes
```

Don't assume "JWT means impossible to revoke."

---

# 92.25 Token Versioning

A user can have a security version:

```text
securityVersion = 7
```

Token:

```text
securityVersion = 7
```

When all sessions must be invalidated:

```text
securityVersion = 8
```

Existing tokens become invalid.

This can be useful for:

```text
Password reset
Account compromise
Administrative logout
Security incident
```

---

# 92.26 Logout

Logout should have a defined security model.

Possible approach:

```text
Logout
 ↓
Revoke refresh token/session
 ↓
Client deletes local credentials
```

For immediate access-token invalidation, additional mechanisms are needed.

---

# 92.27 RBAC

Role-Based Access Control assigns permissions through roles.

Example:

```text
STUDENT
INSTRUCTOR
ADMIN
```

Mapping:

```text
STUDENT
 ├── COURSE_READ
 ├── QUIZ_ATTEMPT
 └── PROGRESS_READ_SELF

INSTRUCTOR
 ├── COURSE_READ
 ├── COURSE_WRITE
 └── QUIZ_MANAGE

ADMIN
 └── ADMIN_*
```

---

# 92.28 Roles vs Permissions

Do not hard-code every authorization decision around roles.

Prefer:

```text
User
 ↓
Role
 ↓
Permissions
 ↓
Authorization
```

This is more flexible.

---

# 92.29 Permission-Based Authorization

Example:

```text
COURSE_READ
COURSE_CREATE
COURSE_UPDATE
COURSE_DELETE

QUIZ_READ
QUIZ_CREATE
QUIZ_UPDATE
QUIZ_PUBLISH

USER_READ
USER_MANAGE
```

Then:

```text
INSTRUCTOR
→ COURSE_CREATE
→ COURSE_UPDATE
```

---

# 92.30 Role Explosion

Avoid creating dozens of roles:

```text
STUDENT_BASIC
STUDENT_ADVANCED
STUDENT_PREMIUM
INSTRUCTOR_BASIC
INSTRUCTOR_SENIOR
...
```

This becomes difficult to maintain.

Prefer roles plus explicit permissions and contextual rules.

---

# 92.31 ABAC

Attribute-Based Access Control considers attributes.

Example:

```text
User:
  role = INSTRUCTOR
  institution = ABC

Resource:
  institution = ABC

Action:
  UPDATE
```

Authorization:

```text
role allows UPDATE
AND
same institution
```

---

# 92.32 RBAC + ABAC

A mature Mediverse authorization model may combine both:

```text
Role
 +
Permission
 +
Resource ownership
 +
Tenant
 +
Context
```

Example:

```text
Instructor
AND
COURSE_UPDATE
AND
course.institutionId == user.institutionId
```

---

# 92.33 Resource Ownership

Students may access:

```text
/progress/{their-own-id}
```

but not:

```text
/progress/{another-student-id}
```

Authorization must verify ownership.

---

# 92.34 Hierarchical Roles

If needed:

```text
ADMIN
 ↓
INSTRUCTOR
 ↓
STUDENT
```

But don't automatically assume hierarchy.

A role hierarchy should be explicitly defined.

---

# 92.35 Method-Level Security

Spring Security can enforce authorization at service/method level.

Conceptually:

```java
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('COURSE_UPDATE')")
```

This is preferable to scattering authorization checks throughout business logic.

---

# 92.36 Controller vs Service Authorization

Do not put every security rule only in controllers.

A safer architecture is:

```text
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Authorization Policy
 ↓
Business operation
```

This reduces the chance that another entry point accidentally bypasses authorization.

---

# 92.37 Gateway Authorization

The gateway can perform coarse-grained checks.

Example:

```text
/api/v1/admin/**
```

requires authenticated admin access.

But resource-level authorization should still happen in the service responsible for the resource.

---

# 92.38 Service-to-Service Identity

Microservices need identities too.

Example:

```text
Progress Service
      ↓
Course Service
```

Course Service should know:

```text
Who is calling me?
```

Possible mechanisms:

```text
OAuth2 client credentials
mTLS
Service account tokens
Workload identity
```

---

# 92.39 Client Credentials

For machine-to-machine communication:

```text
Service A
 ↓
Identity Provider
 ↓
Access Token
 ↓
Service B
```

There is no human user involved.

---

# 92.40 Human vs Service Identity

Do not confuse:

```text
Human identity
```

with:

```text
Service identity
```

Example:

```text
student-123
```

is different from:

```text
quiz-service
```

Both may need authentication, but their security models differ.

---

# 92.41 Service Account Permissions

Give services the minimum permissions they require.

Bad:

```text
course-service
→ ADMIN_ALL
```

Better:

```text
course-service
→ COURSE_READ
→ COURSE_UPDATE
```

---

# 92.42 Least Privilege

Every identity should receive only the permissions necessary to perform its responsibilities.

Applies to:

```text
Users
Services
Database accounts
Kubernetes service accounts
CI/CD systems
Cloud identities
```

---

# 92.43 MFA

Multi-factor authentication SHOULD be considered for:

```text
Administrators
Instructors
High-privilege accounts
Sensitive operations
```

Factors may include:

```text
Password
Authenticator app
Passkey
Hardware security key
```

---

# 92.44 Passkeys

For modern authentication, passkeys/WebAuthn can significantly improve resistance to phishing.

Potential architecture:

```text
Browser
 ↓
WebAuthn
 ↓
Identity Provider
 ↓
Authenticated session
```

Do not force passwords into every authentication flow if passwordless authentication is appropriate.

---

# 92.45 Email Verification

If email identity matters:

```text
Registration
 ↓
Verification token
 ↓
Email
 ↓
Verification
 ↓
Account activated
```

Verification tokens should:

```text
Expire
Be single-use
Be unpredictable
Be invalidated after use
```

---

# 92.46 Password Reset

Password reset is an authentication workflow and must be treated as highly sensitive.

Typical flow:

```text
Forgot Password
 ↓
Generic response
 ↓
Secure reset token
 ↓
Email
 ↓
Reset password
 ↓
Invalidate relevant sessions
```

---

# 92.47 Account Enumeration

Do not reveal whether an account exists.

Bad:

```text
"Email does not exist."
```

Better:

```text
"If the account exists, a password-reset email will be sent."
```

This prevents attackers from harvesting valid accounts.

---

# 92.48 Authentication Error Messages

Avoid:

```text
"Password is wrong but email exists."
```

Prefer a generic authentication failure.

The backend logs can contain more diagnostic information securely.

---

# 92.49 Session Management

A user may have:

```text
Laptop
Phone
Tablet
```

Each may have a separate session.

Store session metadata where appropriate:

```text
sessionId
userId
createdAt
lastSeen
device
IP metadata
revokedAt
```

Avoid retaining unnecessary sensitive information.

---

# 92.50 "Logout All Devices"

A useful security feature:

```text
User
 ↓
Logout all sessions
 ↓
Revoke refresh sessions
 ↓
Invalidate session state
```

This is especially important after suspected account compromise.

---

# 92.51 Concurrent Sessions

Define whether the platform allows:

```text
One session
Multiple sessions
Limited number of sessions
```

Don't implement this accidentally.

---

# 92.52 Token Theft

If an access token is stolen:

```text
Attacker
 ↓
Bearer token
 ↓
API
```

The API may accept it until expiration unless additional revocation mechanisms exist.

Therefore:

```text
Short-lived access tokens
+
Secure refresh-token handling
+
MFA
+
Monitoring
```

provide defense in depth.

---

# 92.53 Token Storage in Browser

Avoid casually storing long-lived sensitive tokens in:

```text
localStorage
```

because JavaScript-accessible storage can be exposed if an XSS vulnerability exists.

For browser applications, evaluate secure, HttpOnly cookie-based session/refresh designs where appropriate.

---

# 92.54 XSS and Authentication

Authentication architecture cannot compensate for unsafe frontend code.

Protect against:

```text
Stored XSS
Reflected XSS
DOM XSS
```

Use framework escaping, CSP where appropriate, safe rendering practices, and dependency hygiene.

---

# 92.55 CSRF and Cookies

If authentication uses cookies:

```text
Browser
 ↓
Cookie
 ↓
API
```

CSRF must be considered.

Controls may include:

```text
SameSite
CSRF tokens
Origin checks
Secure cookie configuration
```

---

# 92.56 JWT and CSRF

Bearer tokens sent explicitly in an authorization header have a different CSRF profile than automatically attached cookies.

But that does **not** mean the architecture is automatically secure.

You still need to address:

```text
XSS
Token theft
CORS
Storage
Refresh-token security
```

---

# 92.57 Identity Provider

For larger systems, consider a dedicated Identity Provider rather than implementing every authentication feature from scratch.

Possible architecture:

```text
React
 ↓
Identity Provider
 ↓
Access Token
 ↓
Mediverse APIs
```

An IdP can manage:

```text
Login
MFA
OAuth2
OIDC
Password reset
Federation
Sessions
```

---

# 92.58 OAuth2

OAuth2 primarily defines authorization delegation.

It is commonly combined with:

```text
OpenID Connect
```

for user authentication/identity.

Do not casually call every JWT login implementation "OAuth2."

---

# 92.59 OpenID Connect

OIDC adds an identity layer on top of OAuth2.

It provides concepts such as:

```text
ID Token
User identity claims
UserInfo
Discovery
```

Use OIDC when integrating with an identity provider for user authentication.

---

# 92.60 Authorization Code + PKCE

For browser/mobile public clients, Authorization Code with PKCE is a strong modern OAuth/OIDC flow.

Conceptually:

```text
Client
 ↓
Authorization Server
 ↓
Authorization Code
 ↓
PKCE verification
 ↓
Tokens
```

Avoid the old implicit flow for modern applications.

---

# 92.61 Audience Validation

A service should not accept a token merely because:

```text
Signature valid
```

It should also validate relevant claims such as:

```text
Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Not-before
Signature
Algorithm
```

---

# 92.62 Algorithm Confusion

Do not allow attackers to choose arbitrary JWT algorithms.

The accepted signing algorithms must be explicitly configured.

Never blindly trust the token header's algorithm selection.

---

# 92.63 Signing Keys

JWT signing keys must be protected.

Architecture:

```text
Private Key
     ↓
Auth Service
     ↓
Signs Token

Public Key
     ↓
API Services
     ↓
Verify Token
```

Private signing keys should never be distributed unnecessarily.

---

# 92.64 Key Rotation

Signing keys should support rotation.

Conceptually:

```text
Key A
 ↓
Key B
 ↓
Key C
```

During rotation, old public keys may need to remain available temporarily so valid existing tokens can still be verified.

---

# 92.65 JWKS

Identity systems commonly publish public signing keys through a JWKS endpoint.

Services can retrieve and cache public keys.

This avoids manually copying public keys into every service.

---

# 92.66 Key Compromise

If a signing key is compromised:

```text
Stop trusting compromised key
 ↓
Rotate keys
 ↓
Invalidate affected sessions/tokens
 ↓
Investigate
 ↓
Monitor
```

This should be part of the incident-response plan.

---

# 92.67 Identity Data Ownership

Define which service owns what.

Example:

```text
Auth Service
→ Credentials
→ Authentication state

User Service
→ Profile
→ User preferences

Course Service
→ Course ownership

Progress Service
→ Learning progress
```

Avoid duplicating authoritative user data across every service.

---

# 92.68 Identity Events

Identity changes may produce events:

```text
UserRegistered
PasswordChanged
UserDisabled
RoleChanged
SessionRevoked
```

Other services can consume these events where necessary.

---

# 92.69 Disabled Users

Every request should account for account status when required.

Example:

```text
User status = DISABLED
```

Potential behavior:

```text
Existing sessions revoked
Refresh denied
API access denied
```

---

# 92.70 Role Changes

Suppose:

```text
Instructor
 ↓
Role revoked
 ↓
Now Student
```

An already-issued token may still contain:

```text
INSTRUCTOR
```

until it expires.

Therefore sensitive role changes may require:

```text
Short token lifetimes
Token/session versioning
Centralized authorization lookup
Explicit session revocation
```

---

# 92.71 Don't Put Everything in JWT

Bad:

```json
{
  "user": {
    "name": "...",
    "email": "...",
    "phone": "...",
    "institution": "...",
    "permissions": [...],
    "progress": [...],
    "preferences": {...}
  }
}
```

JWTs should remain small and focused.

Large tokens increase:

```text
Network overhead
Processing cost
Exposure
```

---

# 92.72 Authorization Cache

Permissions may sometimes be cached.

But when permissions change:

```text
Role updated
 ↓
Permission cache invalidated
```

Do not let stale authorization information remain indefinitely.

---

# 92.73 Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed

For authorization:

```text
Authorization system unavailable
```

the default should generally be:

```text
DENY
```

not:

```text
ALLOW
```

Security controls should fail closed unless there is a carefully justified exception.

---

# 92.74 Audit Logging

Sensitive security events SHOULD be auditable.

Examples:

```text
Login success
Login failure
Password reset
MFA change
Role change
Permission change
Account disable
Session revocation
Admin actions
```

Audit logs should be tamper-resistant and access-controlled.

---

# 92.75 Audit Log Example

```json
{
  "event": "ROLE_CHANGED",
  "actor": "admin-123",
  "target": "user-456",
  "oldRole": "STUDENT",
  "newRole": "INSTRUCTOR",
  "timestamp": "...",
  "requestId": "..."
}
```

Do not log secrets or passwords.

---

# 92.76 Identity Monitoring

Monitor:

```text
Failed logins
Successful logins
Token failures
Refresh-token reuse
Impossible travel
Privilege escalation
Mass account changes
Admin activity
```

---

# 92.77 Security Alerts

Potential alerts:

```text
Multiple failed login attempts
Refresh token reuse
Sudden admin role assignments
Mass password resets
Unusual API access
Repeated authorization failures
```

---

# 92.78 Kubernetes Identity

For workloads running in Kubernetes, use:

```text
ServiceAccount
```

for workload identity.

Do not put static cloud credentials directly into application images.

---

# 92.79 Kubernetes Service Accounts

Example:

```text
course-service
 ↓
Kubernetes ServiceAccount
 ↓
Workload identity / RBAC
```

Grant only required permissions.

---

# 92.80 Kubernetes RBAC

Kubernetes RBAC is separate from application RBAC.

Do not confuse:

```text
Kubernetes ADMIN
```

with:

```text
Mediverse ADMIN
```

They protect completely different layers.

---

# 92.81 Database Identity

Services should ideally use separate database identities where practical.

Example:

```text
course-service-db-user
quiz-service-db-user
progress-service-db-user
```

Avoid one universal:

```text
postgres-admin
```

credential for every application service.

---

# 92.82 Identity Boundary

A good architecture looks like:

```text
                 Identity Provider
                        │
                        ▼
                  Access Token
                        │
             ┌──────────┴──────────┐
             ▼                     ▼
        Course API             Quiz API
             │                     │
      Course Authorization    Quiz Authorization
```

Every service enforces the permissions relevant to its own resources.

---

# 92.83 Authentication Checklist

* [ ] Passwords hashed securely
* [ ] Login rate limiting
* [ ] Password reset secured
* [ ] Email verification where required
* [ ] MFA for privileged users
* [ ] Secure token handling
* [ ] Short-lived access tokens
* [ ] Refresh-token rotation where appropriate
* [ ] Token revocation strategy
* [ ] Signing-key rotation
* [ ] Issuer validation
* [ ] Audience validation
* [ ] Expiration validation
* [ ] Algorithm allowlist
* [ ] Secure session handling

---

# 92.84 Authorization Checklist

* [ ] RBAC defined
* [ ] Permissions defined
* [ ] Object-level authorization
* [ ] Resource ownership checks
* [ ] Tenant isolation
* [ ] Least privilege
* [ ] Admin access separated
* [ ] Service identities separated
* [ ] Authorization fails closed
* [ ] Permission changes invalidate stale authorization where required

---

# 92.85 Definition of Done

Identity architecture is production-ready when:

* [ ] Authentication flow is documented
* [ ] Authorization model is documented
* [ ] Roles and permissions are explicit
* [ ] User ownership rules are explicit
* [ ] Token lifecycle is defined
* [ ] Refresh-token lifecycle is defined
* [ ] Logout behavior is defined
* [ ] Password-reset workflow is defined
* [ ] MFA strategy exists
* [ ] Service-to-service identity exists
* [ ] Key rotation exists
* [ ] Audit logging exists
* [ ] Security monitoring exists
* [ ] Authorization tests exist
* [ ] Token validation tests exist
* [ ] Security failure scenarios have been tested

---

# 92.86 Core Principles

1. **Authentication ≠ authorization.**
2. **Never trust the client to tell you what it is allowed to do.**
3. **Every resource needs an authorization decision.**
4. **Roles should map to permissions, not directly to every business rule.**
5. **Ownership and tenant boundaries must be enforced server-side.**
6. **Access tokens should be short-lived.**
7. **Refresh tokens require stronger protection and lifecycle management.**
8. **Authorization should fail closed.**
9. **JWT signature validation alone is insufficient.**
10. **Validate issuer, audience, expiration, and algorithm.**
11. **Rotate signing keys.**
12. **Keep JWTs small.**
13. **Do not store long-lived browser credentials carelessly.**
14. **Treat password reset as seriously as login.**
15. **Service identities are different from human identities.**
16. **Least privilege applies to users, services, Kubernetes, databases, and CI/CD.**
17. **Security-sensitive actions must be auditable.**
18. **Authorization bugs are usually more dangerous than authentication bugs because a perfectly authenticated attacker can still become an unauthorized user.**

> **The most dangerous security mistake is not "someone bypassed login." It's "login worked perfectly, but the system trusted the user's requested resource or role without verifying authorization." A valid JWT proves very little by itself. The real security boundary is the authorization decision made for every sensitive operation.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 93: Data Security, Privacy & Protection Standards — encryption at rest/in transit, PII, medical/educational data classification, secrets, masking, retention, deletion, backups, auditability, privacy boundaries, and data-loss prevention.**


# CSDG — Chapter 93

## Data Security, Privacy & Protection Standards

This chapter defines how Mediverse should protect data throughout its lifecycle:

```text
Collection
   ↓
Processing
   ↓
Storage
   ↓
Transmission
   ↓
Backup
   ↓
Archival
   ↓
Deletion
```

Core principle:

> **Do not protect data merely because it is in a database. Protect it according to its sensitivity, business value, legal obligations, and potential impact if compromised.**

---

## 93.1 Data Security Architecture

Recommended model:

```text
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │     Client      │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │ TLS
                             ▼
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │   API Gateway   │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │ Application     │
                    │ Services        │
                    └───────┬─────────┘
                            │
              ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
              ▼             ▼             ▼
         PostgreSQL       Redis       Object Store
              │
              ▼
          Encrypted
           Backups
```

Security must exist at every layer.

---

# 93.2 Data Classification

Every important data category should have a classification.

Recommended:

```text
PUBLIC
INTERNAL
CONFIDENTIAL
RESTRICTED
```

---

# 93.3 PUBLIC Data

Information intentionally available to everyone.

Examples:

```text
Course titles
Public descriptions
Public educational content
Public announcements
Public documentation
```

Compromise generally has limited impact.

---

# 93.4 INTERNAL Data

Information intended for authenticated organizational users.

Examples:

```text
Internal operational metrics
Non-public course metadata
Internal configuration documentation
Operational dashboards
```

---

# 93.5 CONFIDENTIAL Data

Information where unauthorized access could cause meaningful harm.

Examples:

```text
User profiles
Instructor information
Learning analytics
Internal reports
Business information
```

---

# 93.6 RESTRICTED Data

Highest protection level.

Potential examples:

```text
Passwords
Authentication secrets
Refresh tokens
Encryption keys
Security credentials
Highly sensitive personal information
```

The exact classification should be determined by the actual data and applicable regulatory requirements.

---

# 93.7 Data Inventory

Maintain a data inventory.

Example:

```text
Data
 ├── Owner
 ├── Classification
 ├── Location
 ├── Purpose
 ├── Retention
 ├── Encryption
 ├── Access roles
 └── Deletion policy
```

Without knowing what data exists, security becomes guesswork.

---

# 93.8 Data Ownership

Every important dataset should have an owner.

Example:

```text
User profile
→ User Service

Course content
→ Course Service

Quiz attempts
→ Quiz Service

Learning progress
→ Progress Service

Audit logs
→ Security/Audit subsystem
```

Ownership determines who is responsible for correctness and protection.

---

# 93.9 Data Minimization

Collect only information actually required.

Bad:

```text
Registration
→ Name
→ Email
→ Phone
→ Date of birth
→ Address
→ Government ID
→ Photograph
→ Other unrelated information
```

if the application only needs:

```text
Name
Email
Password
```

More data means:

```text
More attack surface
+
More storage
+
More compliance burden
+
More breach impact
```

---

# 93.10 Purpose Limitation

Data should have a defined purpose.

Example:

```text
Email
→ Authentication
→ Notifications
```

Do not silently reuse it for unrelated purposes.

---

# 93.11 Data Lifecycle

Define lifecycle stages:

```text
Created
 ↓
Active
 ↓
Archived
 ↓
Retention expires
 ↓
Deleted
```

Do not allow data to remain forever simply because storage is cheap.

---

# 93.12 Encryption in Transit

All sensitive communication should use TLS.

```text
Browser
   │
 HTTPS
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
 TLS where appropriate
   │
   ▼
Services
```

Avoid plaintext HTTP for production authentication or sensitive data.

---

# 93.13 TLS

Use modern TLS configurations.

Avoid outdated protocols and weak cipher suites.

Certificate management should be automated where practical.

---

# 93.14 Internal Encryption

Do not automatically assume internal Kubernetes traffic is safe.

Potential architecture:

```text
Service A
   │
 encrypted/authenticated communication
   ▼
Service B
```

For highly sensitive environments, consider mTLS/service-mesh-based identity.

---

# 93.15 Encryption at Rest

Sensitive data should be encrypted at rest.

Potential layers:

```text
Database storage
Object storage
Backup storage
Persistent volumes
Secrets
```

Cloud/platform-level encryption provides an important baseline.

---

# 93.16 Application-Level Encryption

Some extremely sensitive fields may require encryption beyond storage-level encryption.

Example:

```text
Database
 ┌───────────────────────────┐
 │ encrypted sensitive data │
 └───────────────────────────┘
```

But application-level encryption creates key-management complexity.

Do not encrypt everything blindly.

---

# 93.17 Hashing vs Encryption

These are different.

### Hashing

```text
Input
 ↓
Hash
```

Used for:

```text
Passwords
Integrity
Fingerprints
```

Generally one-way.

### Encryption

```text
Plaintext
 ↓
Encryption + Key
 ↓
Ciphertext
```

Can be decrypted with appropriate key material.

---

# 93.18 Passwords

Passwords should be:

```text
Hashed
Salted
Slow to brute-force
```

Do not encrypt passwords so they can later be recovered.

---

# 93.19 Sensitive Tokens

Do not store:

```text
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
API keys
Secrets
```

in plaintext unless there is a deliberate, justified design.

Where persistence is necessary, consider appropriate hashing or encryption depending on whether the original value must be recovered.

---

# 93.20 Encryption Keys

Encryption is useless if key management is weak.

Bad:

```text
application.properties
ENCRYPTION_KEY=abc123
```

Better:

```text
Application
    ↓
Secret Manager / KMS
    ↓
Encryption Key
```

---

# 93.21 Key Management Service

A KMS or equivalent system can manage:

```text
Key creation
Key storage
Key rotation
Access control
Key usage auditing
```

Examples include cloud KMS systems and enterprise key-management platforms.

---

# 93.22 Envelope Encryption

For large-scale systems:

```text
Master Key
   ↓
Data Encryption Key
   ↓
Actual Data
```

The master key protects the data encryption key.

This reduces the need to use a high-value master key directly for every piece of data.

---

# 93.23 Key Rotation

Keys should support rotation.

Example:

```text
Key V1
 ↓
Key V2
 ↓
Key V3
```

Existing encrypted data may need a controlled re-encryption strategy depending on the system.

---

# 93.24 Secret Management

Secrets include:

```text
Database passwords
JWT signing keys
OAuth client secrets
API keys
Cloud credentials
Encryption keys
```

Do not commit them to Git.

---

# 93.25 Kubernetes Secrets

Kubernetes Secrets are useful but should not automatically be treated as equivalent to a dedicated enterprise secret manager.

Consider:

```text
External Secrets
Vault
Cloud Secret Manager
KMS-backed systems
```

depending on deployment requirements.

---

# 93.26 Secret Rotation

Secrets should be rotatable.

Example:

```text
DB Password V1
       ↓
Create V2
       ↓
Update application
       ↓
Verify
       ↓
Disable V1
```

Avoid designs where changing a credential requires rebuilding the entire platform manually.

---

# 93.27 Database Security

Database security includes:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Network restrictions
Encryption
Auditing
Backups
Least privilege
Connection security
```

---

# 93.28 Database Users

Avoid one universal database administrator account.

Prefer:

```text
course_app
quiz_app
progress_app
reporting_app
```

with appropriate permissions.

---

# 93.29 Database Least Privilege

A read-only service should not have:

```text
DROP DATABASE
CREATE ROLE
ALTER SYSTEM
```

permissions.

Give the application only what it requires.

---

# 93.30 SQL Injection

Never build SQL using raw user input.

Bad:

```java
String sql = "SELECT * FROM courses WHERE title = '" + input + "'";
```

Use parameterized queries / ORM mechanisms appropriately.

---

# 93.31 ORM Security

Using JPA/Hibernate does not magically eliminate all security problems.

Review:

```text
Native SQL
Dynamic queries
JPQL construction
Sorting
Filtering
Stored procedures
```

especially when user input influences query structure.

---

# 93.32 PII

Personally identifiable information may include:

```text
Name
Email
Phone
Address
User identifiers
```

Classification depends on context and applicable legal requirements.

---

# 93.33 Educational Data

Mediverse may handle learning-related data such as:

```text
Course enrollments
Quiz attempts
Scores
Learning progress
Instructor activity
Completion history
```

Treat these as sensitive where appropriate.

---

# 93.34 Medical/Educational Boundary

This distinction is critical.

A medical education platform may contain:

```text
Educational medical content
```

without necessarily holding:

```text
Clinical patient records
```

Do not design the platform as if it stores patient health information unless the actual product requirements say so.

If patient/clinical data is introduced later, the security and compliance architecture must be reassessed.

---

# 93.35 Sensitive Data in Logs

Never log:

```text
Passwords
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
Authorization headers
Encryption keys
```

Be careful with:

```text
Email
Phone
User IDs
Request bodies
```

because these may also be sensitive depending on context.

---

# 93.36 Log Redaction

Example:

```text
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
```

should become:

```text
Authorization: [REDACTED]
```

Similarly:

```text
password=[REDACTED]
```

---

# 93.37 PII Masking

Example:

```text
Original:
john.doe@example.com
```

Possible log representation:

```text
j***@example.com
```

Masking rules should be consistent.

---

# 93.38 Data in URLs

Avoid putting sensitive information in URLs.

Bad:

```text
GET /reset-password?token=secret-token
```

Query strings may appear in:

```text
Logs
Browser history
Proxy logs
Monitoring systems
Analytics
```

Use carefully designed flows that minimize exposure.

---

# 93.39 Sensitive Headers

Do not accidentally log:

```text
Authorization
Cookie
Set-Cookie
X-API-Key
```

---

# 93.40 Data in Error Messages

Bad:

```json
{
  "message": "User john@example.com failed because password hash abc123..."
}
```

Good:

```json
{
  "message": "Authentication failed."
}
```

---

# 93.41 API Response Minimization

Do not return unnecessary fields.

Bad:

```json
{
  "id": "...",
  "name": "...",
  "email": "...",
  "passwordHash": "...",
  "securityVersion": 4,
  "internalFlags": [...]
}
```

Good:

```json
{
  "id": "...",
  "name": "...",
  "email": "..."
}
```

---

# 93.42 Data Masking

Different users may see different representations.

Example:

```text
Student:
john.doe@example.com

Instructor:
j***@example.com

Admin:
full email
```

The exact policy depends on business requirements.

---

# 93.43 Multi-Tenant Data Isolation

If Mediverse supports institutions:

```text
Institution A
 ├── Users
 ├── Courses
 └── Progress

Institution B
 ├── Users
 ├── Courses
 └── Progress
```

A user from A must never access B's data unless explicitly authorized.

---

# 93.44 Tenant ID

Requests may carry tenant context:

```text
tenantId = institution-123
```

But never blindly trust:

```text
X-Tenant-ID: institution-999
```

from the client.

Tenant identity must be derived from trusted authentication/authorization context.

---

# 93.45 Tenant Isolation

Every relevant database query should enforce tenant boundaries.

Conceptually:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM courses
WHERE id = ?
AND tenant_id = ?;
```

Not:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM courses
WHERE id = ?;
```

if the resource is tenant-scoped.

---

# 93.46 Cross-Tenant Authorization

Explicitly test:

```text
Tenant A user
       ↓
Request Tenant B resource
       ↓
403 / 404 according to policy
```

This should be part of automated security testing.

---

# 93.47 Database-Level Tenant Protection

For stronger isolation, PostgreSQL Row-Level Security can be considered.

Conceptually:

```text
Application
 ↓
Database
 ↓
RLS Policy
 ↓
Tenant-specific rows
```

This provides an additional defense layer.

---

# 93.48 Backup Security

Backups contain the same sensitive information as production databases.

Therefore:

```text
Production DB
      ↓
Encrypted Backup
      ↓
Secure Storage
```

Backups require:

```text
Access control
Encryption
Retention policy
Auditability
Recovery testing
```

---

# 93.49 Backup Retention

Define:

```text
Daily backups
Weekly backups
Monthly backups
Retention period
```

according to business and regulatory requirements.

Do not retain everything forever without justification.

---

# 93.50 Backup Encryption

Backup encryption should be independent enough that compromise of ordinary application credentials does not automatically expose all backup data.

Use appropriate KMS/secret-management controls.

---

# 93.51 Disaster Recovery

Define:

```text
RPO
RTO
```

### RPO

How much data can potentially be lost?

Example:

```text
RPO = 15 minutes
```

### RTO

How quickly must service recover?

Example:

```text
RTO = 1 hour
```

---

# 93.52 Backup Restore Testing

A backup that has never been restored is an assumption, not a proven backup.

Test:

```text
Backup
 ↓
Restore
 ↓
Validate
 ↓
Application recovery
```

regularly.

---

# 93.53 Data Retention

Every important dataset should have a retention policy.

Example:

```text
Audit logs → defined retention
Temporary files → short retention
Sessions → short retention
Course content → long retention
Deleted accounts → defined deletion period
```

Actual durations must be determined by product, contractual, and legal requirements.

---

# 93.54 Data Deletion

Deletion should be deliberate.

Possible strategies:

```text
Hard delete
Soft delete
Anonymization
Cryptographic erasure
Archival
```

Choose based on the data and requirements.

---

# 93.55 Soft Delete

Example:

```text
deleted_at
```

Advantages:

```text
Recovery
Auditability
Accidental deletion protection
```

But soft delete is not equivalent to true deletion.

The data still exists.

---

# 93.56 Hard Delete

Physical deletion:

```text
DELETE FROM users ...
```

may be appropriate when data truly needs to be removed.

But investigate:

```text
Backups
Caches
Search indexes
Logs
Replicas
Object storage
Analytics systems
```

before claiming the data is completely deleted.

---

# 93.57 Anonymization

Instead of:

```text
John Doe
john@example.com
```

analytics might retain:

```text
anonymous-user-8472
```

where identity is no longer required.

---

# 93.58 Pseudonymization

Pseudonymization replaces identifiers but retains the ability to re-identify under controlled conditions.

Example:

```text
Real User ID
      ↓
Pseudonymous ID
```

This is not the same as irreversible anonymization.

---

# 93.59 Cache Security

Sensitive data can leak through caches.

Be careful with:

```text
Redis
CDN
Browser cache
Proxy cache
Application cache
```

Never accidentally make personalized responses publicly cacheable.

---

# 93.60 Redis Security

Redis should not be treated as an open internal database.

Configure:

```text
Authentication
Network restrictions
TLS where appropriate
Least privilege
Persistence protection
```

---

# 93.61 Object Storage

Educational media may be stored in object storage:

```text
Videos
PDFs
Images
3D models
Audio
```

Do not make private content publicly accessible simply because a frontend needs to download it.

Use appropriate:

```text
Private buckets
Signed URLs
Access policies
Expiration
```

---

# 93.62 Signed URLs

Typical flow:

```text
Client
 ↓
API
 ↓
Authorization check
 ↓
Signed URL
 ↓
Object Storage
```

The client gets temporary access rather than permanent public access.

---

# 93.63 Content Encryption

For highly sensitive stored content, consider encryption at rest and appropriate key management.

But don't introduce application-level encryption without considering:

```text
Performance
Searchability
Key rotation
Recovery
Operational complexity
```

---

# 93.64 Data Export

Users may need access to their own information.

A secure export process should include:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Data scope
Rate limiting
Audit logging
Secure delivery
Expiration
```

---

# 93.65 Data Import

Imports are dangerous because uploaded data may contain:

```text
Malicious files
Oversized files
Unexpected formats
Embedded scripts
Malformed records
```

Validate everything.

---

# 93.66 File Security

For uploads:

```text
Validate extension
Validate MIME type
Inspect actual content
Limit size
Generate server-side filenames
Store outside executable paths
Scan where appropriate
```

Never trust the filename supplied by the user.

---

# 93.67 Filename Security

Bad:

```text
../../../../etc/passwd
```

Do not use user-supplied filenames directly as filesystem paths.

Generate internal object keys.

Example:

```text
media/2026/08/uuid-generated-name
```

---

# 93.68 Data Integrity

Security is not only confidentiality.

The three classic properties are:

```text
Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
```

---

# 93.69 Confidentiality

Prevent unauthorized disclosure.

Example:

```text
Student A
 ↓
Student B's private progress
 ↓
DENY
```

---

# 93.70 Integrity

Prevent unauthorized modification.

Example:

```text
Student
 ↓
Modify own quiz score
 ↓
DENY
```

Scores should be controlled by trusted business logic.

---

# 93.71 Availability

Ensure systems remain usable.

Controls include:

```text
Rate limiting
Capacity planning
Timeouts
Circuit breakers
Backups
Disaster recovery
Autoscaling
```

---

# 93.72 Data Integrity Controls

Important records may require:

```text
Versioning
Optimistic locking
Audit trails
Immutable event records
Database constraints
Transactions
```

---

# 93.73 Optimistic Locking

For concurrent updates:

```text
Course version = 5

User A reads version 5
User B reads version 5

User A updates → version 6
User B updates using version 5
        ↓
Conflict
```

This prevents silent overwrites.

---

# 93.74 Auditability

For sensitive business changes, record:

```text
Who
What
When
Which resource
Previous value
New value
Request ID
```

Example:

```text
Instructor changed course status
DRAFT → PUBLISHED
```

---

# 93.75 Immutable Audit Logs

For security-sensitive auditing, avoid allowing ordinary application users to modify audit records.

Potential architecture:

```text
Application
 ↓
Audit Event
 ↓
Append-only storage
```

---

# 93.76 Privacy by Design

Privacy should be considered during architecture rather than added after implementation.

Ask:

```text
Do we need this data?
Who needs it?
Why?
How long?
Where is it stored?
Who can export it?
Who can delete it?
```

---

# 93.77 Privacy Threat Modeling

For each sensitive dataset:

```text
Asset
 ↓
Threat
 ↓
Attack
 ↓
Impact
 ↓
Control
```

Example:

```text
Student progress
 ↓
Unauthorized access
 ↓
IDOR
 ↓
Privacy breach
 ↓
Object-level authorization
```

---

# 93.78 Third-Party Data Sharing

Before sending user data to:

```text
Analytics
Email provider
AI service
Cloud service
Monitoring platform
Search engine
```

determine:

```text
What data is sent?
Why?
Who receives it?
How long?
Is it necessary?
```

---

# 93.79 Third-Party API Keys

Never expose:

```text
OPENAI_API_KEY
AWS_SECRET
STRIPE_SECRET
DATABASE_PASSWORD
```

in React.

Frontend code is public to the user.

Use:

```text
React
 ↓
Mediverse Backend
 ↓
Third-party API
```

---

# 93.80 Client-Side Secrets

There is no real secret in browser JavaScript.

Anything shipped to the browser can potentially be inspected.

Therefore:

```text
Secret
 ↓
Backend
```

not:

```text
Secret
 ↓
React bundle
```

---

# 93.81 Data Loss Prevention

DLP controls can detect sensitive information leaving approved boundaries.

Potential controls:

```text
PII scanning
Secret scanning
Git pre-commit checks
CI secret detection
Log scanning
Storage policies
```

---

# 93.82 Git Secret Scanning

CI should detect accidental commits such as:

```text
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
DATABASE_PASSWORD=...
PRIVATE_KEY=...
```

before they reach production.

If a secret is committed:

> Removing it from Git history is not enough. Assume it was exposed and rotate it.

---

# 93.83 Container Security

Do not put secrets into Docker images.

Bad:

```dockerfile
ENV DB_PASSWORD=mysecret
```

Images can be inspected and cached.

Inject secrets at runtime.

---

# 93.84 Kubernetes Security

Avoid embedding secrets in:

```text
Dockerfile
Helm chart values committed to Git
ConfigMaps
```

Use appropriate secret-management mechanisms.

---

# 93.85 Data Security Monitoring

Monitor:

```text
Unexpected database exports
Large object downloads
Repeated authorization failures
Mass data access
Mass account downloads
Unusual admin operations
```

---

# 93.86 Security Incident Response

If sensitive data may have been exposed:

```text
Detect
 ↓
Contain
 ↓
Investigate
 ↓
Eradicate
 ↓
Recover
 ↓
Assess impact
 ↓
Notify where required
 ↓
Improve controls
```

Do not improvise during an incident.

---

# 93.87 Security Testing

Test:

```text
Unauthorized access
Cross-tenant access
IDOR
SQL injection
XSS
CSRF where relevant
File upload attacks
Secret exposure
Broken access control
Rate-limit bypass
Data leakage
```

---

# 93.88 Data Security Testing Example

Test:

```text
User A
 ↓
GET /api/v1/progress/user-B
```

Expected:

```text
DENIED
```

Then test:

```text
Admin
 ↓
GET /api/v1/progress/user-B
```

Expected:

```text
ALLOWED
```

according to policy.

---

# 93.89 Security Headers

Where appropriate, configure headers such as:

```text
Content-Security-Policy
Strict-Transport-Security
X-Content-Type-Options
Referrer-Policy
```

Exact configuration depends on the frontend and deployment architecture.

---

# 93.90 Data Security Architecture Review

Before production, review:

```text
Data inventory
Classification
Encryption
Key management
Secrets
Access control
Logging
Backups
Retention
Deletion
Third-party sharing
Tenant isolation
Incident response
```

---

# 93.91 Definition of Done

Data security is production-ready when:

* [ ] Data classification exists
* [ ] Data owners are identified
* [ ] Sensitive data inventory exists
* [ ] TLS is enforced
* [ ] Sensitive storage is encrypted
* [ ] Secrets are centrally managed
* [ ] Key rotation exists
* [ ] Database least privilege exists
* [ ] Tenant isolation is enforced
* [ ] PII is minimized
* [ ] Sensitive logs are redacted
* [ ] Backups are encrypted
* [ ] Backup restoration is tested
* [ ] Retention policies exist
* [ ] Deletion policies exist
* [ ] Object storage is secured
* [ ] File uploads are validated
* [ ] Audit logging exists
* [ ] Data export is controlled
* [ ] Security monitoring exists
* [ ] Incident response exists
* [ ] Security testing exists

---

# 93.92 Core Principles

1. **Collect less data.**
2. **Classify what you collect.**
3. **Encrypt data in transit.**
4. **Encrypt sensitive data at rest.**
5. **Protect encryption keys separately from encrypted data.**
6. **Never commit secrets to Git.**
7. **Never put backend secrets into React.**
8. **Never trust tenant IDs supplied by clients.**
9. **Treat backups as sensitive production data.**
10. **Soft delete is not true deletion.**
11. **Anonymization and pseudonymization are different.**
12. **Logs can become a secondary data-breach channel.**
13. **Object storage must be private by default when content is restricted.**
14. **Signed URLs should be temporary and scoped.**
15. **Least privilege applies to databases and infrastructure, not only application users.**
16. **Security must protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.**
17. **Data retention must have a reason.**
18. **A system cannot claim strong privacy while collecting and retaining data it never needed in the first place.**

> **The biggest data-security mistake is treating encryption as the whole solution. Encryption protects data from some forms of exposure; it does not stop an authorized-but-malicious user, a broken authorization rule, an overprivileged database account, leaked credentials, insecure logs, public object storage, or a developer accidentally committing secrets. Data security is an entire lifecycle, not a database checkbox.**

**Next `.` → CSDG Chapter 94: Application Security & OWASP Standards — secure coding, input validation, XSS, CSRF, SQL injection, SSRF, deserialization, file-upload attacks, dependency security, security headers, SAST/DAST, and DevSecOps integration.**

# CSDG — Chapter 94

## Application Security & OWASP Standards

This chapter defines how Mediverse applications should defend against common application-layer attacks and how security controls should be integrated into development rather than bolted on after deployment.

Core principle:

> **Never trust input, identity, client state, network location, or external systems. Validate at the boundary, authorize at the resource, and encode at the output.**

---

# 94.1 Application Security Architecture

Security should exist across the complete request path:

```text
Browser
   ↓
TLS
   ↓
CDN / WAF
   ↓
API Gateway
   ↓
Spring Security
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Validation
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Service Layer
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
Database
```

Every layer has a different responsibility.

---

# 94.2 OWASP

Use the OWASP principles as a major security reference.

The important lesson is not memorizing the OWASP Top 10.

The important lesson is understanding **why vulnerabilities occur and how architecture prevents them**.

---

# 94.3 Security by Design

Security requirements should be defined before implementation.

For every feature ask:

```text
Who can access it?
What data does it expose?
What input does it accept?
What could an attacker control?
What happens if a dependency fails?
What happens if the request is repeated?
What happens if the user is malicious?
```

---

# 94.4 Trust Boundaries

Identify where trust changes.

Example:

```text
                 UNTRUSTED
                     │
                     ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │   Browser   │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │
             TRUST BOUNDARY
                     │
                     ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │ API Gateway │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │
              TRUST BOUNDARY
                     │
                     ▼
              Application
```

Never assume data becomes trustworthy merely because it came through the frontend.

---

# 94.5 Input Validation

Validate every external input.

Sources include:

```text
HTTP body
Query parameters
Path parameters
Headers
Cookies
Uploaded files
Webhooks
Kafka messages
External APIs
```

---

# 94.6 Validation Layers

A robust system can validate at multiple levels:

```text
Request syntax
      ↓
DTO validation
      ↓
Business validation
      ↓
Authorization
      ↓
Database constraints
```

These controls complement each other.

---

# 94.7 Bean Validation

Spring Boot can use Jakarta Bean Validation.

Example:

```java
public record CreateCourseRequest(

    @NotBlank
    @Size(max = 200)
    String title,

    @Size(max = 5000)
    String description
) {}
```

Do not rely exclusively on frontend validation.

---

# 94.8 Frontend Validation Is Not Security

React may reject:

```text
title = ""
```

But an attacker can bypass React entirely:

```text
curl
Postman
custom script
Burp Suite
```

Therefore:

```text
Frontend validation
       +
Backend validation
```

is required.

---

# 94.9 Input Allowlisting

Prefer defining what is allowed.

Example:

```text
status ∈ {DRAFT, PUBLISHED, ARCHIVED}
```

rather than accepting arbitrary strings and hoping downstream code handles them safely.

---

# 94.10 Input Length Limits

Every input should have reasonable limits.

Examples:

```text
title → 200 chars
description → 5,000 chars
search query → 200 chars
page size → 100
```

Limits reduce:

```text
Memory abuse
Database abuse
Log abuse
Denial-of-service risk
```

---

# 94.11 SQL Injection

SQL injection occurs when attacker-controlled data becomes SQL syntax.

Dangerous:

```java
String sql =
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'";
```

Attacker input can alter the query.

---

# 94.12 Parameterized Queries

Use:

```text
Prepared statements
JPA parameters
Spring Data repositories
Safe query APIs
```

Example:

```java
@Query("""
    SELECT c
    FROM Course c
    WHERE c.title = :title
""")
List<Course> findByTitle(@Param("title") String title);
```

---

# 94.13 Dynamic SQL

Dynamic queries require additional care.

Never blindly insert user-controlled values into:

```text
table names
column names
ORDER BY
SQL fragments
```

Use allowlists.

Example:

```text
allowedSortFields = {
    "title",
    "createdAt",
    "updatedAt"
```
