# Chapter 120 — Advanced DevSecOps Architecture

This is where we stop treating DevSecOps as **“put SonarQube and a security scan into Jenkins”** and start designing security as an architectural property of the entire software delivery system.

The target is:

```text
Developer
   ↓
Source Control
   ↓
Commit Security
   ↓
CI
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Test
   ↓
SAST / SCA / Secrets / IaC
   ↓
SBOM
   ↓
Artifact Signing
   ↓
Artifact Repository
   ↓
GitOps
   ↓
Kubernetes Admission
   ↓
Runtime Security
   ↓
Monitoring / SIEM
   ↓
Incident Response
   ↓
Feedback → Developer
```

The key idea:

> **Security controls should form a continuous chain of trust from source code to running workload.**

---

## 120.1 What Makes DevSecOps "Advanced"?

Basic DevSecOps:

```text
Git
 ↓
Jenkins
 ↓
Build
 ↓
SonarQube
 ↓
Deploy
```

Advanced DevSecOps:

```text
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │ Threat Model  │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            │
Developer                   ▼
   │                 Secure Design
   ▼                       │
Git ───────────────► Code Security
 │                       │
 ▼                       ▼
Pre-commit              CI
 │                       │
 ▼              ┌────────┼─────────┐
Secrets         │        │         │
Scanning       SAST     SCA       IaC
 │              │        │         │
 └──────────────┴────────┴─────────┘
                            │
                            ▼
                           SBOM
                            │
                            ▼
                      Signed Artifact
                            │
                            ▼
                    Trusted Registry
                            │
                            ▼
                         GitOps
                            │
                            ▼
                       Kubernetes
                            │
                      ┌─────┴─────┐
                      ▼           ▼
                  Admission    Runtime
                      │           │
                      └─────┬─────┘
                            ▼
                         SIEM
                            │
                            ▼
                     Incident Response
                            │
                            ▼
                    Security Feedback
                            │
                            └──────► Git
```

That's the architecture we're aiming for.

---

# 120.2 The Software Supply Chain

Your application isn't just your source code.

It depends on:

```text
Application
    │
    ├── Java
    ├── Spring Boot
    ├── Maven dependencies
    ├── npm packages
    ├── Docker base image
    ├── OS packages
    ├── CI plugins
    ├── Build tools
    └── Deployment tooling
```

Therefore:

```text
Source Code Security
        ≠
Supply Chain Security
```

You need both.

---

# 120.3 Chain of Trust

A mature architecture establishes:

```text
Source
  ↓
Build
  ↓
Artifact
  ↓
Registry
  ↓
Deployment
  ↓
Runtime
```

At every transition ask:

> **Can I prove that this artifact is the thing I intended to deploy?**

For example:

```text
Git commit
   ↓
CI build
   ↓
Artifact digest
   ↓
Signature
   ↓
Registry
   ↓
Kubernetes admission
   ↓
Running image
```

---

# 120.4 Source Control Security

Git is part of your security boundary.

Controls include:

```text
Branch protection
Required reviews
CODEOWNERS
Signed commits where appropriate
Secret scanning
Protected tags
Least-privilege repository access
Audit logging
```

Don't allow:

```text
Developer
   ↓
push directly to production branch
```

without appropriate controls.

---

# 120.5 Pull Request Security

A mature PR pipeline might require:

```text
PR
 ↓
Compile
 ↓
Unit Tests
 ↓
SAST
 ↓
SCA
 ↓
Secret Scan
 ↓
IaC Scan
 ↓
Container Scan
 ↓
Policy Checks
 ↓
Review
 ↓
Merge
```

A security check that happens only after production deployment is too late for many classes of defects.

---

# 120.6 Shift Left — But Don't Shift Everything Left

"Shift left" is useful but often misunderstood.

You want:

```text
Find cheap problems early.
```

Example:

```text
Developer
   ↓
Secret accidentally committed
   ↓
Pre-commit scan
   ↓
Blocked
```

Much better than:

```text
Production
   ↓
credential discovered
   ↓
incident
```

But runtime controls are still required.

Therefore:

```text
Shift Left
+
Shift Right
=
Defense in Depth
```

---

# 120.7 Security Gates

A pipeline can have explicit gates.

Example:

```text
Build
 ↓
Tests
 ↓
Security Scan
 ↓
   ┌───────────────┐
   │ Security Gate │
   └───────┬───────┘
           │
      ┌────┴────┐
      ▼         ▼
    PASS       FAIL
      │         │
      ▼         ▼
 Deploy       Stop
```

---

# 120.8 But Gates Need Risk Policies

Don't create:

```text
Any vulnerability = pipeline failure
```

That can make the pipeline unusable.

Instead define:

```text
Critical vulnerability
AND
exploitable
AND
production relevant
→ block
```

while perhaps:

```text
Low severity
No exploit
Development-only dependency
→ warning
```

The exact policy depends on organizational risk tolerance.

---

# 120.9 SAST

Static Application Security Testing examines source code.

For Java/Spring Boot, it can identify patterns involving:

```text
SQL injection
XSS
command injection
path traversal
unsafe deserialization
weak cryptography
authentication problems
authorization flaws
```

Conceptually:

```text
Java Source
     ↓
SAST
     ↓
Potential vulnerability
```

---

# 120.10 SCA

Software Composition Analysis examines dependencies.

Example:

```text
pom.xml
   ↓
Spring dependency
   ↓
transitive dependency
   ↓
known CVE
```

This matters because:

> Your code can be secure while your dependencies are vulnerable.

---

# 120.11 Secret Scanning

Look for accidental credentials:

```text
AWS access key
database password
API token
private key
OAuth secret
cloud credential
```

Pipeline:

```text
Git
 ↓
Secret scanner
 ↓
Credential detected
 ↓
Block commit/PR
```

But remember:

> Removing the secret from the latest commit does not necessarily remove it from Git history.

A leaked credential should generally be treated as compromised and rotated/revoked.

---

# 120.12 IaC Security

Terraform and Kubernetes manifests are code too.

Example:

```hcl
resource "aws_security_group" "app" {
  ...
}
```

Potential problems:

```text
0.0.0.0/0
overly broad IAM
public database
unencrypted storage
missing logging
```

Therefore:

```text
Application Code
+
Infrastructure Code
+
Configuration
```

all require security analysis.

---

# 120.13 Container Security

Container pipeline:

```text
Dockerfile
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Image
   ↓
Vulnerability Scan
   ↓
SBOM
   ↓
Sign
   ↓
Registry
```

Important checks:

```text
base image vulnerabilities
OS packages
application dependencies
secrets
privileges
user
file permissions
image provenance
```

---

# 120.14 Don't Run as Root

Bad:

```dockerfile
USER root
```

Better:

```text
non-root user
```

Why?

If the application is compromised:

```text
Application compromise
      ↓
Container compromise
```

A non-root workload can reduce the attacker's privileges.

But don't misunderstand:

> Non-root containers do not magically make containers secure.

---

# 120.15 Image Provenance

Suppose your registry contains:

```text
backend:1.4
```

How do you know:

```text
Who built it?
From which commit?
With which dependencies?
Using which build environment?
```

That's where provenance comes in.

Conceptually:

```text
Git commit
   ↓
CI build
   ↓
Build metadata
   ↓
Artifact
```

---

# 120.16 SBOM

SBOM answers:

> **What components are inside this artifact?**

Example:

```text
Application
├── Spring Boot
├── Jackson
├── Hibernate
├── PostgreSQL driver
├── Tomcat
└── Other dependencies
```

When a new vulnerability appears:

```text
New CVE
   ↓
Search SBOM
   ↓
Which applications contain affected component?
```

This drastically improves response speed.

---

# 120.17 Artifact Signing

After successful build:

```text
Artifact
   ↓
Hash
   ↓
Signature
   ↓
Registry
```

At deployment:

```text
Image
   ↓
Verify signature
   ↓
Trusted?
 ┌─┴─┐
Yes No
 │   │
 ▼   ▼
Run Reject
```

This creates a much stronger deployment boundary.

---

# 120.18 Kubernetes Admission

Kubernetes shouldn't blindly execute everything pushed to it.

Think:

```text
Developer
   ↓
CI
   ↓
Registry
   ↓
Kubernetes API
   ↓
Admission Policy
   ↓
Pod
```

Admission can enforce rules such as:

```text
Must not run privileged
Must use approved registry
Must not use latest tag
Must run as non-root
Must have resource limits
Must satisfy security policy
```

---

# 120.19 Runtime Security

Even perfect CI doesn't guarantee runtime safety.

An attacker might exploit:

```text
application vulnerability
stolen credential
zero-day
misconfiguration
dependency vulnerability
```

Therefore:

```text
Runtime
 ↓
Behavior monitoring
 ↓
Detection
 ↓
Alert
 ↓
Response
```

---

# 120.20 DevSecOps Feedback Loop

The real maturity model is:

```text
Developer
   ↓
Secure Code
   ↓
CI Security
   ↓
Secure Artifact
   ↓
Secure Deployment
   ↓
Runtime Monitoring
   ↓
Incident
   ↓
Root Cause
   ↓
Engineering Fix
   ↓
Developer
```

Security findings should become engineering improvements.

---

# 120.21 Security as Code

This is one of the most important concepts in advanced DevSecOps.

Instead of manually configuring:

```text
Security policies
IAM
Network rules
Kubernetes policies
CI security gates
```

define them declaratively.

For example:

```text
Git
 ├── terraform/
 ├── helm/
 ├── policies/
 ├── pipelines/
 └── security/
```

Now security becomes:

```text
version controlled
reviewable
testable
repeatable
auditable
```

---

# 120.22 Policy as Code

Example:

```text
Policy:
Production containers must not run privileged.
```

Instead of:

```text
Security engineer manually checks cluster
```

use:

```text
Policy
 ↓
Automated evaluation
 ↓
PASS / FAIL
```

This is much more scalable.

---

# 120.23 Separation of Duties

A mature pipeline should not allow one identity to:

```text
write code
+
approve code
+
build artifact
+
approve production
+
deploy production
```

without controls.

Better:

```text
Developer
   ↓
PR
   ↓
Reviewer
   ↓
CI
   ↓
Artifact
   ↓
Deployment approval/policy
   ↓
Production
```

This reduces insider-risk and accidental changes.

---

# 120.24 CI/CD Identity

CI systems are extremely powerful.

If Jenkins can:

```text
access AWS
access Kubernetes
push images
deploy production
```

then:

> **Compromising Jenkins may effectively compromise production.**

Therefore CI should use:

```text
short-lived credentials
least privilege
isolated agents
protected secrets
strong authentication
audit logs
```

---

# 120.25 Jenkins Security Architecture

For your stack:

```text
Developer
   ↓
Git
   ↓
Jenkins
   │
   ├── SAST
   ├── SCA
   ├── Secret Scan
   ├── Tests
   ├── SBOM
   ├── Image Scan
   └── Sign
        │
        ▼
      Nexus
        │
        ▼
      GitOps
        │
        ▼
      Argo CD
        │
        ▼
     Kubernetes
```

Jenkins shouldn't necessarily directly hold unrestricted production credentials.

---

# 120.26 GitOps Security

A stronger model:

```text
CI
 ↓
Build + Test + Sign
 ↓
Artifact Registry
 ↓
Update deployment repository
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
Kubernetes
```

This creates separation:

```text
CI → creates artifact
GitOps → declares desired deployment
Argo CD → reconciles state
```

---

# 120.27 Why This Is Better

Suppose Jenkins is compromised.

If Jenkins directly has:

```text
kubectl admin
```

the attacker may immediately control the cluster.

With stronger GitOps separation:

```text
Jenkins
 ↓
artifact
 ↓
Git change
 ↓
policy/review
 ↓
Argo CD
 ↓
cluster
```

the blast radius can be reduced.

Still not perfect, but significantly better.

---

# 120.28 Environment Promotion

Don't build separate artifacts for:

```text
DEV
UAT
PROD
```

Prefer:

```text
Build once
   ↓
Artifact
   ↓
DEV
   ↓
UAT
   ↓
PROD
```

This creates stronger artifact consistency.

Conceptually:

```text
Same artifact
       │
       ├── DEV
       ├── UAT
       └── PROD
```

---

# 120.29 Configuration vs Artifact

Environment-specific configuration should not require rebuilding the application.

Example:

```text
Artifact:
backend:v2.4.1
```

DEV:

```text
DB_HOST=dev-db
```

UAT:

```text
DB_HOST=uat-db
```

PROD:

```text
DB_HOST=prod-db
```

Same artifact.

Different configuration.

---

# 120.30 Secure Promotion

Promotion should verify:

```text
artifact identity
artifact signature
SBOM
vulnerability status
approval
environment policy
```

Then:

```text
DEV
 ↓
UAT
 ↓
PROD
```

---

# 120.31 Progressive Delivery

Don't always do:

```text
100% traffic
     ↓
new version
```

Instead:

```text
1%
 ↓
5%
 ↓
25%
 ↓
50%
 ↓
100%
```

Monitor:

```text
errors
latency
security events
resource behavior
business metrics
```

If abnormal:

```text
Rollback
```

---

# 120.32 Security Canary

You can use the same concept for security.

Deploy:

```text
5%
```

Then observe:

```text
authentication anomalies
unexpected outbound connections
errors
CPU/memory anomalies
security alerts
```

If safe:

```text
increase traffic
```

---

# 120.33 Automated Rollback

A mature platform can detect:

```text
error rate ↑
security alert ↑
latency ↑
```

and trigger:

```text
rollback
```

But be careful:

> Automatic rollback based on a weak signal can itself become an attack vector.

Controls need appropriate confidence thresholds.

---

# 120.34 Observability Integration

DevSecOps shouldn't isolate security from observability.

You want:

```text
Logs
Metrics
Traces
Security Events
Audit Events
```

correlated together.

Example:

```text
Request ID
    │
    ├── Application log
    ├── API trace
    ├── Database event
    └── Security event
```

This makes investigation much faster.

---

# 120.35 Security Telemetry Pipeline

```text
Application
Kubernetes
AWS
CI/CD
IAM
Network
   │
   ▼
Collectors
   │
   ▼
Central Logging
   │
   ▼
SIEM
   │
   ▼
Detection
   │
   ▼
SOAR / Incident Response
```

This connects Chapters 117–120.

---

# 120.36 Advanced Architecture

Putting everything together:

```text
                              ┌──────────────┐
                              │ Threat Model │
                              └──────┬───────┘
                                     │
Developer                            ▼
   │                            Secure Design
   ▼                                 │
Git ──────► PR Security ─────────────┤
 │                                   │
 │                              ┌────┴────┐
 │                              ▼         ▼
 │                            SAST      SCA
 │                              │         │
 │                              └────┬────┘
 │                                   ▼
 │                              Secret Scan
 │                                   │
 │                              IaC Security
 │                                   │
 │                              Container Scan
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                                  SBOM
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                              Sign Artifact
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                              Nexus/Registry
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                              GitOps Repo
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                                Argo CD
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                              Kubernetes
 │                              ┌────┴────┐
 │                              ▼         ▼
 │                         Admission   Runtime
 │                              │         │
 │                              └────┬────┘
 │                                   ▼
 │                             Observability
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                                  SIEM
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                            Incident Response
 │                                   │
 │                                   ▼
 │                              Root Cause
 │                                   │
 └───────────────────────────────────┘
```

This is the architecture you should understand—not merely memorize.

---

# 120.37 DevSecOps Maturity

### Level 1 — Reactive

```text
Incident
 ↓
Fix
```

### Level 2 — Basic Security

```text
CI
 ↓
SAST
```

### Level 3 — Integrated

```text
SAST
SCA
Secrets
IaC
Container scanning
```

### Level 4 — Trusted Supply Chain

```text
SBOM
Provenance
Signing
Verification
Policy
GitOps
```

### Level 5 — Resilient Platform

```text
Security
+
Observability
+
Runtime Detection
+
Automated Response
+
DR
+
Continuous Improvement
```

That's the target.

---

# 120.38 What This Means for Your Project

For your Spring Boot + React + PostgreSQL + Docker + Jenkins + Kubernetes + Helm + Terraform + Argo CD stack, the final security delivery chain should look like:

```text
Developer
   ↓
GitHub
   ↓
Pull Request
   ↓
Code Review
   ↓
Jenkins
   │
   ├── Unit Tests
   ├── SAST
   ├── SCA
   ├── Secret Scan
   ├── IaC Scan
   ├── Docker Scan
   └── SBOM
   ↓
Security Gate
   ↓
Build Image
   ↓
Sign Image
   ↓
Nexus / Registry
   ↓
GitOps Repository
   ↓
Argo CD
   ↓
Kubernetes
   ↓
Admission Policies
   ↓
Runtime Security
   ↓
Prometheus / Grafana
   ↓
Central Logs / SIEM
   ↓
Incident Response
   ↓
Post-Incident Engineering
```

That is a **real DevSecOps architecture**.

Not:

```text
Jenkins + SonarQube = DevSecOps
```

That simplistic definition is wrong.

---

# 120.39 The Five Principles

Remember these:

### 1. Security starts before code reaches CI

```text
Design → Code → Build → Deploy → Runtime
```

### 2. Every artifact should have provenance

```text
Where did this artifact come from?
```

### 3. Deployment must verify trust

```text
Is this artifact authorized?
```

### 4. Runtime security remains necessary

```text
Secure CI ≠ Secure Runtime
```

### 5. Incidents feed engineering

```text
Incident
 ↓
Root Cause
 ↓
Code / IaC / Policy change
 ↓
Pipeline
 ↓
Improved system
```

# Chapter 121 — Security Testing & Red Teaming

This chapter moves from **building security controls** to **actively trying to break them**.

The objective isn't simply:

> "Find vulnerabilities."

It's:

> **Prove whether your security architecture actually withstands realistic attacks.**

---

## 121.1 Security Testing Landscape

Security testing has several layers:

```text
                    SECURITY TESTING
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                   ▼
   Code Testing       Application Testing   Infrastructure
       │                   │                   │
      SAST                DAST                 IaC
      SCA                 API testing         Cloud
      Secrets             Fuzzing             Kubernetes
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ▼
                    Offensive Security
                           │
                  ┌────────┴────────┐
                  ▼                 ▼
                Red Team         Pentest
```

These activities overlap, but they aren't identical.

---

# 121.2 SAST

**Static Application Security Testing**

Analyzes source code without executing the application.

```text
Source
  ↓
SAST
  ↓
Potential vulnerability
```

Typical findings:

```text
SQL injection
Command injection
Path traversal
Unsafe deserialization
Weak cryptography
Authentication weaknesses
```

Useful because defects can be caught before deployment.

---

# 121.3 DAST

**Dynamic Application Security Testing**

Tests the running application.

```text
Running application
       ↑
       │
   DAST scanner
       │
       ▼
HTTP/API behavior
```

It can discover issues that aren't obvious from source code alone.

For example:

```text
POST /api/users
```

might behave incorrectly under unexpected input even if static analysis doesn't flag the implementation.

---

# 121.4 SCA

Software Composition Analysis:

```text
pom.xml
package.json
Docker image
      ↓
Dependency analysis
      ↓
Known vulnerabilities
```

Example:

```text
Spring Boot
   ↓
Library A
   ↓
Library B
   ↓
Known CVE
```

Your application may never directly import Library B.

It can still be vulnerable because of transitive dependencies.

---

# 121.5 Secret Testing

Security testing should detect:

```text
AWS credentials
Private keys
Database passwords
API tokens
JWT signing secrets
Cloud credentials
```

At multiple stages:

```text
Developer machine
 ↓
Git
 ↓
CI
 ↓
Artifact
 ↓
Container
```

Don't rely on one scanner.

---

# 121.6 IaC Security Testing

Terraform:

```text
Terraform
 ↓
Security analysis
 ↓
Misconfiguration
```

Kubernetes:

```text
Deployment
Service
Ingress
RBAC
NetworkPolicy
 ↓
Policy analysis
```

Typical findings:

```text
public database
0.0.0.0/0
privileged container
hostNetwork
excessive IAM
missing encryption
missing logging
```

---

# 121.7 API Security Testing

For your Spring Boot applications, APIs are a major attack surface.

Test:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Input validation
Rate limiting
Object-level authorization
Mass assignment
File upload
Error handling
Session/token handling
```

A particularly important category is:

### Broken Object Level Authorization

Example:

```text
GET /api/users/100
```

Authenticated user:

```text
userId = 50
```

If they can access:

```text
userId = 100
```

without authorization, you have an access-control vulnerability.

Authentication succeeded.

Authorization failed.

---

# 121.8 Authentication Testing

Test:

```text
Valid credentials
Invalid credentials
Expired token
Modified token
Missing token
Wrong issuer
Wrong audience
Wrong signature
Revoked credential
```

Also test:

```text
Brute force
Credential stuffing
Account enumeration
Password reset abuse
MFA bypass
```

---

# 121.9 Authorization Testing

Never assume:

```text
"Endpoint requires JWT"
```

means the endpoint is secure.

You need:

```text
Identity
+
Role
+
Resource ownership
+
Action permission
```

Example:

```text
Doctor
 ↓
Can access patient records
```

doesn't automatically mean:

```text
Doctor
 ↓
Can access every patient's records
```

Authorization must match the business model.

---

# 121.10 Fuzz Testing

Fuzzing sends unexpected or malformed input.

Example:

```text
Normal:
username=ganesh

Fuzz:
username=<very large input>
username=../../../../
username=${...}
username=<unexpected encoding>
```

Goal:

```text
Find crashes
Find parser bugs
Find validation failures
Find unexpected behavior
```

---

# 121.11 File Upload Testing

For applications with file upload:

```text
filename
MIME type
file size
extension
content
path
metadata
```

should all be treated as untrusted.

Testing should verify:

```text
Executable file rejected
Oversized file rejected
Unexpected MIME rejected
Path traversal blocked
Malicious content handled
Storage access controlled
```

---

# 121.12 SSRF Testing

SSRF:

**Server-Side Request Forgery**

Conceptually:

```text
Attacker
   ↓
Your API
   ↓
Server makes request
   ↓
Internal resource
```

Potential targets include:

```text
internal services
metadata endpoints
private APIs
administrative interfaces
```

Cloud environments make SSRF especially important because metadata services can expose sensitive information if improperly protected.

---

# 121.13 Injection Testing

Test boundaries where user-controlled data reaches interpreters:

```text
SQL
OS commands
LDAP
NoSQL
Template engines
Expression languages
Shells
```

Example:

```text
User Input
   ↓
Application
   ↓
SQL query
```

The safe design is:

```text
User Input
   ↓
Validation
   ↓
Parameterized query
```

not string concatenation.

---

# 121.14 Security Unit Tests

Security shouldn't exist only in scanners.

Write tests.

Example:

```text
User A
 ↓
attempts User B's resource
 ↓
403 expected
```

Another:

```text
Unauthenticated request
 ↓
protected endpoint
 ↓
401 expected
```

These become regression tests.

---

# 121.15 Security Regression Testing

Suppose you fixed:

```text
Broken authorization
```

Six months later a refactor accidentally reintroduces it.

A security regression test should catch:

```text
Regression
 ↓
CI
 ↓
Test fails
 ↓
Deployment blocked
```

This is much stronger than relying on manual testing.

---

# 121.16 Penetration Testing

A penetration test is an authorized attempt to exploit vulnerabilities.

Typical phases:

```text
Reconnaissance
      ↓
Enumeration
      ↓
Vulnerability identification
      ↓
Controlled exploitation
      ↓
Impact assessment
      ↓
Reporting
      ↓
Remediation
      ↓
Retesting
```

The key word is:

> **Authorized**

Without authorization, the same technical activity can become illegal or harmful.

---

# 121.17 Vulnerability Scan vs Penetration Test

### Vulnerability scanning

```text
Automated
Broad
Repeatable
```

Example:

```text
"Port 443 exposes vulnerable software."
```

### Penetration testing

```text
Human-driven
Context-aware
Exploit-oriented
```

Example:

```text
"This vulnerability can be chained with weak authorization to access another user's data."
```

A scanner finds weaknesses.

A skilled tester demonstrates realistic impact.

---

# 121.18 Red Teaming

Red teaming is broader than a normal penetration test.

The goal is to simulate a realistic adversary against defined objectives.

For example:

```text
Objective:
Access production customer data.
```

The red team may attempt:

```text
Initial access
      ↓
Privilege escalation
      ↓
Credential discovery
      ↓
Lateral movement
      ↓
Persistence
      ↓
Data access
```

while staying within the engagement rules.

---

# 121.19 Red Team vs Blue Team

```text
RED TEAM
Attacks
   │
   ▼
BLUE TEAM
Defends
   │
   ▼
Detection / Response
```

Red team asks:

> "Can I get in?"

Blue team asks:

> "Can I detect and stop you?"

---

# 121.20 Purple Team

Purple teaming combines them.

```text
Red Team
   │
   │ attack technique
   ▼
Blue Team
   │
   │ detection
   ▼
Improved control
```

Example:

```text
Red:
Simulates credential abuse

Blue:
Checks whether SIEM detects it

Purple:
Improves detection rule
```

This is often more useful than treating red and blue teams as competing groups.

---

# 121.21 MITRE ATT&CK

A useful framework for organizing adversary behavior is **MITRE ATT&CK**.

Think:

```text
Initial Access
      ↓
Execution
      ↓
Persistence
      ↓
Privilege Escalation
      ↓
Defense Evasion
      ↓
Credential Access
      ↓
Discovery
      ↓
Lateral Movement
      ↓
Collection
      ↓
Exfiltration
      ↓
Impact
```

The important lesson:

> Security testing should evaluate the entire attack path, not isolated vulnerabilities.

---

# 121.22 Attack Chain

A realistic compromise may look like:

```text
Internet-facing API
       ↓
Application vulnerability
       ↓
Initial access
       ↓
Container compromise
       ↓
ServiceAccount token
       ↓
Kubernetes API
       ↓
Privilege escalation
       ↓
Secret access
       ↓
Database credentials
       ↓
Data access
```

A scanner checking each component independently might miss the chain.

That's why adversarial testing matters.

---

# 121.23 Attack Surface Management

Before attacking anything, identify:

```text
Internet-facing domains
APIs
Load balancers
Cloud services
Kubernetes ingress
Admin interfaces
CI/CD endpoints
VPN
Remote access
Third-party integrations
```

Then classify:

```text
Internet
 ↓
DMZ / Edge
 ↓
Application
 ↓
Data
```

The larger the attack surface, the more opportunities attackers have.

---

# 121.24 External Attack Surface

For production:

```text
DNS
 ↓
CDN
 ↓
WAF
 ↓
Load Balancer
 ↓
Ingress
 ↓
Application
```

Every component is part of the attack surface.

Don't only scan the application.

---

# 121.25 Internal Attack Surface

Once an attacker gets inside:

```text
Pod
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Kubernetes API
 ↓
Other services
 ↓
Database
 ↓
Cloud APIs
```

This is why:

```text
NetworkPolicy
RBAC
IAM
ServiceAccount isolation
```

matter so much.

---

# 121.26 Kubernetes Red-Team Perspective

Suppose:

```text
frontend Pod
```

is compromised.

A security assessment might ask:

```text
Can it access Kubernetes API?

Can it access other Pods?

Can it read Secrets?

Can it access cloud metadata?

Can it reach PostgreSQL?

Can it create a privileged Pod?

Can it escalate privileges?
```

The objective is not to destroy the cluster.

The objective is to measure the blast radius of compromise.

---

# 121.27 Blast Radius Testing

This is extremely valuable.

Assume:

```text
Service A compromised
```

Ask:

```text id="pblm13"
What can A access?
```

Ideally:

```text
Service A
 ├── Own database
 ├── Required API
 └── Required storage
```

Not:

```text
Service A
 ├── All databases
 ├── Kubernetes admin
 ├── AWS admin
 ├── Every Secret
 └── Internal network
```

---

# 121.28 Cloud Red-Team Perspective

If an AWS identity is compromised:

```text
What can it do?
```

Test whether it can:

```text
read S3
modify IAM
assume roles
access secrets
modify security groups
access EKS
modify logging
disable security controls
```

This directly validates least privilege.

---

# 121.29 CI/CD Attack Surface

This is often neglected.

Attackers may target:

```text
GitHub
Jenkins
CI agents
build scripts
dependency files
Dockerfiles
artifact repositories
deployment credentials
```

Why?

Because CI/CD often has:

```text
high privilege
+
access to secrets
+
production deployment ability
```

Therefore:

> **Your CI/CD system is part of your production security boundary.**

---

# 121.30 Dependency Confusion

A potential supply-chain attack:

```text
Internal package:
company-utils
```

An attacker publishes a malicious package with the same/similar name in a public repository.

If the build system resolves the wrong package:

```text
CI
 ↓
malicious dependency
 ↓
build environment compromised
```

Controls include:

```text
private registries
dependency pinning
package allowlists
trusted sources
lock files
dependency verification
```

---

# 121.31 Malicious Build Script

Suppose:

```text
package.json
```

contains a malicious install script.

Or:

```text
pom.xml
```

references a compromised plugin/dependency.

Then:

```text
Developer
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Malicious code executes
```

This is why the build environment itself must be treated as sensitive.

---

# 121.32 Build Isolation

CI agents should ideally have:

```text
minimal privileges
ephemeral environments
restricted network access
no unnecessary production credentials
```

Bad:

```text
Jenkins Agent
 ↓
permanent machine
 ↓
AWS admin
 ↓
Kubernetes admin
```

Better:

```text
Jenkins
 ↓
Ephemeral build agent
 ↓
Short-lived credentials
 ↓
Minimum permissions
```

---

# 121.33 Security Test Pyramid

A practical testing hierarchy:

```text
                 Red Team
                    ▲
                Pentest
                    ▲
               DAST / API
                    ▲
             Integration Tests
                    ▲
          SAST / SCA / IaC / Secrets
                    ▲
              Unit Tests
```

The lower layers should run frequently.

The upper layers are more expensive and specialized.

---

# 121.34 Continuous vs Periodic Testing

Continuous:

```text
SAST
SCA
Secrets
IaC
Container scanning
Security unit tests
```

Periodic:

```text
Penetration test
Red team
Purple team
Architecture assessment
Disaster recovery exercise
```

You need both.

---

# 121.35 Security Testing in Your CI/CD

Your pipeline can become:

```text
Commit
  ↓
Unit Tests
  ↓
Security Unit Tests
  ↓
SAST
  ↓
SCA
  ↓
Secret Scan
  ↓
IaC Scan
  ↓
Build Image
  ↓
Container Scan
  ↓
SBOM
  ↓
Sign
  ↓
Artifact Repository
  ↓
Deploy to Test
  ↓
DAST / API Security
  ↓
Security Gate
  ↓
Promotion
```

This is a serious security pipeline.

---

# 121.36 Don't Make CI Unusable

A common mistake is adding 20 scanners and making developers wait an hour for every PR.

Instead classify:

```text
Fast checks
 ↓
PR

Medium checks
 ↓
Merge

Deep checks
 ↓
Nightly / scheduled

Offensive testing
 ↓
Periodic
```

Security has to be operationally sustainable.

---

# 121.37 Risk-Based Testing

Prioritize:

```text
Internet-facing
+
high privilege
+
sensitive data
+
business critical
```

Example:

```text
Public authentication API
        ↓
High priority
```

versus:

```text
Internal development dashboard
        ↓
Lower priority
```

Not because the second is irrelevant, but because resources are finite.

---

# 121.38 Finding Severity

A useful model:

```text
Severity
   +
Exploitability
   +
Business impact
   +
Exposure
   +
Data sensitivity
```

A theoretically critical vulnerability in an isolated development environment may be less urgent than a high vulnerability exposed on an internet-facing production API.

Context matters.

---

# 121.39 Vulnerability Lifecycle

Finding:

```text
Detected
   ↓
Triaged
   ↓
Assigned
   ↓
Fixed
   ↓
Tested
   ↓
Verified
   ↓
Closed
```

Don't stop at:

```text
"Ticket created."
```

The vulnerability isn't fixed until the remediation is verified.

---

# 121.40 Retesting

After remediation:

```text
Original vulnerability
       ↓
Fix
       ↓
Retest
       ↓
Still vulnerable?
   ┌───┴───┐
  YES     NO
   │       │
   ▼       ▼
Rework   Close
```

This prevents false closure.

---

# 121.41 False Positives

Security tools will produce false positives.

Example:

```text
Scanner:
Critical vulnerability
```

But after investigation:

```text
affected component
not actually reachable
```

Therefore:

```text
Scanner finding
      ↓
Human/contextual validation
      ↓
Risk decision
```

Don't blindly ignore scanners.

Don't blindly obey them either.

---

# 121.42 Security Testing Evidence

For compliance and engineering maturity, retain:

```text
scan results
test reports
remediation tickets
retest results
approval records
exceptions
risk acceptance
```

This creates an audit trail.

---

# 121.43 Security Exceptions

Sometimes a vulnerability can't immediately be fixed.

Don't simply suppress it.

Create:

```text
Exception
```

containing:

```text
Vulnerability
Reason
Risk
Compensating controls
Owner
Expiration date
Review date
```

Critical rule:

> **Exceptions should expire.**

Otherwise temporary exceptions become permanent vulnerabilities.

---

# 121.44 Red Team Rules of Engagement

Before a red-team exercise define:

```text
Scope
Objectives
Allowed techniques
Prohibited actions
Time window
Systems included
Systems excluded
Emergency contacts
Stop conditions
Evidence handling
```

For example:

```text
Production database deletion
→ prohibited

Controlled exploitation
→ allowed

Denial-of-service
→ prohibited
```

Without rules of engagement, testing can become an operational incident.

---

# 121.45 Red Team Success Criteria

Don't measure success only by:

```text
"Did we get shell?"
```

Better metrics:

```text
Could we obtain initial access?
Could we escalate privileges?
Could we move laterally?
Could we access sensitive data?
Did detection trigger?
How quickly did defenders respond?
Could containment stop the attack?
```

This connects red teaming to blue-team effectiveness.

---

# 121.46 Purple-Team Example

Scenario:

```text
Compromised AWS credential
```

Red team:

```text
Simulates credential abuse
```

Blue team:

```text
Detects CloudTrail anomaly
```

Then measure:

```text
MTTD
MTTA
MTTC
```

Then improve:

```text
Detection rule
+
IAM control
+
alerting
```

Run the test again.

That's real security improvement.

---

# 121.47 Mediverse Security Testing Architecture

For your platform:

```text
                       INTERNET
                           │
                           ▼
                         WAF
                           │
                           ▼
                       Ingress
                           │
                           ▼
                      Spring Boot
                           │
             ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
             ▼             ▼             ▼
            Auth          API          Upload
             │             │             │
             └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                           ▼
                         RDS
```

Testing layers:

```text
Git
 │
 ├── SAST
 ├── SCA
 ├── Secret Scan
 └── IaC Scan
 │
 ▼
Docker
 │
 └── Image Scan
 │
 ▼
Kubernetes
 │
 ├── Policy testing
 ├── RBAC testing
 ├── Network testing
 └── Runtime testing
 │
 ▼
Application
 │
 ├── API security
 ├── Auth testing
 ├── Authorization testing
 ├── Fuzzing
 └── DAST
 │
 ▼
Red/Purple Team
```

---

# 121.48 The Attack-Defense Loop

The mature model is:

```text
                  ATTACK
                    │
                    ▼
                Detection
                    │
                    ▼
                Response
                    │
                    ▼
                Root Cause
                    │
                    ▼
               Architecture
                  Change
                    │
                    ▼
                 Testing
                    │
                    ▼
               Deployment
                    │
                    └──────────► ATTACK
```

This is continuous security engineering.

---

# 121.49 What You Should Actually Master

For your DevOps + Full-Stack goal, don't try to become a professional exploit developer.

You should be able to:

```text
Understand attack surfaces
Understand common attack chains
Run vulnerability scanners
Interpret findings
Test APIs
Test authentication/authorization
Test containers
Test Kubernetes security
Test cloud IAM
Assess CI/CD security
Understand red-team methodology
Build detection around attacks
Validate remediation
```

That's much more valuable for a DevSecOps engineer.

---

# 121.50 Final Mental Model

Don't think:

```text
Security Testing
=
Run a scanner
```

Think:

```text
Security Testing
=
Can an attacker realistically compromise this system?
+
How far can they go?
+
Will we detect them?
+
Can we stop them?
+
Can we recover?
+
Did we permanently fix the weakness?
```

That is the difference between **checking security** and **engineering security**.

# Chapter 122 — Threat Modeling

Threat modeling answers a question that security scanners cannot:

> **“What can go wrong with this system, who can cause it, and what should we design to prevent or limit it?”**

This comes **before** penetration testing. If you don't understand the system's trust boundaries and attack paths, your security testing becomes a random collection of scans.

---

## 122.1 Threat Modeling in the SDLC

A mature flow is:

```text
Requirements
     ↓
Architecture
     ↓
Threat Modeling
     ↓
Security Requirements
     ↓
Implementation
     ↓
Security Testing
     ↓
Deployment
     ↓
Runtime Monitoring
```

Threat modeling is therefore primarily a **design activity**, not just a testing activity.

---

# 122.2 What Are We Protecting?

Start with assets.

For a typical application:

```text
Assets
│
├── User credentials
├── JWT / refresh tokens
├── Personal information
├── Business data
├── Database
├── Files
├── Encryption keys
├── Cloud credentials
├── Kubernetes secrets
├── Source code
├── CI/CD credentials
└── Production infrastructure
```

Not all assets have equal value.

For example:

```text
Public blog post
        ↓
Low sensitivity

Patient record
        ↓
Extremely high sensitivity
```

Security priorities should follow business impact.

---

# 122.3 Identify Actors

Next identify who interacts with the system.

Example:

```text
                    SYSTEM
                       │
       ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
       ▼               ▼                ▼
    Student          Doctor            Admin
       │               │                │
       └───────────────┼────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
                   Backend API
```

But also include hostile actors:

```text
Internet Attacker
Compromised User
Malicious Insider
Compromised Dependency
Compromised CI Agent
Compromised Cloud Credential
```

---

# 122.4 Trust Boundaries

This is one of the most important concepts.

A **trust boundary** exists where data crosses from one security context to another.

Example:

```text
Internet
   │
   │ untrusted
   ▼
┌───────────────┐
│ WAF / Ingress │
└───────┬───────┘
        │
        │ trust boundary
        ▼
┌───────────────┐
│ Application    │
└───────┬───────┘
        │
        │ trust boundary
        ▼
┌───────────────┐
│ PostgreSQL     │
└───────────────┘
```

Every boundary deserves security controls.

---

# 122.5 Data Flow Diagrams

A practical threat model starts with a DFD.

Example:

```text
User
 │
 │ HTTPS
 ▼
Frontend
 │
 │ HTTPS
 ▼
Ingress
 │
 ▼
Spring Boot API
 │
 ├──────────────► Redis
 │
 ├──────────────► PostgreSQL
 │
 ├──────────────► Object Storage
 │
 └──────────────► External API
```

Then mark:

```text
Trust boundaries
Data stores
External systems
Authentication points
Sensitive data flows
```

---

# 122.6 Threat Modeling Questions

For every component ask:

### What can enter?

```text
Input
API request
File
Token
Message
Configuration
```

### What can leave?

```text
Response
Database query
External request
Log
Event
```

### What can be manipulated?

```text
Request
Identity
Headers
Parameters
Files
Messages
Configuration
```

### What happens if this component is compromised?

That's the blast-radius question.

---

# 122.7 STRIDE

One of the most commonly used threat-modeling frameworks is **STRIDE**.

```text
S — Spoofing
T — Tampering
R — Repudiation
I — Information Disclosure
D — Denial of Service
E — Elevation of Privilege
```

Let's understand each.

---

# 122.8 S — Spoofing

Question:

> Can someone pretend to be another identity?

Examples:

```text
Stolen JWT
Compromised session
Credential theft
Fake service identity
```

Example:

```text
Attacker
   ↓
stolen token
   ↓
API
   ↓
impersonated user
```

Controls:

```text
Strong authentication
Token validation
Short-lived credentials
MFA where appropriate
Credential rotation
```

---

# 122.9 T — Tampering

Question:

> Can an attacker modify data or communication?

Examples:

```text
Modified request
Modified database record
Modified deployment manifest
Modified container image
```

Controls:

```text
TLS
Integrity checks
Authorization
Digital signatures
Immutable artifacts
Database constraints
```

---

# 122.10 R — Repudiation

Question:

> Can someone perform an action and later deny having done it?

Example:

```text
Admin
 ↓
Deletes user
```

If you have no audit record:

```text
Who did it?
When?
From where?
What exactly changed?
```

unknown.

Controls:

```text
Audit logs
Immutable logging
Identity tracking
Request IDs
Timestamping
Centralized log collection
```

---

# 122.11 I — Information Disclosure

Question:

> Can sensitive information reach an unauthorized party?

Examples:

```text
Stack traces
Database credentials
PII
Patient information
JWT secrets
Internal IP addresses
Cloud credentials
```

A classic mistake:

```java
return exception.getMessage();
```

to an external client.

Internal exception details shouldn't automatically become API responses.

---

# 122.12 D — Denial of Service

Question:

> Can an attacker make the system unavailable?

Examples:

```text
Huge request
Expensive query
Large file upload
Connection exhaustion
CPU-intensive operation
Memory exhaustion
API flooding
```

Controls:

```text
Rate limiting
Timeouts
Request limits
Connection limits
Resource quotas
Caching
Autoscaling
WAF
Circuit breakers
```

---

# 122.13 E — Elevation of Privilege

Question:

> Can a low-privileged actor obtain higher privileges?

Example:

```text
Student
  ↓
changes role field
  ↓
Admin
```

Or:

```text
Application
  ↓
Kubernetes ServiceAccount
  ↓
excessive permissions
  ↓
cluster administration
```

Controls:

```text
RBAC
Least privilege
Authorization
Policy enforcement
Privilege separation
```

---

# 122.14 STRIDE Table

| Threat                 | Question                       | Example           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------ | ----------------- |
| Spoofing               | Can identity be impersonated?  | Stolen JWT        |
| Tampering              | Can data be modified?          | Modified request  |
| Repudiation            | Can action be denied?          | Missing audit log |
| Information Disclosure | Can data leak?                 | PII exposure      |
| DoS                    | Can availability be disrupted? | API flooding      |
| Elevation              | Can privileges increase?       | User → Admin      |

Memorize the six categories, but more importantly learn to **apply them to architecture**.

---

# 122.15 Threat Modeling Example

Suppose:

```text
Student
   ↓
React
   ↓
Spring Boot
   ↓
PostgreSQL
```

Potential threats:

```text
Spoofing
→ stolen JWT

Tampering
→ modified request

Repudiation
→ missing audit trail

Information Disclosure
→ unauthorized student data

DoS
→ expensive API requests

Elevation
→ student changes role to admin
```

Now threat modeling has produced actual security requirements.

---

# 122.16 Security Requirement From Threat

Threat:

```text
Student changes:
role=STUDENT
```

to:

```text
role=ADMIN
```

Requirement:

```text
Role assignment must be server-controlled.
```

Implementation:

```text
Client
  ↓
role ignored
  ↓
Backend determines role
```

That's better than trying to detect malicious manipulation after it happens.

---

# 122.17 Authentication vs Authorization

Threat modeling forces you to separate:

```text
Authentication
=
Who are you?
```

from:

```text
Authorization
=
What are you allowed to do?
```

Example:

```text
Authenticated:
Ganesh

Authorized:
Can read own profile
Cannot read another user's private data
Cannot delete users
```

---

# 122.18 Data Classification

Classify data before deciding controls.

Example:

```text
PUBLIC
↓
Course descriptions

INTERNAL
↓
Operational configuration

CONFIDENTIAL
↓
User information

HIGHLY SENSITIVE
↓
Credentials / medical records / financial data
```

Then ask:

```text
Where is this data stored?
Where does it travel?
Who can access it?
How long is it retained?
Is it encrypted?
```

---

# 122.19 Data Flow Threats

Example:

```text
Student
   │
   │ medical information
   ▼
React
   │
   │ HTTPS
   ▼
API
   │
   ▼
Database
```

Threats exist at every transition.

```text
Student → API
    ↓
Authentication

API → Database
    ↓
Authorization + parameterized queries

Database → Backup
    ↓
Encryption + access control
```

---

# 122.20 External Dependencies

Don't threat-model only your own code.

Example:

```text
Spring Boot
   ↓
Payment API
   ↓
Cloud Storage
   ↓
Email provider
   ↓
OAuth provider
```

Ask:

> What happens if this dependency is compromised?

For example:

```text
OAuth provider compromised
        ↓
Authentication trust compromised
```

That's a major architectural dependency.

---

# 122.21 Supply Chain Threat Modeling

Your build pipeline:

```text
GitHub
   ↓
Jenkins
   ↓
Maven
   ↓
Docker
   ↓
Nexus
   ↓
Argo CD
   ↓
Kubernetes
```

Each is a trust relationship.

Potential attack:

```text
Compromised dependency
       ↓
Jenkins build
       ↓
Malicious image
       ↓
Nexus
       ↓
Production
```

Controls:

```text
Dependency scanning
SBOM
Artifact signing
Provenance
Registry controls
Admission verification
```

---

# 122.22 Kubernetes Threat Model

Example:

```text
Internet
   ↓
Ingress
   ↓
Frontend
   ↓
Backend
   ↓
PostgreSQL
```

Potential threats:

```text
Ingress compromise
Pod compromise
ServiceAccount abuse
Secret theft
RBAC escalation
Network lateral movement
Privileged container
Host escape
```

Therefore:

```text
NetworkPolicy
RBAC
Pod Security
Secrets controls
Admission policy
Runtime detection
```

must be considered together.

---

# 122.23 Cloud Threat Model

For AWS:

```text
Internet
   ↓
ALB
   ↓
EKS
   ↓
RDS
   ↓
S3
```

Threats:

```text
IAM compromise
Public S3 bucket
Over-permissive security group
Compromised workload identity
Exposed database
Credential theft
```

The question isn't:

> "Is AWS secure?"

The question is:

> **"How can our specific architecture be abused?"**

---

# 122.24 Attack Trees

Another useful technique is an attack tree.

Goal:

```text
Access sensitive database
```

Possible paths:

```text
                    Access DB
                       │
            ┌──────────┴──────────┐
            ▼                     ▼
       Compromise API        Compromise IAM
            │                     │
       ┌────┴────┐           ┌────┴────┐
       ▼         ▼           ▼         ▼
    Exploit    Stolen      Token     Misconfig
    API        Secret
```

This helps identify multiple attack paths.

---

# 122.25 Attack Path Analysis

Suppose:

```text
Public API
   ↓
Application vulnerability
   ↓
Container access
   ↓
ServiceAccount
   ↓
Kubernetes API
   ↓
Secret
   ↓
Database
```

You shouldn't treat these as six unrelated findings.

They're one attack chain.

The architectural question becomes:

> **Where can we break the chain?**

Maybe:

```text
API vulnerability
       ↓
container compromise
       X
ServiceAccount cannot access secrets
```

One control can break the entire chain.

---

# 122.26 Defense in Depth

Never rely on one control.

Example:

```text
Application
    │
    ├── Authentication
    ├── Authorization
    ├── Input validation
    ├── NetworkPolicy
    ├── RBAC
    ├── Secret isolation
    ├── Runtime detection
    └── Audit logging
```

If one fails, others remain.

---

# 122.27 Single Point of Security Failure

Be suspicious of:

```text
One admin account
One API key
One CI credential
One security gateway
One cluster admin
```

If compromise of one component gives total control:

```text
Component A
    ↓
Everything
```

you have a major architectural weakness.

---

# 122.28 Threat Modeling CI/CD

For your Jenkins architecture:

```text
Developer
   ↓
GitHub
   ↓
Jenkins
   ↓
Nexus
   ↓
Argo CD
   ↓
Kubernetes
```

Ask:

```text
Can a developer modify pipeline definitions?

Can Jenkins access production credentials?

Can a compromised build agent access other agents?

Can someone upload an arbitrary artifact?

Can Argo CD deploy unsigned images?

Can Kubernetes pull from an untrusted registry?
```

These questions are more useful than simply installing another scanner.

---

# 122.29 Threat Modeling Terraform

Terraform can create security problems before the application even exists.

Example:

```text
Terraform
   ↓
Security Group
   ↓
0.0.0.0/0
   ↓
Database exposed
```

Threat model:

```text
Internet
 ↓
Database
```

Security requirement:

```text
Database must not be publicly reachable.
```

Then enforce it through:

```text
Terraform
+
Policy as Code
+
Cloud controls
```

---

# 122.30 Threat Modeling Helm

Suppose Helm allows:

```yaml
securityContext:
  privileged: true
```

An unsafe values file could deploy:

```text
Privileged Pod
```

Therefore:

```text
Helm
 ↓
Policy validation
 ↓
Admission policy
```

Security should not depend solely on developer discipline.

---

# 122.31 Threat Modeling Secrets

Trace a secret:

```text
Secret
 ↓
Where generated?
 ↓
Where stored?
 ↓
Who reads it?
 ↓
How injected?
 ↓
Where logged?
 ↓
How rotated?
 ↓
How revoked?
```

A secret that is secure in Vault but printed into Jenkins logs is not secure.

---

# 122.32 Threat Modeling Logging

Logging can create a new attack surface.

Bad:

```text
Authorization:
Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
```

in logs.

Or:

```text
password=...
```

Security requirement:

```text
Sensitive credentials must never be logged.
```

This is an example of threat modeling revealing an operational security problem.

---

# 122.33 Threat Modeling Availability

Security isn't only confidentiality.

Suppose:

```text
Search API
```

performs an expensive database query.

An attacker repeatedly calls it:

```text
100,000 requests
 ↓
Database CPU 100%
 ↓
Application unavailable
```

Controls:

```text
Rate limiting
Caching
Query optimization
Timeout
Resource limits
Autoscaling
```

---

# 122.34 Threat Modeling Human Factors

Attackers don't always attack technology.

They may target:

```text
Developer
Administrator
Support engineer
DevOps engineer
```

Examples:

```text
Phishing
Social engineering
Credential theft
Malicious insider
```

Therefore:

```text
MFA
Least privilege
Approval controls
Audit logging
```

matter.

---

# 122.35 Risk Matrix

A simple model:

| Likelihood | Impact | Risk     |
| ---------- | ------ | -------- |
| Low        | Low    | Low      |
| Low        | High   | Medium   |
| High       | Low    | Medium   |
| High       | High   | Critical |

But don't blindly multiply arbitrary numbers and pretend the result is objective.

Risk scoring is a decision-support mechanism, not mathematical truth.

---

# 122.36 Threat Prioritization

Prioritize threats that are:

```text
Internet exposed
+
Highly exploitable
+
High business impact
+
Sensitive data involved
+
High privilege
```

Example:

```text
Public API
+
Authentication bypass
+
Admin access
=
Extremely high priority
```

---

# 122.37 Threat Model Output

A threat model should produce concrete artifacts.

Example:

```text
Threat:
Broken object authorization

Asset:
Private user data

Attacker:
Authenticated malicious user

Attack path:
API → resource ID manipulation

Impact:
Unauthorized data access

Mitigation:
Object-level authorization

Detection:
Audit logs + anomaly detection

Test:
Security integration test

Owner:
Backend team
```

That's useful.

A document saying:

```text
"Security is important."
```

is worthless.

---

# 122.38 Threat Model → Test

Every important threat should ideally map to a control and test.

```text
Threat
 ↓
Security requirement
 ↓
Control
 ↓
Automated test
 ↓
Monitoring
```

Example:

```text
Unauthorized admin access
        ↓
RBAC
        ↓
Authorization filter
        ↓
403 integration test
        ↓
Audit alert
```

This is mature security engineering.

---

# 122.39 Threat Model → Architecture

The strongest result of threat modeling is architectural change.

Example:

Initial:

```text
Frontend
 ↓
Backend
 ↓
Database
```

Threat:

```text
Backend compromise
 ↓
Direct DB access
```

Improved:

```text
Frontend
 ↓
API
 ↓
Service layer
 ↓
Restricted DB identity
```

Then:

```text
Network isolation
+
least privilege
+
audit logging
```

Now compromise has reduced blast radius.

---

# 122.40 Mediverse Threat Model

For your medical learning platform, consider:

```text
                         INTERNET
                             │
                             ▼
                           WAF
                             │
                             ▼
                          Ingress
                             │
             ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
             ▼                               ▼
          React                         Spring Boot
                                             │
                       ┌─────────────────────┼──────────────────┐
                       ▼                     ▼                  ▼
                    PostgreSQL             Redis            Storage
                       │
                       ▼
                    Backups
```

Actors:

```text
Student
Faculty
Admin
Attacker
Support
Developer
CI/CD
External identity provider
```

Assets:

```text
Accounts
Learning content
Progress
Assessment data
Personal information
Credentials
Tokens
Administrative configuration
```

---

# 122.41 Mediverse STRIDE Example

### Student → API

**Spoofing**

```text
Stolen JWT
```

Mitigation:

```text
Secure token validation
Short-lived access tokens
Refresh-token protection
```

### Student → API

**Tampering**

```text
Modify course completion request
```

Mitigation:

```text
Server-side authorization
Server-side state validation
```

### API → Database

**Information Disclosure**

```text
Student accesses another student's records
```

Mitigation:

```text
Object-level authorization
```

### API

**DoS**

```text
Expensive search request
```

Mitigation:

```text
Rate limiting
Pagination
Query limits
Timeouts
```

### Student → Admin API

**Elevation**

```text
Manipulate role
```

Mitigation:

```text
Server-controlled role assignment
RBAC
```

---

# 122.42 Threat Modeling Is Not a One-Time Document

Architecture changes.

Dependencies change.

Cloud services change.

Attack techniques change.

Therefore:

```text
Architecture change
      ↓
Threat model review
      ↓
Security tests
      ↓
Deployment
```

Trigger reviews when:

```text
New service
New external API
New database
New authentication mechanism
New cloud service
Major architecture change
Sensitive-data change
```

---

# 122.43 The Most Important Principle

Don't ask:

> "What vulnerabilities does our scanner find?"

Ask:

> **"If an attacker controls component X, what can they reach next?"**

That question naturally leads to:

```text
Trust boundaries
Least privilege
Network isolation
RBAC
Identity security
Secret isolation
Monitoring
Attack-path analysis
```

That's where threat modeling becomes powerful.

---

# 122.44 Final Mental Model

```text
                    THREAT MODEL
                         │
        ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
        ▼                ▼                ▼
      Assets           Actors           Data
        │                │                │
        └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                         ▼
                 Trust Boundaries
                         │
                         ▼
                  Attack Surfaces
                         │
                         ▼
                     STRIDE
                         │
                         ▼
                  Attack Paths
                         │
                         ▼
                     Controls
                         │
                         ▼
                      Tests
                         │
                         ▼
                   Monitoring
                         │
                         ▼
                   Improvements
```

The objective is not to create a huge document.

The objective is to **turn architectural threats into enforceable controls and tests**.

## Chapter 123 — Security Architecture Review

This is the final **architecture-level security review** before the capstone.

The key distinction:

> **Threat modeling identifies what can go wrong. Security architecture review checks whether the actual architecture has enough controls to prevent, contain, detect, and recover from those threats.**

### 123.1 Review the Architecture, Not Just the Code

Use this hierarchy:

```text
Business Requirements
        ↓
Security Requirements
        ↓
Architecture
        ↓
Trust Boundaries
        ↓
Security Controls
        ↓
Implementation
        ↓
Testing
        ↓
Monitoring
```

A secure piece of code inside an insecure architecture is still an insecure system.

---

## 123.2 Architecture Review Checklist

Review these areas systematically:

| Area          | What to verify                          |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Identity      | Authentication, MFA, identity lifecycle |
| Authorization | RBAC/ABAC, least privilege              |
| Network       | Segmentation, ingress/egress            |
| Data          | Encryption, classification, retention   |
| Secrets       | Storage, rotation, access               |
| APIs          | Validation, rate limits, authorization  |
| Containers    | Image security, runtime restrictions    |
| Kubernetes    | RBAC, NetworkPolicy, admission          |
| Cloud         | IAM, security groups, logging           |
| CI/CD         | Pipeline isolation, credentials         |
| Supply chain  | SBOM, signing, provenance               |
| Monitoring    | Logs, metrics, alerts                   |
| Resilience    | Backup, recovery, incident response     |

---

## 123.3 Identity Architecture

Bad:

```text
User
 ↓
Username/password
 ↓
Application
```

Better:

```text
User
 ↓
Identity Provider
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Token
 ↓
Application
 ↓
Authorization
```

Review:

* How are identities created?
* How are they disabled?
* How are credentials rotated?
* What happens when an employee leaves?
* How are service identities managed?

---

## 123.4 Authorization Architecture

Don't review only roles.

Review the complete authorization model:

```text
WHO
 │
 ├── User
 ├── Service
 └── Admin
       │
       ▼
WHAT
 │
 ├── Read
 ├── Write
 ├── Delete
 └── Administer
       │
       ▼
WHICH RESOURCE?
```

Example:

```text
User A
 ↓
READ
 ↓
User A's document
```

should not automatically imply:

```text
User A
 ↓
READ
 ↓
Every user's document
```

---

## 123.5 Network Architecture

Review:

```text
Internet
   ↓
WAF
   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓
Ingress
   ↓
Application
   ↓
Database
```

Ask:

* Is the database publicly accessible?
* Can frontend pods access the database directly?
* Can backend pods access arbitrary internet endpoints?
* Is east-west traffic restricted?
* Are administrative interfaces isolated?

A strong architecture minimizes unnecessary connectivity.

---

## 123.6 Kubernetes Review

For Kubernetes:

```text
Cluster
│
├── RBAC
├── NetworkPolicy
├── Pod Security
├── Admission
├── Secrets
├── ServiceAccounts
├── Resource limits
├── Audit logs
└── Runtime monitoring
```

Check especially:

```text
privileged: true
hostNetwork: true
hostPID: true
hostPath
runAsRoot
excessive capabilities
wildcard RBAC
```

These aren't automatically vulnerabilities in every context, but they deserve explicit justification.

---

## 123.7 CI/CD Security Review

Review the complete chain:

```text
Developer
   ↓
Git
   ↓
CI
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Artifact Repository
   ↓
GitOps
   ↓
Kubernetes
```

Critical question:

> **Can a compromised developer account or CI worker deploy arbitrary code to production?**

If yes, identify the controls that limit that path.

For example:

```text
Git
 ↓
PR approval
 ↓
CI
 ↓
Security gates
 ↓
Signed artifact
 ↓
GitOps
 ↓
Admission verification
 ↓
Production
```

---

## 123.8 Secrets Architecture

A good review traces every secret:

```text
Generation
   ↓
Storage
   ↓
Access
   ↓
Injection
   ↓
Use
   ↓
Rotation
   ↓
Revocation
```

Red flags:

```text
Secrets in Git
Secrets in Dockerfile
Secrets in images
Secrets in logs
Long-lived cloud keys
Shared credentials
```

---

## 123.9 Data Protection

For sensitive data:

```text
At Rest
   ↓
Encryption

In Transit
   ↓
TLS

During Processing
   ↓
Access Control

During Logging
   ↓
Redaction

During Backup
   ↓
Encryption + Access Control
```

Security architecture must cover the **entire lifecycle**, not just the database.

---

## 123.10 Logging Architecture

You want:

```text
Application
   │
   ├── Security events
   ├── Authentication
   ├── Authorization
   ├── Administrative actions
   └── Important changes
          ↓
    Central Logging
          ↓
         SIEM
          ↓
       Alerting
```

But don't log:

```text
Passwords
Private keys
Access tokens
Session secrets
Sensitive personal information
```

unless there is a carefully justified and protected reason.

---

## 123.11 Detection Architecture

Ask:

> If an attacker successfully bypasses a preventive control, what detects them?

Example:

```text
Attack
 ↓
Application logs
 ↓
SIEM
 ↓
Detection rule
 ↓
Alert
 ↓
Incident response
```

This is the difference between **prevention-only** and **defense in depth**.

---

## 123.12 Resilience Review

Security architecture also asks:

> What happens after compromise?

Review:

```text
Backup
Recovery
Credential rotation
Incident isolation
Failover
Disaster recovery
Forensics
Business continuity
```

If the only security strategy is:

```text
"Prevent the breach."
```

the architecture is incomplete.

---

## 123.13 Architecture Risk Register

Create a concrete register:

| Risk                   | Impact   | Likelihood | Control                   | Status  |
| ---------------------- | -------- | ---------- | ------------------------- | ------- |
| Excessive RBAC         | High     | Medium     | Least privilege           | Open    |
| Public DB              | Critical | Low        | Private subnet            | Fixed   |
| Secret leakage         | Critical | Medium     | Secret manager + scanning | Fixed   |
| Missing API rate limit | High     | High       | Gateway limits            | Open    |
| Unsigned image         | High     | Medium     | Image signing             | Planned |

The purpose is to turn architecture review into actionable engineering work.

---

## 123.14 Security Architecture Decision

For every major control ask:

```text
Threat
 ↓
Risk
 ↓
Control
 ↓
Residual Risk
 ↓
Decision
```

Example:

```text
Threat:
Compromised application

Control:
Restricted ServiceAccount

Residual risk:
Application can still access its own database

Decision:
Accept residual risk
```

This is much more realistic than pretending risk can reach zero.

---

## 123.15 Mediverse Architecture Review

For the medical-learning platform architecture we've been using, the review should look approximately like:

```text
                         INTERNET
                             │
                             ▼
                            WAF
                             │
                             ▼
                         Ingress
                             │
                    ┌────────┴────────┐
                    ▼                 ▼
                 React            API Gateway
                                      │
                                      ▼
                                Spring Boot
                                      │
              ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────┐
              ▼                       ▼                   ▼
          PostgreSQL                Redis              Storage
              │
              ▼
           Backups
```

Security boundaries:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
Edge Boundary
   │
   ▼
Application Boundary
   │
   ▼
Data Boundary
```

Each boundary needs explicit controls.

---

## 123.16 Final Architecture Questions

Before approving the design, answer **yes** or provide a documented exception:

```text
□ Authentication is centralized and secure
□ Authorization is enforced server-side
□ Least privilege is implemented
□ Sensitive data is classified
□ Sensitive data is encrypted appropriately
□ Secrets are not embedded in source/artifacts
□ Network paths are minimized
□ Kubernetes workloads are restricted
□ CI/CD credentials are isolated
□ Dependencies are monitored
□ Artifacts have integrity/provenance controls
□ Security testing exists in CI/CD
□ Logs support incident investigation
□ Critical security events generate alerts
□ Backups are protected
□ Recovery has been tested
□ Threat model is maintained
□ High-risk attack paths have mitigations
□ Residual risks have explicit owners
```

---

# 123.17 The Hard Truth

A security architecture review isn't successful because the checklist is green.

It's successful when you can answer:

> **If one layer fails, what prevents the attacker from reaching the next critical asset?**

For example:

```text
Application compromised
        ↓
Can attacker access Kubernetes API?
        ↓
If yes → what permissions?
        ↓
Can attacker read Secrets?
        ↓
If yes → which Secrets?
        ↓
Can attacker reach database?
        ↓
If yes → which database identity?
        ↓
Can attacker access sensitive data?
        ↓
If yes → what detects and contains this?
```

That is the level at which you should review architecture.
