# Chapter 124 — Capstone Security Project

This is where we stop studying individual security concepts and **build one end-to-end security architecture** that proves you understand them.

The capstone should integrate the major areas you've covered:

```text
Threat Modeling
      ↓
Secure Architecture
      ↓
Secure Development
      ↓
Secure CI/CD
      ↓
Supply Chain Security
      ↓
Container Security
      ↓
Kubernetes Security
      ↓
Cloud Security
      ↓
Runtime Security
      ↓
Detection
      ↓
Incident Response
      ↓
Recovery
```

## 124.1 Capstone Objective

Build a production-style application platform with security controls at every layer.

For your existing DevOps/full-stack direction, use:

```text
Frontend       React
Backend        Spring Boot
Database       PostgreSQL
Cache          Redis
Container      Docker
Orchestration  Kubernetes
Packaging      Helm
IaC            Terraform
Config         Ansible
CI/CD          Jenkins
GitOps         Argo CD
Registry       Nexus
Quality        SonarQube
Monitoring     Prometheus + Grafana
Logging        ELK/OpenSearch-style stack
Security       SAST + SCA + Secrets + IaC + Container scanning
```

The important point is **integration**.

Don't build 20 disconnected demos.

---

# 124.2 Capstone Architecture

A reasonable target:

```text
                         INTERNET
                            │
                            ▼
                           WAF
                            │
                            ▼
                       Load Balancer
                            │
                            ▼
                         Ingress
                            │
                 ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                 ▼                     ▼
              React               Spring Boot
                                       │
                       ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
                       ▼               ▼               ▼
                  PostgreSQL         Redis          Object Storage
                       │
                       ▼
                    Backup
```

Deployment:

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Git
    │
    ▼
Jenkins
    │
    ├── Unit Tests
    ├── SAST
    ├── SCA
    ├── Secret Scan
    ├── IaC Scan
    └── Container Scan
    │
    ▼
Nexus
    │
    ▼
GitOps Repository
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Kubernetes
```

---

# 124.3 Security Boundaries

Explicitly define:

```text
Boundary 1
Internet → Edge

Boundary 2
Edge → Application

Boundary 3
Application → Data

Boundary 4
Developer → CI/CD

Boundary 5
CI/CD → Artifact Repository

Boundary 6
GitOps → Kubernetes

Boundary 7
Kubernetes → Cloud Resources
```

For each boundary document:

```text
Who crosses it?
What data crosses it?
What authentication is used?
What authorization is used?
What validation occurs?
What is logged?
What happens if the boundary is compromised?
```

---

# 124.4 Threat Model

Create a STRIDE-based threat model.

Minimum threats:

```text
Spoofing
    → stolen JWT

Tampering
    → modified API request

Repudiation
    → missing audit trail

Information Disclosure
    → unauthorized database access

Denial of Service
    → API/resource exhaustion

Elevation of Privilege
    → normal user → admin
```

Then add infrastructure threats:

```text
Compromised Pod
Compromised ServiceAccount
Compromised CI worker
Malicious dependency
Compromised container image
Stolen cloud credential
```

---

# 124.5 Security Requirements

Convert threats into requirements.

Example:

```text
Threat:
Stolen JWT

Requirement:
Access tokens must be validated for signature,
issuer, audience, expiry, and required claims.
```

Another:

```text
Threat:
Compromised application Pod

Requirement:
Application ServiceAccount must have only
the Kubernetes permissions required by the service.
```

Another:

```text
Threat:
Malicious container image

Requirement:
Only approved and verified images may enter production.
```

This mapping is essential:

```text
Threat
 ↓
Requirement
 ↓
Control
 ↓
Test
 ↓
Monitoring
```

---

# 124.6 Application Security

Spring Boot should implement:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Input validation
Global exception handling
Rate limiting
Secure headers
CORS policy
CSRF strategy where applicable
Secure file handling
Audit logging
```

Do not trust frontend authorization.

This:

```text
React
 ↓
Hide admin button
```

is not security.

The backend must enforce:

```text
Request
 ↓
Authenticated identity
 ↓
Authorization decision
 ↓
Business operation
```

---

# 124.7 JWT Security

Implement:

```text
Access Token
+
Refresh Token
```

Validate:

```text
signature
issuer
audience
expiration
algorithm
claims
```

Don't put sensitive information into JWT claims merely because JWTs are convenient.

Remember:

> A JWT is usually signed, not encrypted.

---

# 124.8 Authorization Model

Use explicit permissions.

For example:

```text
ROLE_USER
ROLE_ADMIN
ROLE_OPERATOR
```

with permissions such as:

```text
USER_READ
USER_UPDATE
POST_CREATE
POST_DELETE
ADMIN_USER_MANAGE
```

Then enforce:

```text
Role
 ↓
Permission
 ↓
Resource
 ↓
Action
```

This is stronger than scattering `if (role == ADMIN)` throughout the application.

---

# 124.9 Database Security

PostgreSQL should use:

```text
Dedicated application user
Least privilege
Encrypted connections where appropriate
Restricted network access
Strong credentials
Backup protection
Audit capability
```

Avoid:

```text
Application
 ↓
Postgres superuser
```

Instead:

```text
Application
 ↓
Restricted DB role
 ↓
Only required schema/table privileges
```

---

# 124.10 Kubernetes Security

Your application should have:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
```

and appropriate:

```text
readOnlyRootFilesystem
drop capabilities
seccomp
resource limits
```

where compatible with the workload.

Also:

```text
NetworkPolicy
RBAC
ServiceAccount
Pod Security controls
Admission policies
```

---

# 124.11 NetworkPolicy

Your desired model might be:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
Ingress
   │
   ▼
Backend
   │
   ├──► PostgreSQL
   └──► Redis
```

But:

```text
Frontend ──X──► PostgreSQL
Frontend ──X──► Redis
```

and:

```text
Backend ──X──► Kubernetes API
```

unless explicitly required.

The objective is to reduce lateral movement.

---

# 124.12 CI/CD Security

Your Jenkins pipeline should resemble:

```text
Checkout
   ↓
Unit Tests
   ↓
SAST
   ↓
SCA
   ↓
Secret Scan
   ↓
Build
   ↓
Container Scan
   ↓
SBOM
   ↓
Image Sign
   ↓
Push to Nexus
   ↓
GitOps Update
```

A security failure should block promotion where the policy says it should.

---

# 124.13 Supply Chain Security

Generate an SBOM for the application/container.

Track:

```text
Application dependencies
OS packages
Container libraries
Build tooling
```

Then:

```text
SBOM
 ↓
Vulnerability analysis
 ↓
Risk decision
```

For production artifacts:

```text
Build
 ↓
Sign
 ↓
Store
 ↓
Verify
 ↓
Deploy
```

---

# 124.14 Secrets

Use a secret-management mechanism rather than:

```text
application.properties
.env
Git repository
Dockerfile
Helm values
```

for real production secrets.

The architecture should support:

```text
Secret
 ↓
Secure storage
 ↓
Controlled retrieval
 ↓
Workload
```

and:

```text
Rotation
Revocation
Audit
```

---

# 124.15 IaC Security

Terraform must be scanned before deployment.

Check:

```text
Public databases
Open security groups
Excessive IAM
Unencrypted storage
Public buckets
Missing logging
Weak network boundaries
```

Use policy-as-code where appropriate.

---

# 124.16 Container Security

Build a minimal image.

Avoid:

```text
root
unnecessary packages
debug utilities
embedded credentials
latest tag
```

Prefer:

```text
Pinned base image
Non-root execution
Minimal packages
Read-only filesystem where possible
Signed image
SBOM
```

---

# 124.17 Runtime Security

Assume preventive controls can fail.

Monitor:

```text
Unexpected process execution
Unexpected network connections
Privilege escalation
Container anomalies
Suspicious API behavior
Authentication anomalies
```

This connects the capstone to your previous runtime-security chapter.

---

# 124.18 Security Monitoring

Collect:

```text
Application logs
Authentication events
Authorization failures
Kubernetes audit events
Ingress logs
Cloud audit logs
CI/CD events
Container/runtime events
```

Then:

```text
Logs
 ↓
Central platform
 ↓
Detection rules
 ↓
Alert
 ↓
Incident response
```

---

# 124.19 Attack Scenario #1

Simulate:

```text
Attacker
 ↓
Login endpoint
 ↓
Credential abuse
```

Your system should demonstrate:

```text
Rate limiting
Authentication monitoring
Suspicious activity detection
Account protection
Audit logging
```

---

# 124.20 Attack Scenario #2

Simulate:

```text
Authenticated user
 ↓
GET /api/users/{id}
 ↓
Change ID
 ↓
Attempt access to another user's data
```

Expected:

```text
403 Forbidden
```

and ideally:

```text
Security event
 ↓
Audit log
```

This validates object-level authorization.

---

# 124.21 Attack Scenario #3

Simulate:

```text
Compromised application Pod
       ↓
Attempt Kubernetes API access
       ↓
Attempt Secret access
       ↓
Attempt lateral movement
```

Expected:

```text
RBAC → deny
NetworkPolicy → deny
Admission controls → protect
Monitoring → detect
```

This is an excellent capstone test.

---

# 124.22 Attack Scenario #4

Introduce a vulnerable dependency.

Pipeline:

```text
Dependency
 ↓
SCA
 ↓
Vulnerability detected
 ↓
Pipeline fails
```

Then remediate:

```text
Upgrade dependency
 ↓
Scan
 ↓
Pass
 ↓
Continue pipeline
```

---

# 124.23 Attack Scenario #5

Attempt deployment of an unsigned image:

```text
Unsigned Image
      ↓
Kubernetes Admission
      ↓
REJECT
```

This proves your artifact trust model actually works.

---

# 124.24 Attack Scenario #6

Attempt a privileged deployment:

```text
privileged: true
        ↓
Admission Policy
        ↓
REJECT
```

Again, the important thing isn't that the policy exists.

The important thing is:

> **The deployment actually fails.**

---

# 124.25 Incident Response Exercise

Simulate:

```text
Compromised credential
        ↓
Suspicious API calls
        ↓
Detection
        ↓
Alert
        ↓
Incident
```

Response:

```text
Identify
 ↓
Contain
 ↓
Revoke credential
 ↓
Investigate
 ↓
Eradicate
 ↓
Recover
 ↓
Retest
```

Document the entire timeline.

---

# 124.26 Recovery Exercise

Delete or corrupt a test workload/database snapshot.

Then demonstrate:

```text
Backup
 ↓
Restore
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
Application recovery
```

Measure:

```text
RTO
RPO
```

A backup you have never restored is only a theory.

---

# 124.27 Security Evidence

Your capstone should produce:

```text
/docs/security/
```

with something like:

```text
security/
├── threat-model.md
├── architecture-review.md
├── security-requirements.md
├── risk-register.md
├── incident-response.md
├── disaster-recovery.md
├── penetration-test.md
├── security-test-results.md
└── exceptions.md
```

And:

```text
/docs/architecture/
├── architecture.md
├── network.md
├── identity.md
└── data-flow.md
```

---

# 124.28 Capstone Acceptance Criteria

The project should not be considered complete until you can demonstrate:

```text
✅ Authentication works
✅ Authorization works
✅ Object-level authorization works
✅ Secrets are protected
✅ Database is isolated
✅ Kubernetes RBAC is restricted
✅ NetworkPolicy works
✅ Images are scanned
✅ Images are signed
✅ Unsigned images are rejected
✅ Dependencies are scanned
✅ Secrets are scanned
✅ IaC is scanned
✅ SAST is integrated
✅ DAST/API testing exists
✅ SBOM is generated
✅ Security logs are centralized
✅ Critical events generate alerts
✅ Incident response is documented
✅ Backup restoration works
✅ Threat model exists
✅ Security architecture review exists
```

---

# 124.29 What Makes This a Real DevSecOps Project?

Not the number of tools.

This:

```text id="rx7t5m"
                 SECURITY
                     │
        ┌────────────┼────────────┐
        ▼            ▼            ▼
       PREVENT      DETECT       RESPOND
        │            │            │
        ▼            ▼            ▼
       IAM          SIEM       IR
       RBAC         Logs       Isolation
       WAF          Alerts     Recovery
       Policies     Runtime    Retest
```

And underneath:

```text
             AUTOMATION
                 │
     ┌───────────┼───────────┐
     ▼           ▼           ▼
    Code        Build       Deploy
     │           │           │
   SAST        SCA        Admission
   Secrets     SBOM       Policy
   Tests       Sign       Verification
```

That's the actual DevSecOps mindset.

---

# 124.30 Capstone Deliverable

At the end you should be able to show an interviewer:

```text
Architecture
     ↓
Threat Model
     ↓
Security Controls
     ↓
CI/CD Pipeline
     ↓
Kubernetes Deployment
     ↓
Security Tests
     ↓
Attack Simulation
     ↓
Detection
     ↓
Incident Response
     ↓
Recovery
```

And answer:

> **"Show me one attack, show me how you prevented it, show me how you detected it, and show me how you recovered from it."**

If you can demonstrate that end-to-end, you have something substantially more valuable than a list of DevOps tools on a résumé.

# Chapter 125 — Final CSDG Architecture Review

This is the **final chapter of the CSDG track**.

The goal here is not to introduce another technology. It is to prove that you can take everything you've learned and reason about a production system as a **single security and DevSecOps platform**.

---

## 125.1 The Complete CSDG Model

Your final mental model should be:

```text
                         BUSINESS
                            │
                            ▼
                     Requirements
                            │
                            ▼
                    Threat Modeling
                            │
                            ▼
                  Security Architecture
                            │
        ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
        ▼                   ▼                   ▼
     Identity            Network              Data
        │                   │                   │
        └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
```

That is the complete lifecycle.

---

# 125.2 Architecture Review: Identity

Ask:

```text
Who can access the system?

How are they authenticated?

How are service identities created?

How are privileges assigned?

How are privileges revoked?

How are credentials rotated?

What happens if an identity is compromised?
```

A mature design should follow:

```text
Identity
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Least Privilege
   ↓
Audit
```

---

# 125.3 Architecture Review: Application

For Spring Boot:

```text
Request
  ↓
TLS
  ↓
Authentication
  ↓
Authorization
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Business Logic
  ↓
Data Access
  ↓
Audit
```

Don't allow:

```text
Request
  ↓
Business Logic
  ↓
Database
```

without security boundaries.

---

# 125.4 Architecture Review: Data

For every sensitive dataset:

```text
Where is it stored?
        ↓
Who can access it?
        ↓
How is it encrypted?
        ↓
How is it transmitted?
        ↓
How is it backed up?
        ↓
How long is it retained?
        ↓
How is it deleted?
```

If you can't answer those questions, the data architecture isn't finished.

---

# 125.5 Architecture Review: Network

A secure architecture should minimize communication.

Instead of:

```text
Everything
   ↕
Everything
```

prefer:

```text
Frontend
   │
   ▼
Backend
   │
   ├────► PostgreSQL
   │
   └────► Redis
```

and explicitly deny unnecessary paths.

This limits lateral movement.

---

# 125.6 Architecture Review: Kubernetes

Review the complete Kubernetes security chain:

```text
User
 ↓
Ingress
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Pod
 ↓
ServiceAccount
 ↓
Kubernetes API
 ↓
Cloud identity
```

At each stage ask:

```text
Who is this?
What can it access?
What can it modify?
What happens if it is compromised?
```

---

# 125.7 Architecture Review: CI/CD

Your CI/CD system deserves the same security attention as production.

```text
Developer
    ↓
Git
    ↓
Jenkins
    ↓
Build Agent
    ↓
Artifact
    ↓
Nexus
    ↓
GitOps
    ↓
Argo CD
    ↓
Kubernetes
```

The critical question:

> **Can one compromised CI component bypass every production security control?**

If yes, that's an architectural weakness.

---

# 125.8 Architecture Review: Supply Chain

Your final trust chain should look conceptually like:

```text
Source
  ↓
Trusted Build
  ↓
Verified Dependencies
  ↓
SBOM
  ↓
Security Scan
  ↓
Signed Artifact
  ↓
Trusted Registry
  ↓
Signature Verification
  ↓
Production
```

You are establishing:

> **What code was built, how was it built, and can we prove that the deployed artifact is the artifact we intended to deploy?**

---

# 125.9 Architecture Review: Runtime

Assume:

> **Something will eventually be compromised.**

Then ask:

```text
If Pod A is compromised:

Can it reach Pod B?

Can it reach PostgreSQL?

Can it read Secrets?

Can it access the Kubernetes API?

Can it access cloud credentials?

Can it execute privileged operations?

Will we detect it?
```

This is the **blast-radius test**.

---

# 125.10 Architecture Review: Detection

Prevention alone is insufficient.

Your architecture should support:

```text
Attack
 ↓
Telemetry
 ↓
Detection
 ↓
Alert
 ↓
Investigation
 ↓
Containment
```

For example:

```text
Repeated failed authentication
        ↓
Application logs
        ↓
SIEM
        ↓
Detection rule
        ↓
Alert
```

---

# 125.11 Architecture Review: Incident Response

Your architecture should make response possible.

When an incident occurs:

```text
Detect
  ↓
Triage
  ↓
Contain
  ↓
Investigate
  ↓
Eradicate
  ↓
Recover
  ↓
Lessons Learned
  ↓
Architecture Improvement
```

If you cannot identify what happened, your logging architecture is inadequate.

If you cannot isolate the compromised workload, your network/identity architecture is inadequate.

If you cannot recover, your resilience architecture is inadequate.

---

# 125.12 Architecture Review: Disaster Recovery

Final questions:

```text
What happens if PostgreSQL disappears?

What happens if Kubernetes fails?

What happens if a cloud credential is compromised?

What happens if the artifact repository is unavailable?

What happens if the primary region fails?

What happens if an attacker deletes data?
```

Then verify:

```text
Backup
 ↓
Restore
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
Production recovery
```

**Untested recovery isn't recovery.**

---

# 125.13 The Five Security Questions

For every component in the architecture, ask:

### 1. Prevent

```text
How do we stop the attack?
```

### 2. Limit

```text
If prevention fails, how much can the attacker access?
```

### 3. Detect

```text
How do we know something abnormal happened?
```

### 4. Respond

```text
How quickly can we contain it?
```

### 5. Recover

```text
How do we restore the system?
```

This is an excellent mental model for architecture reviews.

---

# 125.14 Final Threat Chain

Consider:

```text
Internet Attacker
       ↓
API vulnerability
       ↓
Container compromise
       ↓
ServiceAccount abuse
       ↓
Kubernetes API
       ↓
Secret access
       ↓
Database credentials
       ↓
Sensitive data
```

Now break the chain:

```text
API vulnerability
       ↓
Container
       ↓
NetworkPolicy ──────────── X
       │
       ▼
Kubernetes API
       │
       ▼
RBAC ───────────────────── X
       │
       ▼
Secrets
       │
       ▼
Least privilege ────────── X
```

Even if the attacker gets the first foothold, the architecture prevents escalation.

**That's what defense in depth actually means.**

# 125.16 Final Architecture Principles

You should now be able to defend these principles:

### Least privilege

```text
Only the access required.
```

### Zero trust

```text
Never trust merely because something is inside the network.
```

### Defense in depth

```text
Multiple independent controls.
```

### Secure by default

```text
Unsafe configuration should require deliberate override.
```

### Assume breach

```text
Design for compromise containment.
```

### Immutable infrastructure

```text
Replace rather than manually modify where practical.
```

### Continuous verification

```text
Don't assume controls work.
Test them.
```

### Security automation

```text
Security should become part of the delivery system.
```

---

# 125.17 What You Should Be Able to Explain Now

If you're interviewing for a DevSecOps / DevOps role, you should be capable of explaining:

```text
Why Kubernetes RBAC exists
Why NetworkPolicy matters
Why containers shouldn't run as root
Why secrets shouldn't be stored in Git
Why image signing matters
Why SBOM matters
Why SAST isn't enough
Why DAST isn't enough
Why threat modeling matters
Why least privilege matters
Why CI/CD is a security boundary
Why GitOps improves deployment control
Why admission policies matter
Why runtime monitoring matters
Why backups must be tested
Why security testing must be continuous
```

But don't memorize definitions.

You should be able to explain **the attack scenario that each control prevents or limits**.

# 126. Mediverse Core Engineering & Coding Standards

## 126.1 Three.js / WebGL Rendering & Memory Deallocation Rules
```typescript
// Rule 1: Always dispose geometries, materials, and textures on unmount
useEffect(() => {
  return () => {
    scene.traverse((object) => {
      if (object instanceof THREE.Mesh) {
        object.geometry?.dispose();
        if (Array.isArray(object.material)) {
          object.material.forEach((m) => m.dispose());
        } else {
          object.material?.dispose();
        }
      }
    });
    renderer.dispose();
  };
}, [scene, renderer]);

// Rule 2: Zero object allocations inside 60 FPS animation loop
const _scratchVec3 = new THREE.Vector3(); // Pre-allocated outside render loop
useFrame((state, delta) => {
  _scratchVec3.set(state.pointer.x, state.pointer.y, 0.5).unproject(state.camera);
  organMeshRef.current.lookAt(_scratchVec3);
});
```

## 126.2 Physiological Mathematical Simulation Coding Standards
```typescript
// Rule: Use TypeScript branded types to prevent mixing physiological units
export type Millivolts = number & { readonly __brand: unique symbol };
export type MillimetersMercury = number & { readonly __brand: unique symbol };
export type LitersPerMinute = number & { readonly __brand: unique symbol };

// Rule: Defensive guard against division by zero and NaN in differential steps
export function calculateVascularResistance(
  deltaP: MillimetersMercury, 
  flowQ: LitersPerMinute,
  epsilon = 1e-7
): number {
  if (Math.abs(flowQ) < epsilon) {
    return 0; // Guard against infinite resistance on zero flow
  }
  const resistance = deltaP / flowQ;
  return Number.isFinite(resistance) ? resistance : 0;
}
```

## 126.3 AI Socratic Tutor SSE Streaming Hook Standard
```typescript
export function useSocraticChatStream(sessionId: string) {
  const [messages, setMessages] = useState<ChatMessage[]>([]);
  const [isStreaming, setIsStreaming] = useState(false);

  const sendMessage = async (promptText: string) => {
    setIsStreaming(true);
    const response = await fetch('/api/v1/ai-tutor/chat/stream', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ sessionId, message: promptText }),
    });

    const reader = response.body?.getReader();
    const decoder = new TextDecoder();
    let assistantMessage = '';

    while (reader) {
      const { value, done } = await reader.read();
      if (done) break;
      const chunk = decoder.decode(value);
      // Process SSE data: chunk
      assistantMessage += chunk;
      setMessages((prev) => [...prev.slice(0, -1), { role: 'ASSISTANT', content: assistantMessage }]);
    }
    setIsStreaming(false);
  };

  return { messages, sendMessage, isStreaming };
}
```
